According to the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), CD sales exploded in the first half of 2026. A new report from the organization says 17.5 million CDs were sold in the first six months of the year, up from just 12 million during the same period in 2025. That’s a jump of 45.7 percent, and 58.6 percent in dollars, which reached $171.1 million. What makes this all the more shocking is that CD sales actually shrank 22 percent from 2024 to 2025.
CD sales are booming as physical media continues its resurgence
But don’t think that means people are abandoning streaming.
The RIAA isn’t the only one to notice the boom in CD sales. In July, research firm Luminate released a report saying that 16.3 million units were sold in the first half of 2026. It suggested that much of that increase was due to special editions from K-Pop acts like BTS and that Gen Z and millennials were treating them mostly as collectibles, saying that only about half of buyers actually owned a CD player.
Vinyl continued its resurgence as well, with the number of units sold climbing by nearly 21 percent from last year to 26.5 million. “Other physical” media, which includes CD singles, DVDs, cassettes, SACD, DVD-Audio… basically anything besides “standard vinyl and CD albums,” also surged by over 73 percent, to 1.6 million units.
Despite the increased interest in physical media and the ongoing iPod revival, people are not leaving streaming in droves. Streaming revenue grew by 4.7 percent to $4.9 billion — dwarfing all physical media combined.

At least two dead in blast at Bolivia military barracks
- Published
At least two people have been killed after an explosion at a military barracks in Bolivia but authorities fear the toll could be higher.
Bolivian Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said at least 58 people had been injured when "pyrotechnic material" detonated at the barracks, where an artillery regiment is stationed, about 14:30 (18:30 GMT) on Friday.
Health official Rita Nebraska told local television between 10 and 15 people were believed to have died in the incident in Viacha, about 30km (19 miles) from La Paz, according to Reuters.
Police said dozens of homes had been damaged - largely windows shattered in the blast - and emergency workers are searching the rubble.
Nebraska said there was a risk of further explosion and urged people to stay at least 150m away from the military base.
Police spokesman Roger Roca told AFP news agency that fireworks had been stored at the barracks, and the cause of the blast remained under investigation.
Viacha's authorities have declared three days of mourning.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

A 27-second long video has gone viral on social media over the past week. The clip shows a mob, predominantly comprising men, kicking and attacking a woman in the middle of a busy street, while police personnel in the vicinity do little to nothing to prevent the attack.
The X user, Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst), posted the clip on August 31, claiming that a female Hindu teacher had been attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh. At the time of this article being written, the post had been reshared over 3000 times. (Archive)

Pokhariyal later posted a reply to his tweet, attempting to correct his earlier claim. “Correction: The woman was reportedly assaulted by shopkeepers and salesmen after she complained about the shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law,” the tweet read.
Another X user, Deepak Sharma (@SonOfBharat7), posted the same clip, with a seperate claim that in Bangladesh, a Dalit teacher had allegedly offered water to an upper-caste Muslim child, following which she was chased down in the streets and thrashed. (Archive)

— Yati Sharma (@yati_Official1) August 31, 2026
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claims surrounding the viral clip, Alt News broke it down into keyframes. A reverse image search on one keyframe led us to a news report published by the Bangladeshi news portal BD News 24 on August 30.
According to the report, the incident took place at Bangladesh’s Rajbari clothes market, on August 29. The victim in the video is reportedly a female shop owner, who managed her own clothing shop in the market for 12 years. She had allegedly found that one of her female employees had started working in a different shop on August 22. In response, she dismissed the worker from her role at the shop and asked her collect payment in the following month.
Further, another news report published by The Dhaka Tribune on August 30, identifies the female shop owner as one Zakia Sultana, and the ex-employee as Shahana Parveen Bristy. In another report by the outlet Ajker Patrika, Sultana accused Bristy of turning up at her shop with 15-20 men on August 23 and intimidating and verbally abusing her.
This prompted Sultana to launch a protest at the clothes market on August 29 afternoon, along with her female employees. Enraged by this, several shop-owners from the Rajbari clothes market then attacked her, in the presence of police officers who had turned up at the spot to offer her protection, the report states. However, in the video it is visible the that men continue to kick and attack Sultana despite police presence.
We also found a video report from BBC News Bangla, uploaded on August 31, which shows recorded evidence of the attack.
News reports from Bangla TV, Views Bangladesh, and Jago News 24, dated September 1, also reveal that three people have been arrested in relation to the violent attacks on Sultana, as recorded in the viral video.
In conclusion, the viral clip which shows a woman being violently attack is indeed from Bangladesh, but the woman seen in the clip is Muslim, thereby refuting any allegation of a communal angle at play.
Further, the reason for the attack arises from a business dispute as reported by several credible news outlets, thus the aforementioned claims, including that Sultana is a Dalit teacher who was beaten up for offering water to a Muslim child or that she complained about the other shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law, are false and misleading.

Tata Consultancy Services’ (TCS) data centre subsidiary, HyperVault, and its partners will invest up to ₹70,000 Cr to build and operate a large-scale AI data centre campus in Hyderabad with a capacity of up to 1 GW capacity. In a filing with the exchanges, TCS said that it has secured 264 acres of land in Hyderabad to develop the facility. Once completed, the campus aims to offer high-density, liquid-cooled compute workloads for frontier AI companies and hyperscalers. The project will be executed in phases according to the market demand. Once fully developed, the campus will likely rank among India's largest AI infrastructure sites, incorporating green energy and water-neutral design principles. As per the IT giant, the project will also generate several thousand direct and indirect jobs in the region. “HyperVault advances TCS’ infrastructure-to-intelligence strategy by bringing together AI-ready infrastructure with our cloud, engineering, enterprise transformation and AI capabilities,” said TCS managing director and CEO K Krithivasan. TCS established HyperVault in October last year to build AI-focussed data centres across India. In November 2025, the IT giant also brought in global investment firm TPG as a major investor and strategic partner to scale the new data centre subsidiary. At the time, the two companies said that they would invest up to ₹18,000 Cr (about $2 Bn) in a mix of equity and debt over the next few years in order to set up HyperVault’s data centres. Notably, HyperVault has also partnered with AI juggernaut OpenAI to build the latter’s AI infrastructure in India. TCS’ latest move underscores a broader shift among India’s legacy conglomerates, who are now building the local AI infrastructure layer. For instance, HCLTech has partnered with portfolio startup Sarvam to set up an AI data centre in Odisha, while L&T also has set up its Vyoma.AI subsidiary to build data centres and AI infrastructure. The Adani Group has also joined hands with US-based manufacturing company Jabil to build AI data centre infrastructure in India. Meanwhile, Reliance plans to invest up to ₹10 Lakh Cr in AI over the next seven years, including setting up a 168 MW AI-enabled data centre in Gujarat’s Jamnagar.

‘No cash, no complications’: Raghav Chadha highlights UPI-UZQR link to simplify payments for Indians in Uzbekistan
Chadha had been nominated to represent the Parliament of India at the 12th Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) Global Conference of Young Parliamentarians.
BJP leader and Rajya Sabha MP Raghav Chadha, while speaking 12th Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) Global Conference of Young Parliamentarians in Uzbekistan, highlighted India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) as a model of digital inclusion.
Chadha said that UPI's integration with Uzbekistan's UZQR system will allow Indian travellers to make direct payments from their bank accounts by scanning QR codes at shops.
The Rajya Sabha member had been nominated to represent the Parliament of India at the 12th Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) Global Conference of Young Parliamentarians. The event was held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan from September 4 to September 6.
‘India believes digital rights rest on access, agency, safety and opportunity’
Chadha, during his speech, highlighted India's belief that digital rights rest on four pillars, identifying these as access, agency, safety and opportunity. He said that the Union government had launched the Digital India Initiative in 2015 with the “belief that technology must be a bridge and not a divider.”
“Today, the cost of 1 GB of data has fallen from Rs. 269 in 2014 to just Rs. 8 per GB. That is a reduction of 97%,” the BJP leader said.
He said that in the context of agency, the payment system “belongs to no bank or technology company.” “The clearest example of that, as I said, is India's UPI. When it was started in 2016, UPI had only 90,000 transactions in its first month and in the last financial year, that is 2025-26, UPI processed more than 240 billion transactions worth ₹314 trillion.”
The Rajya Sabha MP also spoke about safety, while underscoring the Supreme Court ruling on privacy being a fundamental right and the Parliament enacting the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
On opportunity, Chadha said young people will skills and technology, “become creators, innovators and leaders”. “The test of this era will not be how clever our machines have become, it will be whether the young women with the cheapest phone in the poorest district gets the same data protection, same data access and the same digital rights as everybody else,” the BJP leader said.

The Gyirong border crossing separating China’s Tibet and Nepal became a grisly emblem of the devastation that followed the collapse of a glacier on the Nepal side of the border on August 26.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

The Trump administration is reportedly preparing a major change to the US federal child-care subsidy system that could allow some married couples with a stay-at-home parent to receive government assistance.
The proposal, backed by Vice President JD Vance, would expand the use of federal child-care funds to families where one parent stays home to care for the couple's children while the other works.
If implemented, it would represent a significant shift in the purpose of federal child-care assistance, which has traditionally been aimed at helping working and low-income parents pay for child care so they can remain employed, attend school or undergo job training.
What is the proposed change?
The administration is considering changes to the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), a federal programme administered by the Department of Health and Human Services.
Under the draft rule, a married couple could qualify for assistance even if one parent does not work outside the home and instead provides care for the couple's child, The New York Times reported.
The proposal calls this a new category of “parent-based child care.”
Under the draft document, one married parent could receive CCDF assistance to care for their own child if the other spouse works at least 35 hours a week.
The subsidy would effectively help offset some of the income the family loses because one parent has chosen to stay home.
How is this different from the current system?
The federal child-care programme was created in the 1990s largely to help low-income and working-class parents afford child care while they work, attend school or receive job training.
The proposed change would broaden that purpose.
Instead of federal money being used primarily to pay for outside child-care arrangements, some of the funds could effectively support a parent providing care at home.
The programme currently provides about $9,000 per child each year, according to the information cited in the report.
Who could qualify?
The proposal would apply only to certain married families that meet income requirements.
-The parents must be married.
-One parent must stay home and provide care for the child.
-The other spouse must work at least 35 hours per week.
-The family must meet the programme's income requirements.
-Household income generally must be below 85% of the state's median income, although some states use a lower 60% threshold.
Unmarried couples in which one parent stays home would not qualify under the proposal.
Single parents who do not work would also remain ineligible.

The U.S. Postal Service said on its website that it handles prepaid and stamped mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services.
In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that adding postage to a prepaid mail-in ballot would "force" the U.S. Postal Service to treat it as first-class mail, a service that allows postcards and small envelopes to be delivered in one to five days.
The claim circulated as states began sending out mail-in ballots for the 2026 midterm elections, despite the Trump administration's ongoing court battles to enforce an executive order that would restrict voting by mail.
One Threads user who shared the claim wrote:
By adding a 1st Class Postage Stamp to your postage prepaid ballot, it will then force USPS to handle it as 1st Class Mail, instead of Bulk Mail! SHARE EVERYWHERE!
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. According to the USPS, the service always handles mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services. In other words, adding additional postage will not expedite the delivery of a standard mail-in ballot.
The USPS included the following message on its webpage about "Election Mail" (emphasis ours):
Mailpieces containing a completed ballot are handled as First-Class Mail® service, regardless of whether they are prepaid by election officials or mailed with a stamp affixed by the voter. The only situation where a completed ballot is not handled as First-Class Mail is when the voter opts to pay for a premium service like Priority Mail® service or Priority Mail Express® service.
Who pays postage on a mail-in ballot varies by state. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan, nonprofit organization that represents lawmakers in the 50 U.S. states, 19 states and Washington, D.C. require local election officials to pay postage while voters in other states must pay.
In a June 2026 FAQ, the USPS said its policy directs employees to deliver ballots with insufficient postage and attempt to recoup the payment from the local election board.
Mail-in ballot return deadlines vary by state. The USPS advises that voters mail their ballots "before Election Day, and at least one week prior to the deadline by which your completed ballot must be received by your election office."
Voters can check deadlines for returning mail-in ballots with their local election office. Some states also allow voters to deliver completed ballots to drop boxes that are emptied by election officials, which eliminates the need to use the postal service to vote.
At the time of this writing, the Trump administration sought to implement new federal regulations on mail-in ballots that could require states to submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal and follow a uniform envelope style. In an August 24, 2026, opinion, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to proceed with implementing the proposed regulations but did not rule on whether they were legal.
The Associated Press reported that "legal wrangling" continued over Trump's executive order in lower courts. Therefore, it was unclear at the time of this writing if, or how, the proposed changes to mail voting would affect the 2026 midterm elections.
Despite having previously voted by mail himself, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized mail voting, including after he lost the 2020 presidential election.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Doubling down on India, South Korean gaming giant KRAFTON plans to invest an additional $250 Mn (₹3,300 Cr) in Indian startups over the next three to four years. Beyond gaming, KRAFTON said that the new corpus will expand its focus to emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, deeptech, among others. This is in addition to the $250 Mn that the gaming giant has already invested in the country, taking its total planned investment in India to $500 Mn (₹6,600 Cr). Separately, KRAFTON, in partnership with Mirae Asset Global Investments and NAVER, had also launched a $670 Mn (₹6,000 Cr) venture fund to back Indian startups last year. The announcement came as KRAFTON chairman Byung Gyu Chang met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi today. In a statement, the company said that Chang, during the meeting, reaffirmed KRAFTON’s commitment to India and its rapidly growing gaming, technology and digital entertainment ecosystem. The two also discussed opportunities for India and the Republic of Korea to work closely in areas of gaming, innovation and emerging technologies. “... Through our investments, skill-development initiatives and focus on emerging technologies, we look forward to working alongside India’s growing community of creators, developers and entrepreneurs to build globally relevant experiences and technologies,” added Chang. The BGMI maker has been making investments in India since March 2021. Its India portfolio counts the likes of names such as esports startup NODWIN, streaming platform Loco and self-publishing platform Pratilipi. It also acquired a controlling 75% stake in Pune-based gaming studio Nautilus Mobile last year. Besides investments, India is also a key market for KRAFTON given the country’s high smartphone penetration and ease of access to digital payments, which enable micro transactions. The South Korean gaming giant’s flagship product is Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI), formerly known as PUBG, which has surpassed 260 Mn downloads in the country. KRAFTON is expanding its investment focus in India as the ban on real-money gaming (RMG) last year suffered a big blow to the local ecosystem. Many big names have either crumbled since then or pivoted to new business models, while early stage funding activity has remained tepid for the sector. As a result, KRAFTON likely sees deeptech and AI as the next big frontier for its investments in India. And it is not without reason. Buoyed by policy clarity, government sops, capital inflows, growing demand and brewing investor confidence, Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn during the first six months of 2026. As per Inc42 data, India’s AI economy is projected to become a $126 Bn opportunity by 2030.

A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.
“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

The eyewitness said the collapsed building was called ‘Hostel Daze’
NEW DELHI: Five people were killed and five were rescued after a five-storey boys' paying guest (PG) accommodation collapsed in southwest Delhi's Satya Niketan area on Sunday, officials said. Rescue operations were under way to search for any remaining people trapped under the rubble.The collapse involved a building known as 'Hostel Daze', which was being used as a boys' PG. An adjacent building also collapsed, according to eyewitnesses.JPN Apex Trauma Centre (AIIMS), on late Sunday, informed that it received 10 patients from the Satya Niketan building collapse. Four were brought dead, while one critically injured patient later succumbed. Three are admitted and undergoing treatment, one underwent limb surgery, and one with minor injuries was discharged after observation.
3 killed among 9 rescued as rescue operation continues
The AIIMS Trauma Centre said eight injured people were brought to hospitals following the incident. Seven were taken to the AIIMS Trauma Centre, while one was admitted to Safdarjung Hospital. Two of those brought to AIIMS were declared brought dead.The death toll later rose to three, with authorities confirming that six people had been rescued from the rubble.
Two National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams were deployed at the site, while two additional teams were kept on standby, NDRF Inspector General NS Bundela said. Rescue teams were working in coordination with the State Disaster Response Force, Delhi Fire Service and other agencies.
Eight fire tenders on spot
The Delhi Fire Service received information about the collapse at around 1.30 pm, following which eight fire tenders and multiple rescue teams were rushed to the spot. Police also cordoned off the area as rescuers searched through the debris.Eyewitnesses said several students were believed to be inside the building when it collapsed. A local resident claimed the PG had around 15 rooms, with two to three students staying in each room, and that around 35 to 40 students were residing on its upper floors.Residents said many students were inside their rooms because it was Sunday. Several locals joined the rescue operation, removing debris with their hands and whatever tools were available.
Basement construction work under scanner
Residents alleged that construction or repair work was under way in the basement and that water had accumulated there. A local resident who has lived in the area for around two decades claimed the building's foundation was weak.
Another resident said he had been inside the building shortly before the collapse and managed to get out minutes before the structure came down.The adjacent building was also reportedly leaning after the collapse, raising concerns about the safety of nearby structures.
Students from several states among residents
Residents said most students staying at the PG were from Kerala, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and attended colleges including Motilal Nehru College, Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College and Sri Venkateswara College.One resident said students were paying around Rs 12,000 per bed at the accommodation. Residents also raised concerns about the condition of buildings in the congested locality, where several residential properties have reportedly been converted into student PG accommodations.
CM Rekha Gupta visits collapse site
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta visited the site and reviewed the ongoing search and rescue operation. Emergency teams continued clearing the rubble and searching for anyone who may still be trapped."No one will be spared," she says.
The Rekha Gupta-led Delhi government has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident and directed that an FIR be registered against the building owner, the chief minister’s office (CMO) said.The decision was taken following an on-site review and a preliminary assessment of the incident, the CMO said.“Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, the chief minister has ordered a Magisterial Inquiry of the incident and an FIR against the building owner,” the CMO said.
It added that those found responsible for the incident would be held fully accountable and face the strictest provisions of the law.
PM Modi expresses condolences
Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed condolences over the deaths in the Satya Niketan building collapse and prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured. He said authorities were working at the site and assisting people affected by the incident.

In a village on the edge of Germany’s Harz mountains, families gathering at a beer-and-bratwurst summer picnic lined up for autographs and selfies from the man they want to lead the country’s first far-right state government since World War II.
Ulrich Siegmund, leader of the Alternative for Germany party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, beamed with confidence that he’ll secure a victory that will deliver him a majority to lead the state after Sunday’s election. Should he fall short, he said, so be it. The political chaos that’s bound to ensue will last “a few months” — and the party will simply win the next election.
“Either way, we are the future, and I am looking positively toward this election,” Siegmund, an affable 35-year-old former businessman with a crisply side-parted coif, said in an interview in Roblingen am See last week. “We can only win.”

Spotify Technology co-founder Martin Lorentzon said he would leave Sweden immediately if the country introduces new wealth taxes, escalating concerns that proposals being debated ahead of this month’s election could drive entrepreneurs and capital abroad.
“Yes, absolutely,” Lorentzon said in emailed comments when asked whether he would consider moving. “I would prefer to stay, but such a tax would mean I have to leave immediately.”
The warning from the Stockholm-based billionaire comes as the country’s Left Party campaigns for a tax on billionaires and the Greens are proposing a separate levy on the wealthiest. Both are part of the center-left opposition led by the Social Democrats, which is ahead of the governing right-wing bloc in recent polls, and could wield influence over tax policy after the Sept. 13 vote.
A wealth tax is opposed by the current center-right government, as well as by Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, who has ruled out restoring Sweden’s former wealth, inheritance and gift taxes. Even so, investors are trying to assess what compromises might emerge after the election.
Lorentzon, who has an estimated net worth of more than $11 billion according to the Bloomberg Billionaire’s Index, urged politicians to consider higher taxes on capital or dividends instead.
“It benefits no one if entrepreneurs and job creators have to sell parts of their companies to pay tax,” he said. “It would mean fewer companies, fewer innovations, less investment in areas such as environmental and climate technology, fewer taxpayers and fewer shared resources for welfare. The tax is directly counterproductive.”
Lorentzon’s comments are one of the most dramatic indications yet of how some wealthy Swedes would react to the introduction of new wealth taxes. Nordic Capital executive Klas Tikkanen previously told Bloomberg that the proposals could produce “a real exodus,” while entrepreneurs and advisers have said some are already examining the option of relocating abroad.
Lorentzon said the discussions about new taxes have already done some damage by creating uncertainty. “I get a great many questions from entrepreneurs about whether it is still OK to start a company in Sweden,” he told Bloomberg. “It was bad in the 1970s and 1980s, and it is just as bad today.”
In an opinion piece published in Expressen on Saturday, Lorentzon said he supports progressive taxation but opposes an annual levy on wealth. Such fortunes often consist of illiquid company stakes rather than cash, he argued, meaning founders could be forced to sell shares to meet their tax bills.

In some ways Lee Chang-dong‘s first film in 8 years, Possible Love (original title: Ganeunghan sarang) which is South Korea’s official entry into the International Film Oscar race and premiered in competition at the Venice Film Festival today, might remind you of the class divide in Bong Joon Ho’s Oscar winning Parasite which set the cinematic world on fire in 2019, but now with a pandemic between that release and this one, director Lee’s film carries a poignant subtext, a certain desire for love and longing in a world more split apart than ever, and one which for many seems like it all is out of reach.
The genesis of this film actually started around 2009 when a devastating mass layoff at one of South Korea’s major companies and the cruel suppression of the workers strike there was like an earthquake in the society at the time. The filmmaker though put it on the back burner because the reality of the situation did not feel possible to turn into narrative fiction at the time. The director whose much awarded filmography includes Oasis, Burning, Poetry, and Secret Sunshine, only now after 8 years of no new film was able to find a way in through the art of filmmaking itself as a story device, The changing nature of labor in the country added to his ability to make it not only relevant to his home country, but something that is recognizable around the world.
In Possible Love, a two year workers strike has taken its human toll, notably in the household of Mi-Ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) who is a factory worker who makes masks and whose once proud husband Ho-Seok (Sul Kyung-gu) has been laid off his job, his quiet demeanor now trying to hide his own inner shame, his actions in the strike emotionally crippling. They live with their son, Cheol and try to keep the family upbeat against trying circumstances. Mi-Ok though is still quite spirited and hopeful, protesting the company and longing for better days when their attendance at a funeral leads to meeting a filmmaker, Ye-Ti (Cho Yeo-Jeung) who is doing a documentary on the striking workers and sees Mi-Ok as a promising subject, even moreso when she learns of her husband’s plight and wants to find a way to interview him, even though he adamantly refuses to go on camera.
Watch on Deadline
Possible Love follows this storyline to the point when Ye-Ti, in an effort perhaps to create an environment where Ho-Seok would sit down and talk invites the family to spend time at her house which, class-wise, is much different than the modest lifestyle of Mi-Ok and Ho-Seok. They arrive at the lavishly appointed modern home located in a remote area near the sea where Ye-Ti and her attractive wealthy husband, Sang-woo ( Zo In-sung) live. Though Sang -woo may have business connections not exactly in line with the striking workers concerns he seems very welcoming, and as some time passes Ye-Ti gets Ho-Seok in front of her camera. Meanwhile Mi-Ok increasingly finds herself drawn to Sang-woo, notably an encounter in the ocean that becomes quietly intense. As the lives of these two married couples intersect between affluent and struggling, the human desires and need for love – on many levels – comes to the surface.
As you might expect from this master filmmaker, if you have any experience with his previous films, he takes his time developing the story, and at nearly three hours it takes a little too long here, but once the dichotomy of the situation appears between these two couples, the film comes into focus in a haunting manner, not simply exclusive to life and times in South Korean society, but a situation happening more frequently around the world and in America where the class divide and billionaire indifference to their workers is becoming more pronounced each day.
The cast of top South Korean actors here is well chosen, each of the four main stars given plenty to work with and delivering director Lee’s vision on the screen in this handsomely filmed and pertinent work that even those not familiar with this celebrated filmmaker’s pedigree will find much to admire.
Producers are Pinehouse Film Co., Ltd., Anonymous Content, LLC, NOWFILM Co., Ltd. It will debut on Netflix November 6 preceded by a two week theatrical run stateside.

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.
The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.
“I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.
Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.
Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.
But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.
In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”
As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.
Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.
In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”
It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.
However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

Allahabad HC dismisses plea seeking FIR against spiritual leader Rambhadracharya
Prayagraj , The Allahabad High Court has dismissed a writ petition seeking the registration of an FIR against spiritual leader Rambhadracharya over his alleged objectionable remarks about the Upadhyay community and revered religious personalities, including the Shankaracharyas.
A two-judge bench comprising Justices Chandra Dhari Singh and Tarun Saxena observed that a person aggrieved by the non-registration of an FIR must ordinarily first exhaust the statutory remedies available under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita prior to invoking the high court's extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226.
In its order dated September 1, the court dismissed the writ petition filed by Ramesh Upadhyay of Varanasi. However, he was granted liberty to avail an appropriate remedy under law.
According to the petitioner, certain statements made by Rambhadracharya, the founder and head of Tulsi Peeth in Chitrakoot, caused "grave mental agony, humiliation and insult" to him and other members of the Upadhyay community.
The petitioner alleged that Rambhadracharya also made objectionable statements against the four Shankaracharyas, hurting the religious sentiments of several followers.
Videos of his statements were circulated on social media platforms, including YouTube, he claimed.
The petitioner apprised the court that he had submitted a complaint to the Commissioner of Police, Varanasi, on October 8, 2025, seeking the registration of an FIR against the spiritual leader under appropriate penal provisions. However, no FIR had been registered till date.
The State opposed the petition contending that the petitioner had not approached the concerned police station and had directly approached the high court without first availing the remedy under Section 175 BNSS before the magistrate.
"This Court is of the considered view that if a person has a grievance that his FIR has not been registered by the police, or that having been registered, a proper investigation is not being done, then the remedy of the aggrieved person is not to approach the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution, but to approach the Magistrate concerned under Section 175 BNSS," the court said.

Qantas passengers on Sydney-bound flight recount panic after seeing flames spit from engine
In short:
Passengers have spoken out after their Sydney-bound Qantas flight had to be diverted due to flames shooting from the left-hand side engine.
They have recalled people's "nervous energy", panic and screams.
Qantas says an investigation into the incident is ongoing, and the plane has been temporarily grounded for inspection.
People screaming and widespread panic are how passengers have described the moment they heard loud bangs and saw fire spitting from an engine on a Sydney-bound Qantas flight.
On Saturday afternoon, Flight QF122 had just left Queenstown in New Zealand when it had to be diverted to Christchurch in what the airline said was a "suspected engine issue".
Kriti Sethi was on her way home after her holidays, and was sitting towards the back of the plane where she "could see the fire" coming from the left-hand side.
"It happened around five times, so we hear bang, bang, bang and there was five times fire coming out," she told the ABC from Sydney Airport after spending the night in Christchurch.
"And then the people were screaming; people were like, 'Oh my God.' It was quite scary."
Despite the cabin crew initially blaming the landing gear, Ms Sethi said that, because of her seat's location, she could see everything.
"So we were like, 'No, it's actually fire coming out of the engine, it's not landing gear'."
Adding to the panic and fear was the turbulence.
"So the plane was shaking as well. So it was fire and then went straight into shaking; it was just so scary," she said.
Announcements from captain
Sari-Elle Kraemer, who was sitting on the right-hand side of the plane, said there was a lot of nervous energy on board, especially after the lights went off.
While she could not see the fire, she could hear other passengers talking about it and did not know what to think.
"I've never experienced something like that," Ms Kraemer said.
"Just the noise and the fact that people could see fire on the plane was scary, but obviously the pilots are trained to deal with that, and I felt it was under control after a few minutes."
Throughout the ordeal, passengers were kept informed of what was happening.
Ms Sethi said the flight's captain told passengers in one announcement that the plane had experienced a chemical failure with the engines, forcing the aircraft to make an emergency landing in Christchurch.
Fire engines and emergency services were on hand at the tarmac.
Both women have commended the professionalism of the cabin crew, praising their handling of the incident, and were grateful for the safe landing.
"The cabin crew were amazing, and the captain was amazing,' Ms Sethi said.
"Once we landed, everyone was clapping."
She was still nervous on her trip home, but again the captain "made an announcement, saying 'That we understand what happened yesterday. It was a traumatic experience for you guys'."
Incident under investigation
A spokesperson for Qantas said the plane had been grounded in Christchurch as engineers carry out an inspection and examination.
It will remain there until it is cleared to resume flying, with an investigation underway into what caused the fire.
In a second incident in two days, another Qantas plane has been grounded temporarily and is under inspection after it was forced to return to Sydney Airport this morning.
Flight QF121 was en route to Queenstown when an incident took place halfway into the trip.
"A flight deck alert indicated a potential issue with the aircraft's anti-skid system," the airline told the ABC.
A recovery flight is being organised for Monday, with passengers forced to stay in Sydney overnight.
'Aircraft is designed for these sorts of things'
International aviation consultant Neil Hansford said that while it remained unclear what caused the issue, an engine blade might have detached.
"And obviously when it's a piece of metal going at that many revs, it's hit a fuel line and the fuel's ignited," he said.
"So the captain's able to shut the engine down, use the fire suppression system and put the fire out.
"The aircraft is designed for these sorts of things, so if an engine loses power on take-off, it's designed to fly on safely and continue to climb.
"These are all controllable circumstances, and you don't necessarily want them, but at least with the training of Qantas pilots, they totally know how to handle it; they're tested in the simulator."

How Man Utd plan to compete at top with richer rivals
- Published
Manchester United believe they can challenge for major honours despite being unable to match the spending power of their rivals.
United spent £148m on new players this summer, less than newly promoted Ipswich, the £300m-plus invested by Chelsea and Tottenham and the record £458m spent by Manchester City.
In their victory at Ipswich on Friday night, Liverpool fielded three players, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz, who each cost more than £100m.
By contrast, United's most expensive signing this summer was Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton in a deal that could reach £70m, still £19m short of the club-record £89m they paid for Paul Pogba a decade ago.
Head coach Michael Carrick says money in itself is not the answer to building a successful side and is adamant the club can compete.
"I certainly feel we can," he said. "The challenge is getting the right dynamics, the right balance and the right group together; getting the best players in the group to enhance the rest. Whether you need experience, or some younger players."
There has been some criticism of United's transfer approach, with the lack of a left-back to compete with Luke Shaw and no striking support for Benjamin Sesko two areas highlighted.
Carrick has rejected the notion restrictions have been placed on summer spending by United's hierarchy.
"The actual amount of money I understand can be a big thing but it doesn't always have to be the answer," he said.
United can manage debt and compete for trophies, says Berrada
Has United's debt has restricted the club's spending power?
Questions about that issue were raised at the Fans Forum at the end of June and respected finance blogger Swiss Ramble estimated in September 2025 that United had paid £852m in interest alone since the Glazer family's takeover in 2005.
The club's latest quarterly figures showed total borrowings of £1.29bn, including outstanding transfer fees.
United also took on an additional £91.92m when refinancing bonds in June and are yet to outline how they will fund a proposed new stadium expected to cost more than £2bn.
The club's full year accounts to 30 June are due out in the next few weeks and will show the latest picture after a season without any European football.
Against that backdrop, fans continue to protest against the Glazers at virtually every match. Yet chief executive Omar Berrada insists the club can remain competitive while managing its debt and stadium ambitions, arguing United's challenge is to operate sustainably while continuing to compete for major trophies.
"We have shown that with debt, we can not only [be] profitable, but more importantly, win trophies," Berrada told the club's Fans Forum on 30 July,. "And our aim is to do that again.
"Our role as management is to be able to operate competitively with a financial structure that's sustainable.
"We also aspire to build a new stadium, but we have to do it in a way that allows us to continue being competitive.
"We need to stay very disciplined and continue to take the right decisions on the pitch and put us in a position where we can do everything, where we can sustain the debt, aspire to build a new stadium and importantly, try to win as many trophies as we can."
The arrivals of Baleba, Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, plus the emergence of 19-year-old forward Shea Lacey leads Carrick to conclude his squad is in a better position now than when they ended last season, when they finished third after winning 12 of his 17 games in charge.
"Being at this club, you've got to strive to win," said Carrick.
"That's where we want to be, and we want to try and get to that on a consistent level.
"I don't like to keep looking back, but they know what it's taken to put that run together. Granted, there was one competition, and we need to do that an awful lot more this season, but we have strengthened the group, so we feel good about what's possible."
Whether that optimism is justified will become clearer over the coming months, but Carrick believes United have assembled a squad capable of challenging despite spending significantly less than many of their rivals.

U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner land for talks in Kyiv after meeting Putin in Moscow
KYIV, Ukraine — U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Their trip follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, seeking to revive peace talks during escalating aerial attacks by both sides.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that Kyiv is ready for a "constructive" discussion with U.S. representatives.
"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared," he said in a post on Telegram.
Washington's push to end the fighting has lost momentum, with the United States focused for the past six months on the Iran war. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks with Putin at the Kremlin.
No breakthroughs in Moscow talks
Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than three hours behind closed doors and ended without announcements of any breakthroughs. Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, described them afterward as constructive, frank, and useful but didn't discuss specific outcomes.
While Moscow offered its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Ushakov said, the talks were not purely focused on the war in Ukraine.
"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.
Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks take place. Still, the two traded fire overnight into Sunday, officials said.
Russian attacks across multiple Ukrainian regions killed one person and injured at least 10 others overnight into Sunday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
In Zaporizhzhia, drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, injuring seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region.
Ukraine's air force said Sunday that it intercepted 82 drones out of the 108 launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.
In Russia, a man was killed and a woman seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, local authorities in the Belgorod border region said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Sunday that its air defenses overnight shot down 258 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the waters of the Black and Azov seas.
Mixed hopes on the ground
In Kyiv on Sunday, dozens gathered for a nationwide 9 a.m. moment of silence honoring Ukraine's fallen soldiers, a daily ritual held in cities across the country.
Among them was Nataliia Lipei, 67, whose son Viktor was killed in December 2022. Despite a health condition, she has traveled from city to city to take part, and she said she hopes the talks in Moscow and Kyiv will finally bring an end to the war.
"I hope these steps and these meetings will definitely produce results, because there has been so much bloodshed and so many deaths here that we have to stop all of this," she told The Associated Press.
Not everyone shared her hope for the talks. Oleksandr Pastukhov, 27, a video editor who joined the commemoration, was skeptical the envoys' visit would change anything.
"We've already seen delegations like this come here before," he said. "We've seen this so-called ceasefire for three days, which ended after just a couple of hours, and now we're supposed to naively think that two people will come and change something."

‘Israel’s military gave me just minutes to leave my apartment before it was bombed. I’m lucky to be alive’
Neveen and Mohammed had recently married and were hoping to get their life back on track after nearly three years of Israeli attacks. But in the space of just minutes, those hopes were once again shattered, Alex Croft reports
Just after midnight, Neveen Abu Hatab and her husband Mohammed were awoken suddenly by the sound of shouting from their neighbours.
The panicked screams would save their lives. Shortly after they fled their Gaza home with just a work laptop, an Israeli missile reduced the building to rubble.
“I cried uncontrollably because I lost everything in an instant, for no reason at all,” Neveen says, speaking of the moment she saw footage of her new home in the Zeitoun neighbourhood the burning on social media on Thursday 30 July.
The destruction of the house was heartbreaking for the couple, who had recently married and hoped to get their lives back on track after nearly three years of a brutal Israeli bombing campaign.
Israel has continued launching attacks on Gaza and seized more territory since a ceasefire deal was agreed last October, killing at least 1,222 Palestinians during that time, according to figures from the Gaza health ministry.
Meanwhile, Hamas has stated that it will disarm, but only if Israel ends “all forms of aggression” against it and withdraws its forces from Gaza.
The Israeli military said it killed two Hamas commanders in its overnight strikes on 30 July. Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that three Palestinian citizens were killed in the Gaza City strikes overnight, and another 21 killed across the Strip by Israeli shelling and gunfire after dawn.
Asked for comment about the strike on Neveen’s home, the Israeli military said it had “struck in several areas in the Gaza Strip and dismantled four Hamas weapon storage facilities”. They claimed the facilities held “Kalashnikov guns, explosive devices, additional ammunition and military equipment”.
“The weapons were intended to harm Israeli civilians and IDF troops operating in the area of the Yellow Line and were dismantled to eliminate the threat,” it added.
The prospects for the a second phase of the truce look bleak, after Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a 15-point document put forward by Donald Trump earlier this year, declaring Israeli forces would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas was disarmed.
For Neveen and Mohammed, both aged 28, the possibility that there will be no immediate end to the ongoing military strikes in Gaza, has shattered their efforts to rebuild their lives amid the rubble.
She recalls details of the night of the attack tearfully during an interview with The Independent.
“I grabbed my personal bag and work laptop, then we left to get away from the apartment unless than 10 mins before it was targeted,” she recalls.
“We spent the night at my husband’s family home, where I still am to this day. We were shocked later to find out the missiles had rained down on the buildings, burning and fully destroying our apartment.”
The Israeli military added that it takes “great measures to mitigate harm to the civilian population” and that it “works to distance civilians from combat zones and areas where military activity is expected, by issuing advanced warnings and calls to move to safer areas”.
Neveen and Mohammed had waited for years to get married and buy their first home, as the war in Gaza raged. Over nearly three years, the Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza health ministry, during a bombardment and invasion it launched after the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October in which militants killed 1,195 people, according to Israeli tallies.
“We have not even been married for four months,” says Neveen. “We were postponing our wedding until the Gaza war ended. We finally got married dreaming of stability, only to feel that everything we tried to build was shattered once again, resetting us back to zero.”
“We decided to set up our home despite resources being so scarce.”
With no sign of a stable political future for the Strip, the outlook for Palestinians in Gaza remains bleak.
Former British prime minister Tony Blair, whose role in the Gaza “Board of Peace” has grown in recent months, has been drafted in to try and fast-track the peace process.
Along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, he met with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, for a nearly-four-hour meeting aimed at saving the 15-point roadmap for peace in Gaza.
But the talks failed to make a breakthrough on the stalled deal, after Netanyahu reiterated the Israeli stance that there will be no progress on the deal or on Israel’s withdrawal from the enclave before Hamas disarms.

While warning that breaching the 1.5°C global warming limit would bring irreversible losses that no adaptation initiatives could undo, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on Wednesday (September 2, 2026), for the first time, set out a detailed “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway.
This is a route under which the world overshoots the 2015 Paris Agreement’s central goal — limiting the rise in average global temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels — which a UNEP report said was now unavoidable, but holds the peak as low as possible and then brings temperatures back down below the limit by the end of the century.
The report, Limiting Overshoot, released in Nairobi, said global warming would cross 1.5°C “in the next few years”. Even a scenario in which every country delivers on its national climate plan and net-zero target puts peak warming at 1.8°C, it said. According to the report, current policies point to a rise of about 2.6°C by 2100, with a range of 1.9–3.6°C. The pathway, the report said, "is by no means an acceptable or preferred pathway; it is simply the best remaining option."
The diplomatic grounds for that framing were laid at the 30th UN Climate Change Conference, COP30, held in 2025 in Brazil’s Belém, where the consensus “Global Mutirão” decision became the first COP text to concede that a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C limit was likely, given how fast the remaining carbon budget was being spent. At the conference, countries also committed, for the first time, to limiting the size and duration of the overshoot and to closing adaptation gaps, which would require deep, rapid and sustained emission cuts.
Given that cuts alone will no longer suffice, a steep scaling up of nature-based removals such as large reforestation programmes was needed, COP30 CEO Ana Toni said in a statement. UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres also released a statement, saying, “This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition."
Compounding costs
The UNEP report suggested that time spent above 1.5°C carries compounding costs such as faster sea-level rise, coral reef collapse, glacier loss exceeding a quarter of global mass by 2100, declines of up to 14% in global food production by 2050 without effective adaptation, and rising odds of irreversible tipping points in the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and the Amazon.
Moreover, it gets harder to roll back the effects of a tonne of emitted carbon. The report computed that every five years of continued high emissions adds roughly 0.1°C to peak warming. Reversing that same 0.1°C afterwards means pulling about 220 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide back out of the atmosphere over and above whatever is still being emitted. Very broadly, a single large tree growing for about 30 years can cut out only a tonne of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide removal, the report stresses, is needed in addition to, not instead of, emission cuts, and can credibly cool temperatures back to the 1.5°C limit only if peak warming stays well below 2°C. Even the most optimistic scaling up of emission cuts is unlikely to reverse more than a few tenths of a degree this century, the report underlined.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen was explicit that the report is not a concession. “Let’s be very clear, the 1.5 target is still the goal. But now we need to approach it differently from above,” she said.
The report arrives at a moment of uncertainty over whether countries will cut emissions at all. The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, formally exited the Paris Agreement earlier this year and has also announced its withdrawal from the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Green Climate Fund. Separately, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the conflict in West Asia has produced what the International Energy Agency calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, with output from affected countries down more than 14 million barrels a day. Sustained high energy prices could push governments toward coal and other short-term fossil responses.
Methane targets
The report, in a first for the UN, placed significant stress on methane, which currently contributes about 0.5°C of warming. Cutting it is described as the most effective way to slow warming in the near term. Human activity currently puts out roughly 350–400 million tonnes of methane a year, mostly from fossil fuel operations, livestock, rice paddies, landfills and wastewater. When modellers build the pathways that underpin net-zero targets, they typically assume that about half of this gets cut by mid-century through “cheap, technically easy” interventions such as plugging leaks and venting from oil and gas. But the other half, roughly 150–200 million tonnes a year still being emitted in 2050 from agriculture and waste, is harder to cut; though shaving 60–70 million tonnes from it could reduce temperature rise to the same extent as removing 220 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Over 155 countries have joined the Global Methane Pledge to cut anthropogenic methane at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. India, China, Russia and Iran remain outside it.
The UNEP report co-author Richard Betts of the University of Exeter said, “It is a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world."

‘He didn’t know how to shoot': Jhiram Valley attack convicts' kin dispute court judgment, claim innocence
Twenty nine people were killed in Jhiram Valley attack in Chhattisgarh in 2013 after Maoists ambushed a Congress convoy.
Over 13 years after a Maoist attack on a Congress convoy left 29 people dead in Chhattisgarh's Jhiram Ghati, a special NIA court on Saturday convicted all 10 accused in the case. Two women are among the 10 accused in the case that virtually wiped out the top Congress leadership in the state.
But now, family members of some of the convicts are disputing the allegations of their involvement in the deadly attack.
What the kin of the accused are saying
Family members of convict Joga Markam, also known as Joga Madkami, have spoken out against the judgment, asserting that he was wrongly implicated.
Durjan Markam, the brother of Markam, expressed his frustration over the legal process and the shifting dates for the final verdict.
"My elder brother is Joga Markam. He had no hand in the Jhiram Ghati case incident. They brought him in, saying he carried out such an attack. We were told on August 31 that a decision would be made that day. When we came that day, they said it would be on the 5th. Today, they also say it won't be today; come on the 16th. They are saying like this... what does this mean?" Durjan was quoted as saying by news agency ANI.
He further argued that his brother "didn't know how to shoot an arrow or use a gun."
Similar claims were made by the kin of Kosa Kavasi. His brother Guddu Kavasi Kosa and Mukka Mandavi were falsely implicated in the case. He claimed Kosa Kavasi was involved in preparations for a family wedding when the attack took place, while Mandavi was also engaged in marriage preparations in the village.
"They were not there at the time of the attack. Those who were involved have surrendered and are living freely, while those who were not involved are paying the price. The families are distressed and shattered," Guddu told HT.
Others convicted in the case are: Pramila Modiyam, Chaitu Lekam, Sumitra Punem Modiyam, Aayata Markam, Madkami Deva, Banjami Sanna and Mahadev Nag.
Who were killed in the attack?
The attack took place on May 25, 2013, when Maoists ambushed the Congress' 'Parivartan Rally' on a national highway in Jhiram Valley under Darbha police station limits in Bastar district. The leaders were going for a rally organised ahead of the Chhattisgarh assembly elections later that year.
Those killed included then-state Congress chief Nand Kumar Patel and his son Dinesh, former leader of Opposition in the assembly Mahendra Karma, former union minister Vidya Charan Shukla, and senior Congress leader and former MLA Uday Mudliyar. However, then chief minister, Amit Jogi, escaped with injuries, HT reported earlier.
