As the summer crowds slowly begin to fade and the trees turn fiery shades of red, orange, and yellow, fall in New England has officially begun. It's time for sweater weather, pumpkin spice, and apple orchards.
Being from Rhode Island myself, I know many people think the Ocean State is most exceptional in the summer, with iconic Westerly beach days and summer mansion tours in Newport. Yet, in my opinion, fall is the perfect time to plan a quiet escape.
One of my favorite lesser-known places, Middletown, is home to local farms, quiet beaches, and a beautiful vineyard, making for a quiet, fun-filled fall day.
I always start a fall day with a pumpkin-spice latte and a farm trip
Nothing says fall more than an iced pumpkin-spice latte. One of my favorite local coffee spots is Custom House Coffee, which always has delicious seasonal beverages.
Walking in, guests can smell the beans roasting on-site and even pick up a fresh bag. If I want a sweet treat, I'll also grab a cheese danish for the road.
Then, it's time to head to the farm. Picking apples and pumpkins at a local spot is one of my favorite seasonal pastimes, and Sweet Berry Farm is my go-to.
Because apple-picking season ends in mid-October and pumpkin season starts in September, I've found late September or early October to be the best time to visit. I love walking through the neat rows of trees searching for the ripest and juiciest apples to add to my bucket.
From summer golden to honeycrisp, Fuji, and McIntosh (my personal favorite), there's a wide variety of apples available — plus, a pumpkin patch where you can find the perfect specimen for your front porch.
Fall is the best time of year for a quiet beach walk
Fall is the prime time of year to grab a cozy crewneck and walk along Second or Third Beach.
These beaches are always bustling in the summer with hordes of tourists lying blanket to blanket, but now, they're quiet and perfect for taking in the beauty of the ocean or strolling hand-in-hand with your loved one.
Second Beach is within walking distance of the Sachuest Point National Wildlife Refuge, which is a great place for a fall hike. The main loop is around 2 ½ miles, or you can opt for the Ocean View Loop at around 1 ½ miles.
While walking around, you may even spot migratory birds or other wildlife.
The Newport Vineyards are perfect for wine and a snack
Although this spot is called the Newport Vineyards, don't be fooled: It's actually located in Middletown.
After a beach walk, a glass of their famous Great White usually starts to call my name. Fruity and light, the wine pairs well with their cheese boards.
I'll often pick a funky blue cheese, a sharp cheddar, and a soft goat cheese from their list of offerings, many of which come from New England farms and dairy producers.
Fall is peak harvest season, when visitors can tour the property. Maybe you'll even be lucky enough to show up during the annual Harvest Festival in October, where you can watch guests squash grapes with their feet in an exciting competition.
At the vineyard, you'll often hear live music — and, if you're chilly, you can find a place to sit by a fire pit. I find this to be the best spot to warm up with friends after a long day of fall adventures.

Steinem led a CIA-backed organization that reportedly recruited young Americans to disrupt Soviet Union-supported festivals and share alternatives to communist ideas. She maintained through her life that her involvement with the CIA was an innocent arrangement and claimed in a 1967 New York Times article that the CIA never asked her to report on other Americans or foreign nationals.
After American journalist and feminist activist Gloria Steinem died at age 92 on Sept. 3, 2026, a rumor spread online that she once worked with the CIA.
Social media users on X, TikTok and Reddit claimed she was a CIA "asset," "cop" or "operative," or that she led an organization that was actually a front for CIA operations.
Steinem repeatedly and publicly acknowledged working with the CIA. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, she ran the Independent Research Service, a CIA-backed organization that recruited young Americans, reportedly to disrupt Soviet Union-supported festivals and promote alternatives to communist ideas.
As such, we have rated this claim as true.
Whether she actively spied for the CIA is unclear. In 1967 news articles, Steinem insisted she was never asked to pass information to the CIA.
Steinem admits involvement after exposé
"This was the organization that made life so miserable for the organizers of the communist-leaning world youth festivals in Vienna in 1959, and in Helsinki in 1962," the 
According to a 2016 New York Times article about Steinem, after the Ramparts issue ran, Steinem publicly acknowledged to the Times and The Washington Post that the CIA was a major financial backer of the Independent Research Service.
While the Times said the Independent Research Service simply received financial support, the Post said Steinem "worked closely with the Central Intelligence Agency" and "had great praise for the CIA agents whom she collaborated with."
"I found them liberal and farsighted and open to an exchange of ideas," Steinem said, according to the Post. "I never felt I was being dictated to at all." Steinem told both newspapers that very few people involved in the Independent Research Service knew of the CIA's involvement.
The Post's article also quoted another director of the Independent Research Service, Dennis Shaul, who said, "The Helsinki Festival was a disaster from their (the Communist world's) point of view, and I think we can take a good deal of credit for that."
In March 1967, Steinem appeared on a CBS documentary, "In the Pay of the CIA: An American Dilemma," to tell her story about her time taking "secret CIA funds," per a CBS news release archived in the CIA's public records.
A clip of her interview in that documentary appears to be available on YouTube. In the clip, she acknowledges working for the CIA and, again, says the CIA did not interfere with her point of view.
"I had the conventional liberal's view of the CIA as a right-wing incendiary group, and I was amazed to discover that this was far from the case, that they were enlightened, liberal nonpartisan activists," she said (at 2:17).
We reached out to CBS to ask for an official copy of the documentary and await a response.
Steinem responds to feminist 
In 1975, Redstockings, a radical feminist group, attacked Steinem's involvement with the CIA and called Steinem's insistence that she was never asked to gather information for the CIA a "serious lie."
"The Report on the Vienna Youth Festival, published with her name on it as Director of the Independent Research Service, contains 13 pages devoted solely to biographies, political affiliations, and even pseudo-political analyses of individuals from all the countries participating in the festival," Redstockings wrote.
Redstockings also said it questioned Steinem's motives for entering the women's movement and was "suspicious of her sudden rise to prominence as a 'women's liberation leader' at a time when, unlike other prominent women's liberationists, she was active in no women's group, she had not written a feminist book, won a Congressional seat or played a superb game of tennis."
The New York Times reported in 2016 that Steinem said the criticism from other feminists "hurt more than anything."
"They never called to ask me what I did," she said.
In the same 2016 article, Steinem maintained that her relationship with the CIA was innocent.
"It's so interesting now, because the initials C.I.A. will make people believe anything," she said. "It just wasn't like that. It just was so uncontrolled. As I remember saying at the time, if this was our grandmother's money we'd be doing the same thing."

The company says it is guided by a commitment to treat teens as teens, and to encourage real-world support.

Republicans have been turning transgender athletes into a wedge issue since Idaho passed the first state ban in 2020. This year, it’s already playing a major role in midterm ads, with Democrats in competitive races almost always on the defensive. At this point, the fight doesn’t even need a trans athlete: The WNBA spent the summer at the center of a culture war over a hypothetical conflict, after two ex-NBA players declared themselves eligible for the women’s draft as a stunt. There have been no known trans women on any team, and the league confirmed it had “no immediate eligibility matters” on its hands.
What happens when a blue state votes on trans sports?
Four states have midterm ballot measures on the issue. Washington’s would go further than any law in the country.
Key takeaways
- Twenty-seven Republican-controlled states have imposed measures to restrict trans athletes from playing in girls’ and women’s sports since 2020, but this year is the first time voters will have a chance to weigh in on the question directly.
- Washington state’s proposed measure to verify sex assigned at birth would apply to all girls seeking to play sports, not just players whose eligibility has been challenged.
- Democrats are split on how loudly to fight it. Washington’s congressional and legislative leaders oppose the measure, while the governor and both US senators have stayed quiet.
It became such a political priority in part because it polls well: Surveys show most Americans, including many otherwise Democratic-leaning voters, favor barring trans women from sports leagues. This November, though, marks the first time voters will confront the issue directly at the ballot box themselves.
Most notably, in Washington state, the public will decide whether to go further than any red-state legislature has even managed. A ballot initiative, I-638, would require every girl who wants to play school sports to first prove their sex assigned at birth, via an inspection of their reproductive anatomy or a test of their sex chromosomes or hormone levels. Competing campaigns in the state are mobilizing voters for and against the measure, which will deliver the clearest test yet of how liberal and moderate voters feel about this issue.
Twenty-seven other states have already imposed measures to restrict trans athletes from participating in girls’ and women’s sports in recent years, and the US Supreme Court ruled earlier this summer that such bans are constitutional. Yet nearly all of those bans passed through Republican-controlled legislatures, mostly in states Donald Trump won three times, and none went directly before voters. That changes this fall, not only in Washington but also with Arizona, Colorado, and Nebraska voters weighing in.
The blue-state ballot battle comes at a time when the Democratic Party is still struggling to figure out how it wants to talk about transgender athletes. Democrats have broadly supported anti-discrimination protections for trans people, but on the specific questions that have dominated the political debate — namely whether trans women and girls should play on sports teams matching their gender identity, and whether minors should have access to gender-related medical treatment — most Democrats have been reluctant to adopt clear positions, while some swing-state candidates have actively distanced themselves from the party.
But the Washington state referendum is forcing its opponents, and allied Democratic politicians, to tackle the issue head-on. And they think they may have found a way to win — by convincing even voters who agree with the ban’s goals that enforcing it will create more problems than it solves.
What’s different about the Washington sports ban
The measure in Washington state is more far-reaching than other state bans in one key way, as it would require verification from every student seeking to join a girls’ sports team, not just those whose eligibility has been challenged. According to the text for I-638, athletes would need to document their sex assigned at birth based “only on one or more of the following: the student’s reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.”
Opponents, organizing under the banner of No Hate in WA State, are seeking to defeat the measure by framing it as the most extreme proposal of its kind. On paper, they face an uphill battle: 73 percent of Americans told Pew last year they were uncomfortable with transgender athletes playing on teams that don’t match their assigned birth sex. Opponents are also being massively outspent by Let’s Go Washington, the PAC campaigning for the measure, which is bankrolled by the conservative hedge fund manager Brian Heywood.
But No Hate in WA State hopes the ballot text will help them show that the proposed ban on transgender athletes would be a nightmare to implement. Even if Let’s Go Washington didn’t intend the outcome, they argue, no defensible reading of I-638 could avoid the conclusion that thousands of children will face either invasive new genital exams or the loss of a spot on a girls’ team altogether because their families can’t afford the genetic or testosterone testing the initiative offers as alternatives.
“Brian Heywood’s Initiative Wants To Inspect Your Daughter’s Body” reads a typical post from the No Hate in WA State campaign account, warning the initiative would yield “medically unnecessary” and “potentially traumatizing” genital or pelvic exams.
Let’s Go Washington disputes this, saying documentation of a genital exam from any routine past checkup, including the physical performed at birth, would suffice. But more than 150,000 school-age girls in Washington lack a regular family doctor with the medical records the campaign says would already be on file, and many schools conduct sports physicals publicly in group settings, where examining a student’s reproductive anatomy would be unthinkable.
Let’s Go Washington could not connect me with an attorney willing to defend its interpretation of the legislative text on the record, though campaign spokespeople Darren Littell and Hallie Herzberg said they consulted lawyers while crafting the ballot language. “I agree with you that it should have been explicit to say, ‘Here’s all the ways in the universe that you could verify a child’s sex’ and we didn’t do that, and that’s where we are now,” Herzberg told me.
Critics of the initiative warn the campaign will stir up more anti-trans sentiment and put vulnerable students in danger. The lead supporters say I-638 is necessary to protect the “integrity and fairness” of girls’ sports, and has nothing to do with targeting trans children. “This is not being motivated because we don’t like trans kids,” Littell said. “I’ve got family members who are trans, and I still love them and care about them.”
The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association is aware of about 10 transgender middle and high schoolers who play sports, out of more than 200,000 student-athletes statewide. Since 2007, the organization has allowed trans students to play on teams that align with their gender identity, with their handbook stating once a student-athlete is granted eligibility, they do not need to seek to renew eligibility every season or school year.
“School sports is a place where kids can belong, a place of inclusion, where they can learn to work as a team and learn dedication,” Kelsey Gellner, a pediatric nurse based in Seattle, told me. “Tens of thousands of girls will be impacted by this to purposely exclude 10 children. That’s insane.”
Some opponents doubt the measure is really about protecting competition in female sports at all. Earlier this summer, the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with the Trump administration, released a report attacking Title IX, the federal law barring sex discrimination in federally funded schools and programs. The report argues for “unwinding our current regime” and blames the law for imposing a male model of competition on women, encouraging girls toward dominance and aggression, and pulling them away from femininity and motherhood.
“Preventing girls from playing sports is the whole point,” Megan Rapinoe, a two-time World Cup champion and Olympic gold medalist, wrote in a recent op-ed lambasting the ballot measure in Washington. “Spaces that leave girls and women feeling empowered are the spaces they want to constrict — and then eliminate.”
Bringing adult restrictions down to children
The initiative’s proponents point to alternative means of verifying sex at birth, rather than genital exams. But hormone and genetic testing, the less invasive alternatives on offer, are very unusual for minors, and typically have only been required for certain elite adult athletes.
Earlier this summer, for example, the Women’s Tennis Association announced it would require all players to undergo genetic sex testing in order to compete on the WTA Tour, a move that came on the heels of World Athletics requiring the same for participation in the female category for world ranking competitions. The goal would be to provide blood, saliva, or a cheek swab to test for any presence of the gene associated with the Y chromosome.
These tests are expensive, though, and require specialized training that public school staff virtually never have.
“The language in the [Washington state] measure is quite alarming because it quite literally would codify sex testing for youth athletes into law,” Anna Posbergh, a professor at the University of Illinois Department of Recreation, Sport, and Tourism, told The Cut.
I-638 doesn’t specify how these tests would work in practice or who would pay for them. The ballot measure is also silent on intersex students, whose anatomy, chromosomes, and hormones may not point to the same answer. Littell says they would leave these questions “up to the doctors and patients, and at the end of the day this is common sense.”
I asked the Washington State Medical Association what share of primary care and family medicine practices in the state could even run genetic or hormone testing in-house, and what referrals would look like for a rural practice.
“We don’t have that level of data, unfortunately,” Graham Short, a spokesperson for WSMA, told me. He added that his association does not yet have a formal position on the ballot measure, though their policymaking delegation convenes in September and may formulate a stance then.
The Washington State Nurses Association has come out against the proposal. Gellner, who sits on its board, said it’s been disturbing to watch the idea of sports physicals shift from checking whether a student is healthy to play — i.e., checking their muscles, joints, blood pressure, and signs of asthma — to determining “whether the child themselves is a risk.”
The state chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, which has not taken a formal position, asked Let’s Go Washington to stop invoking the national group in the state’s official voter pamphlet, where the campaign cites AAP guidelines on routine childhood checkups. (The campaign refused.) Dr. Erica Li, a Spokane-based pediatrician who has been Let’s Go Washington’s most vocal physician in support of the measure, insisted to me that the process outlined in I-638 just “does not pose any barriers to any female” looking to participate in school sports.
Yet other states have backed away from language like this. A 2021 Florida law signed by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis originally had language saying that students would have to undergo a genital exam or get hormone or genetic testing if there were ever disputes over a student’s eligibility. That language sparked major controversy and was ultimately stripped from the final bill. House Republicans in Ohio also passed a bill in 2022 that would have required any student athlete whose sex was disputed to prove their sex assigned at birth through those same three options. After backlash, lawmakers removed the language from the Senate version, and put in a birth certificate requirement instead.
A time of Democratic hesitance
Democrats have broadly supported anti-discrimination protections for trans people, but on sports specifically, the party has struggled to find agreement.
The Biden administration proposed a Title IX rule in 2023 that would have rejected blanket bans but allowed schools to restrict trans athletes’ participation in some cases, but the president never spoke about this nuanced rule publicly. Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign didn’t raise trans rights either, even as Republicans made them a centerpiece of their attacks against her.
Democratic strategists have urged candidates to address transgender-related attacks more directly this time, but that hasn’t translated to a policy consensus. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger spent millions on ads acknowledging concerns about fairness and safety in school sports, for example, although even Spanberger’s actual position on the subject remains vague.
Nationally, as the New York Times recently reported, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts appears to be the only high-profile Democrat “eagerly campaigning as a supporter of transgender rights” this cycle.
In Washington state, some prominent Democrats have come out against I-638, including five Democratic members of Congress, such as Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the House Democratic Caucus, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus. The state’s top two legislative leaders, Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen and House Speaker Laurie Jinkins, have also come out against it. Gov. Bob Ferguson and Sens. Patty Murray and Maria Cantwell, though, have not publicly joined them.
Polling thus far is unclear. A September 2025 poll of Washingtonians found 69 percent statewide support for the school-sports initiative, although the survey used language highly favorable to the measure, describing it as protecting “integrity and fairness” and did not explicitly say it would bar transgender girls from girls’ teams.
No Hate in WA State referred me to May polling conducted by the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, a progressive group that tracks state ballot measures. Their survey rated I-638 a toss-up, finding voters sharply divided, with 43 percent strongly in favor, 21 percent strongly opposed, 17 percent fully undecided, and another 11 to 14 percent not firmly committed. BISC said they did not have more recent polling to share.
The measure, however it ultimately goes at the ballot box, will be a verdict on how the issue is playing out beyond red states, and directly with voters. For the handful of trans students the WIAA knows about, and for every other girl who wants to play sports, November will decide something more immediate. Voter pamphlets go out in October.

Russia hits Ukrainian security headquarters in drone attack, Zelensky says
- Published
A Russian drone has hit the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) during a strike in the heart of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The unmanned aerial vehicle crashed into the SBU headquarters on Friday afternoon, targeting a room used by security chief Oleksandr Poklad.
It is not clear whether Poklad was in the building, but Zelensky said he had since spoken to him to order an "appropriate, tangible response".
"The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Zelensky confirmed. It suggests Russia's new drones are growing in accuracy and signals Moscow could step up strikes before possible US mediation talks this weekend.
- Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv over weekend, reports say 
  - Published40 minutes ago
"All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram.
"I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."
Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses".
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.
A nearby café was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike.
Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third café to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion.
"Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added.
The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.
In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.
In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.
The strike on the SBU building is a rare example of Russia successfully hitting a government building.
The SBU - which is just over the road from the St Sophia cathedral, the oldest building in Kyiv - is a key part of Ukraine's war efforts as it conducts deep strikes to damage Russian infrastructure.
The drone came during yet another air raid alert. There was a brief whine before an explosion echoed across the roof tops and smoke rose into the sky.
Despite the ongoing exchanges, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war continue.
The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials.
Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, without a breakthrough so far.

A clever technique used to hide malicious prompts in attacks on AI agents has been adopted by spammers to evade filters on email platforms that are designed to flag unwanted messages used in mass campaigns.
The technique is broadly known as ASCII smuggling. It gained attention two years ago as a means of making a class of AI attack known as prompt injections more stealthy. Malicious instructions embedded in emails or other untrusted content to be processed by an LLM aren’t written in ordinary text. Instead, they’re rendered by a special range of Unicode tags. For example, the tag point U+E0041 mirrors “A,” and U+E0061 mirrors “a.”
No longer just for obscuring prompt injections
The block of 128 tags mimics a portion of the American Standard Code for Information Interchange almost perfectly, with one major difference: the characters they encode are readable by computers but, by design, are almost completely invisible to humans. By expressing the malicious prompts in these tags, LLMs detect the instructions, but people reading the email never see them. There’s much more about ASCII smuggling here.
Earlier this year, Microsoft started seeing a massive increase in spam messages that used the technique. Beginning on one day in early February, the number of ASCII smuggling signatures detected by Microsoft Defender for Office spiked from roughly 21,000 per day to more than 1.3 million. Within four days, signature detections jumped to 2.5 million. The deluge persisted for months and then fell off sharply in mid-May.
“Because tag characters are invisible to humans but exist at the text-processing level, the same property that makes them useful for smuggling instructions into a model also makes them useful for obfuscating keywords before a detector evaluates them,” Microsoft explained Thursday. “The intent is inverted, but the mechanism is similar, and a user’s suspicions are not raised.”

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
- Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark 
  - Published7 June
- Antonelli says he still has questions to answer 
  - Published11 June
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Is 256GB enough for an iPhone? Here's when you should go bigger
Looking at you, gamers.
New iPhones are on the way, and upgrading can be tempting — especially with Apple's first foldable phone on the way. But picking the right model is about more than just choosing between shades of space gray. Storage matters too, and choosing the wrong capacity is a headache you'll be living with it for years. Deleting vacation photos just to clear room for new ones gets old fast. So does watching an iOS update fail because three apps need to go first.
Most new iPhones start at 256GB now, which is more than enough for many people. A single photo eats up roughly 3MB, so some back of the envelope math suggests a 256GB phone has room for something like 70,000 of them — more than most people will ever shoot. The problem shows up when storing 4K video or bigger AAA games. That's usually the point where it's worth paying extra for more storage instead of fighting your phone every few months.
When you should upgrade to a 512GB iPhone
Although 4K video offers incredible definition, it's also the fastest way to use up your storage space. One minute of standard 4K footage runs about 440MB. Switch to a codec like Apple ProRes, though, and that same minute can hit 6GB. At that rate it doesn't't take long to fill up a 256GB iPhone. RAW photos also take up a lot more space than regular photos and can be as large as 50MB each.
Gamers have their own reasons to pay for extra storage. Resident Evil 4 alone eats over 30GB. Now imagine downloading five or six games like that. Going bigger also means no more deleting your favorite games to make room for new releases. That matters most when you're traveling and can't count on a solid connection to redownload anything.
Then there are the things you don't really see or think about. iOS itself takes up as much as 24GB of space right out of the box, and that number goes up when the system downloads additional content such as AI models and offline maps.
The iCloud factor
Choosing iPhone storage also depends a lot on how you prefer to manage your data. Maybe you're fine with paying for an iCloud plan and streaming most of your music and movies. 256GB is ideal when you can store everything in the cloud. iCloud subscribers can even enable an option to automatically offload older photos and videos, so that only the most recent ones are saved in high resolution on your device for offline access. You can also clear the cache for certain apps on your iPhone to save some storage.
However, if you're the type of person who hates relying on the cloud, or if you frequently travel to places with poor or no internet connection, having more local storage is essential for keeping an offline copy of all your content. If having your entire photo library with you, recording lots of 4K videos or downloading lots of large games is what you want, you should definitely spend the extra money to upgrade to 512GB or more.

Could the man who murdered a Christian missionary and his sons walk free in India?
- Published
Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressing
One of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.
The Supreme Court is hearing a petition seeking release from prison by a man who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.
Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).
Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.
The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.
Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.
On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.
As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.
In a sensational interview, external with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries".
"Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."
Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.
His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.
In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.
The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.
He received life sentences, external for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.
Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".
Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.
Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.
In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.
The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition, external seeking early release.
"The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago.
"In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.
Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.
At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.
The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."
On Wednesday, though, the court did not hear the case. The date for the next hearing is yet to be announced.
Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.
In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."
If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions".
"The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.
In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane".
But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008, in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced.
"The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes.
"What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda

The sandwich shop had struggled to maintain supply of the cola for the last eight years as the distributor cut back production due to the rising cost of aluminium.
But it didn't expect the cans to vanish permanently. Now it has switched to a locally-made version, which the venue's customers have largely embraced.

A team of Indian researchers has produced the first comprehensive molecular and functional profile of the venom gland of Stegodyphus sarasinorum, a colonial spider species found across the Indian subcontinent, to identify numerous proteins and small molecules that could serve as promising leads for future drug discovery.
Published in Springer Nature’s peer-reviewed, open-access journal Scientific Reports, the study identifies bioactive compounds associated with anti-cancer, antimicrobial and immune-related functions, while also demonstrating that venom gland extracts can kill cancer cells under laboratory conditions.
The researchers caution, however, that the findings represent an early stage of biomedical research and require extensive validation before any clinical application becomes possible.
Lead researcher A.P. Ajay Kumar of the Department of Zoology at Sree Neelakanta Government Sanskrit College, Pattambi, led the multidisciplinary study.
Unlike most spiders, which are solitary hunters, S. sarasinorum lives in permanent colonies, constructs communal silk nests and captures prey cooperatively. It is among only a small number of permanently social spider species known worldwide, thereby making it an important model for studying both spider behaviour and venom biology.
Although spider venom has long attracted scientific interest for their diverse biological activities, this is the first study to comprehensively analyse the molecular composition of the venom gland of this species using an integrated multi-omics approach, the researchers emphasise.
The research team combined transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy to examine the spider’s venom gland in great detail. Their analysis identified 31 protein components through transcriptomic profiling and 32 proteins through proteomic analysis. In addition, Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) detected 81 metabolites, including amino acids, biogenic amines and organic acids to provide a detailed molecular inventory of the venom gland.
To investigate the biological activity of these molecules, the researchers tested venom gland extracts against Dalton’s Lymphoma Ascites (DLA) cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The extracts exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, meaning that higher concentrations destroyed a greater proportion of cancer cells.
The findings suggest that the venom gland contains molecules with anti-cancer potential, the experiments were conducted only in cultured cells. Nonetheless, further studies involving additional cancer models, healthy cells, animals and eventually clinical trials will be required before any therapeutic use can be considered.
Among the most significant discoveries was the identification of several protein families that are already known for their biomedical relevance. These include hemocyanin proteins, which are known to stimulate immune responses and have attracted considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy research. The study also detected U12 and U20 lycotoxins, peptide molecules that can disrupt the membranes of bacteria and cancer cells, making them promising templates for the future development of antimicrobial peptides and targeted anti-cancer compounds.
The experimental work was carried out by research scholar Veena Venugopal, with contributions from collaborators from Calicut University, S.N. College, Nattika, St. Joseph’s College, Devagiri, PSG Institute of Advanced Studies, Coimbatore; GITAM University, Andhra Pradesh; and Ajman University, UAE.

Listed EV maker Ola Electric’s board has approved a fresh fundraise of up to ₹1,500 Cr, three months after the company raised ₹780 Cr through a QIP. In an exchange filing, the Bhavish Aggarwal-led company said it plans to raise the capital by issuing equity shares and/or securities convertible into or exchangeable for equity shares. The fundraise may be undertaken through one or more routes, including a further public offer, rights issue, QIP, private placement, or the issuance of instruments such as convertible debentures, warrants, American Depository Receipts, and Global Depository Receipts. The proposal is subject to approval from shareholders and other regulatory or statutory authorities. The filing did not disclose the proposed use of the proceeds. The latest proposal follows Ola Electric’s ₹780.24 Cr QIP in June. The QIP formed part of an earlier approval to raise up to ₹1,500 Cr, which Ola Electric’s board cleared in October 2025 and shareholders approved the following month. Of the net QIP proceeds of ₹744.87 Cr, the company earmarked ₹225 Cr for repaying or prepaying borrowings and ₹335 Cr for organic growth initiatives. Another ₹184.87 Cr was set aside for general corporate purposes. According to its QIP placement document, Ola Electric and its subsidiaries had outstanding borrowings of ₹1,637.61 Cr as of May 20, 2026. The fresh fundraise proposal comes as Ola Electric invests in its EV, battery cell manufacturing, and battery energy storage system businesses, while trying to revive sales and narrow its losses. Last month, the company launched the S1Z escooter range, powered by its locally developed 46-series LFP Bharat Cell. It also expanded its energy storage portfolio with the second-generation residential Ola Shakti, the industry-focused Shakti Rack, and the utility-scale Mahashakti. Ola Electric is also overhauling the sales model it has followed since launching its first escooter five years ago. The company opened its first dealer-operated stores across seven states yesterday and plans to build a network of more than 500 dealerships over the next two quarters. The changes come as the company looks to regain ground in India’s electric two-wheeler market. Ola Electric’s registrations declined 7.7% MoM to 13,132 units in August from 14,226 units in July, according to Vahan data. However, its market share improved to 7.6% from 6.8% during the period as overall electric two-wheeler registrations fell more sharply. On the financial front, Ola Electric’s consolidated net loss narrowed 22% YoY to ₹336 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹428 Cr. However, its operating revenue plunged 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, revenue rose 72% from ₹265 Cr, while loss narrowed from ₹500 Cr. The company’s board also approved an increase in its authorised share capital to ₹8,721.87 Cr from ₹8,318.50 Cr today, subject to shareholders’ approval. Meanwhile, in another senior management change, Ola Electric’s COO Hyun Shik Park resigned due to personal reasons, effective from the close of business today. The company’s board also approved the reappointment of Manoj Kumar Kohli and YourStory founder Shradha Sharma as independent directors for a second five-year term beginning December 6, subject to shareholders’ approval.

AFLW results: Fremantle star Mim Strom turns ruck coach after shoulder injury
In short:
Fremantle's All-Australian star Mim Strom has pitched in as a ruck coach to help her side defeat Richmond.
Strom came off the field in the first quarter of Fremantle's 25-point win after hurting her shoulder.
Elsewhere in the AFLW, Geelong comfortably defeated Essendon while Carlton downed Collingwood.
Injured AFLW powerhouse Mim Strom was forced to play ruck coach on the bench as the Dockers steamrolled a Monique Conti-less Richmond by 25 points on the road.
Two-time All-Australian ruck Strom was in agony at Princes Park after a tackle from Tigers midfielder Emelia Yassir in the first quarter of Sunday's clash.
Recruit Eden Zanker was first cab off the rank in the ruck, while Gabby O'Sullivan kicked three goals to help lift the Dockers to a 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) win in Indigenous Round.
Later on Sunday, Aishling Moloney finished with four goals as Geelong posted a 13.5 (83) to 7.9 (51) result to pile the misery on a winless Essendon at Kardinia Park.
Lisa Webb's Dockers (2-2) can finish the fourth week of the 12-fixture competition in the top eight, but are bracing to lose Strom for part of their finals push.
Before Sunday, Strom had played 78 consecutive matches since making her debut in 2020.
"She's been on the bench with a big smile, so she's hard to get a read on, but I'll get a medical update," coach Webb told Seven Plus at three-quarter time.
"She's been a ruck coach on the side. She's been a warrior for us, and we'll look after her."
Richmond, which, like Fremantle, has not reached finals since 2024, drop from sixth and could finish as low as 13th with a 2-2 record.
The Tigers are unsure of how serious Conti's injury is, with the 2023 league best-and-fairest managing Achilles soreness.
The five-time All-Australian midfielder was a late withdrawal alongside Fina Dethlefsen, with recruit Georgia Stubs and Kate Dempsey returning to the side.
Youngster Isabel Bacon (24 disposals, six clearances) led the game in Conti's absence, and Olivia Wolmarans kicked two goals.
The Dockers took the early advantage after three lead changes in the opening quarter, pipping the Tigers by five points thanks to a goal from O'Sullivan.
Strom's absence did little to sap Fremantle's momentum, with O'Sullivan piling on back-to-back goals as the hosts were kept scoreless in the second term.
It was much the same after half-time, with the Dockers maintaining a perfect record against the Tigers across four meetings since season six in 2022.
At Kardinia Park, scores were level at 1.1 (7) for much of the first quarter before Chantal Mason gave away a free kick for a high tackle on Maggie Johnstone in Essendon's forward-50.
Johnstone converted after the quarter-time siren for a six-point lead, but the Bombers' ascendancy did not last long after Moloney came to life.
The star Irishwoman kicked four of Geelong's six goals in the second term, while the visitors managed just two to trail by 18 points.
Geelong improved its record to 3-1 to tighten its grip on a top-four spot, leaving Essendon languishing in 16th.
Mikayla Bowen had a monster 40 disposals, while Cats star Georgie Prespakis matched older sister and Essendon veteran Maddy with 27 disposals and five clearances.

In the wake of the passing of Dolly Parton in August 2026, a story we previously debunked in December 2025 about Parton opening an animal sanctuary resurfaced. Parton's real acts of charity were well documented throughout her career, yet this false story still made the rounds.
This was a type of claim we refer to "glurge," a term originating in the 1990s that we've defined as "a sentimental or heart-rending story that undermines its own inspirational message by distorting — or ignoring — the facts."
Tales like the one about Parton's supposed animal shelter would indeed be inspiring ... if they were true.
These stories often recirculate when a celebrity makes real headlines for something unrelated — and the spread of generative artificial intelligence tools that can fabricate text and realistic images makes it harder than ever to sort through the noise and find the truth
We dug into the Snopes archives to collect 15 false stories about celebrities doing (fake) acts of kindness.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

US President Donald Trump has criticised what he described as an “unacceptable” imbalance involving the Canadian dollar and the United States, saying the situation has persisted for years but would no longer be tolerated.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote: “Canada’s (currency) Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable. It has been that way for years - but no longer!”
Trump did not provide further details in the post about what he meant by the “currency dollar imbalance” or outline any immediate policy measures.
The comments come amid continued tensions between Washington and Ottawa over trade tariffs. Trump has repeatedly raised concerns about the US trade relationship with Canada and has pushed for measures aimed at reducing what he considers unfair economic arrangements.
The Canadian dollar is closely tied to the US economy because the United States is Canada’s largest trading partner. Movements in the Canadian currency can be influenced by interest-rate differences, commodity prices, trade flows and economic expectations in both countries.

The high-end watch world has an understandable affection for Casio. You can easily rock an iconic, brightly colored F-91W in any meeting with a luxury brand, and you'll get nods of approval. It is, after all, the watch that has graced the wrists of Barack Obama and Napoleon Dynamite.
If not the F-91W, you'd be on similar safe ground sporting the famous “CasiOak” that many G-Shock fans love because of its more than passing resemblance to Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak, which was recently given a similarly affordable makeover by Swatch with the Royal Pop. First introduced in 2019, the wallet-friendly G-Shock GA-2100 earned the nickname largely because of its octagonal case shape, and it is considered by some the definition of attainable luxury.
Now, however, it appears Casio has something genuinely new for the G-Shock line. Leaked on Notebookcheck and Instagram, the upcoming GMC-2500 and GAC-2500 series echo the CasiOak's links to high-end brand AP with more than a passing resemblance to Patek Philippe's Nautilus thanks to prominent shoulders on either side of the case.
Casio did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.
In 1972, legendary watchmaker Gérald Genta suggested an angular stainless steel watch design to Audemars Piguet with a high-end movement inside that would, perversely, be more expensive than gold dress watches. The Royal Oak, and the idea of the luxury sports watch, was born. In 1976, Genta repeated the trick for AP's main competitor, Patek Philippe, to create the now equally famous Nautilus.
According to Notebookcheck, the GAC-2500 series is a resin analog lineup supposedly built from the DNA of the DW-5000C, the very first G-Shock made back in 1983. Stainless-steel versions will be labeled the GMC-2500 series. So far, nicknames like the “CasioNaut” and “CasioTilus” are already being thrown around on Instagram. The leaked four resin colorways in November are expected to be white, black, green, and yellow, and the price is estimated at 20,900 Japanese yen (about $134) each. The metal versions will supposedly retail for about $320.
Another striking aspect of the CasioNauts, one that helps the comparisons with Patek even further, is that the watches are fully analog, a rarity in a G-Shock. The brand has always had a digital display somewhere on its main ranges, just like the CasiOak does.
A two-eye dial layout means a small seconds subdial on the left and a date window on the right. A Shock Resist mark is on the tail of the seconds hand. These pieces apparently have Casio's Magnetic Holding Structure, so the hands aren't fixed to a shaft but are instead held magnetically in place. When the rugged watch takes a severe smack, the hands can absorb the impact and won't break.
The metal GMC-2500 dimensions are supposedly 46.7 x 43.8 x 12.9 mm (H x W x D), with the GAC-2500 a shade thinner at 46.7 x 44.5 x 12.7. It looks like the metal versions will offer a choice of colors, along with the bracelet or strap options. The rumored release date for all of the CasioNauts is November, so set your watch.
According to legend, the inspiration for the Nautilus shape was the portholes on transatlantic ocean liners, and the idea struck Genta while he was having dinner at a hotel. Genta supposedly saw Patek executives sitting in a corner on the opposite side of the restaurant. It took him just five minutes to sketch the watch that would later become an icon.
