The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.
After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May.
The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed.
The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing.
The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime.
“They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.”
Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’”
Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January.
At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.
Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent.
Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime.
The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’”
Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.”
Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before.
“My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

Argentina threatens to sanction oil projects around Falkland Islands
On Saturday, oilfield services firms including Schlumberger and Halliburton said they do not and will not work on projects near the islands
Argentina has announced that it will investigate and sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands without authorisation, after President Javier Milei said the “winds of change” favour his country’s claim to the archipelago.
Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, a British overseas territory that Argentines call Las Malvinas.
Argentina’s presidency said in a statement on Friday that it had ordered the opening of proceedings to “investigate and penalise” 45 entities “linked to the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons” around the Falklands.
The statement did not name the entities involved. According to Argentine media, they include British, US, Canadian, Israeli, Danish and Dutch companies.
On Saturday afternoon, oilfield services companies Schlumberger, Halliburton and Baker Hughes issued statements saying they do not and will not work on hydrocarbon projects near the islands.
Later, Milei shared a news item on social media reporting the statements, along with an acronym that translates to “everything is going according to plan”.
The Falklands are located about 600km (372 miles) east of Argentina’s southernmost tip and administered by Britain. The Falklands war in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentine government after 74 days of conflict that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops.

Prashanth Fertility launched ‘Prashanth Fertility at Home’, an initiative to provide select IVF-related support services at patients’ homes across Chennai.
The service is aimed at helping patients maintain continuity during fertility treatment, particularly those who may find it difficult to make frequent visits to the fertility centre because of work and other commitments.
Under the initiative, a dedicated team will provide services such as injection administration, eligible monitoring, follow-ups and treatment coordination at home, while patients continue to remain under the supervision of their treating fertility specialists.
A dedicated vehicle and team will operate across Chennai. Patients can schedule eligible services through the Prashanth Fertility app, which also allows them to manage appointments, follow-ups and treatment-related medical records.
Speaking at the launch, actor Khushbu Sundar, the chief guest, highlighted the stigma and emotional challenges associated with infertility and fertility treatment. She said couples often have to navigate not only the physical and financial demands of treatment, but also social expectations and questions around parenthood.
Samhitha Moturi, Director, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said fertility treatment involves multiple appointments, medication schedules, monitoring and follow-ups, and repeated travel to a fertility centre can be an additional challenge for couples. “The initiative has been conceived to take appropriate, clinically supervised aspects of care closer to the patient,” she said, adding that reducing practical barriers could help patients stay on track with treatment.
Geetha Haripriya, Chairman, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said the initiative was intended to make fertility care “more accessible, more personalised, and more connected to the patient”.
The service is currently available across Chennai. Patients can contact the 24x7 helpline 044-2888-2888 for details about eligibility and scheduling.

Three people have been taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries after an alleged axe attack in Victoria, with police still searching for the suspect.
The alleged attacker, who is known to the victims, came to an address in the Gippsland town of Tyers at about 12.30pm on Saturday, according to a spokesperson for Victoria police.
He is believed to have attacked an elderly man and woman, and a third person with an axe, causing serious injuries.
The man, who is in his 50s, fled the address and the victims were able to call emergency services for help, police said.
A specialist air ambulance and road paramedics were dispatched to the scene and all three victims were treated at the scene.
A spokesperson for Ambulance Victoria said a man in his 70s and a man in his 40s were transported to hospital in a critical condition.
A woman in her 70s was transported to hospital in a serious but stable condition, the spokesperson said.
The man is believed to have left the property on foot.
Victoria police launched a large-scale search for the man yesterday and were continuing to look for him on Sunday.
The man was last seen wearing a black and mustard coloured jacket and carrying a black backpack, police said.
Police warned he may be armed with an axe and handsaw.
Police urged anyone who sees the offender to not approach the man and immediately contact Triple Zero (000).

Iran accuses the US of targeting a tanker near Kharg Island, and other key Mideast developments
Iran has accused the U.S. of attacking an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf
Iran has accused the U.S. of attacking an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. The U.S. did not immediately comment, and there was no sign of retaliation. The past week saw the first exchange of fire after a month of relative calm.
Meanwhile, the U.S. ambassador to Israel has again condemned settler violence in the occupied West Bank. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels accused Yemen's government of killing three people in attacks. Israeli strikes killed three people in southern Lebanon.
Here’s a look at the news in the Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Iranian state TV said four U.S. missiles struck a tanker about six miles (10 kilometers) from Kharg Island, home to a terminal through which the country exports most of its oil. It said there were no casualties.
The report did not provide evidence and did not include comment from Iranian officials. U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Kharg Island been repeatedly targeted during the war, including U.S. strikes on military sites there in March. The latest report comes almost a week after the U.S. resumed strikes on Iranian targets following a monthlong pause, as fighting around the Strait of Hormuz has intensified.
The U.S. ambassador to Israel has again spoken out against Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, calling their behavior an “act of terror.”
Ambassador Mike Huckabee on Saturday referred to the settlers as “terrorists,” a word U.S. officials usually reserve for Palestinian militants. He was speaking to Palestinian American residents in the village of Turmus Ayya.
“If there are squatters that come in and put up their own flags and take possession of something that does not belong to them, if they burn a car, if they torch a mosque, if they go into someone’s home and vandalize it, paint graffiti on the walls, that’s a criminal act. But it extends beyond a criminal act. It’s an act of terror,” Huckabee said.
The ambassador last month spoke out sharply after weeks of unrest in the town of Qusra, where settlers surrounded several homes including one owned by a Palestinian American. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the actions of a “handful of rioters” and the foreign ministry called the settlers’ actions “a disgrace.”
Netanyahu’s government, the most ultranationalist and religious in Israel’s history, has presided over a surge of settlement construction in the West Bank. Most of the international community views settlements as illegal.
Iranian-backed Houthi rebels said government forces in western and southwestern Yemen killed at least three people. The attacks Friday in Hodeida and Taiz provinces came as Yemen’s military said it launched more than 15 airstrikes on the Houthis.
The Houthi authorities in Hodeida said a father and daughter were killed in an attack on their house in southern Jarahi district. In Taiz, shelling killed a man and wounded another, according to the Houthis’ al-Masirah satellite news channel.
Fighting has intensified recently along Yemen’s west coast near an important supply route.
Lebanon's health ministry said Israeli strikes killed three people and wounded nearly two dozen in southern Lebanon and the eastern Bekaa Valley.
Israel's army said it struck positions of the Hezbollah militant group late Friday in response to a drone launched toward Israeli forces in southern Lebanon. The drone was intercepted and no soldiers were injured, it said.
In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a U.S.-mediated framework deal under which Israeli forces are to withdraw from areas they occupy in southern Lebanon in exchange for disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah, but little progress has been made. Hezbollah has vehemently opposed the direct Lebanon-Israel talks.
The latest Israel-Hezbollah war began when Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel days after Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Israel invaded Lebanon and has since occupied a large swath of its south.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty on Saturday called for the U.S. and Iran to return to the negotiating table. The comments came in separate phone calls with the foreign ministers of Bahrain and of Oman, which sits across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran.
Abdelatty urged prioritizing de-escalation, the Egyptian ministry said, and called for maintaining the safety of shipping through the strait, where traffic remains at reduced levels as Iran continues to assert control over the waterway.

Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
His life as a writer and farmer was informed by a simple, clarifying idea: Forget tomorrow, and work toward what is good today.
Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk.
I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him.
The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post.
A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back.
When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “By Heart,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World, contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.”
He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since.
I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorrow” seemed to better describe the ethos of Berry’s longtime nemeses: coal-industry strip miners, big agribusiness, the global financial system.
It was also an odd choice for someone who seemed so concerned about the excesses of modern life. Berry struck me as someone who absolutely would fixate on the general worsening direction of things. Fretting about the future is a favorite preoccupation of the conscientious. Berry occasionally admitted to his own worried state of mind on the page, including in one of his best-known poems: “When despair for the world grows in me,” he wrote, “I wake in the night at the least sound / in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be.”
Nevertheless, in the part of his book that he asked me to read, he wrote, “Taking thought for the morrow is, fairly predictably, a waste of time.” He insisted that what we call “the future” is a flimsy and insubstantial thing at best—a phantom we obsess over that never really arrives, or never arrives in the way we imagine. “Most of the bad possibilities I have worried about have never happened,” Berry wrote. “By taking thought for the morrow we have invested, and wasted, a lot of effort in preparing for morrows that never came.”
Obsessing about the future, he argued, also has devastating moral consequences. It allows people to avoid engaging with the urgent realities of the present.
I don’t know whether Berry, given his extremely offline lifestyle, ever learned about doomscrolling—the way social media can serve as a collective orgy of dread. But he’s right that, when people become too obsessed with a future that may or may not befall them, they tend to turn their back on the moment they’re in. “The time is coming when it will be too late to save the world. Oh, oh, oh,” he wrote, lampooning the handwringer in so many of us. “If that is the way our minds are afflicted, we and our world are dead already. The present is going by and we are not in it.” As I see it, this was the core purpose of Berry’s work: He dared his readers to live in a way that honors the situation at hand, at this very second.
That mandate suffused everything he wrote about. He exhorted readers to enjoy the food on their plates, to bear witness to the places that surround them, and to revel in shared experience with the people in their orbit. Honoring the present was a joyful thing for Wendell Berry. It was also a form of rewarding but very difficult work. It meant slow, careful deliberation about the things he was willing to let into his life, whether that was a new piece of technology or a request from a journalist.
And it meant searching for ways to disentangle himself, by turns and sometimes painfully, from destructive systems. The moral goal of a human being, he often argued, should be to do less harm right now. When one of his most famous essays, 1987’s “Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer,” resulted in astonished and outraged letters from readers, Berry replied by writing, “I did not say that I proposed to end forthwith all my involvement in harmful technology, for I do not know how to do that. I said merely that I want to limit such involvement, and to a certain extent I do know how to do that.” This response boils down to a simple, radical worldview: We must seek to understand the harms caused by the systems we’re implicated in, then strive to become less reliant on them.
Berry was no purist. He understood that no 20th- or 21st-century American can live a wholly blameless life. He lamented needing to drive a truck, the unavoidable, occasional use of gas-powered equipment on his farm. He knew that his ancestors had enslaved their fellow human beings and that he, in direct and indirect ways, had benefited from that obscene bondage. “I am owned by the blood of all of them,” he wrote in an early poem, “My Great-Grandfather’s Slaves.” “We cannot be free of each other.”
Moral blamelessness isn’t possible. But Berry’s larger point was that people should strive for something better, here and now. As he put it in Our Only World, with his trademark aphoristic brilliance: “Maybe we could give up saving the world and start to live savingly in it.” This reframes Jesus’s “sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” as a simple, clarifying injunction: Forget the future, and work toward what is good today.
I did speak with Berry a second time. We talked a little while about the Sermon on the Mount, but I didn’t get him to agree to a formal interview. I could tell he wanted to help me, to be a sport. Still, I sensed something else nagging at him: the irresistible presence of the now. He was here, living on this Earth. He had land to tend to, animals to care for, a wife to love, books to write—more than 50 of them, by the end. Maybe someday, in some dimly glimpsed future, he would find some more time to talk with me. But right then, at that moment, there was just too much to do.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
"Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says.

You're probably wasting these keys on your keyboard — here's how to remap them
Put those dusty keys to much better use.
Most of the keys on your keyboard have an important purpose, but that's not the case for all of them. While the letters, numbers, most symbols and modifier keys like Shift are all vital, when was the last time you intentionally pressed a key like F7 or Scroll Lock? These keys are useless at best, and in some cases hitting the wrong one (like Caps Lock or Insert) can interrupt you and waste time.
In addition to disabling annoying keys, it's also easy to remap any key to another function. If you never type in all caps, changing the Caps Lock key to do something else justifies its prime real estate on the keyboard. Take some time to map your keys more sensibly, and the time you spend typing will become more efficient.
The best way to remap keyboard keys
There are a couple of ways to change what keys do on Windows. For most people, the best option is Keyboard Manager, one of the many tools inside Microsoft's free PowerToys suite. If you don't have PowerToys installed already, grab it from the Microsoft Store or GitHub.
Once it's open, select Keyboard Manager on the left sidebar and turn on the Enable Keyboard Manager slider. Next, click Remap a key to open a panel, followed by Add key remapping. Under Select, choose the key you want to overwrite by either clicking Select and typing it, or choosing it from the dropdown below this. Then, do the same under To send: to pick what the remapped key becomes.
For example, if you select Caps Lock on the left and Delete on the right, then pressing Caps Lock will have the same effect as the Delete key; it won't toggle caps anymore. You can repeat this process multiple times to remap different keys.
You have a few other options beyond single keys for the To send: section. Key combos work, allowing you to enter shortcuts like Ctrl + Shift + Esc to launch Task Manager. The dropdown menu also has controls like Help, Play/Pause Media and Start Mail that are easy to miss. Pick Disable from the top of the list to shut off a key without changing its function.
Alternatively, change the Send Key/Shortcut box to Send Text, and your remapped key will write the text you enter in the box below. While this can be helpful for common text like your email address or phone number, a text expansion utility like Beeftext or a clipboard manager like ClipClip are better productivity tools for entering these repeated snippets.
Finally, try the Remap a shortcut panel to change shortcuts in a given app or across the system. For instance, if you use Ctrl + P all the time but find it uncomfortable to reach, change it to Ctrl + Q.
Keys that are good nominees for remapping
Look down at your keyboard, and you'll probably recognize a handful of keys you barely use, which are the best candidates for remapping:
- Unless you need to type in all caps for your work, the Caps Lock key is something most people hit without realizing that results in having to fix a bunch of text later. I've set this to another Backspace key so it's easy to erase with either hand.
- The Insert key toggles between Insert and Overtype modes, but this isn't consistent across apps, and you probably prefer one or the other. I have this remapped to the Browser Search function, which also opens Windows search.
- The Scroll Lock key is only used to change what the arrow keys do in Excel. If you don't use it, try remapping it to something like Browser Favorites or Browser Home.
- Pause/Break does almost nothing aside from Win + Pause opening the About panel of Settings, so you can put it to better use.
- If you only use the Alt and Control keys on one side, the others are good remapping candidates.
- The F1 through F12 keys are of varying usefulness. Some are common (like F5 for refreshing a browser page), while others (like F9) are barely used.
What actions to remap depends on your workflows and keyboard. If yours doesn't have media keys, try remapping another key to Play/Pause for easy music control without having to buy a new keyboard.
PowerToys is a great solution for key remapping because it's simple and easily reversible (toggle the app off to remove all changes temporarily). If you close its background process, keys will go back to normal, so it's important to keep the app running at startup. It only affects your user account, and changes don't apply on the Windows login screen. Plus, PowerToys has tons of other great features and is a first-party tool.
SharpKeys does a similar job, but because it makes changes to the Registry, the key remaps affect everyone and aren't as easy to reverse. Utilities from top gaming keyboard manufacturers like Logitech and Razer are a good option for game-specific changes.

Every morning, many of us drink one or two cups of coffee and feel good, refreshed, and ready for the day. Some of us drink one or two more cups at work before lunchtime. Some use pure coffee while others add chicory to it. We prepare the powder using a filter, add milk and sugar, and take a swig.
While many Indians have a fondness for coffee, almost everyone in the U.S. and Europe drinks coffee, and more of it, every day.
Now, what are the effects of drinking coffee? How many cups per day? Should it be black coffee or can it include milk and sugar? And how does this affect our health? These are some questions that have been on our minds — and for which research has offered contradictory answers in the past. Fortunately, a new publication, titled ‘Caffeine and Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association’, may clear some doubts. The authors of the statement analysed several studies that examined the effects of caffeine, the active molecule in coffee that stimulates the brain and the central nervous system and encourages the body to produce and use more energy.
The statement reported that moderate caffeine intake, especially through coffee, may lower the risks of type-2 diabetes, stroke, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation. However, high doses, especially from energy drinks, may harm cardiovascular health, and unfiltered coffee can also raise LDL cholesterol levels.
Data from the Nurses Health Study at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Medical School and an analysis of 3 lakh people from the U.K. Biobank and Health Canada have indicated that drinking four cups a day may lower the risk of developing cancer, type-2 diabetes, heart diseases, and age-related disorders like dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. However, analyses also suggest that it would be prudent for pregnant and lactating women to limit their coffee intake to three cups a day.
Drinking hot black coffee is recommended, with little or no additives like sugar or milk. However, a group from Copenhagen, Denmark, pointed out in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Science in 2023 that adding milk to black coffee can be good as milk contains antioxidants, minerals, and vitamins and allays the bitter taste.
Chicory-blended coffee
Many people in South India prefer to have pure coffee, i.e. with no additives like chicory, which comes from a perennial herbal plant with coloured flowers. This herb contains no caffeine but a polysaccharide called inulin, which supports digestion and can help control blood sugar.
The benefits of a coffee and chicory blend and their implications for nutrition and health implications were discussed in a recent review paper by a group led by Pushpa S. Murthy at the Central Food Technology and Research Institute, Mysuru, published in the Journal of Food Science and Technology. Chicory contains several compounds that help protect the liver from inflammation, shield the stomach from damage, and may help defend against cancer. Adding chicory to coffee also improves coffee’s fragrance and taste.
The optimal blend of coffee and chicory was suggested to be 70:30 or 60:40, coffee to chicory, to strike a balance between taste and benefits. In fact, most coffee sellers across India have these ratios, unless of course a customer asks for ‘pure’ coffee. This writer himself used to prefer pure coffee until he read the review article by the Mysuru group!

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Maybe I just read too much science fiction, but xenotransplantation has got to be one of the coolest words out there (shout-out Octavia Butler’s “Xenogenesis” series).
Scroll down for the latest eye-popping update in pig-human technology.
Lindsay Clancy case exposes dangers of fragmented U.S. health system
Fragmented care is the norm for Americans with private health insurance. Unfortunately for Lindsay Clancy, that fragmentation made it difficult for providers to intervene as her mental condition deteriorated.
Clancy’s ongoing murder trial has laid bare the psychological challenges new mothers can face during the postpartum period and the inadequate resources available to them in a fragmented health care system. In the four months before killing her three children and attempting to kill herself, she received 13 medications across 30 different prescriptions. Five clinicians. Two hospitals.
Read more about the highly publicized trial from STAT’s Tara Bannow, including contentious exchanges between lawyers and Clancy’s doctors.
Can a transplant recipient get a human kidney after getting a pig kidney?
Yes. Or at least, two patients have.
Last night, eGenesis announced that two of its first recipients of genetically engineered pig kidneys have now successfully gotten organs from human donors. The biotech company is one of a handful racing to develop xenografts, as these interspecies transplants are called.
The whole project of putting pig kidneys in humans is motivated by the fact that there aren’t enough human organs for everyone who needs them. Many die waiting. But scientists weren’t sure if temporary replacement pig organs would cause someone to produce antibodies that could complicate a human-to-human transplant.
Early returns are promising, though not without hiccups. STAT’s Eric Boodman has the write-up, and the complications.
What does an EMT need? A healthy heart
EMTs, firefighters, Marine pilots, Navy SEALs, astronauts: These “tactical athletes” often do their job in unpredictable or even extreme conditions. Their well-being can mean life or death for the people they serve.
The biggest health risk that this group of roughly 4 million Americans faces while on the clock? Cardiovascular disease.
To address this risk, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association published new cardiovascular guidance for clinicians on Thursday. Many of the authors also helped develop similar guidance for competitive athletes.
One of the most unique features of these professions is that they must quickly transition from a high-alert state at rest to highly intense physical activity, while potentially being at risk of harm or death. Elizabeth Cooney has the full scoop on the new clinical guidelines for these “tactical athletes.”
ADA report on conference controversy is ‘confidential’
The American Diabetes Association has completed its internal review of members being ousted from its June conference (background here), but that doesn’t end the controversy. In a press release Tuesday, the ADA described its conclusions: The five violated a code of conduct for attendees and the New Orleans police were not called. (Off-duty officers were part of security.)
Steven Kahn, one of the five, asked CEO Charles Henderson for the report. “We feel it is only fair that we, just as you did, get to see its contents,” Kahn wrote in an email shown to STAT.
“I understand your interest in reviewing the full report,” Henderson wrote back. “The report is confidential and will not be shared.”
Kahn said this is at odds with a July promise to share the findings. ADA did not respond to a request for comment. This may turn on how to define “findings.” — Elizabeth Cooney
Disabled workers at greater risk of losing health insurance
Disabled workers are less likely to have health insurance through their employer, which means they are at greater risk of losing coverage once Medicaid work requirements kick in next year, according to a report published Wednesday.
The research paper, published by the Center for Economic and Policy Research, found that 57.9% of people with disabilities had employment-based health insurance coverage, compared with 70.6% of people without disabilities. These disabled workers were much more likely than their nondisabled counterparts to be on Medicaid, but many of them do not meet the required hours they will need to stay on the federal health insurance next year.
Read the report for more details.

A Tesla launch event tends to cause a hoopla. Fans crowd into an event space; loud electronic beats are the warm up act. Finally, the star himself, the ringmaster of this electric circus, CEO Elon Musk, emerges to a roar. There are demos, powerful verbs, and sometimes, a “one more thing,” a last-minute surprise product unveiling. Fans and investors the world over look on—and post—online.
But for the road debut of the Cybercab, the driverless car that Tesla promises is not only the future of the company but also the global economy, an event in Austin came with no livestream. Invitees, many of them online Tesla influencers, were reportedly barred from posting about the event until hours after it started. And Musk wasn’t there at all.
It was a somewhat peculiar start for the Cybercab, a matte gold two-seater first introduced in 2024. Now 45 of the vehicles, which do not have steering wheels or pedals, are registered to operate on Tesla’s robotaxi network in Texas. On Thursday night, after the news embargo lifted, the online influencers who attended the event began to post sanguine reviews and clips from their first Cybercab rides.
The Cybercab is a make-or-break vehicle for Tesla. Musk and other executives have argued that investors should no longer think of the world’s most valuable carmaker as a carmaker. “Really, we should be thought of as an AI robotics company,” the CEO said last year. “If somebody doesn’t believe Tesla is going to solve autonomy, I think they should not be an investor in the company.” Musk has said that hitting its marks in those areas would make Tesla not only the most valuable company in the world, but worth upwards of three times more than Nvidia, today’s market leader.
But hitting Wall Street-ready milestones hasn’t been easy for Tesla’s autonomous vehicle program, at least so far. Musk said in 2013 that Teslas would do 90 percent of their miles autonomously within three years; that didn’t happen. He said that 1 million Tesla autonomous vehicles would be on the road by 2020. (Today, 420 Tesla robotaxis are registered in Texas.) He said that the Robotaxi network would reach 50 percent of the US population by 2026. Now Tesla needs a robotics win.
Driving a Win
Tesla’s robotaxi network officially launched in Austin in June of last year, with a handful of Model Y electrics. At the time, those cars came with human safety monitors in the front passenger seats, ready to intervene if the technology made mistakes. Since then, Tesla says that it’s taken human monitors out of many of its cars. The service is now picking up riders in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida, and has permits to operate in Arizona and Nevada. A ride-hail service in California must have a human driver behind the wheel of each “robotaxi” because Tesla does not have permits to operate driverlessly there.
Tesla executives say it will win the self-driving race because the cars depend on just inexpensive cameras to operate, making them much cheaper than those from competitors including Waymo and Zoox. (Those companies also use more expensive radar and lidar setups.)
Right now, though, the automaker feels behind. Tesla AI software head Ashok Elluswamy announced at Thursday’s event that the company’s vehicles had collectively traveled 1 million miles without humans behind the wheel. Waymo, which now operates in 14 US metros, said it reached 1 million driverless passenger miles in January 2023.
Tesla’s Cybercab vision is ambitious and wide-ranging. It plans to not only deploy the driverless vehicles on an Uber-like network, but to sell cars without driving controls directly to customers—and before the end of 2026, Musk posted months ago. (This scheme would likely require several major changes to the law.) It also plans to offer entrepreneurial Tesla fans the opportunity to operate their own fleets of Cybercabs. An "interest form” posted on Tesla’s website today allows people to indicate whether they're interested in Cybercab fleet vehicle purchasing.
Open Questions
It’s not clear how the Cybercabs will legally operate in public. Federal safety rules require that vehicles come with steering wheels and brake pedals, and also the systems that power those human driver-centric systems. Last month, the government granted its first-ever exemption for a purpose-built autonomous vehicle for the Amazon subsidiary Zoox, whose box-like vehicles don’t have human driving controls. The US federal government said this summer that it intends to fast track new rules that will make it easier for autonomous vehicles without those features to deploy in great numbers. But those rules aren’t finalized yet.
A spokesperson for the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration told WIRED that Tesla has not filed an exemption request for the Cybercab. “NHTSA is in contact with Tesla and is evaluating the situation,” the spokesperson said. A Tesla executive has said that the company does not need to apply for an exemption.
And the Cybercab is just one part of Tesla’s projected future. Musk has said many times that the Optimus humanoid robot project “has the potential to be the biggest product of all time.” Eventually, he has projected, the robot will usher in an “age of abundance” that will render human labor moot. “The robots will actually make so many robots and AI that they will actually saturate all human needs,” Musk said earlier this year. “You won’t be able to even think of something to ask the robot for at a certain point. Like there would be such an abundance of goods and services.”
Questions remain about how exactly the robotaxi service works. Like other autonomous vehicle developers, Tesla says it has human remote operators ready to help or intervene if something goes wrong inside the car or on the road around it. Unlike other companies, Tesla allows remote operators to directly drive its cars from afar, at speeds up to 10 mph. These human operators have been involved in at least three minor robotaxi crashes, according to government data, including one in which a human drove an autonomous Model Y into a “hidden tree stump.” (Tesla reports that one has been hurt in these incidents.)
Still, Tesla executives seemed determined to have fun on Thursday, showing off the 22-inch screen in the center of the Cybercab’s console. If you don’t have to drive, why not watch TV? “You can choose to be entertained or choose to be productive,” engineering director Silvio Brugada told the crowd. “Anything you can possibly do as long as you have your seatbelt on.” The crowd didn’t quite roar, but it did “woo” suggestively.

India's GDP growth defies oil shock but stirs up controversy
- Published
"Doomsayers were doomed and India bloomed… Yet again," wrote Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on X, external, reacting to smart first quarter GDP data that came out earlier this week, widely beating forecasts, but also sparking a major controversy over its credibility.
On the face of it, the 7.8% number was a shot in the arm for the prime minister who's recently faced scathing student anger over his government's handling of exam paper leaks and rising youth unemployment.
While those longstanding concerns have not gone anywhere, the better-than-expected growth print suggests that his government may have deftly weathered the Middle East oil shock despite heavy dependencies on imported crude.
According to Sajjid Chinoy, chief India economist at JP Morgan, India's "cyclical growth recovery" had been visible for the past six months, driven by a huge fiscal stimulus, including direct tax cuts in February last year, a reduction of consumption taxes in September and interest rates which have come off by about 1.5% since early 2025.
"But the question was, could India insulate that recovery from events in the Middle East, and this is where the government deserves enormous credit," Mr Chinoy told India Today, external news channel, adding that the urgency with which Delhi diversified its energy imports in the face of the Hormuz blockade helped the country protect its growth.
What also helped Asia's third largest economy power ahead amid the disruption in global energy markets was a strong acceleration in exports and a surge in private corporate investments, which has long been a point of great concern for economists.
Exports grew by a sharp 12% despite tariff uncertainties on the back of strong global demand and a weak exchange rate. Economists reckon a 15% slump in the Indian rupee against the US dollar may have helped companies improve their competitiveness, driving up demand for Indian goods.
Corporate India, meanwhile, seems to be finally putting money into new buildings and factories. India's gross fixed capital formation, which serves as a core indicator of total domestic public and private investment rose, nearly 12% in the first three months of this year.
"Non-government data also points to the fact that investment intentions of companies have gone up in recent months, with announcements especially concentrated in industries like data centres, renewable energy and metals," Madan Sabnavis, chief economist with the state-run Bank of Baroda, told the BBC.
"Of course, private investment is not broad-based yet, but these are definitely signs of a pick up."
While the robust numbers pushed several private brokerages to revise their full year growth forecasts upwards, they also stirred up a roaring debate online and a war of words between politicians.
Opposition leaders like Jairam Ramesh , externalcalled the numbers "statistical gymnastics", accusing the government of repeatedly tweaking methodology to conceal what he said was "India's dire economic reality".
A former finance secretary also raised serious doubts, saying the GDP got a pop because it was calculated on the basis of newly revised numbers and a lower base for the same period last year - a view the government strongly rebuffed, external, saying revisions are a part and parcel of GDP calculations.
The government's view was supported by the World Bank's executive director for the country, Neelkanth Mishra, who said the new GDP series "cleaned up the data and also significantly improved the methodology", enhancing the credibility of the estimates.
But beyond the statistical minutiae, others like the former central bank governor Raghuram Rajan questioned why if the growth indeed was so rapid was India not creating more jobs or attracting more foreign direct investment.
To make matters worse, the stock markets also largely shrugged off the positive news.
The debate has muddied the picture for authorities who will have hoped the numbers would help them counter growing criticism about the uneven nature of India's growth trajectory.
There are also other more mundane reasons why it might be too early to celebrate a growth bump.
For starters, government spending is expected to ease off in the coming months as the compulsions to meet deficit targets get stronger. The impact of the goods and services tax cuts on spurring consumption is also soon likely to peter out, according to HSBC.
Moreover a sub-par monsoon and El Niño-like weather conditions have taken a toll on India's agrarian rural economy, which supports livelihoods for half of the country. As of 27 August, cumulative rainfall stood at 13% below the long-period average.
This will pose "clear risks to agriculture, rural demand and food inflation [even though] India appears better prepared than in past episodes", CareEdge, a rating agency, said in a note.
Sugar and onion prices have already spiked across the country, forcing the government to run special trains to cities to meet demand. India's retail inflation, meanwhile, hit a 15-month high of 3.9% in May and further rises are expected, with some economists predicting the rate will hit the upper band of the central bank's comfort level amid a weak monsoon.
Given the high-growth and high-inflation scenario, most brokerages are pencilling in a hike in borrowing costs. This, coupled with expectations of lower global growth (and hence lower demand for Indian exports), higher costs of inputs and energy because of volatile geopolitics could all mean this growth bonanza - credible or not - may well be nearing its peak.

My toddler son wasn't sure what to make of the situation.
We'd just finished touring Costa Rica's Manuel Antonio National Park, and were strolling through the adjacent village of Naranjito. He had his trusty stuffed toy, Grover, in tow. It wasn't long before a group of local children spotted it and approached him.
"Elmo, Elmo," they gleefully shouted. My boy first looked confused, then beamed.
"It's not Elmo, it's Grover," he exuberantly explained.
A friendly conversation all about "Sesame Street" characters ensued. His dad and I watched the bilingual interaction, both bemused and proud.
Fast forward more than 15 years. Our then-3-year-old is now a nimble, independent young man attending college nearly 2,000 miles from home.
I'm firmly convinced that our early family travels helped shape the confident person he's become.
My son took his first trip at 8 months old
That Costa Rica adventure wasn't the first time we took our son overseas. He's had a passport since he was an infant, and it was first stamped when he was 8 months old. Friends and family thought we were crazy, but we couldn't imagine leaving him behind.
Honestly, that initial jaunt was a bit of a nightmare. Our little guy got sick on the transatlantic flight, and we went through an entire pack of diapers plus several sets of clothes to keep him and the folks around us as comfortable as possible given the circumstances.
When we arrived at our destination, we sent out our laundry and immediately hit the drug store for electrolytes and extra rash cream; thankfully, his symptoms resolved quickly. We washed his bottles in our suite sink, he tried new foods (including mushy peas at a London pub!), and peacefully napped in his stroller while we were on the go.
That first trip helped set the tone for my infant son's continued resiliency. During subsequent adventures, he saw firsthand the inevitable curveballs travel can bring. From flight delays and language barriers to ATM snafus and navigation challenges, he's come to understand that how you respond to what you can control tends to make or break most situations.
Traveling at a young age has cognitive, social, and emotional benefits
Travel taught him to adapt, and it's a skill that continues to serve him well. But he also learned so much more.
Children are naturally curious, and seeing different corners of the world was the perfect way to channel our son's inquisitiveness.
As he encountered each new place and learned about its customs, religions, and language, his mind opened. Our kid asked questions, made observations, and started to connect cultural dots between his everyday experiences and those of the people he met. He'd try to say "please" and "thank you" in the foreign language of the place we visited.
We could see him soaking up as much of the environment as he could, which nurtured a love of learning he retains today.
Every time he interacted with a new person, he learned how to see past his own background and truly consider others. He built empathy for others, deepening his emotional intelligence. Each journey lifted his confidence, boosted his brain, and made him a more compassionate person.
He's now a self-assured adult
Bringing our son along with us during our globetrotting meant he could experience travel's unexpected twists, but knew everything would be OK because his mom and dad were right there with him.
Now that our son is away at college, he moves through the world with a quiet maturity, knowing he can handle whatever comes up. He's become friends with classmates from around the world. He constantly, confidently explores his new hometown's many nooks, crannies, and neighborhoods. And he's recently started traveling internationally, all on his own. I couldn't be prouder.
It wasn't always easy for us to travel with a little guy, but prioritizing travel (and yes, budgeting for it) was one of the best parenting decisions we made.
Sure, there were occasional tantrums and minor mishaps when we hopped time zones or skipped routines. But the older our son got, the more he could roll with those proverbial punches with ease.
His assuredness was forged with every journey, and that's a benefit I know will continue to pay dividends for him.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

A team of astronomers discovered a strange polygonal atmospheric structure on Saturn near the planet’s south pole. This 10-sided shape, known as a decagon, joins one of the gas giant’s most famous features: a hexagon near the north pole that was first observed 44 years ago. Images of the new decagon were captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, and the discovery was recently published in the journal Science Advances.
The formations at both the north and south poles aren’t solid structures, like a wall or a rock formation. Saturn doesn’t even have a defined solid surface like Earth’s crust. If you were to descend through the atmosphere of the ringed planet, the pressure and density would progressively increase, but you would never reach a “ground” on which to land. Instead, what astronomers have witnessed are patterns formed by clouds, albeit very unusual ones.
Each side of the decagon measures approximately 16,800 kilometers, which is a few thousand miles longer than the diameter of Earth. Near the feature is a jet stream reaching speeds of 116 meters per second, or nearly 260 miles per hour. By way of comparison, a Category 5 hurricane—the most intense storm level possible on Earth—is defined by winds above 157 miles per hour. Interestingly, although the jet stream circulates at tremendous speed, the decagon pattern shifts at a mere 2.5 meters per second—less than 6 miles per hour.
The south pole feature appears to have formed recently. For decades, scientists have been searching for a counterpart to the famous northern hexagon. However, major missions that observed the planet have previously not been able to find an equivalent, long-lasting structure in the south. The search was further complicated because, due to Saturn’s tilt, its southern hemisphere was not clearly visible from Earth for many years.
The first clues of the decagon came from ground-based observations, some by amateur astronomers. As the images accumulated, it became evident that something strange was happening in Saturn’s southern cloud bands. Data from the Hubble Space Telescope made it possible to trace the pattern back to images taken in 2023. Monitoring continued, and by 2025 its 10 vertices had become much more clearly defined, confirming the presence of a new polygonal feature in the ringed planet’s atmosphere. Science, however, hasn’t settled on an explanation for how these structures came to be.
Various hypotheses have been proposed since the discovery of the north polar hexagon. One is that the polygons are the visible manifestations of enormous atmospheric waves confined by powerful jet streams. You can think of these as similar to ocean waves, which are not simply objects traveling across the ocean but rather disturbances propagating through the water.
A wave’s behavior changes depending on the space in which it moves and the boundaries it encounters. On Saturn, waves of atmospheric gases may be encountering jet streams that confine them, in a sense, like the edge of a beach. Except in this case, the “beach” wraps all the way around the planet.
Various other factors, such as Saturn’s rapid rotation, exact wind speeds, and variations in the currents, could all contribute to the distinct geometries of the shapes. A current that coils around the planet six times can form a hexagon; one that does so 10 times, a decagon. This is one of the more likely explanations for how an atmosphere without any solid structure can end up forming something that looks like a gigantic polygon, but there are still many unanswered questions.
We don’t know how deep these geometric figures extend, how long the new decagon might last, whether its appearance is related to Saturn’s seasons, and—most importantly—what sparked its formation in the first place. Researchers hope to find some answers by tracking the decagon’s evolution. To do so, they plan to continue observations with the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes and use more advanced atmospheric models to reconstruct possible conditions that could give rise to such a structure.

The sky was still ink black where we were in South Africa. My son Ben and I grabbed our flashlights, lighting our way along the walking path to the main building at the lodge where we were staying, ready for our last game drive with ranger Dion and tracker Bongi. 
We were nervous after hearing a lion roaring outside our window the night before. We were watching for the little thief monkeys along the path who loved to jump out and scare us, hoping we might drop any food we carried. We were giggling and excited and happy, just plain happy.
We were, for the first time in our lives, adults together. And children together. Equals together. Because for the first time in our lives, I was a passenger on an adventure with my adult son.
I've been in charge for so long
Back in our real lives at home, I have always been the decider. The planner of parties, the organizer of road trips and weeks at the cottage, and the one who gives out birthday reminders. Back in our real lives, I am a single mother of four sons who has never handed the reins over to anyone. Back in our real lives, Ben is 30, now a husband. He is a man with his own life. He is trying to make his own plans. He has bills to pay. He is, I am just now realizing, my son in peripheral. I wanted to get to know this man. I wanted time with this man. To look him in the eye, to hear him.
And so, when I had the chance to go on a luxury safari thanks to my job, organized completely by a tour company, something in me released. An exhale. I could let them drive the car for our trip and just hop in the backseat with Ben. If someone else planned the flights, the packing list, the hotels, and all the other details, we could talk. Just the two of us. We could think about what snacks we want to eat, a constant conversation between us since forever.
I was able to learn a lot on this trip
Ben is braver than me. From our first game drive after arriving at our bush lodge, where we stayed in a two-bedroom villa bigger than our first home when he was a baby, Ben was surefooted.
We saw a family of rhinos on our game drive. A herd of curious elephants sidled up to the jeep, so comfortable and relaxed. A cheetah eating a recently killed impala. On our drive back in the evening, a female lion passed us on the road and looked us dead in the eye. I nearly had a heart attack. My son was steady, calming me down. A solid presence in the seat beside me. A shadow of the father he might become someday, on full display in the African wild. And I got to see it first hand.
Ben is friendly. And charming. He and our ranger Dion became friends on this trip. The same age, the same good smiles, the same open-hearted love of nature, bonding them fast and sweet. I watched him chat with fellow travelers, with the bartender, with Dion and Bongi when we had our sundowner cocktails out in the bush. After watching him struggle with shyness and anxiety as a boy, it felt like a miracle to see him now. A confident man.
More on multigenerational travel
If I had planned this trip, I would have been focused on the outcome. I would not have had the bandwidth to just sit by the bonfire with Ben at the end of the day, watching the local watering hole for hippos and giraffes, quiet in ourselves. I would not have been able to fall into bed with that particular giddy sleepover feeling I remembered from being a little girl. Because that was what this trip felt like. Some mom somewhere arranged a sleepover safari for Ben and me for a week. And we just packed our little bags and went off together.
Ben felt it too. As we left the bush for the airport, bumping along the back roads for our final ride in the jeep, the impala were leaping alongside us. He got a little choked up, told me, "I never thought I'd see anything like this."
I looked him full in his grown-up face, stubbly and happy and grown, and thought, "me neither."

This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
The $70 Xteink X3 puts Silicon Valley to shame.
No matter how you read it, The Power Broker is a serious undertaking. The paperback weighs as much as a brick; to avoid lugging around all 1,344 pages, people have cut it apart at the spine and chunked it into sections. Others have organized in-person Power Broker marathon readings that run continuously for three full days. I decided to try something else.
Over the past several weeks, I’ve spent 10 hours paging through Robert Caro’s masterpiece on an e-reader the size of a credit card. It’s magnetic, and small enough to attach to the back of my iPhone without adding any real bulk to my pocket. (Yes, this does mean that I have a screen on the back of another screen.) It’s called the Xteink X3, and at a glance, it looks like a cheap gimmick: more electronic junk made by unknown brands and sold on Temu and TikTok Shop—the kind of thing influencers are always hawking. (Can I interest you in a programmable LED hat for $11.60? Or how about $20 AirPod look-alikes made by “Fhumsh”?)
In a sense, it is that. Xteink sounds less like a real brand name than the kind of garbled text you’ll find in AI-slop memes. (Speaking of which, the official website of the China-based company is full of AI-generated photos of people posing with the device.) And indeed, since the X3’s release on Amazon in May, TikTokers and YouTubers have raved about how the device is a steal and you should buy it right now—just click the link in bio.
And so I did. On Amazon, the X3 is $69 and tops the “hot new releases” list for e-readers, beating out a slew of Kindles. In person, the Xteink is many things: plasticky. Flawed. Finicky. Nevertheless, it is the single best piece of technology that I have purchased in years. In the two months before getting this cartoonishly tiny e-reader, I finished only one book. In one month with the X3, I read three books without even really trying—and my iPhone’s average daily screen time dipped by 25 minutes.
The X3 is great because of its size, not in spite of it. (For once, “fun-size” actually lives up to the billing.) Because this is such a runt of a device, you can stick it to your phone and have an e-reader in your pocket at all times. As a result, I’ve found myself reading on my morning commute, in line at a museum, even while waiting through Netflix ads. The display on my Xteink may be roughly half the size of the smallest Kindle, but the text is big enough to easily read. Even after three straight hours of inching through The Power Broker, my eyes weren’t strained.
The device’s size actually helped me develop a different relationship to reading altogether: Because each “page” on the Xteink amounts to just a paragraph or two—and sometimes less—I’m compelled to finish it. And now that I’m onto the next page, I might as well finish that one too. A YouTuber who recently reviewed the Xteink had the same experience—she referred to the uniquely addictive experience of using the device as the “TikTokification of reading.” I know how terrifying that sounds, but consider the outcome: Whenever there’s even a couple of minutes of free time, I now have a healthy alternative to doomscrolling on Instagram. I don’t even have to put my phone down. Flip over the Bad Screen and fire up the Good Screen.
For all of its charm, the Xteink is a pretty basic piece of hardware. For $70, you get what you pay for. Other popular e-readers now come with AI-powered recaps, high-definition displays, and Android operating systems. Meanwhile, the Xteink has no touch screen, color display, or backlight for reading in the dark. (Xteink recently launched the X4 Pro, a slightly larger and more expensive model that has a reading light and a touch screen.) Just reading a book on the device isn’t necessarily seamless: The preloaded software is horrific and can’t even display book covers or properly format some text. Unlike with a Kindle, you can’t port over books from Amazon with one click.
In spite of itself, the Xteink X3, in all of its 3.7 inches of glory, has become a viral hit. Online, people have posted photos of their Xteink on trips to the Austrian mountains or the Aegean Sea; one anesthesiologist says he tucks it into his scrubs. People are mounting the Xteink X3 to their kitchen hood to display recipes and are making all sorts of bespoke accessories, including 3-D-printed reading lights and a case that looks like a gun (I’m serious). Fans have built their own open-source firmware, Crosspoint, that considerably upgrades the device. The version I downloaded displays reading stats and an array of fonts, and it lets me screenshot pages as I read. Late last month, Crosspoint added the ability to access books on Libby, the popular library ebook app.
The best thing about the Xteink is not any one feature. It’s that this tiny e-reader is fun in a way so few gadgets are anymore. Despite all our advances, the consumer-electronics landscape of 2026 is predictable and banal. Our laptops, smartphones, and tablets are thinner and more powerful than ever, but that feels like a weak substitute for innovation. Next week, Apple is poised to launch one of its most hyped products in years: a folding iPhone. But even folding smartphones are old news; Samsung released its version in 2019. After shelling out hundreds or thousands of dollars for a new gadget, you might still have to pay for subscriptions and endure annoying ads. Sometimes, your purchases aren’t even really yours. Amazon recently removed the ability to download ebooks you already own and transfer them to non-Kindle devices.
In other words, we need more gadgets like the Xteink: cheap, simple, and customizable. With few exceptions, these products are now coming out of China. Neck fans from brands such as JisuLife and Civpower have become sensations for helping people endure the summer heat. Anker’s portable projectors and earbuds are both Wirecutter-recommended. Silicon Valley has left a gaping hole in the gadgets markets, and Americans are more than willing to look elsewhere.
