Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway
- Published
The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced.
Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII.
The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89.
Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state.
Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral.
Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital.
At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals.
The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress.
Among the tributes to King Harald was an emotional televised speech by his son King Haakon, who said: "Thank you for being such a good dad."
Harald had been seen as a down to earth "people's king" who had helped to modernise the monarchy, broken with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure.
His son said he represented the values of a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".
King Charles's message praised his cousin King Harald for serving his people with "unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility".
King Haakon assumes his role at a difficult time, with the Norwegian royal family facing scandals this year.
His wife, Queen Mette-Marit, came under scrutiny when it was revealed she had maintained a three-year friendship with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.
Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.
While Prince William will be in Norway, King Charles has returned to Scotland, after meeting President Macron of France at the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London this week.
The King will be hosting Andy Burnham at Balmoral this weekend, in the traditional annual visit of the prime minister to stay with the monarch.

Hunt 'not afraid of anyone' after 100m second-place finish
- Published
Amy Hunt says she is "on the up" and "not afraid of anyone" after finishing second in the 100m at the Diamond League final in Brussels.
The 24-year-old Briton finished in 11.06 seconds, behind Jamaica's Tina Clayton who won in 10.93, just one day after a third-placed finish in the 200m.
Hunt's performance surpassed American Olympic silver medallist Sha'Carri Richardson, who came third in 11.07.
It continues Hunt's fine late season form after winning four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month.
"I am 24 and on the up and up and up. I am not afraid of the other girls," said Hunt.
"I have so much love and respect for them and they are absolute icons but I love the challenge of going head to head with them.
"It takes me back to younger days racing boys in the school playground."
Hunt is planning to compete in the 100m and 200m again at the inaugural Ultimate Championships event in Budapest, which begins on 11 September.
"To come away with two podiums is no mean feat, and I am the only athlete to double up in the sprints and I came away with a second and a third," added Hunt.
Fellow Briton Georgia Hunter Bell came fourth in the 1500m despite being among the pre-race favourites.
Hunter Bell has won three international titles this year, including the world indoor 1500m, Commonwealth Games 800m and European 1500m, but never looked like threatening the top three in Brussels.
Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska came first with a time of three minutes 54.05 seconds, with Kenya's Dorcus Ewoi second and Australia's Jessica Hull third.
Hunter Bell said her performance was a result of a "long hard season", with the 32-year-old having competed in 19 races this year.
"I have done three championships so I am starting to feel it in my body," said Hunter Bell.
"I am struggling a little bit, even mentally to get my adrenaline up again week in, week out, but I am really lucky to be racing and to be happy and healthy.
"I just have to regroup before the Ultimate Championships next week, but I have to be happy with my consistency this season."
Elsewhere, Switzerland's Audrey Werro won the women's 800m final but was pushed all the way by Dutch athlete Femke Broeders-Bol.
With British Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson missing through injury, Werro hung on during the final straight with Broeders-Bol at her heels.
Werro, who has set the third, fourth and fifth fastest 800m times in history this year, finished in 1:54.75, which was 0.06secs in front of Broeders-Bol.
Brazil's Alison dos Santos and America's Masai Russell, who set world records in the men's 400m hurdles and women's 100m hurdles last week respectively, repeated their victories in Brussels but could not better the times they set in Zurich.

Germany plans anti-sabotage shield after airport drone attack
A national ‘cyberdome’ would be established, with a network of digital sensors to detect and intercept attempted hacking attacks
Germany is planning a broad package of measures to strengthen its defences against drone attacks, cyber intrusions and other forms of Russian sabotage after a failed airport drone attack last month, an interior ministry spokesperson said on Sunday.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper, which first reported the plans, that Russia’s hybrid attacks had become a part of daily reality.
“These attacks will increase, but we can defend and protect ourselves,” Dobrindt was quoted as saying.
Russia has long rejected allegations it is carrying out operations in western Europe and has denied involvement in the German airport attack, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov saying the accusations were “the start of a real war”, according to state news agency TASS.
According to the ministry spokesperson, police mobile drone defence capabilities would be expanded under the plan, with rapidly deployable counter-drone units stationed in cities to protect the airspace above critical transport hubs and government districts.

A video (here & here) claiming to show the bodies of victims who died in the Nepal flash floods on 26 August 2026, is circulating widely on social media. Let’s examine the veracity of this claim.
Claim: Video showing the deceased victims during the flash floods that struck Nepal on 26 August 2026.
Fact: This video is unrelated to the Nepal floods. It is a staged video shot for entertainment purpose by an Instagram creator. The Nepal floods occurred on 26 August 2026, but this video was uploaded on 03 August 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is misleading.
A reverse image search of the keyframes from the viral video revealed that the same video (archive) was uploaded to Instagram on 03 August 2026 by a content creator named Simran SK. This confirms that the video has no connection to the Nepal floods, as it was uploaded well before the actual disaster took place.
A closer review of Simran SK’s Instagram account indicates a pattern of uploading comedy and scripted videos. We also found other scripted videos (archive) on the account featuring individuals pretending to be dead. Furthermore, during the Assam floods in July 2026, another scripted video from this very account was falsely circulated as a real incident. Our previous fact-check article regarding that instance can be read here.
To sum it up, a scripted video is being falsely shared as genuine footage of deceased victims from the 2026 Nepal floods.

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.
A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.
The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.
The People’s Insurance Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish its capital.
The initiative could help bolster state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.
The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.
“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.
The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corp and its subsidiaries.
The two lenders said the proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans on state banks to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

Manipur: 2 banned UKNA cadres killed, 2 injured in Churachandpur
Two UKNA cadres were killed and two injured in a joint Assam Rifles-Army operation in Manipur’s Churachandpur district, with arms and ammunition recovered.
Two cadres of the banned United Kuki National Army (UKNA) were killed and two others injured during an operation in Manipur’s Churachandpur district, officials said, adding that arms and ammunition were recovered from their camp.
The Assam Rifles and the Indian Army launched a joint operation based on specific intelligence input on August 29 in Phaibong village, Henglep sub-division, Churachandpur district. The forces established surveillance over a UKNA camp and commenced tactical operations at 5 am on September 2.
The UKNA cadres opened fire on the security forces at around 5.30 am. The security forces retaliated, leading to a heavy exchange of gunfire.
Assam Rifles on its X official account stated as “Intel confirms 2 UKNA cadres neutralised and 2 injured. Search of the camp yielded 2 MA Rifles (5.56 mm), 1 AK-56 Rifle (7.62 mm), 1 Lathode Gun (40 mm), 7 Lathod Grenades, 15 AK Magazines, 371 AK-56 rounds, 601 MA Rifle rounds, 172 SLR rounds, 15 combat uniforms, 7 ammunition pouches, 5 backpacks, 3 combat bags and 5 pairs of jungle shoes. Operations continue in surrounding jungles.”
Manipur Home Minister Govindas Konthoujam Singh had informed the Manipur Legislative Assembly that the banned UKNA outfit was found to be involved in the Tronglaobi IED bomb attack that killed two minors while they were sleeping.
According to statements by the Manipur Police and security agencies, the arrested UKNA cadre, identified as S Palal Kuki, had admitted that he was serving as the self-styled finance head/finance secretary of the banned outfit.
The violence in Manipur, which began on May 3, 2023, has claimed 306 lives, while 49 people are still missing..

Part of the Kennedy Center’s ceiling collapses – sparking calls to allow Trump’s renovations
‘President Trump has been right: America’s cultural center needs to close, renovate, and be restored—now,’ the Kennedy Center said in a statement
A piece of the Kennedy Center’s ceiling collapsed, sparking renewed calls to allow President Donald Trump’s renovations at the historic performing arts center to go forward.
The damage occurred in the building’s Grand Foyer following heavy rainfall in the nation’s capital, the center said in a statement on Saturday. No one was injured.
Photos show the room’s red carpet coated in debris as well as a large, round hole in the white ceiling.
The Kennedy Center described the issue as “another warning we can’t ignore,” adding that “decades of deferred maintenance made this inevitable.”
“President Trump has been right: America’s cultural center needs to close, renovate, and be restored—now,” the organization added.
The center’s board is currently locked in a long-running legal battle over its plan to shutter the venue for two years while it undergoes $250 million in renovations — and to add Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade.
The center — whose board is dominated by Trump loyalists and chaired by the president himself — says the overhaul will include repairs to plumbing and electrical systems, along with new seating and carpeting.
Administration officials have warned the institution could face “financial ruin” unless Trump’s name is added.
However, confidential documents acquired by the Washington Post last month suggested the Kennedy Center had gone into financial meltdown since Trump’s involvement began and he put his name on the front of the building.
Meanwhile, employees have questioned the need for a two-year shutdown, noting the center has previously completed repairs while remaining open and continuing to host performances, according to The Washington Post. One unnamed staffer described the move as a “self-inflicted crisis.” Meanwhile, Democrats have denounced Trump’s effort to attach his name to the venue as a vanity project.
After the ceiling collapse, the main building closed briefly on Friday and was expected to reopen Saturday, per WUSA9. The Grand Foyer will remain off limits to visitors through the weekend.
Roma Daravi, vice president of public relations, told the outlet the incident highlights the need for repair work.
“Another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed,” Daravi said. “There's no justification for further delays in restoring America's cultural center.”
Trump’s appointees originally voted to rename the building – a living memorial to the assassinated President John F. Kennedy – as “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts.” A judge ordered Trump to remove his own name.
However, the center is now planning to add his name in a different context by putting the phrase “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” directly under Kennedy’s name.
Beyond the Kennedy Center, Trump has pursued an array of building and restoration projects across the capital. Since returning to office, he has broken ground on a massive White House ballroom and advanced plans for a 250-foot triumphal arch, among other initiatives.

The deadliest ever Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now claimed the lives of more than 3,000 people, according to the latest official toll released on Wednesday.
The epidemic, which has hit the conflict-hit east and northeast of the country, has caused 3,007 deaths and infected 6,186 people, the Congolese National Institute of Public Health said.
The fatality rate is 48.6%. A total of 1,409 people have been reported to have recovered, it added.
Ebola, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and causes haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa in the last 50 years.
The worst outbreak previously recorded in DR Congo left nearly 2,300 people dead from 3,500 reported cases between 2018 and 2020.
The current outbreak originated in the remote northeastern province of Ituri and is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or treatment.
The virus has spread to six provinces and is ravaging areas where the presence of the Congolese state is weak and insecurity is widespread due to the presence of armed groups.
The health response lacks sufficient resources and has been overwhelmed by the surge in cases, while there has been widespread mistrust in parts of the community.
Several treatments and vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo strain. Approved vaccines are only effective against the Zaire strain, which is responsible for the largest-known Ebola outbreak to date.
The World Health Organization has in the meantime recommended the implementation of a phase three clinical trial using the Ervebo vaccine deployed against the Zaire strain.
WHO experts are still unclear as to whether Ervebo protects humans against Bundigbugyo but initial data suggests that it could offer a degree of protection.
A batch of 16,250 doses for use by frontline medical personnel arrived in DR Congo at the end of last month and vaccination began shortly afterwards in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province in the northeast.

Uttam Kumar Ghosh, Officer-in-Charge of Rajbari Sadar Police Station, confirmed that there was no religious angle to the incident. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several Bangladeshi media reports covering the incident and featuring the same visuals (here, here, here, here). Based on these reports, we learned that the woman seen in the viral video is Zakia Sultana, a woman entrepreneur who runs a clothing business called ‘Astha Poshak Shilpa’ at Kaderia Market in Rajbari. The incident reportedly stemmed from a business dispute between Zakia and her former employee, Shahana Parveen Brishti.
According to Zakia, Brishti left her shop without settling the accounts and later started her own business. Zakia alleged that Brishti, along with several others, went to her shop and threatened her. She further claimed that she was assaulted while she was at the market seeking a resolution to the dispute. However, reports quoting traders and other local sources said that the dispute arose after Brishti left Zakia’s shop and started her own business in the same market.
Rajbari Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Uttam Kumar Ghosh said the incident was related to a business dispute. He said police reached the spot after receiving information, rescued Zakia from the situation, and took her to the police station for her safety. The viral video shows her being attacked by several men while police officers are present.
We also contacted Uttam Kumar Ghosh, Officer-in-Charge of Rajbari Sadar Police Station, over a WhatsApp call. He confirmed that there was no religious angle to the incident. According to Ghosh, the victim, Zakia Sultana, is Muslim, and three individuals accused in connection with the incident are all Muslims and have been arrested.
To sum up, this video does not show a Hindu teacher being beaten up by Muslims in Bangladesh.

Whatever happened to the U.S. campaign to ban child marriage?
Our team of global health reporters has covered child marriage –- when one partner is under age 18. The United Nations calls it a "human rights violation," citing a litany of concerns for child brides: "early pregnancy and social isolation, interrupting her schooling, limiting her opportunities for career and vocational advancement and placing her at risk of domestic violence." Yet every year, the U.N. estimates that 12 million girls become child brides.
Child grooms, the U.N. further notes, may be forced into "an adult role for which they are unprepared," with pressure to drop out of school and support a family.
The U.N. has set the goal of ending child marriage by the year 2030.
This year there are new efforts to make child marriage illegal — a bill introduced by U.S. legislators in July and a resolution adopted by the U.N. General Assembly on September 4 establishes November 27 as the International Day to End Child, Early and Forced Marriage. As part of our "Whatever happened to …" series, we asked contributor Kamala Thiagarajan to examine the ongoing effort to end this practice.
Over the next week, we'll be looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
Nations around the world are seeking to meet the U.N. goal of ending child marriage by 2030.
Since 2021, countries as diverse as Sierra Leone, England, the Philippines and the Dominican Republic have been passing legislation to set the marriage age at 18, with no exceptions.
In the United States, the current push for a national law is controversial — some have criticized provisions in the proposed legislation, and others oppose it altogether.
And legislation is not necessarily the solution. In India, marriage under age 18 is illegal, yet the latest National Family Health Survey conducted in country found that one in five women ages 20 to 24 married before turning 18. UNICEF estimates that at least 1.5 million girls under the age of 18 are married in India each year.
The U.S. effort
On July 16, U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin and Sens. Dick Durbin, Brian Schatz and Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Child Marriage Prevention Act, a federal bill aimed at combating child marriage.
This legislation would push states toward a nationwide minimum marriage age of 18. "In 34 states, including Wisconsin, child marriage is legal. Many of these marriages are between young girls and adult men. It's time we end this predatory practice," Moore said in a statement emailed to NPR. "I know that advocates have pushed for reform at the state level, which has led some states to change their laws. This federal legislation would help bolster and support those efforts, including helping states get the data to understand its prevalence in their jurisdictions and then take action to address it."
In announcing the bill, its four congressional cosponsors cited data showing that more than 314,000 minors were legally married in the United States between 2000 and 2021, including girls as young as 10. The figures, compiled by child-marriage advocacy groups from state marriage records, indicate that most of the underage girls were married to adult men.
Unchained At Last, a nonprofit worked to end forced and child marriage in the U.S., estimates that at least 66,415 of these marriages — about one in five — occurred when the bride was at an age when sexual relations would be considered a crime (the age varies from 14 to 18 depending on the state). In roughly 90% of that subset, according to the organization's founder, Fraidy Reiss, marital exemptions in state statutory-rape laws shielded the adult spouse from prosecution. Married minors may also face legal barriers to hiring an attorney, filing for divorce or obtaining protection from abuse.
The Tahirih Justice Center, an organization with a long history of advocating for survivors of forced and child marriage, has been a key partner in developing and supporting this legislation.
"The one thing we hear all the time from places — Cameroon, Guatemala, you name it — is: 'It makes my work harder when a politician can say to my face, the United States allows child marriage, so why should I do anything?' The best thing that we can do to help the global movement is to get our house in order," says Casey Carter Swegman, director of public policy at Tahirih.
Swegman says that a child's apparent consent does not necessarily mean that the decision to marry was made freely. "A 15-, 16- or 17-year-old who has been pressured and coached by family members may tell a judge that she consents because refusing could expose her to punishment or violence at home," she says. This is especially troubling, Swegman says, when pregnancy, potential evidence of sexual abuse, is treated as justification for allowing the marriage to proceed.
"A child is coming before your court pregnant by an adult person — that should be a red flag for statutory rape, not a green light for marriage," she says.
Although the proposed bill has won support from many child-marriage advocates, others have questioned whether its provisions go far enough and warn of possible unintended consequences that it has overlooked.
"If I could heart a provision of this bill, it would be [the proposal] to provide financial incentive to states that have banned child marriage — that I can get behind," says Reiss. "While I applaud Congress for introducing and considering legislation to combat child marriage at the federal level, I am appalled that two sections of the Child Marriage Prevention Act would make a mockery of the bill's title."
Section 6, she says, would provide federal grants to states to "study" child marriage instead of banning it. "If states are given money to examine something that's a human rights violation instead of banning it outright, it would be devastating," says Reiss, who says she was forced to marry at age 19.
Section 10 would allow some minors as young as 16, whether in the United States or abroad, to qualify for a U.S. spousal visa under certain circumstances. This would actually encourage a particularly heinous form of child marriage, says Reiss: the trafficking of minors to the U.S. under the guise of marriage, and it would discourage U.S. states from setting their marriage age at 18, no exceptions. "If the bill were amended to set the spousal visa age at 18, it would be a 'game-changer' by sending a clear message to states and halting legal trafficking," she says.
And there is opposition to the very idea of the bill. In some states, Oklahoma and Missouri, for instance, Republican lawmakers have opposed state bans on child marriage, arguing that such restrictions constitute government overreach and interfere with parental authority.
In 2024, in an interview with the Missouri Independent, Republican state Rep. Dean Van Schoiack called a proposed ban "government intrusion in people's lives." Asked what would be lost if 16- and 17-year-olds could no longer marry, he replied, "Liberties that people currently have."
How the U.S. bill compares to other global efforts
As Congress prepares to debate the U.S. bill this fall, other countries have already adopted more sweeping national restrictions. The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2024 in Sierra Leone sets 18 as the minimum age of marriage without any exceptions for parental consent, religious marriage or pregnancy. Section 15 declares that any child marriage contracted after the Act took effect to be void. The legislation even penalizes people who facilitate or attend a child marriage.
In November 2024, Columbia, where 23% of girls are married before they're 18, passed a law banning such marriages outright. In a similar move, on Sept. 25, 2025, Bolivia banned child marriage without exceptions, removing provisions allowing 16- and 17-year-olds to marry with parental consent or judicial approval.
But laws are not always a solution. In many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and in India, there are national laws banning child marriage but weak enforcement often limits their effectiveness.
"In countries like India, child marriage persists despite strong laws due to deeply ingrained cultural factors, making solutions very complex," says Renu Singh, executive director of Young Lives India, a research program that studies how poverty and inequality shape children's lives as they grow into adulthood.
The Young Lives study began in 2002, in India, Ethiopia, Peru and Vietnam.
In India, Young Lives has followed 3,000 children in the southern Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — from childhood into their late 20s. Researchers have repeatedly interviewed them and their families about education, health, employment, marriage, fertility, household circumstances and personal aspirations. They found that many of the children they'd followed married early.
Working with India's National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, they analyzed 2011 Census data to map child marriage at the state and district levels. That research reported 12.1 million marriages involving people below India's respective legal marriage ages (21 for boys and 18 for girls) and identified hotspots that could help the government target interventions.
"We found that there were so many varied and complex reasons driving these marriages," says Singh. "It wasn't just low-income groups who got their children married off." Some parents, she says, who were deeply concerned about the safety of an unmarried daughter, saw marriage as a security net. Young Lives found that girls with older brothers were more at risk of being married early because of the social custom of giving dowries — when the bride's family gifts the bridegroom's family money at the time of marriage. In a household with a boy and a girl, the girl was married especially early, so that her older brother could get married too.
"Boys were often married off early as well, especially if the family wanted to get dowries for their sons to offset the financial losses they faced when they gave their own daughters away in marriage. And this was the case across all income groups," says Singh.
India's national law has helped establish that child marriage is unacceptable and punishable, Singh says — but lasting change also requires communities to stop accepting and supporting the widespread practice.
NPR has reported on how this practice unfolds in India: "Our parents just hold the weddings in secret," a 16-year-old told our correspondent. "At night - very rushed." Our story continues: "She was married when she was 9 years old. A bunch of other girls nod. They were all married around that age, too. A shy girl in a pink T-shirt says she didn't even understand what was happening at the time."
For legislation to be effective, Singh says, parents, relatives, religious leaders and others must no longer regard an early marriage as normal, protective or beneficial for a girl.
"The U.S. also has major issues with deeply entrenched gender roles, with patriarchy, with extreme — I would say almost obsession over the control of female sexuality. These are the [reasons] the social pressure for this practice continue," says Swegman. In addition to a national law, it's clear that attitudes must change too. "This requires belief and behavior change, services, support, thoughtful conversations on the community level," says Swegman.
The campaign for stronger laws in the United States is a part of a growing international effort to move child marriage higher up the global political agenda.
One of the key figures behind the U.N. resolution declaring a day "to end child, early and forced marriage" is Bhuwan Ribhu, a lawyer and the founder of Just Rights for Children, a child rights network. Just Rights for Children has filed 60 Public Interest Litigations in India that would reframe child marriage as child rape, securing legal protections for the young women.
"Establishing an official International Day to End Child, Early and Forced Marriage gives us an annual platform to hold governments accountable and enforce laws that protect children. Now is the time to build on this commitment and end child marriage by 2030. Today, the world has spoken in one voice: the crime of child marriage must end," Rhibu says.
Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times, The British Medical Journal, the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

- An August 2026 U.S. Department of Health and Human Services report claimed that "watchdog analyses tracking" had determined more than 5,500 minors had undergone "sex change surgeries" from 2019 to 2023.
- The "watchdog analyses tracking" references an anti-LGBTQ+ group that inflated the data by counting a vast number of procedures entirely unrelated to "sex change surgeries," including hair removal, surgical removal of excess eyelid skin and bladder drainage. These procedures were counted in the "sex change surgery" statistic as long as the patient had a gender dysphoria diagnosis or a psychiatric condition related to crossdressing (which is different from being trans). As with any other person's healthcare, there are many reasons why a trans person may need these procedures that have nothing to do with being trans.
- Credible data indicates that gender-affirming surgeries are rarely performed on minors, and most minors who receive them are not actually trans, but cisgender boys getting chest reductions. A peer-reviewed study from Harvard University researchers in 2024 determined that in 2019, only 85 trans minors received gender-affirming surgery and most of them were age 15 to 17. The Harvard study found no gender-affirming surgeries conducted on children under 12.
In August 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services under U.S. President Donald Trump released a report alleging that according to "watchdog analyses tracking," more than 5,500 minors had undergone "sex change surgeries" from 2019 to 2023.
Here's what Page 9 of the report says (emphasis ours):
Watchdog analyses tracking billed charges for minors from 2019 onward estimate almost $120 million in total hospital and clinic billings nationwide, encompassing over 5,500 surgical procedures and 8,500 courses of hormones or blockers. 
(14) 
(14) "What We Found," Stop the Harm Database, accessed March 12, 2026, https://stoptheharmdatabase.com/about/. ($119,791,202 in total submitted charges; 5,747 minors had sex change surgeries; 8,579 minors received hormones and puberty blockers).
Social media users across Facebook repeated the supposed statistic and cited the report, including Republican U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger, a pharmacist from Tennessee (screenshot). Similar posts included a video of Adm. Brian Christine, assistant secretary for health at HHS, who claimed that there were more than "5,500 sex-rejecting procedures" performed on minors (screenshot). Snopes readers searched the website to investigate the legitimacy of this statistic.
The HHS report pulled this number from a database of supposed surgeries created by Do No Harm, an advocacy group that opposes gender-affirming care for trans minors and diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in medicine. The Southern Poverty Law Center, a civil rights organization that tracks extremist organizations, has designated Do No Harm as an anti-LGBTQ+ hate group.
Do No Harm's methodology report lists insurance codes — standardized codes insurance companies use to describe various health care procedures and treatments — that the organization used to come up with the statistic. However, a Snopes review of the report found that many of these codes are entirely unrelated to "sex change surgeries," thus contradicting Do No Harm's claims.
Furthermore, both a peer-reviewed study from Harvard University researchers and a Reuters analysis found far lower rates of gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors. In truth, for minors, these surgeries are exceedingly rare and occur only among older teenagers.
As such, we have rated this claim as false.
A spokesperson for Do No Harm, Caroline Anderegg, said in an email that answers to our questions could be found on Do No Harm's methodology page and report. Anderegg did not return a follow-up inquiry noting that the methodology report and page did not answer our questions about what insurance database the group used and how the group filtered the insurance codes to ensure the data included only "sex change surgeries."
Methodology doesn't hold up to scrutiny
Do No Harm's website for its "Stop the Harm Database" claimed that between 2019 and 2023, "5,747 minors had sex change surgeries."
However, its methodology report said Do No Harm included insurance procedure codes for treatments that do not change a person's sex, including electrolysis for hair removal, bladder drainage, "removal of excessive skin of upper eyelid" and more (pages 17 through 20). These procedures are also not necessarily for gender-affirming care more broadly and can happen for many different reasons.
Do No Harm said it included these procedure codes only when connected to a patient with a gender dysphoria diagnosis or transvestic disorder, a psychiatric condition where a patient experiences clinically significant distress or impairment due to sexual arousal while crossdressing (Page 17).
However, a gender dysphoria code merely indicates that the patient is transgender, not that the procedure was done specifically to alleviate gender dysphoria, said Kellen Baker, senior adviser for health policy at the Movement Advancement Project, a nonprofit think tank known for tracking LGBTQ-related laws and policies.
"I really cannot underscore to you how irregular the Do No Harm analysis is," 
There are many reasons why a trans patient might receive any number of these procedures that are unrelated to being trans. For example, a trans child could have a urine obstruction and need bladder drainage, or require excess skin removal for droopy eyelids impairing their ability to function.
Furthermore, some of the codes, such as codes for intersex surgery, are used for intersex people, not transgender people. Intersex people are born with a variety of different sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary ideas of male or female bodies. Intersex infants and children in the United States sometimes receive surgeries, either for medical necessity or, more controversially, to align their bodies with more "typical" traits.
Baker also pointed out that Do No Harm claims to use "an all-payer claims database" — a database with every open and shut insurance case — but 
Gender-affirming surgeries rarely performed on minors
There are very few studies on the number of gender-affirming surgeries done on minors, largely because the surgeries themselves are so rare, Baker said.
However, Harvard researchers published a peer-reviewed study in 2024 that analyzed 2019 insurance claim data and found no incidences of a child under 12 receiving a gender-affirming surgery.
Out of a total of about 22 million minors sampled, the study found only 85 instances of a minor undergoing a gender-affirming surgical procedure in 2019, with 82 of those instances involving chest-related procedures, presumably either a chest reduction or breast tissue removal, commonly known as top surgery. The vast majority of those instances involved teenagers ages 15 to 17.
The study also found that far more cisgender boys — those who align with their gender assigned at birth — received gender-affirming chest reductions than transgender boys. Cisgender boys often receive these chest reductions because of gynecomastia, or physically harmless enlarged chest tissue that can affect their self-esteem and mental health.
Snopes reached out to the Harvard researchers involved in the study for their thoughts on the Do No Harm database and did not immediately hear back.
In 2022, Reuters, a credible news source, analyzed data from Komodo Health — considered the most complete health insurance database available — and found 238 mastectomies, or top surgeries, in 2019, 256 in 2020 and 282 in 2021 among trans minors. The analysis also found 56 genital surgeries among patients ages 13 to 17 with a prior gender dysphoria diagnosis from 2019 to 2021.
However, the Reuters analysis did not appear to separate out trans youth who received these surgeries due to health issues unrelated to gender identity, unlike the peer-reviewed study from Harvard researchers.
Furthermore, any increase in gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors has likely reversed due to the rise in anti-trans health care policies across the country and on the federal level, Baker said.
The bottom line
The data HHS cited in its report comes from an anti-LGBTQ+ group that used faulty analysis to inflate data on gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors.
It's more accurate to say that from 2019 to 2023, more than 5,500 minors, many of whom had a gender dysphoria diagnosis at one point in time, received various procedures for any number of medical reasons, the vast majority of which were unrelated to being trans.
Peer-reviewed research suggests that gender-affirming surgeries among minors are incredibly rare and usually involve cisgender boys undergoing chest reductions.

Valley Vita Agro (OPC) Private Limited inaugurated its new city office at Hyderpora, Srinagar, with the company positioning the facility as a hub for technology-driven horticulture and modern orchard management in Kashmir.
Located near 14th Avenue, Hyderpora, the office will cater to farmers, orchard developers and horticulture entrepreneurs seeking access to high-density apple orchard technology, planting material, farm machinery and orchard-management services.
The inauguration was attended by Managing Director Muzamil Jabar and special guest Mohd Jabar Dar, besides farmers, business associates and other guests.
AI-enabled spraying technology unveiled a key highlight of the launch was the introduction of an AI-enabled spraying system for orchards. According to the company, the technology is designed to improve the precision and efficiency of spraying operations, reduce dependence on manual labour, minimise wastage and lower operational costs for growers.
The company said the technology is aimed at addressing some of the challenges confronting Kashmir’s fruit industry, including rising labour costs and the increasing need for precision and efficiency in modern orchard management.
The new Hyderpora office is intended to provide growers with a single point of access to orchard planning, nutrition and crop-protection guidance, technical support and mechanisation services.
Valley Vita Agro primarily focuses on high-density apple orchard development and supplies planting material, imported apple rootstocks and orchard systems to growers transitioning from traditional cultivation practices.
Speaking at the event, Managing Director Muzamil Jabar said technology and high-density plantation systems would play an important role in the future of Kashmir’s horticulture.
“The future of Kashmir’s horticulture is not only high-density — it is intelligent, precise and technology-driven,” he said.
Jabar said the new office would help bring artificial intelligence, mechanisation and technical expertise closer to growers across the Valley.

A four-storey paying guest accommodation collapsed near Delhi University's South Campus in South Delhi, resulting in the deaths of three people. Rescue teams from the National Disaster Response Force and Delhi Fire Service are racing against time to clear heavy debris and collapsed roofs using cranes, JCB machines, and heavy cutters. Officials noted that the debris clearance could take several more hours. Heavy deployment of Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel is managing crowds in the student area. The incident has also triggered political reactions, with leaders from the Bharatiya Janata Party and Congress visiting the collapse site alongside student organisations.
Rescue operations led by the Delhi Fire Service and the National Disaster Response Force are underway following a major collapse where the roof fell from a height of five storeys. Officials stated that the complete roof collapse broke into heavy chunks of debris, initially blocking entrance roads before being cleared for aid and assistance. Teams face difficulties as the large concrete chunks must be broken down before JCB machines can remove them from the site. Operations are expected to take several more hours as authorities work through the rubble.
In an interview with India Today, Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) Chairman Siddhesh Kadam discussed the environmental impact of data centers, loudspeaker regulations during festivals, and incidents of violence against healthcare workers. Addressing concerns over upcoming data centers in residential areas, Kadam stated that MPCB is collaborating with IIT Mumbai to formulate a comprehensive policy and operating guidelines regarding siting criteria, buffer zones, water sourcing, energy usage, heat generation, and noise control. On the use of high-decibel DJ systems and loudspeakers during festival seasons, Kadam urged citizens to avoid western sound systems and return to traditional cultural practices such as Puneri Dhol, Nashik Dhol, and Koli brass bands. He remarked, "We should celebrate these festivals in our own traditional way, rather than adopting the Western cultures of having these loudspeakers, laser lights and the DJ system." Furthermore, Kadam condemned assaults on medical personnel, asserting that no individual may take the law into their hands and all offenders will face legal action.
Dramatic visuals from south-west Delhi’s Satya Niketan show locals desperately trying to rescue a man trapped beneath the debris of a collapsed five-storey building, using their bare hands and whatever tools they could find. Two people have died and nine have been rescued so far as the search and rescue operation continues at the site. A sudden tremor-like shake sent residents rushing out of nearby buildings on Sunday, only to find the student accommodation building, Hostel Daze, reduced to a heap of rubble. Locals immediately began clearing concrete slabs in a frantic search for those trapped inside. The building, located in the densely packed area near Delhi University’s South Campus, had around 15 rooms, with two to three students reportedly staying in each. Two NDRF teams comprising around 70 personnel are currently engaged in the rescue operation, using canines, cutting equipment and other technical tools. The teams are working alongside the Delhi Fire Service, Delhi Police and local residents.
Addressing the student tragedy in Delhi, the speaker stressed that it is time for rescue operations rather than political blame games. Noting that three students were evacuated while an estimated 25 to 26 remained affected, the speaker pointed out delays in the arrival of police and ambulances. The speaker questioned civic bodies including the MCD and NDMC over alleged corruption, negligence, and lack of safety norms for student accommodations. Citing past incidents in Saket and Satya Niketan, the speaker demanded accountability from authorities and called for scrutiny into the role of the local MLA regarding paying guest operations in the area.

Tottenham picked up its first point of the season with a 0-0 draw at Nottingham Forest, and Newcastle remains unbeaten under new coach Matthias Jaissle thanks to a late equalizer from Jacob Ramsey in a 2-2 draw with Bournemouth.
Crystal Palace twice came back against Fulham to eventually win 3-2 at Craven Cottage for its first points of the campaign while Brighton drew 1-1 with Leeds .Brentford and Sunderland also drew 1-1.
Newcastle rallied from 2-0 down to rescue a point at St. James’ Park after Ramsey came off the bench and struck late to salvage a draw with Bournemouth.
Ramsey fired home from inside the box in the 88th to spark wild celebrations from Newcastle fans.
Bournemouth led through Marcus Tavernier’s goal in the ninth minute and went 2-0 ahead when Malick Thiaw deflected the ball into his own net in the 35th.
Harvey Barnes responded two minutes later with a brilliant solo goal by cutting in from the left and curling the ball into the top corner.
Newcastle looked to be heading for its first defeat of the season until Ramsey lashed low past Bournemouth goalkeeper Djordje Petrovic.
It was the third time this season Bournemouth squandered a lead late in games. The Cherries conceded in stoppage time against Manchester City — after allowing a late equalizer — and Everton in their opening two games of the campaign.
Big spending Tottenham got its first point of the season, but it is still without a league goal despite revamping its attack in the transfer window.
Summer signings Omar Marmoush and Savio were both blunted at the City Ground, while on-loan Mykhailo Mudryk also failed to find a breakthrough after coming on to make his debut.
“The problem is the last third, not because we have not the quality. We have great players,” said Spurs coach Roberto De Zerbi. “We have to be better in the last decision, to keep calm when we are in the last third and take the best decision.”
Forest thought it had found the winner through Neco Williams, but the goal was ruled out by VAR because of a handball.
It’s been a difficult start for new Fulham coach Alvaro Arbeloa after three straight league losses.
The former Real Madrid coach might have thought he was set for a first win after his team led 1-0 through Josh King and then 2-1 through Cesar Palacios.
Palace had other ideas, with Tyrick Mitchell twice equalizing and Ben Chilwell scoring the winner in the 77th.
Sunderland secured a late draw at Brentford through Enzo Le Fee’s penalty in the 82nd. Leeds was looking for a third straight win and led Brighton 1-0 thanks to Jayden Bogle until Luka Vuskovic leveled in the 71st.

How to track prices with Safari's Notify Me tool on iPhone, iPad and Mac
Get an update every time a price drops or a product comes back in stock.
One of the features in Apple's iOS 27 update that you may have missed is Safari's new Notify Me tool. Designed for things like product restocks and price drops, it can send you a notification when it detects a particular change on any website.
As well as the iPhone, Notify Me is available in iPadOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, too. It works directly inside Safari, so there's no need to install any third-party apps or browser extensions. It also isn't limited to product changes or price fluctuations, allowing you to use it for things like concert ticket availability, tour dates, news stories on a particular topic or anything else you can imagine.
Tell the tool, using a simple description, what you want it to watch for and choose how often you'd like it to check the page. Notify Me should be able to handle the rest without you lifting a finger.
How to set up Notify Me
Setting it up is easy. Tap or click the three horizontal lines on the left side of Safari's address bar. Select Notify Me and a pop-up will appear, asking you to describe the changes you want it to monitor.
This could be something like:
- "If the price drops below $100"
- "The gray and blue option comes back in stock"
- "The stick of RAM falls under $500"
After that, select the blue edit button to set the exact time it polls for changes and whether you'd like it to check in hourly, daily, weekly or monthly intervals. Once the blue checkmark appears in the upper right, you can confirm the Notify Me alert.
If you haven't set up notifications for Safari, you'll be prompted to do so. Since the feature runs on the device, not in the cloud, make sure you're setting it up on the device where you'll most likely see the alert. If you have an iPhone that always travels with you, it would make sense to set it up on that.
What if you want to delete it or make changes? You can do so by visiting the same page and selecting Edit in the banner at the top. Alternatively, go to Settings > Safari and scroll down to Notify Me near the bottom.

A horror story of sorts is unfolding in the United States. It goes like this: AI has made it so effortless to access information, and short-form video has made it so easy to entertain ourselves, that nobody reads anymore.
It shouldn’t feel impossible to finish a book
Screens have atrophied our reading muscles. Here’s how to get them back.
If you’re familiar with this tale, it’s possible, ironically, that you read about it. A viral Atlantic story from earlier this summer put a chilling headline on trend: “The End of Reading Is Here.” Teachers and professors, the magazine reported, don’t even bother assigning entire books to their students, because excerpts are good enough to prepare for standardized texts. The piece said we’re living in a “postliterate era.”
This is a cultural crisis, yes — but for a lot of us, it’s a personal one. We’re all short on time, and we’d like to read more, but the ascendancy of attention-stealing tech companies has made it feel like we have less of it.
“Reading was and is a crime of opportunity,” said Leah Price, a professor of modern book history at Oxford and the author of What We Talk About When We Talk About Books. “The limiting factor isn’t reading matter, but reading time.”
Key takeaways
- Reading is changing, not dying. The bigger problem is competition for people’s time and attention.
- Print offers productive difficulty. E-readers and audiobooks make reading easier, but the friction of print promotes deeper comprehension.
- Leisure reading should be fun! It’s totally fine to peek at the ending, skip boring parts, or just give up on boring books.
Losing the reading habit is especially bad because it’s a healthy practice in a world obsessed with self-improvement. Studies suggest that reading is an astonishingly good mental exercise, as well as a very accessible one. Reading, especially leisure reading, can improve your language skills. It exposes you to new knowledge and ideas. Reading can help relieve stress, anxiety, and insomnia. It can make you more empathetic and combat cognitive decline. Reading is absolutely great for kids. Reading, perhaps above all, also happens to be fun.
There are, I’m happy to say, some bright spots in this story — and some helpful news.
There’s evidence that reading isn’t over. It’s just changing. A 2025 Pew study found that the number of Americans who say they read books has remained roughly the same in recent years, although the way that they read them is changing. The vast majority of books read in the United States are print, but a growing number of people are reading e-books and listening to audiobooks. The number of print books sold is actually growing on the backs of the science fiction and self-help genres. The number of e-books and audiobooks borrowed from their local libraries, meanwhile, topped 820 million last year, a new record. There’s no shortage of books to read. And it’s never been easier to access any book you want in your preferred format.
The other bit of good news is useful to you: Reading is like a muscle. Even if you feel like your ability to pore over a book has atrophied, that muscle is still there, ready for exercise. The more you do read, the more your vocabulary improves, the more you learn, and the more you’re able to put new information in context. In other words, the more you read, the better you get at it. And probably as a result, the less appealing algorithmic feeds become.
It’s one of those personal habits that extends beyond your own life, too. Becoming a better reader is good for American society. The nation’s founders believed that an informed citizenry was necessary to preserve democracy — and to prevent tyranny. A nation of people passively flipping through 10-second videos on a smartphone or bedrotting with a streaming show can be informed in a sense. You might want to be a better American.
The big question, then, is: How does one become a better reader in an era that increasingly appears to be postliterate? Actually, there are some interesting insights — and ironically, some technology — that can help.
Reduce friction
One thing that keeps a lot of people from reading is simply friction. Reading can be hard — or at least effortful — for a lot of different reasons.
For me, I hit friction every time I pick up all 1,300 dense pages of The Power Broker by Robert Caro. It’s the weight of a doorstop in my hands, as I struggle with the context of mid-century New York bureaucratic history, ultimately unsure if I’ll live long enough to reach the end of the book. Reading is full of friction, and finding ways to reduce friction is one way to read better.
Technology is good at this. Just take the growth in e-book popularity as proof. Whereas people over 65 have historically read more than young people, more than 40 percent of young people have read an e-book in the past year, according to an April Pew study. You can’t blame them. Once you get used to the lack of pages and paper, e-readers are incredibly convenient. The classic Kindle Paperwhite is more portable than a doorstop, and you can keep an entire library on something the size of a side plate. It’s even waterproof, or at least more waterproof than paper. More advanced devices, like the Kobo Libre Colour, offer color e-ink displays and the ability to scribble on the page.
What turned me into a Kindle enthusiast is the existence of Libby, an app that lets you check out e-books from your local library. From the comfort of the New York City subway, I can find, borrow, and download just about any book I’d ever want and start reading it in a matter of seconds. You might call this a frictionless experience. The raw simplicity of the device also means that I can’t easily navigate away from the book to check my email or start doomscrolling.
Audiobooks open up another avenue: the ability to read a book while doing something else, like chores or driving. You might disagree on whether listening to an audiobook counts as “reading,” but there’s evidence that people can comprehend and retain information from audiobooks equally as well as they can from printed material. Audiobooks can even make difficult language more accessible for more readers.
There are drawbacks, too. Audiobooks force you to listen at the speed of the narrator, although you can probably speed it up or slow it down in increments. And it’s difficult to go back and review the text or to skip ahead, which is also true for e-books. This spatial component of reading is something that printed books will always have going for them. Rereading text can improve comprehension, and the spatial nature of books makes it easier to find certain passages. Just think about that effortless feeling of flipping back toward the beginning of a book for that really juicy section. That’s not easy to do on a Kindle or with an e-book.
There’s an interesting paradox here: In order to become a better reader, you need to reduce enough friction that you read more. But you also need to preserve certain kinds of friction that help you fully appreciate what you’re reading.
Embrace useful friction
There’s a good reason your teachers and professors assigned hard books when you were in school. “Learning only happens when there is some cognitive friction, if you’re actually grappling with the ideas,” said Daniel Willingham, a psychology professor at the University of Virginia.
Reading difficult text, scribbling notes in the margins, rereading the difficult text, taking breaks to think about it — this friction-full process leads to deeper comprehension. Certain inconveniences that come with reading print books, including turning physical pages and navigating the spatial elements of the object, invite you to do the mental work that promotes learning. Screens, with their lack of friction, may actually make it harder to comprehend what you’re reading.
The advantage of print is small but meaningful. A 2018 meta-analysis of nearly two decades’ worth of studies showed that paper-based reading had a slight advantage to screen-based reading when it came to comprehension, especially when dealing with informational texts, rather than narratives. Another meta-analysis published a year later suggested that readers were more efficient when reading on paper and, interestingly, seemed to have a more accurate awareness of how well they understood the text. In other words, when you read on your phone, you might think you’re absorbing more than you actually are.
There are other drawbacks to reading on screens. Scrolling alone is bad for comprehension, according to yet another meta-analysis, because it basically forces us to lose our place on the page. There’s also been research into how reading on screens demands more of our cognitive resources than reading on paper, perhaps because the technology requires the reader to process more information, leaving them with a little less gas in the tank to actually comprehend the text. But again, plenty of studies show that the difference in how well we comprehend information by reading on screens versus print is small.
What’s perhaps more meaningful are the vibes we bring when we approach a medium. We’ve been trained to read on screens a certain way, according to Naomi Baron, a professor emerita of linguistics at American University. From the early days of Google, screens became places where we searched and scanned for information, quickly clicking through to the next page in pursuit of an answer. That’s a far cry from the millennia-old tradition of poring over printed manuscripts.
“We got used to thinking a digital device is that which one doesn’t concentrate on,” Baron said. “One keeps moving like a shark. … Print is a medium that encourages stopping.”
It turns out two things can be true. Indeed, keeping a smartphone next to you while you’re trying to read a book is an invitation to distraction. You may also feel like your attention span is already shredded, probably thanks to your smartphone. You just have to be more intentional about your attention and harness your focus. Taking breaks can help restore your attention stamina, especially if you do so in nature. Try reading a book for a few minutes every day, and you’ll soon find that you can read for longer. The next thing you know, you’ll have read a book.
Let’s not lose the plot here
Some people read to learn. Others read because their job demands it. The luckiest of us read for fun. Some people read to escape or to imagine. And depending on your purpose, you might choose a different approach or device to stuff that text into your brain.
If you’re simply trying to become a better reader, it doesn’t matter how you do it.
You should keep reading, again, because reading more makes you better at reading. If you’re trying to learn, printed books can facilitate that, but you can also learn quite a bit by listening to an audiobook. If a Kindle and a library card can unlock all the hard sci-fi and fantasy your eyes could ever consume, go for it and enjoy.
Part of what keeps some people from reading, I have to imagine, is the preconception that reading needs to be difficult to be rewarding. And as many teachers and professors will point out to you, navigating your mind through the difficult text can be especially rewarding, since that friction leads to better comprehension and learning. Still, you don’t need to read everything like you’re trying to get a good grade.
“There are no rules about leisure reading,” Willingham told me. “You can peek at the end. If you’re not enjoying a book, drop it. You can do whatever you want. The whole point is for you to have fun.”
You should read material that feels magnetic to you, that keeps you coming back for more. If reading is going to have any chance of competing with TikTok, it needs to be interesting and compelling, regardless of how literary or sophisticated you might think reading needs to be. You should read books, longform articles, and blog posts on whatever medium makes sense in that moment — and whatever medium makes it easy to keep reading.
That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t try to read the big difficult, doorstopper-sized classics, though, if that’s important to you. Just think twice about using AI to summarize what you’re reading. It’s tempting to ask ChatGPT why Anna Karenina is a classic — I just did, and ChatGPT says “psychological realism, moral complexity, continuing relevance” — but it’s not fun.
Using AI as a reading partner may help initial understanding of reading material, but old habits like note-taking better promote engagement and long-term comprehension. Pia Kreijkes, senior researcher at Cambridge University Press & Assessment and author of a study on this topic published earlier this year, is worried about young people leaning on AI to do more of the cognitive lifting that reading requires.
“Given that children are already on a trajectory of declining reading frequency and enjoyment, and that reading skills are also declining, we should be very concerned about this,” Kreijkes said. “The more we use AI to reduce our reading effort, the more likely reading skills are to decline.”
After all, if the kids stop reading, there’s not a whole lot of hope for future generations to be readers of books. If we let technology remove too much friction from our pursuit of knowledge, we will lose the plot entirely and slide into the postliterate horror so many people are currently afraid of, AI-dominated dystopia and all. When you put it that way, though, this is also a great premise for a sci-fi novel.

U.S. strikes Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for missile attacks on Navy ships
The U.S. military on Saturday said it struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy ships were targeted by missiles.
U.S. Central Command said it struck the vessels after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched two ballistic missiles at two Navy warships patrolling the sea. CENTCOM said a U.S. aircraft carrier and missile destroyer "successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" and that no American personnel were injured.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours," CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement posted on social media. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."
Strikes between the U.S. and Iran resumed last weekend, after a monthlong break from the fighting, when the U.S. hit several sites in Iran in response to a threat of Iran firing sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
An Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf, a key hub for the country's oil-export system, was one of the three vessels the U.S. struck on Saturday. A tanker in the Gulf of Oman also was hit in "multiple critical locations" and its crew had to abandon ship and another tanker near Jask was also struck, CENTCOM said.
The three Iranian oil tankers were part of a "multibillion-dollar shadow network" that funds the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and its regional proxies, CENTCOM also said in the statement.
Shadow fleets are vessels that operate outside of the official shipping system. Iran uses shadow fleets as a way to move oil because it is under sanction. The U.S. has seized Iranian vessels operating under shadow networks, including two in April.
Iran's foreign ministry on Saturday condemned the U.S. strikes, saying that they are "a clear violation of Paragraph 4 of Article 2 of the United Nations Charter, constitute a war crime, and represent an overt threat to international peace and the security of commercial shipping," according to the country's state media.
Lt. Col. Ebrahim Zolfaghari also warned Iranian forces would target American military in the region "more severely than before" if the U.S. continues strikes against ships, according to Iran's state media.
Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth on Saturday said in a social media post that if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, "we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."
"All they have to do is not shoot at @USNavy," Hegseth wrote.
NPR's Carrie Khan contributed to this report.

Children among at least 25 killed in Cabo Verde bus crash
Such incidents are rare in the west African archipelago, where roads are generally in good condition
At least 25 people, mostly children and teenagers, were killed in a bus crash on Cabo Verde’s Fogo Island, public radio network RCV said on Sunday.
Several others were injured in Saturday’s accident, some of them seriously, the head of civil protection for Sao Filipe city, Jose Canuto, told reporters.
Such incidents are rare in the west African archipelago, where roads are generally in good condition.
Canuto and other local authorities said the bus, which was carrying 32 passengers, veered off the road and plunged into a deep ravine on the way back to Sao Filipe after an excursion to the Cha das Caldeiras village inside the Pico do Fogo volcanic crater.
The dead include the bus driver, who organised the excursion to the unique site every year as a present for the pupils he drove to school during term time.
Emergency personnel worked through the night to rescue victims trapped in the wreckage, which came to a halt in a rocky valley that is hard to reach.

On his Facebook page, he has photos with several BJP MPs and MLAs, including Sanjay Bhatia, Rakesh Singh, Kartik Maharaj, Rudranil Ghosh, Krishnendu Mukherjee and Sanjay Singh.
His Facebook and Instagram accounts contain multiple posts in which he addresses the public against the backdrop of BJP Uttar Howrah’s banner, speaking on a range of political issues.

Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc crashed out of the Italian Grand Prix in dramatic fashion at Monza on Sunday.
The Moneqasque lost control of his machine at the iconic Parabolica and heavily crashed into the barriers while dueling with Mclaren’s Oscar Piastri.
The crash brought out the red flag, with the race scheduled to restart at 19:09 PM IST.
It was an eventful opening couple of laps of the Italian Grand Prix as pole sitter Pierre Gasly got a great launch off the line, holding off Mercedes’ George Russell.
However, it didn’t take long for Russell to breeze past the the Frenchman, taking the lead with a move down the inside at the first chicane on Lap 2.
There was no shortage of drama behind the front-runners either as Leclerc momentarily overtook Gasly before losing the place to the Frenchman and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen a few corners later.
Then came the moment of heartbreak for the capacity crowd at Ferrari’s home race.
Leclerc, winner of the race in 2019 and 2024, came under pressure from Piastri after getting overtaken by Verstappen and slipping to fourth place.
The Australian went for a daring move on the inside of the Parabolica, which forced Leclerc to take the outside line.
The Moneqasque then lost control of his rear (as he did in 2020, a race which Gasly won) to bring a premature end to what has been a difficult weekend for the scarlet red outfit.

Dunkley century helps England sweep Ireland 3-0
- Published
Third ODI, New Road, Worcester
England 291 (48.5 overs): Dunkley 119 (119); Murray 4-56
Ireland 177 (44.2 overs): Hunter 39 (58); Filer 3-27
England won by 114 runs; win series 3-0
Sophia Dunkley's sparkling century led England to a comprehensive 114-run win in the third and final one-day international against Ireland at Worcester.
Dunkley's run-a-ball 119 set up England's 291 before Ireland were bowled out for 177 in 44.2 overs, sealing a 3-0 clean sweep for Charlie Dean's side.
England were eyeing a record total after opener Dunkley's second international century, but the innings fell away from 260-4 and they frustratingly lost their last six wickets for just 31 runs to be dismissed with seven balls unused.
Dunkley added 73 for the first wicket with Maia Bouchier, who continued her fine run of form with 39, before Jodi Grewcock also wasted a good start as she was caught and bowled for 35 and Alice Capsey was unlucky to be run out backing up for 10.
All-rounders Freya Kemp and Dani Gibson threatened to push England beyond 300 but it was the former's wicket that kickstarted the collapse as she was caught at long-on for 23 and a run of single-figure scores followed, though Gibson kicked on to an ODI-best 41.
Leg-spinner Cara Murray was the pick of Ireland's bowlers with 4-56 as the visitors fought back admirably, and England only managed to hit seven boundaries after Dunkley's departure in the 36th over.
Despite the disappointing end to the innings, England still had plenty on the board in another non-contest between bat and ball.
Amy Hunter top-scored with 39 but no Irish batter was able to score at a strike-rate above 100 and the run-rate spiralled beyond their grasp, as Mady Villiers and Lauren Filer took three wickets apiece.
The final match of the series concludes England's international summer. Their next confirmed games will come at the Champions Trophy in February, though a multi-format series against West Indies in the autumn and three ODIs against Sri Lanka are in the schedule, but the dates have not been released.
- Ireland women in England 2026 
  - Published13 minutes ago
Dunkley delivers to close the summer
This has been a series with an unusual context for England.
Key stars such as Lauren Bell, Sophie Ecclestone and Nat Sciver-Brunt have been rested, which has presented opportunities to experiment with the likes of fringe players in Grewcock and Tilly Corteen-Coleman.
But the curious cricketing calendar means they have few opportunities to play the format, with the autumn schedule still unconfirmed and their next home ODI coming in the Ashes next summer, meaning they have been simultaneously seeking stability.
The opening partnership was one question that needed answering after Tammy Beaumont's retirement earlier this year, and a century apiece for Dunkley and Bouchier in this series has seen them take their chance.
Of course, Ireland's bowling attack is incomparable to Australia's and to cite this as Ashes preparation would be very unrealistic, but England can only play the schedule they are given.
Dunkley had been threatening in the first two games, falling for 73 at Leicester before she was stitched up by Bouchier's poor running at Derby - but she was not to be denied a third time.
The 28-year-old started patiently, reaching her half-century off 63 balls after Bouchier dominated the strike early on, before kicking on and whacking her next fifty off just 37.
A notable change to her game has been her improvement through the off-side, scoring her runs almost equally split across both sides of the wicket - a big change for a player previously known for her leg-side dominance.
Ireland tested her with the short ball and forced her to hit to the sweepers, which she handled efficiently before her eventual downfall as she was brilliantly caught by Prendergast at deep square leg.
Sciver-Brunt is likely to slot straight back in at number three, and England have a decision to make about whether Capsey keeps the gloves over Amy Jones, but for now, Dunkley and Bouchier have solved one of coach Charlotte Edwards' headaches.
England's bowling stocks improving
The series was also a valuable opportunity for England's crop of seamers to test themselves without Bell leading the attack, another area of their squad that needed strengthening.
With spinners dominating the T20 World Cup earlier this summer, the likes of Filer and Issy Wong were sidelined, but both have stepped up admirably.
Wong starred in the second ODI with her first international five-wicket haul before resting for this final game where Filer troubled the Irish batters throughout with her lively pace, which helped her take 3-27.
Contrastingly, Ryana Macdonald-Gay offered a change of tempo with her niggly medium-pace and Edwards will be hoping for Kemp to return to bowling fitness soon in order to give herself another option in the middle overs alongside Gibson.
Villiers took 3-33 with her off-spin as she claimed the big wickets of Hunter and Orla Prendergast, and with Corteen-Coleman waiting in Ecclestone's wings, England's bowling stocks are in a healthy position.
Ireland barely threatened to reach their target, with captain Gaby Lewis falling early for 16 to dent their hopes almost immediately and fellow opener Alice Tector trudged to 29 off 59 balls, which saw the run-rate climb steadily.
England were made to work hard for their wickets throughout a stalling middle-over phase but eventually they ripped through the lower order with Ireland's last five wickets falling in a heap for just 10 runs.
