Last month, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman. Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere.
Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
Angie Nixon explains her playbook to be Florida’s next senator.
But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale. She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change.
Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state, and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise?
It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money. But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch.
This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing. I am a former union organizer. I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country.
How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida?
It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for.
Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not.
We are not communist. We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like. There’s nothing radical or extreme about that.
Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election. Prominent pundits have said that Democrats should not invest in Florida, and that would amount to wasted money. Political forecasters moved the race in the Republican direction after your primary victory, arguing that the progressive politics makes it easier for Republicans to win in a state like Florida.
I wanted to ask about electability. Can you give me the case for how you can win a statewide race amongst such skepticism?
The same way that I was able to win a primary being outspent and out-raised 18 to 1. I am building a very unique, diverse coalition of people. We’ve had Republicans and independents that crossed over in the primary to vote for me in the primary. They also volunteer in our campaign. They’ve made donations.
We literally have a bunch of Republicans and libertarians who have been stating that they are voting for me because they like that I am no-nonsense. They appreciate that I am trying to put a check on what is coming out of Washington, DC, all of the cruelty and the corruption, and that is the winning message.
Look, we’re up against a woman, [incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody], who allowed the theft of $10 million. She allowed money to be stolen from medically needy and low-income kids, to be diverted toward two citizen-led ballot initiatives that actually caused us to not have better health in our communities.
People are frustrated, and that’s all Ashley Moody has done — just look out for herself, her campaign donors and these billionaires. People are ready for elected officials to stop bailing out these big businesses [and] actually look out for everyday people.
In November 2023, you introduced a resolution to the Florida House calling for “the immediate de-escalation and ceasefire…in Israel and occupied Palestine.” It was rejected 104 to 2. And it earned you some bad blood with some of the members of the Florida Jewish Caucus. The chair actually said that the resolution was born out of ignorance and antisemitism.
Obviously, the Democratic Party base has shifted on that issue over the last several years. There’s been an open discussion about whether Joe Biden and Kamala Harris did themselves damage in the 2024 election by not breaking more explicitly with Israel’s actions in Gaza.
Do you think that was a mistake for Democrats?
I would say yes. I would say that we have to have really uncomfortable conversations amongst our different communities and we just have to talk. But I feel that they did do a disservice in regards to just going along with the AIPAC lobby.
You had mentioned that you don’t support sending any money or any weapons to Israel at this moment, but I also wanted to ask about things like BDS, the movement to boycott, divest, or sanction Israel. Is that something you support?
It is. I’m a Black woman who is a descendant of slaves, and who is the descendant of people from the civil rights movement, and I know how we used boycotts and we used protest to gain our civil rights for our community. So I’m fully supportive of that.
You repeatedly said that you don’t support defunding the police on your website. It says that you support demilitarizing the police. And that “real safety comes from good jobs, strong schools, affordable housing, and healthcare for all — not from more cameras, more cages, and more agents.”
What is the difference between that and defunding?
Whatever folks think the difference is. I’m not going to box myself in because I understand how they’ll try to cut and clip things with me saying certain words.
But doesn’t that sound a little bit like lessening the resources that go to police to focus on other things? I mean, that sounds a little like the same thing.
It sounds like I know that is my position. I want to defund Flock cameras because bad cops are stalking their ex-girlfriends and ex-boyfriends. And so to-may-toe, to-mah-toe. I literally said this before and that is what I am for. I’m not trying to get clipped in any kind of way.
Let me ask you this way. I appreciate the focus on root causes, and I think you’ve laid that out that that’s where you want the energy to go — that real public safety comes from focusing on the things that cause people to commit crimes in the first place, but those often take a long time to show effect.
If we’re talking about the root causes of crime, what is the message to someone whose community is unsafe right now that does not include policing?
What I would say is, making sure that we invest in making sure people have more jobs and we invest in community control of the police. I totally believe in civil review boards and that type of thing, but I believe in making sure that people’s most basic needs are met.
One of the things that I believe could help that right off the bat is things like universal healthcare, or at a minimum, extending the ACA subsidies so that we can drive down these healthcare premium costs. Or fully funding these programs that allow people to have access to first-time homebuyer programs.
I was a single mom for 12 years, and I took part in the first-time homebuyer program that was funded from the federal government. That trickled down to the state and then to the local government. That helped me with down payment assistance as well as closing costs and those types of programs. We need to put policies in place that are allowing people to be good.
We need to push for universal child care. For every $1 that is invested by the government, it puts $3 back into the economy so parents can get to work. They can be able to make sure that they have money to put their children in different programs. We need to invest in programs to keep our children off the streets.
There’s been so much effort to put you in one of the boxes that have defined the Democratic ideological battles — DSA versus establishment. I hear in this interview how that doesn’t neatly fit with what it seems like you’ve done in Florida.
Where do you think this campaign fits into the ongoing question of where do Democrats go next?
We’re coalition builders, we’re aggregators. Folks should know, I was a vice chair of a local Democratic Party. I was also the field director and the political director with the state party. I have never fit in a box. I was a union member and I also led a statewide organization that was straight-up progressive.
We need all these things to fight back against this Donald Trump regime. Look, this man is not going to leave willingly in 2028. He’s created a paramilitary force in the form of ICE that is getting away with shooting people and slaughtering them on camera while they’re masked without any accountability. They’re pushing to see how far they can go.
Granted, Black people have been getting slaughtered on camera without accountability for a while, but now they are doing it to people who aren’t just Black, who aren’t just Latino. They are banking on us being normalized with what’s happening.
First lady Michelle Obama says, “They go low, we go high.” I’m saying, “We get loud, we push back. We organize stronger and harder so that we can win and change this country and build a new vision for the next 250 years, where we have a Florida and an America for all.”

Navi Mumbai: An eight-page suicide note allegedly left behind by an Assistant Police Sub-Inspector (ASI) attached to the Special Branch of the Navi Mumbai Police was recovered from the trunk of his car parked near his residence in Airoli, police said. The officer died by suicide at a lodge in Mahape on Saturday.
Chit In Pocket Led Police To Hidden Note
According to the police, a small chit found in the deceased officer's pocket stated that a detailed suicide note had been kept in the trunk of his car. Acting on the information, police located the vehicle and recovered the eight-page note. The note was subsequently seized, sealed and sent for forensic examination.
The ASI had allegedly first published a video online recorded by the deceased surfaced on social media, in which he allegedly made allegations and named three police personnel, including senior officers. The exact contents of the suicide note and the allegations made in it have not been disclosed.
Family Says They Could Not Read Suicide Note
His daughter, Vaishnavi Patil, said the family did not get an opportunity to read the note as it was immediately taken into police custody and sent for forensic examination.
“We did not get a chance to read the suicide note as the police seized it, immediately sealed it and sent it for forensic examination,” Patil said.
Daughter Alleges Harassment After Officer’s Death
Patil said her father had never discussed anything with the family and that they learnt about the alleged harassment only after his death through some of his colleagues.
“He never shared anything with us. We came to know about the harassment only after the incident,” she said.
Family Claims Officer Faced Threats And Pressure
According to Patil, colleagues told the family that her father had allegedly been harassed by the police personnel named in the purported suicide note. She alleged that he was regularly harassed, repeatedly threatened with transfers and coaxed to collect bribes.
“He was regularly harassed, repeatedly threatened of getting transferred and coaxed to collect bribes. As a police personnel, he was extremely helpful. I cannot accept whatever has happened. Even in the final video, he has earnestly sought for justice and he must get this,” Patil said.
The deceased officer had two daughters. His elder daughter is married, while Vaishnavi is the younger daughter.
Family Demands Action Against Senior Officers
The family has demanded stringent action against the police personnel named in the purported note and video, including the DCP and ACP allegedly referred to by the deceased.
“The culprits named by my brother, including the DCP and ACP, should all be subjected to the strictest action. They should be arrested,” Patil said.
Following the officer's death, his family staged a rasta roko on the Thane-Belapur Road and later protested outside the police station, demanding an immediate FIR and action against the officers named in the purported note and video.
Police officials subsequently spoke to the family and assured them that the matter would be investigated impartially and that necessary action would be taken after the evidence was verified. Following the assurance, the family dispersed from the police station and proceeded for the last rites of the deceased.
Police Commissioner Milind Bharambe has said that necessary action will be taken after the evidence, including the suicide note and the video, is verified.
The officer had been posted with the Special Branch only in May and was earlier attached to the Control Room, according to the police.
The exact nature of the alleged harassment and the contents of the eight-page suicide note are yet to be established. Police are examining the note, the video and other evidence as part of the investigation.

Hong Kong to review bookings for famous Sai Kung trail after high no-show rate
Only 1,560 registered and walk-in patrons arrived at Po Pin Chau on Saturday and Sunday, despite 3,230 people making bookings
Hong Kong authorities will review a new reservation system for a Sai Kung trail famed for its dramatic volcanic rock columns after the National Day “golden week” in October, following large numbers of no-shows during the first two trial runs.
Only 1,560 registered and walk-in patrons arrived at Po Pin Chau on Saturday and Sunday, despite 3,230 people having made bookings under the real-name reservation system.
Lawmakers and a district councillor have called for more on-site quotas, clearer booking status information for walk-ins, and a penalty-points system to curb no-shows.
In a response to the South China Morning Post Sunday, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) said it would step up visitor management, patrols and enforcement around the East Dam and Po Pin Chau area, while continuing publicity and educational efforts, including reminders to book in advance.
“The department will conduct a comprehensive review of the effectiveness [of the trial] after the National Day golden week to assist in formulating long-term countryside management strategies,” a spokesman said.
Golden week refers to either of the two week-long holidays in mainland China around National Day on October 1, and the Chinese New Year, also known as the Spring Festival.

Whatever happened to kindness? Spoiler alert: Our readers prove it's alive and well
In recent years, NPR has explored how small interactions with strangers can do more than just brighten our days — they can improve our well‑being.
Our original story from 2023 traced psychologist Gillian Sandstrom's research back to her experience as a lonely graduate student in Toronto who exchanged a wave and hello daily with a hot dog vendor she passed on campus, even though she never once bought a hot dog. That brief exchange boosted her spirits so much that she began studying the power of "weak ties." Her research found what many people intuitively feel: Even the most casual encounters can boost mood, ease isolation and strengthen our sense of community.
Global health professor Kristin Jenkins of Cornerstone University in Grand Rapids, Mich., wrote to tell us that our story had inspired her to ask her students to intentionally engage with strangers and casual acquaintances. They enjoyed the assignment so much, they wanted to continue doing it! In sharing some of their experiences with NPR, they described moments that echoed Sandstrom's findings. A mechanic started "a wonderful conversation" about nursing school. A hospital worker felt more grounded during a stressful shift: "Something as simple as using someone's name or taking a few extra minutes to listen can actually mean a lot.". These short, simple interactions became reminders that kindness doesn't always have to be grand to be meaningful.
About This Series
We're looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
Now, we've invited readers to share their own moments of connection — small exchanges that lift their spirits and stay with them much longer than they expect.
One woman from California shared a story about her mother, who lost a year of school to polio as a child and has lived ever since with a twisted spine and chronic pain. Even so, for the past two decades, she and her dogs have made weekly visits to nursing homes and hospitals, bringing handwritten cards and goody bags to people who normally don't have visitors.
Another reader in Kenya told us that a quick question about an acronym on a man's T‑shirt while waiting in line at a bakery turned into a lively 15‑minute conversation. They both walked away smiling.
Finally, one open-hearted reader doesn't just limit kindness to other humans. "Even a simple greeting like 'Hello, brother' to a hawk or 'You are so beautiful' to a flower brightens my day."
And the stories kept coming, all reflecting a simple truth: small gestures matter. To keep a smile on your face, here are a few more:
A listening ear, a pack of tissues
It's no mystery that I enjoy talking to strangers. Everyone has a story, and I'm hear (see what I did there?) to listen to it. I actually dated a guy once that said, "Why do you have to talk to everyone?" I knew right then and there he wasn't the one.
When I stumbled across the NPR article, "Why saying hello to strangers can be good for you," I felt inclined to share a story that happened just today.
I work in corporate events, and part of my job includes operating registration desks. Consider me the Welcome Wagon! The role actually requires a lot of project management and organizational skills, but for the point of this story: I smile, check people in and print their badges. There is a lot of interaction with strangers, which I enjoy.
Toward the end of the day, a woman came up to my desk in tears. She was so embarrassed about what had just transpired in a meeting and decided to share with me. She explained she felt behind during the training course. She said the presenter did not assist her in a helpful way and was actually pretty crass. When she packed up her things and left the room early, the heavy door slammed behind her, making everything feel worse.
Out of everyone she could have walked up to, she chose me. I gave her a mini pack of tissues and listened. The woman talked about her struggles of being an older woman in a male-dominated tech environment and about how certain moments could make her feel invisible. I felt like I had a purpose right then to help her in the best way I knew how – just by listening. By the end of our conversation, I felt her mood shift and the heaviness lift. I even managed to get a smile out of her!
What she doesn't know is that she gave me something too. During our exchange, I felt like I was right where I was supposed to be, at the right time. I am proud that I carry myself in a way that makes others feel comfortable to approach me and share.
The article said people feel good after random encounters with strangers, and I would have to agree. I try to remind myself that we never know someone's full story, and a little grace — a smile, a quick hello, or a moment of listening — can really go a long way.
Michelle Sarnosky
Missouri
Puppy love
After moving from South Florida to a small town on Florida's west coast, I discovered the community was more closed-off than I was used to. But as I was out walking my puppy, neighbors — dog owners or not — would stop to talk. Within a month, my new husband, who had lived in this bedroom community for years, was amazed by how many new friends I was making for both of us!
Thank you for writing about this small but powerful way we can make a difference in each other's lives. It truly is a two-sided gift.
Anita Finley Derr
Florida
A stranger's hug
My older brother passed away unexpectedly on December 30, 2019. As my family gathered at my younger brother's apartment in downtown Philadelphia the next day, the mood was deeply heavy. We were all in shock — disbelieving and numb.
My dad was handling payroll for a small organization at the time and had to walk to the UPS on Chestnut Street to overnight some paychecks. I decided to go with him. When we entered the small UPS office and approached the counter, the woman working there made a pleasantry — I can't exactly recall, maybe something like "Oh, are you all together for the holidays?" I decided to be honest. I said in a somber tone that ended more in a whimper, "Yes… but also, unfortunately, my brother died yesterday.."
I will never forget her reaction. Her jaw dropped, she gasped, and she looked at my dad and asked "Your son?" When he said yes, she said nothing more. Without hesitation, she came around the counter and gave us both the most incredible, genuine hugs. She didn't know us at all, but she instantly recognized the weight of our indescribable pain in that moment.
There was something incredibly healing and meaningful about that moment. To feel seen by a stranger who cared enough to step forward — it mattered. I'll never forget this, and since then, I've often tried to pass on that type of compassion, whether to a stranger or friend.
Cordelia Biddle
Pennsylvania
A world of stories
I always chat with strangers, in elevators, walking along the street, waiting in lines. If you pay attention and listen, everybody does have a story to tell.
Donald Pederson
Maryland

'Layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
- Published
A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.
Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.
"It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.
The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.
"I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.
Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.
They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors.
"We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.
Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said.
He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.
At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water.
Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.
Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.
The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.
But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.
Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone'
Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.
Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".
The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers.
"Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."
But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time.
"It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."
Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".
This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located.
"We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

Counter-tariffs won't just affect the cost of goods for Canadians. They'll hit the trailers moving them too
Semi-trailers, largely built in U.S., expected to see 25% counter-tariff take effect Sept. 8
Canadians bracing for billions of dollars in counter-tariffs won't just see prices rise on American aluminum, toilet paper, furniture and more — but on the very semi-trailers hauling those goods into and around the country.
Ocean Trailer, the largest retailer of semi-trailers in Western Canada, is waiting on a $45-million order of 600 trailers from U.S. manufacturers.
The company is rushing to get as many over the border before a 25 per cent Canadian counter-tariff on trailers, and scores of other items, takes effect on Tuesday.
"The extra cost, the 25 per cent, is well above our profit margin on a trailer, so we would have no choice but to pass that along to the customer," said Mack Keay, Ocean Trailer's chief operating officer, told CBC News from Vancouver.
The federal government announced dollar-for-dollar countermeasures will take effect at 12:01 a.m. on Tuesday on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods, in response to the latest round of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration.
Keay said it's possible Ocean Trailer may be able to cancel some of its order, which was expected to flow in trailer by trailer until the end of the year, but it's on the hook for the trailers that are already in the process of being fabricated in the U.S.
The ones the company can't get into Canada by Sept. 8 will have to be parked somewhere in the U.S. or sold to American-based retailers, and Keay said he wouldn't get back what he paid for them.
Industry 'very much concerned'
Ocean Trailer isn't alone.
The head of the Manitoba Trucking Association said the vast majority of semi-trailers in Canada come from the U.S.
"I know a number of members that currently have trailers on order and are very much concerned about the cost of those trailers, because they ordered them before the counter-tariffs," said executive director Aaron Dolyniuk.
"I don't know that they'll be able to afford to pay 25 per cent more for them when they get here."
Dolyniuk said many businesses that rely on those trucking companies to ship product are also "rushing to get things north of the border before the [counter-]tariffs come on."
"I was talking to one member late last week … [who] said normally, they hauled two loads for this one customer northbound, and they wanted 15 this week," he said.
A variety of types of semi-trailers are towed along Canadian roadways, but the two most common are called dry vans and refrigerated vans.
The latter, also known as "reefer" vans, haul groceries, pharmaceuticals and other items that need temperature-controlled conditions during transport to avoid spoilage.
Dry van trailers are used to haul everything from kitchen appliances to car and machine parts, paper products, furniture, televisions, canned goods and other non-perishable items.
'This is not going to be OK'
There are just two semi-trailer manufacturers in Canada — one based in Ontario that doesn't manufacture reefer van trailers and another in Quebec which does, along with making dry vans, flat fright vans and other specialty trailer types.
Neither would have the capacity overnight to absorb the increased demand for trailer orders or rentals from Canadian trucking companies following counter-tariffs.
Ocean Trailer's Keay said Canada's domestic manufacturing capabilities are less than half of what the trucking industry would need to meet demand.
At the industry level, the potential added costs from counter-tariffs are eye-watering.
The average cost across trailer varieties is about $75,000, said Keay. A 25 per cent tariff would drive that closer to $95,000.
Each of the seven Ocean Trailer branches from Manitoba to B.C. is bringing in one or two trailers per day, either associated with orders from trucking companies or to be added to the company's rental fleet, said Dallas Senebald, the branch manager for the Winnipeg office.
"This is not going to be OK. Not just us not being OK, the industry is not going to be OK," said Senebald, whose Winnipeg office employs 40 people.
"There will be a shortage of trailers, which then increases demand, increases the cost of the trailers, and that gets filtered down right to consumer goods that are needed to be shipped."
If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt.- Aaron Dolyniuk, Manitoba Trucking Association
Senebald said trends in semi-trailer sales can be unpredictable year to year, depending on supply and demand of goods that need shipping.
One year, a larger corporate customer might order 100 trailers for purchase, and then none the next year, said Senebald. The Winnipeg branch might bringing in 300 to 400 trailers one year, and 80 the next, he said.
The variability is one reason the industry relies on a mixed model. Ocean Trailer has about eight suppliers — seven in the U.S. and one in Mexico, said Senebald.
On top of being the largest retailer of semi-trailers west of Ontario, it's also the largest business for rentals.
In the short term, Canadian trucking companies may turn to rentals as they hold off on buying U.S. trailers that cost them 25 per cent more due to counter-tariffs, said Senebald — and that's a concern.
"Demand for rentals is going to skyrocket so much so that we probably won't have enough to fulfil customer needs," he said.
"Saying no to customers repeatedly is never a good thing. Eventually, they stop calling."
The trucking association's Dolyniuk said the depth of pain felt will ultimately depend on how long the tariff war goes on.
"If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt within the trucking sector and outside of it," he said.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to work on his Washington, D.C., beautification projects, thus making those workers unavailable for immediate rescue efforts in the aftermath of the Aug. 29, 2026, Grand Canyon National Park flash floods, is unproven.
- The rumor stemmed in part from users sharing a Sept. 1 article from the online publication The Lever, which reported, "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
- The Lever cited a CNN article published days before the flooding reporting hundreds of NPS first responders were reassigned without saying exactly when the staffing shifts occurred. The CNN story cited its own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources.
- Snopes has not been able to review the same internal CNN documentation, nor have we located information confirming or debunking the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hampered flood rescue efforts.
- An Interior Department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers hampered the flood response, "That is 100% false." We reached out to numerous other relevant parties and will update this article if we receive further details.
A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to Washington, D.C., to work on his administration's beautification projects circulated online in early September 2026. People sharing the claim suggested they would have proved key in rescue efforts, possibly saving lives, had they been available immediately following the Aug. 29 flash floods inside Arizona's Grand Canyon National Park. We have not yet found evidence that would confirm or debunk this rumor.
The National Park Service, an agency under the Interior Department, announced closures to bridges, the Colorado River, lodging and trails, as well as confirming two deaths, one person missing and around 80 people rescued or evacuated.
An NPS news release said the two people who died, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, both of Granbury, Texas, were hiking in Bright Angel Canyon and were a part of the same group as the missing person. A key water pipeline sustained severe damage, as well.
In one example of the rumor, on Sept. 1, an X user posted (archived) a message appearing to place blame for the deaths on Trump.
(@factpostnews accessed via X)
Other posts featured the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
Some posts directly cited the online publication The Lever, which published an article on Sept. 1 with the headline "Before Deadly Floods, Trump Diverted Emergency Responders To Beautify D.C." The story's subheading reads: "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
The Lever's article cited a CNN story published prior to the floods on Aug. 25, telling of Trump's administration sending 300 NPS incident management team workers — a division responding to wildfires and other incidents — to work on what CNN dubbed Trump's Washington, D.C., "pet projects," such as the past renovations for the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the future overhaul of the East Potomac Park golf course. The CNN article does not say exactly when the purported staffing shifts occurred.
The CNN reporters cited their own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources regarding other information.
Neither the Lever's article nor users' posts explicitly said the Trump administration's reported diversion of 300 workers hampered rescue efforts surrounding the flash floods. Either way, users inferred it, some believing Trump very recently diverted the workers, with one Snopes reader emailing, "Did tRump divert 300 specialized emergency first responders from American national parks to work on his Reflecting Pool, in the midst of needing them for Grand Canyon rescues?"
Snopes has not been able to review the same internal documentation CNN cited, nor have we located information that might allow us to conclusively rule on the veracity of the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hindered Grand Canyon flood rescue efforts. This claim is therefore unproven and we have left it unrated.
Via email, the White House referred us to the Interior Department, where a department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers to Washington harmed the flood response, "That is 100% false."
We requested documentation, information and/or comment from the Arizona Department of Public Safety, CNN, Coconino County Emergency Response, Grand Canyon National Park, The Lever and NPS, and will update this article if we receive further information.
A brief timeline of rescue efforts
Within three hours of the flooding on Aug. 29, NPS Grand Canyon shared details about officials evacuating 50 people by air. By the next morning, the division reported 62 total evacuations out of the roughly 80 rescues to date, and said it had gotten assistance from the Arizona Public Safety Department.
A Sept. 1 notice from NPS Grand Canyon announced the continuation of search-and-rescue operations, as well as that the "NPS Western Type 3 Incident Management Team" — the same as the incident management teams CNN and The Lever reported about — would be taking over command as of that morning. The Arizona Daily Sun published a photo reportedly showing a member of that same team observing an Aug. 31 news conference, two days following the flooding.
For further reading about Trump's beautification efforts in the nation's capital, we previously reported about an allegation that his administration chopped down dozens of beloved cherry trees to renovate a golf course, as well as that his motorcade ride inside the reflecting pool caused damage he later blamed on others.

HIV is no longer a word that frightens young people. For a generation that has grown up seeing HIV transformed from a feared death sentence into a manageable chronic condition, the virus no longer carries the deterrent power it once did.
But the fading fear of HIV is confronting Keralam with a new public-health challenge. Changing sexual behaviour, gaps in information and awareness, and growing substance use are increasingly putting young people at risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
The numbers seeking care at the 23 District STI/RTI Centres (DSRCs) under the Kerala State AIDS Control Society (KSACS) have been rising steadily. However, these figures do not capture the full picture, as Keralam does not have routine STI surveillance across public and private hospitals. STIs also rarely figure in formal public health conversations.
World Sexual Health Day
On World Sexual Health Day (September 4), experts say Keralam needs more open conversations with young people about sexual health, safe sexual practices, consent and healthy relationships. Equally important is ensuring that youngsters know where they can seek confidential testing, advice and treatment without fear of judgement.
KSACS data compiled up to December 2025 show that attendance at DSRCs rose from 41,417 in 2023-24 to 63,129 in 2024-25. Another 51,243 people visited the clinics during April-November 2025 alone.
The proportion of DSRC clients undergoing RPR screening for syphilis also increased—from 55% in 2023-24 to 70% in 2024-25 and 79% during April-November 2025. The increase in screening means more infections are being detected, and the figures cannot by themselves be taken as evidence of a corresponding rise in prevalence.
Of particular concern is the increase among younger clients. Among those aged up to 19, clinic attendance rose from 1,547 in 2023-24 to 2,255 in 2024-25; another 1,910 had been recorded during April-November 2025. The proportion of newly detected HIV infections among those aged 15-24 also rose from 10% in 2022-23 to 15% during April-October 2025.
Change in societal attitudes
“There is a change in societal attitudes towards casual sex and today, the earlier message of abstinence that we used to give youngsters no longer works. Many youngsters are sexually active today and our only message to them is to remain safe, because their health is at stake,” a senior Health Department official said.
Being safe goes beyond HIV prevention. Condoms significantly reduce the risk of many STIs, including HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia, but do not eliminate the risk of infections such as syphilis, HPV and genital herpes, which can spread through skin-to-skin contact. HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, regular testing, timely treatment and reducing exposure to multiple or unknown partners are also important.
Consent and communication also need to be part of sexual-health messaging. Being safe means being able to say no, respecting a partner’s decision and discussing protection before sex.
Substance use among young people is another concern for sexual-health professionals, who say intoxication can increase risky sexual behaviour and impair the ability to make informed decisions.
Testing is crucial
“One of the most important messages we can give youth today is that testing matters, even without symptoms. Many STIs cause no symptoms, so someone can have and transmit an infection without knowing it. Testing becomes particularly important after a potential exposure or when starting a new sexual relationship,” said V. Sam Prasad, who heads AHF India Cares, an NGO working in HIV.
Keralam’s STI clinics are seeing a range of infections, with syphilis emerging as a particular concern. Doctors also report a resurgence of gonorrhoea, which they say is increasingly being encountered in clinical practice.
KSACS data show that clients found reactive for syphilis on screening increased from 1,206 in 2023-24 to 1,455 in 2024-25, with another 1,121 recorded during the first seven months of 2025-26.
Complicated infections
“We are quite concerned that some STIs are now presenting differently and with serious complications. We have had reports of neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis, which are complicated and require long and intensive treatment,” a Health official said.
At STI clinics, young people diagnosed with an infection are encouraged to bring their partners for testing to prevent reinfection. They are also advised to complete treatment and undergo HIV testing, given the close relationship between HIV and other STIs.
Self-assessment tool
To encourage confidential testing, KSACS has launched a digital self-assessment tool through which users can privately assess their sexual-health risk. By scanning a QR code and answering questions about lifestyle and behavioural practices, users receive guidance on whether testing may be advisable, along with information on the next steps and the nearest STI clinic.

Elbows up or down? Why Alberta is diplomacy-first in the trade war
Alberta's Washington envoy says province's position on alcohol gives it an edge
Alberta’s top U.S. diplomat says playing nice is paying off for his province in the Canada-U.S. trade war.
Nathan Cooper, Alberta’s senior representative to the United States, told CBC’s West of Centre that compared to provinces that have taken a more aggressive approach, Alberta has come out ahead.
“I think the premier’s diplomacy-first approach has really not only been helpful for me, but certainly helpful for the province,” Cooper said.
“If we look at the impact of U.S. tariffs on the Alberta economy, we have a disproportionately low impact.”
Experts have said while Alberta’s industries are not immune to the impact of the trade dispute, they are not seeing the direct hit other provinces are. Despite the trade war, the U.S. continues to increase its imports of Canadian oil.
The comments come as Cooper, the former speaker of the Alberta legislature, spent time in Nashville, Tenn., with Premier Danielle Smith last week.
Cooper said American officials have been “significantly more responsive” to his team than some of his provincial counterparts.
Alberta is the only remaining province with no ban or retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol imports. The province’s position on that is something the Americans have shown “a real appreciation” for, Cooper said.
“I believe that that's actually translated into results for the province of Alberta,” he said.
The premier said her trip to Music City was a personal one, but she took time to meet with business and tourism leaders while there. Ahead of her trip, Smith also appeared on U.S. news networks pushing for a return to the bargaining table.
Honey or vinegar?
Not everyone has been on board with Alberta’s approach.
Following Smith’s trip to Mar-a-Lago last year, she was called out for not being a part of a unified “Team Canada” response.
This summer, Premier Doug Ford pushed for Canadian leaders to take a stronger stance, and called for energy exports to be cut off to the U.S.
Smith’s predecessor, Jason Kenney, has said a modest tax on oil exports should be considered to put extra pressure on the president.
Smith has rejected both ideas and consistently said doubling down on diplomacy is a better approach.
“I think in this scenario, maybe Premier Smith is seen as a dissenting voice or not quite on script,” Evan Menzies, vice-president of Crestview Strategy said in an interview.
But Menzies, who previously worked as a director of communications for Smith’s party, said things look more favourable for Alberta when you zoom out.
“If you're to look at what's bearing good fruit, Alberta's efforts seem to be bearing some good fruit.”
Smith’s too-friendly-to-resist approach contrasts against Ontario Doug Ford’s aggressive advertising and insult slinging.
Cole Hogan, a strategic communications advisor at Alberta Counsel who has worked on Ford and Kenney campaigns, said the divergent tactics make sense considering domestic priorities.
“Ford's approach, while it makes a lot of people feel good … it hasn't garnered the same results that Smith's approach has here in Alberta.”
“They both have different political goals in doing so — they have different industries to serve.”
Separation anxiety
All this comes amid a looming election in Alberta on whether to hold a binding referendum on separation — something U.S. officials are increasingly waking up to.
It's been used by representative Andy Harris to trumpet renewed calls for a 51st state and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as a sign of disunity and failed trade talks.
On the ground, Cooper said the referendum isn’t frequently raised in his meetings with U.S. officials.
“At the end of the day, one of my key jobs is to try to determine the difference between signal and noise and do what I can to get people focused on the big issues that are impacting our province.”

Yoga and Ayurveda have moved beyond their traditional wellness identity and are increasingly becoming part of India’s global health and diplomatic strategy, with the Centre seeking to expand their footprint through medical tourism, international education, practitioner mobility and trade agreements.
The shift is particularly evident in India’s recent trade diplomacy. The India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), operationalised in June 2026, and the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) contain dedicated provisions on health-related services and traditional medicine. These include measures to ease licensing, develop standards and facilitate the mobility of AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors.
The India-European Union (EU) FTA, signed in January 2026, goes further, allowing AYUSH practitioners to use their Indian qualifications in EU countries where no regulatory framework exists and providing for AYUSH wellness centres and clinics.
Also Read | India partners with WHO to mainstream Ayush globally through agreement on traditional medicine interventions
The agreements represent an attempt to transform AYUSH from being a cultural export to a formalised health and services opportunity.
The India-Oman CEPA contains what the government describes as its first comprehensive commitment on traditional medicine across all modes of supply, while the India-New Zealand FTA has a dedicated ‘health and traditional medicine’ annex covering Ayurveda, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy.
The New Zealand agreement also provides structured mobility pathways, including a dedicated visa quota for AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors. The government said the agreement would institutionalise cooperation in education, training, standards development and wellness services.
Comment | The growing relevance of traditional medicine
Need to convert market access to demand
However, the diplomatic push also raises questions about how far formal recognition and market access will translate into actual international demand.
Experts point to the need for credible standards, evidence, regulation, practitioner quality and patient safety if AYUSH is to establish itself in increasingly regulated global healthcare markets.
Senior officials in the Ministry of Ayush said the Ayush visa, overseas training and exchange programmes were also helping expand the sector.
“Foreign medical arrivals rose from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.44 lakh in 2024, as per our data. Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Germany, Russia, Malaysia, Mauritius and Saudi Arabia are among the important markets for AYUSH and Ayurveda treatment. The government does not publish a current consolidated country-wise ranking of AYUSH patients,” an official from the AYUSH Ministry said.
However, the figure of 6.44 lakh refers to overall foreign medical arrivals and not specifically AYUSH patients. The absence of consolidated data makes it difficult to assess AYUSH’s actual share of India’s medical-value-travel market.
The Ayush visa, introduced in 2023, is another component of the strategy. Between January 2023 and December 2025, a total of 3,375 foreign nationals travelled to India on Ayush visas or e-Ayush visas, while another 579 travelled on Ayush attendant visas or e-Ayush attendant visas. Earlier, the Ministry had reported that 1,646 Ayush visas had been issued to nationals of 75 countries between January 2024 and February 2025.
Education is also emerging as another channel of influence. Under the Ayush Fellowship Scheme, 260 students from 32 countries were studying AYUSH in Indian institutions.
The Ministry’s international cooperation programmes also support training, seminars, conferences and knowledge exchange, including Yoga teaching and education overseas.

'The health system in Nepal is not prepared for this'
Nepal flood waters have receded, but threats to physical and mental health are growing
"There's nothing left there," says Shushma Bhusal, the regional lead for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. "There's no village, no sign of anyone there. A lot of houses have just been washed off."
Bhusal is describing parts of Bidur municipality after the flood. Before disaster struck, it was a bustling place, home to about 60,000 people. Hundreds of homes and businesses hugged the Trishuli River, which cuts a winding path through the Nepali Himalayas. It was a central transit hub, about two and half hours from Kathmandu, Nepal's capital.
Now Bhusal sees only devastation.
Across the river, Trishuli hospital served the larger region. But the bridge to get there was destroyed by the enormous torrent of water, mud and debris unleashed by a collapsed glacier on Aug. 26.
"The time taken to cross the bridge in normal times was just 10 minutes," says Bhusal. "Now it takes about 10 hours for people to go and walk through the trail and get to the other side of the river. It leaves the people here in Bidur out of access to health services."
It's a situation playing out across communities along the river, imperiling the physical and mental health of tens of thousands.
"It's an unbelievable disaster," says Padam Simkhada, a global health researcher from the area who is now at the University of Chester. "The health system in Nepal is not prepared for this."
Damaged infrastructure, disrupted care
The floods killed at least 1,200 people in Nepal and neighboring Tibet, according to authorities. The disaster also completely destroyed or damaged at least seven hospitals and health centers, says Allison Gocotano, the World Health Organization representative to Nepal. While some hospitals remain functional, "access remains hindered because of the road blockages," he says. "Continuity of electricity is also an issue across the board."
The damage is making it harder to care for those injured by the floods. It's also disrupting routine medical care.
"We know in the community there are pregnant women who have delivery dates in the next few weeks," says Abhilasha Gurung, a health specialist with UNICEF in Nepal. The aid organization is in the process of setting up medical tents to provide that basic care. She says they've also distributed basic items, including hygiene kits and bed nets to protect against mosquitoes, to 19,000 people.
People with chronic conditions requiring medication, like diabetes, hypertension or cancer, are especially vulnerable in crises like these, says Simkhada.
"Even if they survive because they ran away, they lost their medication. There is no health facility to get that medicine. Even if there is another supply, they don't know [the] dosage," he says. "People who already have chronic conditions even become worse."
As health officials scramble to shore up this basic medical care, they're also on the lookout for new threats.
Clean water is hard to come by, as the floods contaminated water systems and damaged infrastructure. That's raising fear of waterborne diseases, says Simkhada. "There is a high risk of an epidemic that could be cholera, diarrheal disease."
Thousands of survivors are being relocated into cramped temporary shelters where airborne diseases like tuberculosis could spread. The Ministry of Health has deployed technical staff to help beef up surveillance in these centers, says Gocotano, the WHO official.
"The dead are gone, I am the one alive"
The devastating floods have also left a mental health crisis.
Roughly 2,500 to 3,000 people are currently in temporary holding centers, including everyone rescued from the floods, says UNICEF's Gurung. Many are grappling with profound loss.
Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal, visited one such center in Nuwakot earlier this week. His visit was often interrupted by the sound of helicopters overhead, searching for survivors.
"Whenever a helicopter passed by, you would see children in these holding centers looking up in the sky," he says. "Not just one child, it's like every child, they just look up."
Joshi saw flashes of hope on their faces.
"A hope that the security forces will find their family members trapped beneath the rubble or stranded somewhere," he says. "Every helicopter carries, even for a moment, the possibility that someone they love might be found."
Many survivors are holding onto that hope for the thousands still missing, he says, and struggling to come to terms with what's been lost.
"One girl that I spoke to told me that she could not sleep because she had seen four of her best friends being washed away by the flood. She was also separated from her parents while staying at the holding center," he says. "You can imagine the emotional burden that a child has to carry in this situation."
UNICEF's Gurung spoke to one woman who was rescued by a helicopter and who seemed in a state of shock. "I asked 'How are you?' and the response I got was, 'The dead are gone, I am the one alive,' " says Gurung. "I asked, 'Are you OK?' and she said, "I lost my children.'"
Save the Children and other responders are trying to provide support for that acute psychological distress, sending in counselors and providing mental health support at the shelters. But Joshi says mental health care is often treated as an afterthought in disaster situations, and resources can get pulled before people have fully made sense of the trauma.
"It's something that no one talks about, and it has a prolonged, long-term effect," he says. "The focus must go beyond immediate relief."

Small robots and drones have increasingly been used to help respond to disasters, reaching locations that are too hard or too dangerous to send humans, such as collapsed buildings. Many of these efforts have been focused on search and rescue. But new research shows how bugs—with their ability to crawl through even narrower gaps in rubbled—outfitted with electrodes could be used as the next generation of first responders.
A research team from the University of Queensland (UQ) and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) have developed the “Paraborg” to not only help with searching for victims, but also administer first aid. While the idea of receiving medical care from a cockroach might be a little skin-crawling, the new cyborg bug could one day help buy human rescuers valuable time in a disaster zone.
“Cyborg insects have been designed for ‘search and explore’ missions for the past couple of decades,” Tan Vo Doan, a bio-robotics researcher at UQ, says in a press release. “We wanted to take the next step.”
The team relied on a giant burrowing cockroach that inhabits northern Queensland to develop the Paraborg, which they documented in a recent paper published the journal Advanced Science. The armored cockroach is up to 87 millimeters (3.5 inches) in length and weighs up to 40 grams (1.4 ounces).
Taking advantage of this large size, the research team developed two types of Paraborgs with different functions: one equipped with a camera to film the condition of disaster victims, and another with an automatic injection mechanism to administer medication. Cockroaches can carry up to 1.5 times its body weight. In practice, a cockroach equipped with the injection mechanism saw its total height increase by about 15 millimeters and its weight by about 17 grams, which the study found did not significantly impair its normal movements. To create the cyborg cockroaches, the team anesthetized them when the electrodes and microchips were attached, and they lived as normal cockroaches once the equipment was removed.
By applying electrical stimuli to electrodes embedded in the cockroach’s antennae and cerci—a pair of protruding sensory organs at the rear of the abdomen—researchers were able to remotely control the bug’s direction of travel and walking speed.
They were able to steer the roach by stimulating each antenna independently, while stimulating both cerci controlled the pace. The scientists administered different frequencies between 10 and 40 hertz after finding that anything over 50 hertz became ineffective over time.
The injection mechanism is a small device that deploys a syringe using a spring system. That triggers a process that breaks the seal between a chamber containing citric acid and another containing baking soda. The resulting chemical reaction—basically the same one you might’ve done as a kid to make a volcano with baking soda and vinegar—creates enough carbon dioxide to push the plunger on the syringe and administer medication.
For the study, the research team remotely controlled a cockroach to travel from its starting point through three checkpoints and administer an injection to a simulated target.
The results showed that the success rate for injections made at close range—within 150 millimeters of the target—topped out at approximately 95 percent. The success rate for the entire sequence of tasks—from departure to completion of the injection—was 72 percent.
The researchers also successfully demonstrated teamwork, where one cockroach uses a camera to locate a simulated target while another serves as the injector.
Although the research team has previously developed cyborg beetles capable of climbing vertical walls, they note that larger cockroaches are better-suited for carrying specialized rescue and medical equipment.
While the results of the new research are promising, the experiment didn’t replicate the complex environmental conditions found at actual disaster sites, such as debris, uneven terrain, and shifting landscapes.
Vo Doan expressed hope that, if resources can be secured to speed up research and field testing, a rescue team of cyborg insects could be deployed at actual disaster sites within five to 10 years.
“Rather than building one robot to do everything, we can harness the natural strengths of different insects and equip them for different missions,” Vo-Doan says.

J. D. Vance’s Disingenuous Defense of Tucker Carlson
The vice president’s relationship with a conspiracy theorist is, at bottom, a political partnership, not a personal friendship.
When J. D. Vance was asked at a press conference on Thursday about his relationship with Tucker Carlson, the media personality and ultra-right-wing conspiracy theorist, he displayed a surprising side of himself: human, vulnerable, almost touchingly naive.
“Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go. And if you have a disagreement with somebody politically, even over a deeply held issue, you should still be friends with that person, because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another.”
This was a matter not of politics, Vance was at pains to emphasize, but of friendship. If Vance were to renounce Carlson over a matter as trivial as, say, Carlson’s oddly positive assessment of Adolf Hitler, what hope is there for society? The bonds of affection between Vance and Carlson are the very glue holding together the American experiment.
And yet, tempting though it might be to imagine Vance clasping hands with the children of the world and teaching them to sing in perfect harmony, some notes of skepticism are warranted. Perhaps Vance’s affection for Carlson has more to do with holding the loyalty of his friend’s enormous audience.
For one, Vance is not known for cordially disagreeing with people. He has accumulated an unusual number of bitter enemies by flinging insults at people—including Senate Democrats (“You’re full of shit, and everyone knows it”), reporters (“scumbags”), and “childless cat ladies.” Last month, Vance hurled himself into an obscure debate over burrito prices to make a gratuitous swipe at a conservative Washington Post columnist’s weight.
At the very same press conference where he waxed so earnestly about open dialogue, Vance mocked the idea that he would talk to former President Biden at the 9/11 ceremony (“I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden. I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations, and it’ll be great”) and dismissed the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as “a crazy person.”
Vance’s dig at El-Sayed, and the context in which he made it, revealed a lot more about his reasons for maintaining the alliance with Carlson than did his encomium to friendship. Vance was trying to illustrate that he and Carlson do not agree on everything. Carlson had recently praised El-Sayed as “America First” and “literally Trumpian,” apparently calculating that the candidate’s anti-Zionism outweighs his many left-wing positions.
That view was the one Vance chose to highlight as his point of disagreement, rather than several other controversial remarks Carlson has made. Examples include but are not limited to his endorsement of “Great Replacement” and other conspiracy theories, his expressions of sympathy for Russia and its war against Ukraine, and his sympathetic interviews with figures such as Nick Fuentes, Alex Jones, and the World War II–revisionist historian Darryl Cooper, who called Winston Churchill “the chief villain of the Second World War” and described much of the Holocaust as mistaken deaths resulting from poor planning.
All of these statements have left Carlson teetering at the edge of respectability within the Republican Party. He has become one of the most prominent exponents of a strain of right-wing populism that flirts with and in some cases embraces isolationism, anti-Semitism, and general crackpottery. Vance has courted this faction of the right. He and Carlson have a partnership that has lasted nearly a decade and has yielded dozens of interviews.
In the course of this partnership, they may well have formed a genuine friendship. But Vance has discarded plenty of friends as he has cycled through various political identities. The difference between Vance’s ex-friends and Carlson is that Carlson is still a useful ally in a Republican factional conflict. When Carlson upset Fox News in 2021 by endorsing the Great Replacement theory, which holds that Democrats are using illegal immigration to replace the current electorate and cement power, Vance wrote on social media, “Tucker Carlson is the only powerful figure who consistently challenges elite dogma—on both cultural and economic questions. That is why they try to destroy him. Don’t fall for it this time, or any other.”
Vance went on to endorse the same theory in advance of the next midterm elections. “Democrat politicians who have decided that they can’t win reelection in 2022 unless they bring in a large number of new voters to replace the voters that are already here” are orchestrating lax border enforcement, he said on Carlson’s show that year.
The Carlson-Vance partnership has generated more conservative blowback over the past few years as Carlson has progressed from skepticism of Israel into anti-Semitism, which Carlson denies. Traditional Republicans who have supported, or at least gone along with, the party’s attacks on Muslims and immigrants and its rejection of democratic norms have spoken out against cracking the door open for anti-Semites. Building an authoritarian, ultranationalist party that marinates in populist conspiracy theories but that abhors anti-Semitism turns out to be tricky.
Vance, heading into his expected 2028 presidential campaign, has a strong incentive to try to harness this right-wing energy. His political interests would be served if Republicans were to stop attacking Carlson and if Carlson were to tone down his criticism of the GOP. Hence, he seemed less concerned that Carlson had crossed a moral line than that, in the Michigan Senate race, he had crossed party lines. Carlson praising a member of the Democratic Party is more threatening to Vance than Carlson praising an apologist for the National Socialist German Workers’ Party.
At this week’s press conference, the reporter asked Vance, “What do you say to those who are uneasy with your close relationship with Carlson and claim that you’re avoiding addressing a lot of these issues, which may be causing divisions within the GOP?”
“What a travesty it is that in the United States of America, we let political disagreements define who our friends are going to be and not going to be,” Vance said. “So, yeah, Tucker is a friend of mine.”
Suppose Carlson decided to support someone other than Vance for president in 2028. Does anybody think their friendship would survive?

Liverpool target Minteh can still get dream move - Hurzeler
- Published
Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler says Yankuba Minteh could still "fulfil his dream" move in the future after the club rejected Liverpool's offers in the transfer window.
The Reds had bids of £50m and £60m turned down for the winger, with Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola having wanted to bolster his attacking options.
It is understood Brighton were seeking closer to £70m for the 22‑year‑old Gambia international.
Minteh, who joined from Newcastle for £30m in 2024, plays primarily on the right and has scored 10 goals and supplied nine assists in 73 Seagulls appearances.
Speaking before Saturday's Premier League game against Leeds, Hurzeler said: "If the whole team is successful and the individual shines then Yankuba will get a lot of attention again and he can then maybe fulfil his dream in the next transfer window."
- Premier League breaks transfer record for second straight summer 
  - Published3 days ago

Hurzeler said Minteh is "definitely" committed to Brighton despite the failed move to Merseyside.
"He wears the Brighton colours, he wears the Brighton badge. He has been with us for two years now as part of the squad. He has achieved great things together with the boys," said the German.
"It's also about him now to commit. In the end, we always say we want to be successful as a club and then you can shine as individuals.

"He has this motivation of wanting to improve every day," said Hurzeler.
"He comes on the first day and wants to go outside on the pitch, he wants to have ball touches and you can really feel that he is very ambitious...

Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posts bail after arrest
MANILA, Philippines — Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail Saturday after an order was issued for her arrest the previous day on charges that she publicly threatened to arrange the assassination of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and two other people.
Emerging in a black outfit from Quezon City Regional Trial Court in Metro Manila, Duterte consoled her supporters, hugging a woman who was sobbing as supporters chanted "Duterte! Duterte!"
The vice president, who has denied the allegations, showed a court order lifting the arrest warrant issued by the court Friday and said her lawyers instructed her to keep a copy on hand. She urged journalists to surround her on the way to her car because she did not feel safe.
"If possible please go with me, because I do not feel safe with all these police personnel who are harassing those at my home, harassing me since 2023," Duterte said. "What does this administration really want to do with me?"
Paul Lawrence Lim, one of her attorneys, said court staff took Duterte's fingerprints and she posted 360,000 pesos bail ($5,740) for three counts of grave threats.
After the arrest order was issued Friday, he said Duterte would fight the charges.
"She has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies," he said in a statement.
Case based on comments during online news conference
The case is seen as part of a high-stakes political showdown pitting Duterte against Marcos. A conviction may permanently disqualify her from holding public office and prohibit her from seeking the presidency in 2028, when Marcos's six-year term ends.
The charges stem from an alleged threat Duterte, 48, made during a 2024 online news conference. She said she would have Marcos, his wife and then-House of Representatives Speaker Martin Romualdez killed by an assassin if she herself was killed as their political disputes escalated.
The vice president warned during the event that her threat was not a joke.
Duterte later said she was expressing concern for her own safety and not threatening Marcos as the remarks set off a criminal investigation and national security concerns.
The House of Representatives, which is dominated by Marcos' allies, voted overwhelmingly in May to impeach Duterte over allegations of unexplained wealth, misuse of confidential state funds and the online news conference threats. The Philippine Senate, acting as an impeachment court, opened her televised trial in July.
Former political partners turned rivals
Marcos and Duterte were running mates in the 2022 elections in an alliance that combined two of the country's most formidable political dynasties.
Marcos is the son of former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., who held the office from the 1960s to the 1980s, including a period of repression and martial law. The vice president is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the predecessor to the current President Marcos.
Rodrigo Duterte was arrested in 2025 on orders of the International Criminal Court and detained in The Hague, where he is scheduled to face a trial beginning in late November over alleged crimes against humanity connected to a brutal anti-drugs crackdowns that left thousands of mostly poor suspects dead. He has denied authorizing extrajudicial killings but repeatedly threatened suspects with death while in office.
Sara Duterte previously criticized the Marcos administration for surrendering her father to a foreign court, which currently has no jurisdiction over the Philippines.
Marcos and Sara Duterte also have contrasting geopolitical leanings.
Marcos has expanded defense engagements with the United States, a treaty ally of the Philippines, as his administration stood up to China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea.
The vice president has come under fire for not condemning China's assaults, including with the use of powerful water cannons, against Filipino forces and fishermen in the disputed waters.

Clashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel movement killed more than 60 people, including civilians, as the Houthis pushed forward with a military offensive on Yemen’s western coast.
Twenty-six government troops and 31 Houthi fighters were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s south-west on Saturday, medical and military sources told Agence France-Presse (AFP). A missile strike also killed six civilians and injured seven others travelling by bus in the city of Taiz.
The killings were the latest in a series of bloody clashes in recent days as the Houthis continued an offensive in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast. On Friday, 129 were killed in fighting between rebel and government forces, according to an AFP tally.
The fighting is some of the deadliest in years, after the collapse in July of the 2022 ceasefire. The truce fell apart after an Iranian plane attempted to land in Houthi-controlled Sana’a, triggering attacks by the Yemeni government on the airport.
The Houthis are trying to beat back governmental troops to capture strategic hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb in order to advance towards port cities on the coast. So far, they have managed to capture areas in western Taiz.
In Taiz, a government military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” as the Houthis had taken positions near the city a day before. They added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden to try to stem the Houthi advance.
On Friday, government forces said that they had recaptured the al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills west of Taiz, two strategically important areas for controlling the region.
The Houthis had previously controlled the port city of al-Makha overlooking Bab al-Mandeb, before being pushed out by government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition.
The Bab al-Mandeb strait is a crucial maritime chokepoint for ships heading to the Suez canal. About 10% of global maritime trade passes through the strait. Saudi Arabia has been using the strait to export oil for months after the start of the US-Iran war.
If shipping is disrupted in Bab al-Mandeb, it will only further raise the cost of global goods, which has already rocketed as a result of the virtual closure of the strait of Hormuz since March 2026.
If the Houthis manage to recapture the port city and take key areas along the Red Sea coast, it will help them control naval traffic in the Red Sea. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, and they have repeatedly disrupted traffic in solidarity with Gaza since the start of the war there in October 2023.
Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis and allied forces took the capital city of Sana’a and pushed the then government out of power. A Saudi-led coalition then began a military intervention to support the Yemeni government and fight the Houthis, a strategic ally of Iran.
At least 150,000 people in Yemen have been killed in the fighting, and hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes such as hunger and diseases. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by the fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN.
