Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms. Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.
Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.
One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.

Hobart City Council slams trial of statewide building portal PlanBuild
In short:
A new planning portal meant to speed up development approvals has turned into a state government debacle.
PlanBuild was intended as an easy-to-use online catch-all for building development applications, replacing the paper-based system, but the scheme's trial adopter, Hobart City Council, has labelled it "unfit for purpose".
What's next?
The department behind the trial says it is working to fix "user functionality issues" before rolling it out statewide.
The Tasmanian government has suffered a $6.5 million cost blowout on its signature PlanBuild program, a new planning portal that was meant to speed up development approvals but has turned into a debacle.
PlanBuild was intended to be rolled out statewide.
Hobart City Council was the first to adopt the system when it went live in 2024, but the council says its implementation has frustrated council staff, residents and industry alike.
On Monday, the council unanimously backed a motion expressing its concern.
The motion described PlanBuild as "unfit for purpose", and called for an indefinite waiver of the annual $83,000 in fees paid to the Department of Justice — which runs the program — until the system is fixed.
Hobart councillor Louise Elliott, who introduced the motion and has been campaigning on the issue of planning costs and delays, described PlanBuild as "lose, lose, lose".
"Everyone's losing. [Hobart City Council] lose because it's a system that we have and people quite rightly think that it's our system, so we bear the heat and the reputational impact of that," she said.
"The taxpayers lose because we've now spent [more than] $12 million and 10 years on a system that is making people pull their hair out, and the community loses because it's another deterrent and another barrier to housing."
The motion was supported by the council administration, who conceded the program's launch had been "very difficult for officers and applicants".
Scheme 'not up to scratch'
PlanBuild was conceived more than a decade ago, when former premier Peter Gutwein was treasurer and planning minister.
Mr Gutwein had pushed for a uniform statewide planning scheme to cover Tasmania's 29 councils. The idea was to roll out a streamlined, easy-to-use online portal for all building, plumbing and development applications, replacing the paper-based system.
Work started in the 2016-17 financial year, with a budget of $9.7 million — including $6.4 million in Commonwealth Small Business Regulatory Reform Agenda funding — after external tenders were called for by the Consumer, Building and Occupational Services (CBOS) arm of the Justice Department.
According to Benjamin Price, executive director of the Tasmanian branch of the Housing Industry Association, there was strong support at the outset.
"We were big backers of PlanBuild when it was initially brought to industry's attention," Mr Price said.
"We're still wedded to the PlanBuild promise: something that will make it simpler, easier, quicker to manage applications right across the state."
Unfortunately, the trial has not gone well.
"Our members right across Tasmania and particularly here in the south have been saying that PlanBuild is not up to scratch," Mr Price said.
"It's not working as intended and it's not making their lives easier, [and it] isn't delivering the efficiencies that the Tasmanian government had promised.
"What we've seen is a clunky product that isn't delivering benefits to industry and isn't delivering benefits in the Hobart community."
Maree Ashworth, client liaison officer for Hobart-based builders Ronald Young + Co Builders, deals with the PlanBuild system daily, and said she finds it incredibly frustrating.
Ms Ashworth told the ABC that for builds within the City of Hobart, her company hands the documentation over to somebody else to lodge through PlanBuild.
"We would rather put the projects to a planner, than use the system,"
That preference means added costs on all sides.
Mr Price echoed her concerns.
"We hear feedback from members who are architects, designers, builders and plumbers that the PlanBuild portal is too difficult to use," he said.
"We even hear from some members that they are charging more to do work in the City of Hobart area."
Escalating costs
Last year the Justice Department waived the fee for 2025-26 in recognition that the system was not working, after a similar motion by Cr Elliott was passed by Hobart City Council.
In May, the department agreed to a PlanBuild remediation project plan. The plan, obtained by the ABC, aimed to address the council's concerns by February 2027 and lay the foundation for a statewide rollout.
In June, CBOS executive director Robyn Pearce told a parliamentary estimates committee hearing: "We're working with City of Hobart to ensure that some of the user functionality issues that are being addressed are put into place [and] we'll then be looking to roll it out to further councils."
She conceded the PlanBuild budget had increased from the original $9.7 million to $12.8 million.
The $3.1 million difference was attributed mainly to delays with the rollout, which led to a loss of expected revenue from other councils due to take up the scheme.
Additionally, only $3 million of the expected $6.4 million in Commonwealth funding was received, with the final $3.4 million withheld due to the expiry of the original grant.
That blowout has left the state's taxpayers $6.5 million worse off, as the original expected state outlay of $3.3 million has now risen to $9.8 million — a three-fold increase.
In correspondence with Cr Elliott, a spokesperson for the Justice Department said the total spending to date was just more than $11.6 million, of which some $3.45 million had been paid to the external developer.
"Rollout of the system to further councils remains on hold while post-implementation system enhancements are completed," the departmental spokesperson said.
"The final cost of statewide implementation cannot be determined at this point."
Cr Elliott told the ABC that despite the remediation work underway, "I do have genuine concerns that even with that extra work and the extra time and the extra money that it absorbs that we still won't end up with a product that's fit for purpose".
'Sold a pup', council says
At Monday's meeting, Cr John Kelly told the council that PlanBuild was a "disgrace".
"We have been sold a pup. We've got to toughen up here and really put our foot down with state government," he said.
"I note that we are a little bit of a laughing stock out there, not only among the building industry [but] also other councils.
"Other councils in Tasmania … don't want to touch this with a 40-foot barge pole. That is how bad this is."
Hobart councillor Ryan Posselt told the meeting the PlanBuild experience was comparable with the epic Spirit of Tasmania debacle.
"[It's] kind of analogous to the Spirits," Cr Posselt said.
"We are bearing the reputational damage, frankly. We also desperately need homes constructed in the city and commercial buildings constructed in the city."
The ABC understands PlanBuild has experienced a heavy turnover of staff within CBOS amid budget cuts and a hiring freeze at the Justice Department.
The Minister for Justice, Corrections and Rehabilitation, Guy Barnett, told the ABC he was aware of concerns with PlanBuild, and that an additional $2 million had been committed in the recent state budget to "deliver a pathway forward".
"I have asked my Department to work with City of Hobart as a high priority to correct bugs in the system," he said.
"I understand that we are seeing some important improvements to the functionality, but work is ongoing.
"We'll continue to work closely with the local government sector to pursue opportunities to have development applications and permits processed faster."

At our first dinner on Hurtigruten's MS Trollfjord, my parents and I spent most of the meal imagining what my 3-year-old son would have thought.
Aksel would have picked at the bread, asked how many courses of "real food" were left before dessert, and probably driven his Hot Wheels through the butter.
Instead, he stayed home in Denmark with my husband while my mom, dad, and I sailed south from Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago in the High Arctic.
Outside, black mountains and sharp cliffs rose from the Arctic waters. Inside, the aquavit was so strong my mother took one sip, winced, and passed the glass to my father.
Since Aksel was born, I hadn't spent more than a few hours alone with my parents. Without his commentary and toy cars, the quiet felt unsettling.
My parents are grandparents in short bursts. They fly from Connecticut to Copenhagen, where my husband and I have lived for almost a decade, spend a few jet-lagged weeks with us, then go months without seeing Aksel except on FaceTime.
When Aksel was born, they became "Momma G" and "Poppy," and I became "Momma." When they visit, he becomes the main event.
With an ocean between us, they get little time simply to be my parents.
Traveling with my parents made me feel like their daughter again
Before we boarded the ship, we spent three days in Longyearbyen, Svalbard's largest settlement. My parents rarely visit Europe, except to see us.
Svalbard was far from their usual trip to Copenhagen, and they were in awe. On the drive from the airport, my mother leaned so close to the taxi window that her breath fogged the glass. My father kept asking how dark it gets in winter and how the grocery store gets fresh fruit.
Years of solo travel before marriage and motherhood made me efficient but jaded. Seeing Svalbard through my parents' eyes made travel feel extraordinary again.
Their reminders ("Drink water!", "Stay warm!", "Let me carry that!") instantly took me back to high school. A few years ago, I would have rolled my eyes. Now I ask Aksel if he's hungry while he's in the middle of eating.
One afternoon, my mother told me she couldn't remember the last time she had felt so relaxed on vacation.
I laughed because my mom does not relax on vacation. She anticipates everyone's needs and helps before anyone asks. When she visits Denmark, she dresses and feeds Aksel, fully embracing her role as grandmother.
For once, nobody needed anything from either of us. She could drink her coffee and watch the fjords while I sat beside her with nothing to manage. That slower pace of the sailing helped make the week restorative.
We talked about work, family, health, and how my experience of motherhood across an ocean had been both wonderful and disorienting after years of fierce independence.
We also got on each other's nerves. My parents kept asking the same questions, and I grew impatient at times.
But I had missed having enough time together to stop being on our best behavior. They knew me before I had a career, a husband, a Danish address, or anyone calling me Momma.
I realized I couldn't keep saving trips with my parents for later
I missed Aksel, but I knew the trip would have been different with him there: snacks and dropped forks at dinner, bathroom breaks, and tired legs on excursions.
My parents and I would have traveled as a mother and two grandparents.
Living in Denmark while my parents are in Connecticut makes every visit feel too short. The distance makes time more visible. Aksel changes between FaceTime calls, and each visit reminds me that my parents are aging, too.
I want Aksel to know his grandparents beyond a screen, but I also want time alone with the people who raised me. As an immigrant, I rarely feel there is enough time for both.
We talk about how quickly childhood passes, but less about how limited our time with our own parents can feel. They won't always be able to join me on adventures like this.
I didn't leave Aksel home because I needed a break from motherhood. I left him at home because my parents could still make the trip, and I couldn't assume we'd get another chance.
When I returned, Aksel wrapped his arms around me before I had taken off my coat and showed me a toy car I had seen dozens of times.
On our next family trip, he will probably be at the center of everything, and I will be glad he's there. But for one week, my parents didn't have to be Momma G and Poppy, and I didn't have to organize every day around a toddler.

Etsy seller's 'bruh' T-shirts were removed over a trademark complaint. He says it's trademark squatting
Seller says person who complained registered trademark in bad faith — something trademark holder denies
When Sam Joseph Karam received an email from online retailer Etsy saying 11 of his T-shirt designs bearing the slang term "bruh" had been taken down for a trademark violation, he was immediately suspicious.
"It's usually one or two listings. It's not 11 in a row. So that obviously caught our attention pretty quickly," Karam said.
Karam, who owns the U.S.-based apparel company Customized Designs and sells clothing on sites like Etsy, says the platform also revoked his Star Seller badge — a mark given by the platform that means the seller provides top-tier customer service. Following that, he says he noticed an immediate drop in sales.
In the email, Etsy told Karam the shirt had been reported by someone named Malik Yawar Abbas, who holds a Canadian trademark for the term "bruh."
Karam is one of multiple Etsy sellers who told CBC News they've had items taken down from the platform after their use of the word was reported by the trademark holder. CBC News reviewed multiple emails Etsy sent to Karam and two other sellers that showed the takedowns came in response to complaints by Abbas.
Karam says Abbas, the trademark holder, is "squatting" on the trademark, aiming to make money by licensing the use of the word to others rather than by making a product of his own. Some legal experts say it's up to platforms and the legal system to better prevent trademarks from being used in this way.
No clothes for sale, request for payment
A trademark for the word "bruh" was issued by the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) in July 2025 in connection with selling many kinds of clothing, according to the government's trademarks database. Another trademark for the same word was recently granted to Abbas for use in advertising restaurant services.
In an email to CBC News, CIPO did not answer questions about the "bruh" trademark, but said each trademark application the office receives is "examined on a case-by-case basis."
After the listings were removed, Karam found the trademark holder's website and was surprised to find a section detailing how he protects the "bruh" trademark and directing others to license with him in order to get permission to use it.
"We didn't invent the word. the streets did. the internet did. but we realized its power," the site reads.
The site doesn't offer clothes for sale — just mock-ups of clothing and items like energy drinks using the word "bruh."
In an email to CBC News, trademark holder Abbas said those images are there to show "potential commercial applications" of the brand.
When Karam contacted Abbas about the Etsy takedowns to see if he would withdraw his complaint, Abbas said he would if Karam agreed to a number of terms and paid him $1,000.
Karam refused, and says the signs in this case all point toward what he says is "trademark squatting."
"It's quite disheartening," Karam said. "When you have someone immediately turn around and say, 'I want $1,000, simply to go back and retract my complaint,' you know right there that they're acting in bad faith. That's my personal belief."
Abbas told CBC News via email that the $1,000 was a proposed settlement that was "part of a negotiated resolution of a disputed trademark matter. It was not paid, and no monetary settlement was concluded."
He also disagrees with the idea that he is squatting on the trademark.
"BRUH is a lawfully registered Canadian trademark being developed as a commercial licensing brand," Abbas wrote.
He has since withdrawn the complaint to Etsy, which he says he did after the 11 designs were removed and those products were no longer being offered to Canadian consumers.
But Karam says the "damage has been done."
He is currently in contact with an intellectual property lawyer and is considering taking legal action to try to invalidate the trademark on the basis of bad faith.
Bad faith trademarks can be taken down
Under a relatively new part of Canada's trademark laws added in 2019, a trademark can be invalidated if it was filed in "bad faith," explains Carys Craig, a professor at York University's Osgoode Hall Law School specializing in intellectual property law.
While cases arguing bad faith have popped up, she says this part of the law is still somewhat untested, so she's not sure what a court might decide in this case.
Craig says licensing can be a valid way of using a trademark. Overall, she says the way the "bruh" trademark is being presented on the website, along with the takedown orders that are being sought, might be enough to reach the standard of bad faith.
"We just don't quite know what that looks like yet."
Abbas told CBC News he trademarked the term in order to build a "licensing-only brand at the time when there was no BRUH-named brand in Canada," and disagrees that "protecting, enforcing or commercially developing" the brand should be characterized as bad faith.
"If there is a genuine disagreement about the validity, scope, or infringement of the registration, Canadian law provides mechanisms and forums to determine those issues," he said.
Does a trademark mean you own a word?
Despite broad use, general terms and pop culture phrases can be trademarked — it all depends on the context, according to Craig.
The point of a trademark is to differentiate the products or services of one brand from those of another, she explains. So a word like "apple" can't be trademarked to sell fruit because it's simply describing the product, but to sell computers, it works just fine.
There are some other criteria that are considered during a trademark application, but Craig says that because "bruh" isn't describing the product in this case, the word could reasonably function as a trademark.
But trademarking something doesn't mean you own it outright, and experts say the "bruh" clothes on Etsy might not necessarily be infringing just because they use the word.
Paula Clancy, an intellectual property law partner at Gowling WLG, says for courts to determine if there was infringement, they would look at how the alleged infringer was using the trademark — either as a source of origin, to appear as though it was from a specific brand, or in an ornamental way, as part of a design.
Shirts with phrases like "Bruh, we back," which Karam had taken down, "might well fall within those exceptions," Clancy said — meaning they might not infringe.
Despite that, Karam says Etsy didn't give him a way to appeal its decision to take the products down.
For his part, Abbas said he reported listings to Etsy when he "reasonably believed" the listings might conflict with his trademark rights, and never intended to "prevent people from using the word in ordinary speech or everyday communication."
In an email to CBC News, an Etsy spokesperson said the platform assesses and removes items when it receives proper notice of infringement and said sellers are responsible for following all laws and site rules. The spokesperson said sellers should reach out to the person who made the initial complaint if they think their listing shouldn't have been removed.
Clancy says she understands why platforms like Etsy take these trademark takedown requests seriously, but she says a policy that doesn't allow for appeals poses a challenge for sellers who are unlikely to take on the expense of going through the courts.
Testing boundaries of trademark system
Clancy says cases like this are rare in Canada.
"Usually, we see the other way around. We see the infringers using marks without authorization," she said, noting that some people will try to piggyback on the reputation of an established brand.
But Craig worries that because trademark disputes can be so costly, especially for small businesses, cases of trademark squatting or over-enforcement might fly under the radar more often than we think.
She also points out that despite objections from Etsy sellers, the trademark holder in this case has walked a "careful line" that could still be potentially within the bounds of the law, given they were granted the trademark rights and licensing trademarks is allowed.
"This is really testing the sort of boundaries of that trademark system and exploiting some of the … policy weaknesses or loopholes within the system," Craig said.
She says tighter rules might be needed to prevent these kinds of situations. More care might be required in the initial stages of issuing trademarks, she says, especially when it comes to zeitgeist-y phrases where there might be more incentive to try to corner them.
Easier processes for challenging possible bad-faith trademarks, and changes to online marketplaces that allow sellers to appeal trademark takedowns, might also help, according to Craig.
She called it a "worst case scenario" to be in a place where everything is protected, nothing is actually litigated and "everything is automatically taken down as soon as a trademark owner claims their rights."

On August 21, CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka and his colleagues were attacked while visiting a village in Rajasthan under the ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign. The next day, local BJP MLA Kailash Verma gave his version of the incident to the media, placing the entire blame on CJP.
Verma claimed that “around 100 to 150 CJP workers arrived in 30-40 vehicles and descended on the village, terrorising its residents.” He went so far as to allege that CJP workers themselves pelted stones at their own vehicles and smashed the windows merely to garner sympathy.
100-150 लोग आते है गाव वालो के हाथापाई करते है और खुद वीडियो बनाने के लिए खुद पत्थर फेकते है खुद की गाडिया खुद तोड लेते है चोरी और सीनाजोरी दोनो करने के बावजूद आप 48 घंटे का अल्टीमेटम देते हो

मगर वीडियो मे सबसे मजेदार बात ये है जो शख्स गाडियो… pic.twitter.com/yVfoBqZnu5
— एक नजर (@1K_Nazar) August 22, 2026

The same man is also seen beating another person with a stick. Crucially, he later told a camera that he was with the BJP. He was also standing alongside Kailash Verma when the BJP MLA addressed the media.
What Happened in Rajasthan?
CJP workers, led by Ashutosh Ranka, had travelled to Rampura-Kanwarpura village in Rajasthan’s Jaipur district to inspect a government school. They said the school had been operating for several years from a buffalo shed and was in a deplorable condition.
All levels of disgust have been crossed today.
रामपुरा, कंवरपुरा में पिछले काफ़ी सालों से स्कूल भैंसों के तबेले में चल रहा है। लेकिन जब हम वहाँ निरीक्षण करने पहुंचे तो सरेआम मारपीट, पत्थरबाजी की गई। कारों के शीशे फोड़े गए, टीम पर पत्थर बरसाये गए। कपड़े फाड़े गए। ट्यूब में पत्थर… pic.twitter.com/H15osb1ODA

Soon after the team entered the village, however, some people allegedly surrounded the CJP workers. They were allegedly pushed and assaulted, stones were thrown at them, and the windows of their vehicles were smashed. Ranka posted videos of the incident on X.

Ranka said an angry mob broke the hands of several CJP workers, severely damaged their vehicles and pelted stones at women members of the team. He described the incident as a pre-planned conspiracy and accused the police administration of remaining silent spectators.
BJP MLA Kailash Verma, however, presented a diametrically opposite version. He claimed that a large number of CJP workers had attacked the villagers, but offered no evidence to substantiate the allegation.
Significantly, as Verma addressed the media, the man clearly seen in the videos attacking CJP vehicles and smashing their windows was standing right beside him.
The Man Smashing CJP Vehicles
The man is seen attacking at least two vehicles from behind and smashing their windows. The video below corroborates this.
सर जी इनका हाथ कैसे टूटा उसका सबूत इस विडियो मे है जब अपनी कोहनी की ताकत दिखाते हुए इन्होने गाडी को शीशा तोड दिया pic.twitter.com/sXRN6DLfWO

Speaking to the camera of News Nation, the man publicly said, “This is a BJP government, and we will remain with the BJP.”

How do u know they were BJP goons ?

It can be congress people too ,because we all know u r B team of AAP . So there might be chance .

However, a close examination of videos of the incident shared by Ashutosh Ranka on social media led to the identification of one prominent individual in the attacking crowd as Lalchand Sharma.

Kargil, Sep 06: Project Vijayak of the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) on Sunday kicked off its 16th Raising Day celebrations with a motorcycle rally from the its memorial here to Sapi La Pass in the Union Territory of Ladakh, an official said.
The rally, comprising 51 participants, was flagged off by retired Colonel V K Oberoi from the Project Vijayak Memorial in Kargil and culminated at Sapi La, located at an altitude of 14,337 feet, the official said.
He said the rally was attended by Deputy General Officer Commanding, 8-Mountain division, Brigadier Sarit Prakash, Chief Engineer, Project Vijayak, Brigadier Rahul Oberoi, Commander, 121 Infantry Brigade, Brigadier Ashish Joshi, besides officers and personnel from the Army, Project Vijayak and civil participants.
Brigadier Oberoi said Project Vijayak was raised on September 21, 2010, following recommendations of the Kargil War Review Committee, with the objective of improving connectivity across Ladakh region, particularly to forward areas and posts.
"The Project Vijayak has made significant contributions towards strengthening road infrastructure in the region. Several roads have been widened and upgraded from single-lane to double-lane standards, while new roads have been constructed to improve connectivity to forward locations," the chief engineer said.
He said the specifications and standards of National Highways have also been considerably improved, with several tunnel projects currently underway.
Oberoi said as part of the raising day celebrations, Project Vijayak organises motorcycle rallies every year to remember and pay tribute to the personnel who made the supreme sacrifice while serving the nation and developing vital road infrastructure in the challenging Himalayan region.
He said last year's rally had travelled to the Kargil War Memorial at Drass to honour the bravehearts of the Indian Army and the Border Roads Organisation.
Continuing the tradition this year, the rally travelled approximately 54 kilometres to Sapi La Pass, one of the important passes maintained by Project Vijayak in Western Ladakh and the Siachen sector, he said.
The rally culminated at Sapi La, where the Deputy GOC, 8 Mountain Division hoisted the National Flag.
Oberoi said the flag-hoisting ceremony at Sapi La was a proud occasion and a tribute to the brave personnel who sacrificed their lives in the service of the nation.
The Motorcycle Rally marked the beginning of the celebrations leading up to the 16th raising day of Project Vijayak on September 21, he said.

US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”
He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.
He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.
In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.
This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.
Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.
“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.
“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.
Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.
Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.
Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.
According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.
The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.
The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.
The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.
The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

Hong Kong to propel belt and road market expansion, finance chief says
Paul Chan’s pledge comes ahead of 11th Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong this week
Hong Kong will step up support for belt and road enterprises seeking to expand into new markets and tap regional growth, reinforcing its role as a pivotal business hub and platform for deeper exchanges, the city’s financial chief has said.
In his weekly blog on Sunday, Paul Chan Mo-po also pointed to strong growth in emerging markets and developing economies in recent years, citing International Monetary Fund projections of a further 3.8 per cent and 4.5 per cent expansion respectively over the coming two years.
“The gradual relocation of mainland China’s industrial chains towards belt and road regions is a response to this reality,” he wrote.
Chan made the remarks ahead of the 11th Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong this week. The annual event promotes business among participating nations in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s project to build a China-centred global trading network.
This year’s summit is being held under the theme “Advancing high-quality development, embarking on a new journey”. For the first time, there will be a dedicated “Go Global Chapter” to support mainland firms expanding overseas.
Mainland firms have established around 58,000 overseas entities, creating more than two million local jobs annually, with an investment stock of US$3.4 trillion, nearly 90 per cent of which is in developing economies, according to Chan.

US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Kyiv after talks to Putin in Moscow
Saturday’s meeting in Moscow lasted more than three hours behind closed doors and ended without announcements of any breakthroughs
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Their trip follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, seeking to revive peace talks during escalating aerial attacks by both sides.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday that Kyiv is ready for a “constructive” discussion with US representatives.
“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable post-war peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared,” he said in a post on Telegram.
The envoys arrived by train and were welcomed at the station in Ukraine’s capital by high-ranking Ukrainian officials, before being met by Zelensky at a ceremony in St. Sophia Square.
Washington’s push to end the fighting has lost momentum, with the United States focused for the past six months on the Iran war. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks to Putin at the Kremlin.

- You can unlock and upgrade Loot Hacks in Fortnite from the Override menu found in-game using Sprite Dust.
- A total of five Fortnite Loot Hacks can be active at any given time.
- You can refund Loot Hacks in Fortnite for free and get back any Sprite Dust that was spent.
Loot Hacks are a new feature to get loot pool items in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4. They can be purchased and upgraded to give you access to ‘hacked’ items in a Battle Royale or Zero Build match and are available for everyone to use. That said, here’s what you need to know about Loot Hacks in Fortnite and how to unlock and upgrade them.
What Are Loot Hacks in Fortnite?
Loot Hacks in Fortnite is a new feature used to unlock items, weapons, and consumables that you can activate to get from Chests in a Battle Royale match. These items/weapons are part of the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 loot pool, but they won’t appear unless they’re ‘hacked’ in or unlocked. Here’s a list of all current Loot Hacks in Fortnite:
- Caduceus Staff
- Scorpion’s Combat Kit
- Wrecker Revolver
- Deadeye Assault Rifle
- Holo Twister Assault Rifle
Up to five Loot Hacks can be activated at any given time. This could change as Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 progresses, and if it does, we’ll update the information. Until then, you can ‘hack’ in the aforementioned unique weapons/items in every match.
How to Unlock Loot Hacks in Fortnite
Loot Hacks can be unlocked by purchasing it with Sprite Dust in Fortnite. Sprite Dust is obtained in a variety of ways, with the easiest being extracting Sprites. You can also use a few Fortnite Lobby Hack (Admin Panel) Codes to earn some, if needed.
When you have enough Sprite Dust in Fortnite, click on the “Override” section at the top of your main lobby screen. Within this section, you can see Loot Hacks up for sale on the left side of the screen. On the right, you can see their drop rates.
Click on an item, and on the bottom right, an “Unlock” button will appear. Press it to unlock the Loot Hack in Fortnite. This enables it to appear in-game when searching Chests. You can also come across new Sprites in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 while searching Chests, so it’s a win-win situation.
That said, don’t expect to come across a ‘hacked’ weapon or item in every match. They are rather hard to come by. On a side note, we personally recommend unlocking the Caduceus Staff, allowing you to heal your teammates. Alternatively, you can try an Overshield Sprite in Fortnite to boost their defensive capabilities.
How to Upgrade Loot Hacks in Fortnite
To upgrade Loot Hacks, go to the “Override” section. Items/weapons that have been unlocked show an “Upgrade” option on the bottom right of the screen. You can use Sprite Dust to upgrade them one at a time.
Upgrading Loot Hacks in Fortnite improves their drop rate during a Battle Royale match. The more you upgrade, the higher your odds of receiving that particular item/weapon from Chests. If you need more Sprite Dust, consider extracting Cheat Master Sprites in Fortnite.
As a final note, purchasing and upgrading Loot Hacks in Fortnite is an expensive venture. Choose wisely before investing Sprite Dust, as Sprite Dust is needed to summon Sprites that were lost in a match. This includes the elusive Fortnite Crown Sprite.
Can You Reset Loot Hack Upgrades and Get Sprite Dust in Fortnite?
Yes, you can definitely reset Loot Hacks and get your Sprite Dust back in Fortnite. To do so, you need to press and hold the “Reset All Upgrades” button. It is located just below the unlock/upgrade options. Once Loot Hacks are reset, all Sprite Dust is refunded, which you can spend once again.
You can reset Loot Hacks as many times as you want. There is no limit and we’ve tested it out to confirm this feature. If you end up losing your precious Klombo Sprite in Fortnite and need Sprite Dust to bring it back, this is a quick fix you can apply.
Let us know in the comments below which Loot Hacks you’ve decided to purchase and upgrade in Fortnite.
Are Loot Hacks in Fortnite permanent?
No, Loot Hacks in Fortnite are subject to refresh every few days.

The story so far: India’s food regulator has proposed a red, hexagonal warning label on the front of packaged foods high in added sugar, saturated fat or salt, in a move aimed at giving consumers a simple, at-a-glance signal about unhealthy products.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), in an affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on August 28, has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages.
The proposal comes after years of debate over front-of-pack labelling and intervention by the Supreme Court. The Court is scheduled to consider the affidavit on September 10.
Also Read | FSSAI’s proposed warning labels could let unhealthy foods escape scrutiny, says expert
How the proposed system is expected to work?
FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages.
In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase.
The thresholds are proposed to be based on the Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024. However, the FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat.
Single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey, are also proposed to be exempt.
Also Read | Supreme Court slams FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products
What do critics say about the proposed change?
Nutrition advocates say the biggest concern is the decision to initially require a product to be high in two nutrients before it attracts a warning. A product that is high in sugar but low in salt and fat, for instance, could escape a warning altogether.
“This defeats the purpose of a warning label,” Arun Gupta, convenor of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPI), told The Hindu. He has argued for a simpler principle: if a product is high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, it should carry a warning.
Also Read | Why the FSSAI is also putting liquor under the scanner
The distinction could matter particularly for products such as sugary beverages, which may be high in added sugar but contain little or no fat or salt and could therefore fall outside the warning requirement in Phase I.
Dr. Gupta has also raised concerns over the use of “added” rather than total sugar and fat, the size of the proposed warning and the absence of a firm deadline for Phase II. He has called for the warnings to be available in Hindi and English, arguing that language and visibility are essential if the labels are to reach consumers across the country.
He has urged the Court to examine the proposed nutrient thresholds, definition of high-fat/sugar/salt foods, warning size, language requirements and exemptions to ensure that the system remains visible and scientifically robust.
Also Read | From Bournvita to ‘100% Pure’: Why is FSSAI tightening the rules on food claims?
Why is this significant?
Front-of-pack warning labels have been under discussion in India since at least 2018. Draft regulations on high fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods were proposed in 2022, but did not become law.
The issue returned to the centre of the public-health debate in 2026 after the Supreme Court directed FSSAI to move towards interpretive warning labels for unhealthy packaged foods.
The regulator’s approach has also evolved rapidly in recent weeks. An earlier proposal placed before the Court in August relied on displaying nutritional information against recommended daily limits. Following the Court’s intervention, FSSAI returned with the red-hexagon warning framework in its August 28 affidavit.
Also Read | FSSAI proposes front-of-pack red pictorial warnings for foods high in fat, sugar, salt
For consumers, the proposed red hexagon is intended to make it harder for marketing claims such as “natural” or “multigrain” to obscure the nutritional profile of a product.
For the food industry, mandatory warnings could increase pressure to reformulate products by reducing sugar, salt and saturated fat. FSSAI has said the phased approach would give industry time to reformulate.
But the proposal is not yet a notified regulation. The immediate question before the Supreme Court is whether the framework provides a clear and meaningful warning or leaves products high in a single nutrient outside the net for an unspecified period.

The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.
Slogans of “Godi Media” were raised during a gathering in the national capital Delhi. pic.twitter.com/oyZpCVz0EY
— The Nawakadal (@thenawakadal) July 20, 2026
Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!
Yesterday’s Massive Student Protest Delivered The Final Verdict:
Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!
Lakhs of Students who hit the streets got EVERY piece of Real Information from Social Media — not your Biased Propaganda Boxes.… pic.twitter.com/zLIOM5GXP1
— তন্ময় l T͞anmoy l (@tanmoyofc) July 21, 2026
As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.
Wonder whether these are genuine protestors or lumpen elements.https://t.co/Xo4bTJ1DgX
— 🍉 (@DelhiIsNotFar) July 21, 2026
In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.
You are the most vile, most pathetic, most disgusting person @sudhirchaudhary
I always agree to disagree, never hate anyone but you are really a bad person.
You are now labelling innocent students for your propaganda.
Shame on you! pic.twitter.com/lYj5cNlURk
— Arpit Sharma (@iArpitSpeaks) July 21, 2026
Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.
ALSO READ: The fictional strikes on the Karachi port and what it says about Indian media
A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.
Check the thumbnails in the compilations from 2022 below. Each and every bulletin represented by these thumbnails was on communal issues. All on News 18:

Shows hosted by Amish Devgan:
The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Vinoo Ganesh, the 34-year-old CEO of Kepler. He spent over six years at Palantir in the 2010s and later worked at Citadel. He's based in New York. It's been edited for length and clarity.
Palantir had a program we called Project Frontline. The idea behind Frontline was: How do we take software engineers and expose them to life as a forward-deployed engineer?
I actually went through a version of this before the program. I started off on the product development team, did a rotation that lasted for a long time as a forward-deployed engineer, then went back to the product development team.
I was running the program for a good chunk of time. We had a bunch of people go through it. Some folks stayed as forward-deployed engineers; some rotated back to becoming software engineers.
At the time, the state of the world was that forward-deployed engineers were moving really fast, and were very close to the customer. The software engineering team tended to be geographically — literally, some folks were in Palo Alto — culturally isolated from the urgency the FDE team had.
The idea was: walk a mile in the other person's shoes.
Palantir worked really hard to set all of these folks up for success. We would give them mentors. They would have two touch points: a forward-deployed engineering manager and a software engineering manager.
People loved it. They'd be in corporate housing for a few months, displaced somewhere other than their home office. It's not like every FDE went through this program; it was a set of software engineers who expressed interest.
We called it "business engineering" at Citadel. The goal was much more focused on internal portfolio managers and analysts. Palantir's FDEs are much more focused on customers external to the company. At Citadel, we were focused on folks internal to the organization.
It was still the same operating model: Citadel's engineering team has a core product, and our goal is to better inform its development by engaging with portfolio managers, analysts, and associates.
What other companies get wrong about FDEs
I've always modeled forward-deployed engineers as being an extension of the product team. Your job is to solve problems to gain product insights that inform product development.
Some people are modeling it — incorrectly, in my opinion — as sales engineers. Some people are modeling it as quota-carrying salespeople. I've seen everything from a forward-deployed equity researcher to a forward-deployed principal architect.
I think "FDE" is being used incorrectly as a stopgap for lack of product-market fit at some of these companies. Where I see it being used is to force customers to use your product that otherwise may not want to.
Palantir had a culture of autonomy and empowerment. If you identified a problem, you'd be able to be the agent of action and go solve that problem. That's what allowed FDEs to thrive.
I also think Palantir's product is almost perfect for the forward-deployed engineering ecosystem. You've built this horizontal platform that can work in a variety of industries, and FDEs are the individuals creating the vertical applications.
I'd be thinking about our product and whether or not it's relevant for an FDE function. I don't think of an FDE as a way of selling more tokens. I don't think of an FDE as a way to get users to use your product when they haven't had a pain point solved.
It's being used as a catch-all now for a combination of sales, customer success, or marketing functions to show that you care about customers.
I see a lot of organizations focused on trying to get their product in front of as many people as possible, whether or not that actually generates the compounding product returns.
The world isn't black and white. There's a whole bunch of middle grounds to what kind of FDE you need at what point in your trajectory. These are my opinions and not a formal statement around how Palantir did things.
I think this is the future of software engineering. If writing code isn't the differentiator anymore, the opportunity is: how do you understand customers deeply and viscerally?
It's really important to get software engineers globally more customer-aware. For me, the FDE is more of a mindset than a job title.

Indonesia cancels flights at Jakarta airport as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano has erupted, causing flight cancellations at Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports as volcanic ash drifted across parts of western Indonesia.
Indonesia’s Geological Agency said the volcanic island located in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m. Sunday. Closed-circuit camera footage showed lava flares from the volcano.
No casualties were reported and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the active crater.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra’s southern tip, Indonesia’s Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.
AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as four other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
By mid-afternoon, the closure had affected 516 flight movements, with 202 in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport alone that affected about 22,800 passengers, on Sunday. The airport was ordered closed until at least 5:30 p.m.
Indonesia’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation said it was closely monitoring the eruption's impact on air travel and coordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency.
“Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The eruption also disrupted services at Bali’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport and at Medan.
Indonesia’s volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery. One plume rose to 20,000 feet (6,100 meters) and drifted northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters. A second cloud reached 50,000 feet (15,200 meters) and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.
Lana Saria, head of Indonesia’s Geological Agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has intensified since July, with Sunday’s eruption the strongest during the current period of unrest.
The repeated eruptions indicate a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases beneath the volcano, she said, though officials cannot predict whether a larger eruption will occur.
“We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” Saria said in a video briefing.
She said the main hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas and the ejection of hot rocks and other material around the crater area.
Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau,” is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
The eruption caused a tsunami in 2018 that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Scientists said Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption.

Hello there from STAT’s Andrew Joseph, writing to you from London and filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for the day. We just picked up a new bag of coffee beans that boasts notes of cola, cherry, and grape, so we’ll have to see if we pick up on any of that when we grind them up for tomorrow’s cup of stimulation. For now, though, perhaps some headlines will suffice …
An experimental gene therapy for Angelman syndrome from Ultragenyx failed in a Phase 3 study, STAT reports. The medicine showed no benefit compared to a sham treatment in the rare disease, which causes severe intellectual disability and developmental delays. The drug, called GTX-102, had shown powerful results in early trials, raising the hopes of families affected by the devastating condition. The trial failure is also a significant blow to Ultragenyx’s business, and the company said it’s now planning “significant expense reductions.”
Just a week after the landmark U.S. approval of a game-changing drug for advanced pancreatic cancer, the same therapy is showing promise against the world’s biggest cancer killer, Nature tells us. In a small trial in non-small cell lung cancer, the drug, Revolutions Medicines’ Rasonque, shrank tumors in more than 30% of participants. Each patient had tumor-promoting mutations in a member of the RAS family of proteins, and had previously tried other therapies. A larger study in which participants with non-small cell lung cancer are randomly assigned to receive either the drug, also called daraxonrasib, or standard chemotherapy is underway.
