On Sunday, influencer Amanda Hirsch — the creator behind the popular “Not Skinny But Not Fat” podcast, who also hosts Hulu’s “Get Real” podcast — addressed the uproar about having posted partner content with the betting platform Polymarket over the Lindsay Clancy verdict. In a since-deleted post from Friday, after the judge in the case had declared a mistrial, Hirsch posted the news of what happened, and wrote: “On Polymarket it was predicted the verdict would be Not Guilty. Are you surprised? #Polymarketpartner.” 
The reaction to the post was swift and brutal, and Hirsch deleted the reel — but screenshots are forever. Hirsch attempted to post as usual to her Instagram stories on Saturday, but the criticism escalated. On Friday, Hirsch’s rep didn’t respond to Variety’s request for comment.
In the apology posted to her grid — with the comments turned off — Hirsch said, “Posting about the Lindsay Clancy trial in the same breath as a brand partnership was completely insensitive, wrong, and out of character for me — I should have known better, and I feel sick that I didn’t see that in the moment.” She wrote that, as a mother, the case had affected her, and she followed it constantly. “I became so consumed by the trial that I completely lost perspective and didn’t stop to think about how grossly inappropriate it was to discuss something this tragic in that context.”
“I made a terrible judgment call and I feel so fucking awful about that,” Hirsch continued. “I know deleting it doesn’t erase it. Believe me, I’m horrified by the choice I made and please know this lapse in judgment does not represent who I am as a person. I am so deeply sorry.”
	Several days before she’d posted the Polymarket sponsored content on Sept. 4, Hirsch had posted on IG about her conflicted feelings about the trial, which has become a true crime sensation. She expressed compassion for Clancy, and wrote “there were major issues with the investigation,” and then pushed back on the outlandish, unfounded accusations against Patrick Clancy, whom conspiracy theorists have accused of killing his three children (even though Lindsay has said she was at fault). Hirsch then wrote: “And this is where I feel like we’re losing the plot a little bit. Three babies were killed. They had their entire lives ahead of them. Yes, their mother was very sick. That is devastating. But it wasn’t their fault. They were strangled to death methodically and left to die in the basement.” 
Hirsch appeared to be arguing that the public should keep Lindsay Clancy’s children central to the narrative. She wrote that she didn’t know what should happen to Lindsay Clancy, “But the fan base, the GoFundMe, the way people are rallying behind her almost like she’s a celebrity genuinely scares me a little bit about where we are as a society. I just don’t want our compassion to somehow turn into excusing or minimizing what happened to her children.”
Hirsch soon had to turn the comments off on the post, though they remain on throughout the rest of her account — and are now littered with criticism of her for the Polymarket partnership.
The new world of betting prediction markets — led by Polymarket at Kalshi — have proven to be the unregulated Wild West. In the spring, Variety reported on how both companies spoiled who won “Survivor” in its 50th season, prompting the show’s host and showrunner Jeff Probst to slam the companies. “They have figured out a way to capitalize on [the show],” he told Variety. “It doesn’t sit well with me as a human. I get it — they built a great business. They don’t care.”
Given that the Clancy trial was declared a mistrial because there was one holdout juror who appeared not to agree that she was not guilty by reason of insanity, new conspiracy theories have sprung up about whether that juror was also placing bets in prediction markets.

How to check your PC's hard-drive health
A few built-in checks can tell you whether your HDD or SSD is showing signs of trouble.
Storage drives have a tendency to fail when you least expect it. A traditional hard drive may give you a warning with clicking or grinding sounds, but an SSD has no moving parts to make a fuss. Problems with either type can manifest as corrupted files, abnormally slow access, frequent read or write errors, crashes, or a drive that periodically disappears from Windows.
If any of that is already occurring, back up your important files before doing much else. Diagnostics are good, but it's not as much fun to recover the only copy of something when a drive dies.
Windows has several built-in methods for checking the health of drives, but the information it can provide will vary based on the hardware in the computer. Free utilities can go further and read the drive's Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology (SMART) data.
There is one limitation, though. A healthy status can be reassuring, but it's certainly not a lifetime guarantee.
See what Windows knows about your drive
The simplest way to get started in Windows 11 doesn't involve opening a terminal or feigning a love for command lines.
- Open Settings and choose System.
- Go to Storage > Advanced storage settings > Disks & volumes.
- Select your drive and choose Properties.
Windows can display estimated remaining life, available spare capacity and temperature for supported NVMe SSDs. It can also alert you if spare capacity is low, reliability has decreased or if the drive has gone into read-only mode.
There is one thing to look out for here. Microsoft says this health monitoring doesn't cover SATA SSDs or traditional hard drives. If Windows provides little or no health information, don't assume that it's a clean bill of health.
Another quick check can be done via PowerShell. Open a PowerShell tab in Windows Terminal, type Get-PhysicalDisk and check the HealthStatus column. The status can be Healthy, Warning, Unhealthy or Unknown.
Older guides might instruct you to use wmic diskdrive get status instead, but that's old advice. WMIC has been removed from currently supported versions of Windows 11, and Microsoft recommends supported alternatives like PowerShell.
How to act on Healthy, Warning or Bad results
If the result is Healthy and the PC is acting normally, that's a good sign. Keep backing up your data, as drive-health systems can detect some potential issues, but not all failures.
For a second opinion, CrystalDiskInfo is a free tool that can read SMART data from many HDDs and SSDs, including NVMe drives. More importantly for those who don't really want to spend an afternoon trying to understand what the raw storage counters mean, it gives the drive a health status of Good, Caution, Bad or Unknown.
If you get a Caution or Bad result, backing up becomes the priority. You can then verify the issue using the drive manufacturer's own diagnostic software, like Seagate's SeaTools or Samsung Magician (for supported Samsung SSDs). Persistent warnings, an Unhealthy result or obvious mechanical symptoms are all good reasons to stop trusting that drive with the only copy of important data and start considering a replacement.
CHKDSK is also helpful, but for a different task. It checks a volume's file system and metadata for errors. The /f option fixes file-system errors, and the /r option locates bad sectors and attempts to recover readable data.
However, if a file-system problem is corrected with CHKDSK, the questionable hardware is not magically made healthy. For HDDs, CrystalDiskInfo can trigger a Caution status based on three SMART attributes: reallocated sectors, pending sectors and uncorrectable sectors.

What’s the Matter With Moderation?
Hoping to break a 94-year losing streak, Kansas Democrats have turned to Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor whose mood may not match his party’s.
One simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right.
And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter.
Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one.
Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life.
In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.”
Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times. A roiling left has risen to match Trump’s raging right. To win, Hamilton must not only persuade independents and Republicans to vote for him—he must also motivate angry progressives in this time of throat-cutting.
If El-Sayed and others like him are the furious faces of the Democratic future, perhaps Hamilton is a DINO. When I asked him if Democrats should seek to impeach Trump a third time, he ventured his belief that “the impeachments in the first term did not accomplish anything”—a claim that dismisses the expression of righteous anger as a political imperative in itself. Hamilton likes to talk about the good that he could accomplish in partnership with the well-liked Senator Jerry Moran, the senior Republican from Kansas. But maybe that’s not what the people, who truly are pissing mad, really want.
Emporia is the seat of Lyon County, which in 2024 gave 56 percent of its votes to Donald Trump and 41 percent to Kamala Harris. Yet Hamilton was not in hostile territory when he visited one late-August morning. Gravel City Roasters is a combination coffee shop and art gallery located directly across Emporia’s main drag from the county Democratic headquarters. There is a Pride flag on the wall with Refugees welcome superimposed on its rainbow stripes. The chai, served in mismatched mugs, is excellent.
But the comfort zone is narrow here for a 21st-century Democrat. The little city with its college campus is surrounded by farmland that has historically bred beasts, grains, and discontent. In its heyday—the era of William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt—Emporia was home to the journalist William Allen White, whose Gazette newspaper was a sort of proto-Substack. Readers around the world vibed to his grumbling, which often had to do with the eternal sense of Kansas as undervalued and overlooked. “Go east and you hear them laugh at Kansas; go west and they sneer at her; go south and they cuss her; go north and they have forgotten her,” White wrote in his career-launching screed, dated 1896 and titled “What’s the Matter With Kansas?”
Thirteen decades later, an Emporia pharmacist, John Schmidt, picked up the theme, telling me at the coffee shop of the town’s beef processing plant (closed), its Michelin rubber-track factory (downsized), its maker of plastic ice scrapers (victim of a bankrupt holding company), and the nearby drugstore (battered by low reimbursements). The area’s future, too, feels festooned with pink slips.
A few dozen people awaited Hamilton, who arrived in a blue blazer and an open-collared white shirt. He immediately went to work shaking hands and nodding thoughtfully. After watching Hamilton campaign half a dozen or so times, the best description I can manage is “pastoral.” Fair enough, I suppose, for a 62-year-old pastor. Hamilton has a soft voice, and his gaze is gentle, intent, and framed by horn-rimmed glasses. His head moves constantly in tiny yeses and no’s, like a seismograph needle registering each quick conversation.
After working his way to the rear of the shop—pausing to autograph a woman’s copy of his book on the Holy Spirit—Hamilton used a wireless microphone to tell a joke about hypocritical politicians pretending to know the Lord’s Prayer. “I am a Democrat who actually knows the Lord’s Prayer,” he said. “When it says, ‘give us this day our daily bread,’ it’s reminding us to make sure that people have enough to eat.”
A sturdy little stump speech rolled out from there, befitting a man who has been crafting sermons since Seinfeld was new. He said he is a fifth-generation Kansan who married his sweetheart a week after high-school graduation and wants to give his granddaughter “a better country.” He said he built a church from nothing to 24,000 members. He said he prayed a year and a half ago that Trump would govern “with wisdom, grace, and compassion,” but found himself watching something quite different. Somebody’s got to do something became Maybe I should do something.
Rather than take on Trump directly, however, he aimed the balance of his fire at Marshall, who, Hamilton noted, “has voted for nearly everything the president has done.” Hamilton said he is against tariffs because they hurt farmers, against the Iran war because it drives up fuel prices, against Medicaid reductions because they threaten rural hospitals, and against cuts to food aid because more than 14,000 Kansas children need that support. “Since when did it become woke to care about your neighbor?” he asked rhetorically, aware that his audience was already seeing attack ads trying to tie him to left-wing ideas, and that Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas used an X post to denounce one of Hamilton’s sermons as “heretical.”
Don Duncan was part of that audience, having driven to town from nearby Chase County to have a look at the candidate. In the primary, a local Democrat, Christy Davis, drew 113 votes in Chase County, leaving Hamilton with eight; on the Republican side, Marshall got 479. Duncan, a self-described “Democrat who leans independent,” told me he did not think things are as bleak for Hamilton as that would suggest.
“It’s just a matter of people getting to know him,” said the retired school administrator and coach. “We need someone to get us back together.”
Could that be Marshall? I asked. “I can’t say we ever talk about him,” Duncan answered.
About 100 miles north and east, amid the big houses and busy shops of Kansas City’s southern suburbs, stands Hamilton’s monument to open minds, the “church for thinking people” that he founded in 1990. The main sanctuary of Leawood’s United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is visible from all directions, an elliptical edifice clad in glass and stainless steel, vaguely reminiscent of Disney’s Space Mountain. Rising 100 feet above a 77-acre campus of auxiliary buildings and parking lots, it features the largest fused-stained-glass window in the world, a work roughly the size of a basketball court. Nine satellite churches in greater Kansas City—four in Kansas; five in Missouri—carry the COR brand to sites around the area and beyond.
If the words megachurch pastor conjure images of hellfire oratory and $400 haircuts, Hamilton comes as a surprise, as mild as Jake from State Farm. Yet his success stands in contrast to the decline of mainstream Christianity in his lifetime.
Born in 1964 and raised by divorced parents in Prairie Village, one of those same southern suburbs, Hamilton came of age in a time of Protestant crisis. Perplexed by the social upheaval of the 1960s, Hamilton’s United Methodist denomination lost more than 10 percent of its membership in the 1970s and a further 5 percent in the 1980s. What energy there was in American Christianity came from conservative movements energized by opposition to abortion, homosexuality, scientific modernism, and a grab bag of philosophical attitudes derided by evangelicals as “secular humanism.”
Even as a teen, Hamilton found this alienating. Drawn to church for its social possibilities—“I didn’t believe in God, but I believed in girls,” he likes to say—the God he eventually embraced was one who delighted in discovery and gloried in progress. God gave us a brain for a reason, he thought, taking to heart the biblical admonition to worship with all of one’s “heart and soul and mind.”
In college at Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Hamilton “grew more and more interested in the parts of the Gospel that evangelical churches were leaving behind,” he told me during a July interview at a barbecue joint across the state line in Kansas City, Missouri. “I began focusing on scriptures dealing with social justice, ‘rolling down like waters,’ as Amos has it; the caring for widows and orphans; the story of the Good Samaritan. And I noticed that our churches were great at helping the people who came to church, but not so much with the people who were outside.”
Trained as a pastor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Hamilton returned with his young family to Kansas City in the late Reagan years. He soon persuaded his regional bishop to let him start a new congregation for people turned off by what Christianity had become. Though United Methodism suffered a further 29 percent drop in membership from 1990 to 2020, Hamilton’s congregation grew from fewer than a dozen people meeting in a funeral-home chapel to the largest mainline Protestant congregation in America.
He credits an idea known to theologians as the via media, the “middle way,” which has roots in ancient philosophy and scholastic Christianity, but had its flowering in Elizabethan England. At its core the idea involves a belief that truth is not to be found on the extremes and that compromise in pursuit of worthy aims is a virtue. Society as Hamilton envisions it is a sort of Newton’s cradle, the toy that is composed of a line of metal balls suspended by threads. When the ball on one end is lifted and released, it swings into contact with the pack, where its energy is conducted to the ball on the other extreme, which swings away in reaction. Energy might come from extremism, but stability lies with the center.
COR is that stable center, Hamilton maintains, “roughly equal parts Democrat, Republican, and independent,” where inevitable conflicts among freethinking people can be respected and accommodated in pursuit of shared missions. “I am wired to see both sides,” he told me, “which is not the same as saying that all issues are 50–50. I believe cutting Medicaid and closing rural hospitals is just wrong. Making it harder for public schools to serve special-needs students is wrong, and I am willing to talk with anyone to explain why I think so. But I don’t expect everyone to agree with me all the time.”
Hamilton hasn’t shied from hard issues as a pastor. When a faction of American Methodists joined forces with culturally conservative congregations in Africa to try to pass anti-LGBTQ ordinances for the denomination, he led the opposition. Criticizing what he saw as a misguided focus on a few biblical verses over a larger Gospel of inclusion and acceptance, Hamilton ultimately concluded that a schism was inevitable, and he was instrumental in negotiating the many details of separation.
The thing to notice about that story, as Hamilton tries to turn from pastor to lawmaker, is that the via media was the road not taken by Hamilton and the Methodists when the chips were down. There was no middle ground, and now there are two denominations where there used to be one.
Hamilton would likely run into an even more challenging divide in Washington, where the two factions cannot go their separate ways. Can moderation really be an agenda? In the biblical story of King Solomon, when confronted with a seemingly unresolvable impasse, the wise solution was not to split the baby, but for one combatant to surrender for the greater good. That’s not the Washington way.
Electoral politics is, in some ways, just second-grade math: addition and subtraction. Candidates seek to add votes in Column A while subtracting votes from Column B. All of the money, overt or dark; all of the advertisements; all of the pandering and polarizing; all of the door-knocking, the text messages, the awkward TikToks, the yard signs, the stilted visits by candidates to factories, diners, fairgrounds, living rooms, nursing homes, colleges—it’s all about addition and subtraction.
For Hamilton, the problem pencils out at around 80,000 votes. Any combination of addition and subtraction that hits this target, whether raising the Democratic vote share or reducing Marshall’s compared with his 2020 victory, will get the job done. That’s a big number in a state the size of Kansas, where about 1.3 million people voted in 2024, but so is the number of people who cram the pews of Hamilton’s sanctuaries each Christmas and Easter: around 100,000 per holiday.
As shown by the August 4 results, his stronghold is in Johnson County, home to his church and to about a quarter of the state’s voters. Once a bastion of chamber-of-commerce Republicanism, the county turned purple during its explosive growth in the Baby Boom years and has, in the Trump era, become a relatively safe base for Democratic Representative Sharice Davids.
Driving up turnout in Johnson County and other metro centers—working-class Wyandotte County (Kansas City, Kansas), liberal Douglas County (Lawrence, home to the University of Kansas), booming Sedgwick County (Wichita, still the state’s largest city)—will be the keys to Hamilton’s addition problem.
As for subtraction, meet Marshall. A retired ob-gyn who calls himself “Doc”—a nickname that hasn’t caught on with Kansas voters—he has distinguished himself as one of Trump’s most obsequious acolytes, though not always the most on-message. Marshall’s ready-fire-aim approach to public speaking has left his candidacy riddled with self-inflicted wounds. Asked whether he’s okay with Iran having ballistic missiles (the program Trump was promising to destroy), Marshall said, “I would prefer they didn’t. But I don’t think that’s the key issue here. I think that they have to be able to defend themselves.” Of rising gas prices triggered by the war: “Freedom is not free. Americans are going to have to make some sacrifices.” When Kansans died on a plane that collided with an Army helicopter over Washington, Marshall blithely blamed their deaths on DEI, a theory unsupported by crash investigators.
Having sold his house in central Kansas shortly after being elected to the Senate, Marshall is dogged by allegations that his status as a Kansas resident is largely fictitious. He lists as his residence a roughly 1,200-square-foot cabin on a family ranch property, but for several years his congressionally paid travel plans included frequent stops at his “vacation” home in Florida, which he says has been uninhabitable since suffering severe hurricane damage in 2024. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to my requests to discuss the race for this article, but in a recent social-media post he wrote, “Over the last six years, I’ve averaged 185 days per year in D.C. doing the work you sent me to do, 130 days per year in Kansas with over 300 stops per year across the state, about 35 days of official travel, and 20 holiday/personal days.”
When he does visit Kansas, Marshall has avoided open meetings with the public ever since a crowd in a rural community jeered him in March 2025 during Elon Musk’s DOGE fiasco. “The town halls just became non-productive and dangerous,” Marshall told a newspaper in Hays, Kansas.
The odor of weakness around the incumbent helped inspire the GOP-dominated legislature this year to spitball easing Marshall out of office in favor of an appointed successor whose term they would extend through 2028. Voilà! No election needed. The scheme died amid criticism that the Constitution doesn’t allow states to change the length of a Senate term, no matter how lame their senator might be.
With no choice but to defend Marshall, the GOP is probing for Hamilton’s vulnerabilities. A Massachusetts-based super PAC spent a reported $600,000 on a TV ad that pieces together phrases from sermons to portray Hamilton as “mega-woke.” “Black Lives Matter,” Hamilton says in the ad, “marching for righteousness.” In another moment, marked with an ellipsis on-screen, he says, “By virtue of being white … I have to repent.” The Kansas City Star dug up the June 2020 sermon from which the clip is taken and found Hamilton saying “I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, white, and male, right?” adding, almost a minute later, “Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent.”
Ted Cruz’s X post avowing that Hamilton held “heretical” views relied on a sermon in which Hamilton says that non-Christians might enter heaven. Marshall thanked Cruz in his own post and added, “Wait until you hear about the ‘hundreds of mistakes in the Bible’ my opponent claims to have found.” In response, the Hamilton campaign shared a quote from Joshua Leu, a pastor of a church in Great Bend, Kansas, where Marshall once served on the board. HuffPost had asked Leu about Hamilton. “I would say that he’s a middle-of-the-road pastor who is willing to listen to all sides, and then based on his understanding of the gospel, try to make the best decision,” Leu said.
Attacking Hamilton as a fellow traveler of the progressive left, a democratic socialist in gossamer disguise, might work in Kansas. But there are reasons why even Kansans who reject that portrait as grossly inaccurate might still say no to his candidacy. The party of Lincoln still has deep resonance in a state where people were battling years before Fort Sumter. Bob Dole’s success at amassing power in Washington and using it to funnel money to the state taught lessons in the value of seniority that are still remembered. Western Kansas is not only overwhelmingly Republican, but it is also suspicious of what it regards as the citified East, where Hamilton is from. And not even all of his Johnson County congregation’s members are Hamilton supporters, by the candidate’s own assessment. As the church has grown, some members have griped that Hamilton has become less accessible—an issue that his Senate campaign is likely to exacerbate, to say nothing of actually serving in the Senate. He’s taken a leave from sermonizing for now, but would stay on as senior pastor and preach at least a dozen times a year if elected.
A Kansas Democrat starts out in such a deep hole in a Senate race that Hamilton considered running as an independent, but the recent example of the failed independent Greg Orman (who lost a race for Senate in 2014 and governor in 2018) convinced the pastor and his advisers that only a Democrat could unseat Marshall. When voters ask, as they frequently do, how Hamilton would deal with pressure from party leaders, he told me his answer is: “I won’t work for Chuck Schumer; I’ll work for the people of Kansas.”
But other candidates in the region—Dan Osborn in Nebraska, Brian Bengs in South Dakota—have chosen the middlest of ways by running as independents. Perhaps Hamilton’s decision to step off the via media by allying himself with one of our nation’s two political parties is a concession to the reality of politics. Before Hamilton can be as nettlesome for Schumer as, say, West Virginia’s Joe Manchin was during the administration of Joe Biden, he first must win in November. Well-intentioned concessions, however, are the beginning of another, much more famous, road.
With money continuing to pour in from more than 16,000 donors, Hamilton can answer the attacks. And he has another shield in his armory. A prolific author of books on scripture, prayer, and Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White, Hamilton has created texts and instructional videos that are staples at Bible studies and Sunday-school classes in at least 500 Kansas churches, he told me. This makes him something of a known commodity in rural communities that might otherwise be leery of a big-city candidate.
As he calculates, 500 churches averaging 50 people each represents a small army of 25,000 people at least partly inoculated against anti-Hamilton attack ads. He doesn’t expect to win them all in counties where Democrats sometimes number in single digits, and he doesn’t need to. Maybe a handful in each precinct, in the secrecy of the voting booth, stung by the price of tractor fuel and fertilizer, will mark his name, or simply skip Marshall’s.
Hamilton is not a dynamic political performer; he doesn’t suck the oxygen from the room. The son of a service-station manager, a husband and father by the end of his teens, Hamilton instead relies on approachability, on his feeling for life as ordinary people live it: sometimes messy; sometimes painful. He seems to genuinely believe that what people have in common matters more than their differences. You can build a church on that. But can you build a campaign?
Jim Hightower, the former Texas agriculture commissioner turned liberal pundit, used to say, “There is nothing in the middle of the road but yellow stripes and dead armadillos.” But Kansas has—or had—something of a tradition of moderate Republican senators in the not-so-distant past. Nancy Kassebaum, the daughter of former Governor Alf Landon, the Republican Party’s 1936 presidential nominee (even Kansas went for Franklin D. Roosevelt that year), died last month. She served three terms in the Senate, from 1978 to 1997. She was a Republican who worked on health care, voted to ban assault weapons, and opposed, for nearly all of her career, a constitutional amendment to balance the budget. “We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution,” she said. Hamilton might anger partisans on the left and right—in his pews and beyond—by adhering to the middle way. He will need to make compromises in order to win, or, should he win, in order to govern. Politics inevitably sullies religion. But Jesus, in the Gospel of Matthew, also recommends the narrow road instead of the wide and easy one.
As a student of the via media, Hamilton surely knows what came for Queen Elizabeth’s moderate vision. The elegant span she championed connecting Catholic structures and rituals to Protestant individualism proved a bridge to nowhere. The decades after her death belonged to the extremists. Rivers of blood flowed across Europe as Catholics and Protestants waged their Thirty Years’ War. In England, sectarian Puritans staged a regicidal revolution. Refugees from religious violence poured into the Americas.
Some eras in history are like that, obstreperous and irreconcilable. Hamilton likes to point out that Kansas contains the geographical center of the lower 48 states, and he hopes to find America’s political midpoint too. The risk is that, like so much of the Farm Belt, the center has been hollowed out.

Panaji, Sep 6: Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Sunday said it is Prime Minister Narendra Modi's objective that drug-free youth power will lead to Viksit Bharat in 2047, and asserted the Union government has prepared a roadmap to make India drug-free by 2029.
The Modi government is committed to making the country drug-free to realise the dream of a developed India, just as it has worked to end the menace of Naxalism and terrorism, Shah said.
The Centre has adopted a coordinated, nationwide strategy to dismantle the entire narcotics network, from drug trafficking and financing to rehabilitation, as part of its goal of 'Drug-Free India' by 2029, he said.
"It is Narendra Modi’s objective that drug-free youth power will lead to Viksit Bharat in 2047," Shah said while addressing a press conference after chairing a high level meeting on narcotics that was attended by Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant as well as MHA and state government officials.
"Before 2014, the fight against narcotics was largely conducted in small units and isolation. Agencies were often satisfied catching small time accused. Our government is making the fight national security priority," he said.
In 2019, a four-tier National Coordination Committee for Countering Drug Trafficking (NCORD) mechanism was created at the executive, state and district levels to ensure coordinated action against the drug menace.
"Dedicated Anti-Narcotics Task Forces (ANTFs) have been constituted in all states and Union Territories and local police have been linked with the national strategy," Shah said.
He said a Joint Coordination Committee was also formed in 2019 to enable central agencies and state governments to take joint decisions against major drug networks, their international connections and operational gaps.
The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) has been strengthened by reorganising its cadre and enhancing its manpower, zonal presence and operational capabilities, Shah said while emphasising that the fight against drugs was not just limited to enforcement.
The government has linked awareness, treatment, counselling, rehabilitation and livelihood opportunities with the anti-narcotics campaign, he pointed out, adding that the 1933 MANAS helpline has been introduced to support persons with drug addiction.
The government is committed to achieving the goal of 'Drug-Free India 2029' through political will, coordinated enforcement and measures aimed at preventing addiction and rehabilitating victims, he said.
The Modi government's three-year roadmap to a drug-free India is based on a four-pillared approach to destroy narcotic networks, Shah said.
"These pillars include intelligence and operation-based enforcement, control on synthetic drugs, demand and harm reduction and creation of capacity and coordination," he explained.
Under the Narendra Modi regime, Jammu and Kashmir is on the path to progress and development after the decline of terrorism, which is gradually approaching zero there, he said.
The sentiment of separatism has lessened since the abrogation of Article 370, Shah said.
The Modi government's broader internal security strategy had succeeded in addressing three long-standing challenges -- terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir, insurgency in the Northeast and Left-Wing Extremism, Shah said.
"The Modi government has taken various steps to improve and strengthen internal security. Those who dreamt of a 'red' (Maoist) corridor from Tirupati to Pashupati have laid down arms and joined the mainstream," he said.
Referring to the Northeast, Shah said 14 major peace agreements had been signed since 2019 and around 11,000 armed youths had laid down their weapons and joined the mainstream.
He said India ended the nearly six-decade-old challenge of Left-Wing Extremism on March 31, 2026, through a coordinated strategy combining security, development and trust.
"We have eradicated Naxalism and will deal with menace of narcotics in the same manner," the Union minister asserted.
Shah said the Centre has a target to demolish 100 national and international networks by March 2029 and bring back 100 fugitives to the country.
By March 2027, there will be clear end-to-end visibility of the supply chain while at least 75 secret labs would be destroyed in 2026, he said.
He said the government had also adopted a mission-mode approach to bring back fugitives hiding abroad.
Between July 2019 and July 2026, as many as 274 wanted or absconding criminals were brought back to India from 36 countries, he said.
Over the past three years, 401 Red Corner Notices have been issued, including 182 up to July 2026, Shah said.
He said more than 1,400 Central and state agencies were connected through Interpol, facilitating faster information sharing.
Between 2019 and 2026, assets worth Rs 17,874 crore belonging to fugitives were attached, while Rs 18,762 crore was recovered or restored, Shah informed.
Shah also highlighted the government's efforts against cybercrime, saying the cyber system had helped save more than Rs 11,158 crore across 32.8 lakh complaints as of June 30, 2026.
He said strengthening border and coastal security, implementation of three new criminal laws and the Vibrant Villages Programme were among the measures taken to strengthen internal security.
The Union minister said the government has adopted a "zero tolerance" policy towards terrorism and a first-responder approach to disaster management.
He also praised the Goa police for effective implementation of the three new criminal laws saying the conviction rate has increased from 22 percent to 53.2 percent.

Vietnam dentists target Australians on social media amid plans to expand medical tourism industry
In short:
Vietnamese dental clinics are targeting Australians through social media, prompting more people to travel there for cheaper dental work.
The country's Health Ministry says Australians are among the top foreign nationalities receiving medical treatment there.
What's next?
Vietnam hopes to increase its medical tourism sector and attract twice as many international patients over the next four years, which has Australian dentists concerned.
Wendy Middleton used her hands to hide her "awful teeth" when she spoke for more than 20 years.
The 67-year-old from Adelaide's north had stopped going to the dentist years ago because she said she "couldn't afford it".
But two years ago, her teeth were no longer just a cosmetic issue. She was in so much pain, she could not eat properly and needed urgent dental work.
She said the public waiting list was too long and her local dentist quoted her about $40,000 to fix her teeth, which required multiple crowns and extractions.
"There's no way I could afford it," she told the ABC.
"I'd be paying it off for the rest of my life."
Then the casual disability care worker started to see advertisements on social media for dental tourism packages in Vietnam.
For about a third of the cost of the work in Australia, she was promised the same dental procedure along with flights, accommodation, visas, airport transfers, meals and medication.
She was initially worried it was "a scam", but after conducting her own research, she said she was willing to take the risk and booked the package.
Ms Middleton's story is not unique. According to Smartraveller, dentistry is one of the most common medical procedures that Australians travel overseas for.
However, it is hard to know exactly how many head abroad for medical work because Australia does not track this information.
One dental practice operating in Hanoi and Da Nang, Australian Dental Clinic, told the ABC the "majority" of their foreign clients were from Australia.
"We do see an increase in the flow of Australian visitors," practice manager Nguyen Nam said.
Vietnam's Health Ministry also lists Australians as one of the top nationalities receiving medical treatment in the country.
While Ms Middleton's experience of having dental work in Vietnam was positive, consultant prosthodontist Scott Davis said he often saw patients returning from abroad with negative outcomes.
Dr Davis, a spokesperson for the Australian Dental Association, said Australians travelling overseas for dental work had become "a bigger problem" in recent years.
"I see a lot of people who've had complications," Dr Davis told the ABC.
"Ultimately, if I travel a very long way to have dental treatment, I'm trying to condense what normally might take three to six months into two weeks.
"Biology just doesn't listen to that."
He said he wished Australia, like the United Kingdom, collected information about citizens who have adverse outcomes from medical work abroad so the scale of the problem was clearer.
Aussies targeted with social media advertisements
Dentists in Vietnam are actively targeting Australians through social media advertisements and influencers to drum up more business.
It was how Ms Middleton and many other clients of Vietnamese dentistry practices first became aware of the services.
"That's what I've been watching because it has been growing," said associate professor Giannina Warren.
Dr Warren is the senior program manager in communications at RMIT University Vietnam with expertise in place branding — how cities and destinations promote themselves.
She said it was "interesting" how many Australians and New Zealanders were creating content of their dental tourism experiences in Vietnam through TikTok and Instagram.
"This is happening in the digital space, and it's happening in an organic, user-generated way," she said.
She said popular dental clinics in Vietnam were also using targeted Facebook advertisements and online videos to build their brand and business.
Vietnam plans to expand medical tourism industry
Despite warnings from the Australian government about the risks involved, Asia has been a common spot for Australians to seek out dental, medical and cosmetic work.
Almost half of Australian travellers have — or would consider — going overseas for a medical procedure, mostly due to the lower cost of treatment, according to 2025 data from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Insurance Council of Australia.
Now, Vietnam has plans to become one of South-East Asia's leading medical tourism destinations. And that has Australian dentists, including Dr Davis, worried.
About 300,000 foreign residents and visitors currently use medical services including dental, fertility treatment and other cosmetic procedures in Vietnam each year, according to Vietnam's Ministry of Health.
But under a draft scheme being prepared by the Health Ministry, the Vietnamese government wants to more than double that, aiming to attract about 750,000 international medical tourists a year by 2030 by teaming up with the country's Department of Tourism.
"I do think they have a long way to go in terms of building the narrative and working constructively with the private sector," Dr Warren said.
"That's the key thing when it comes to medical tourism, trust is the currency … and that has to come from a layer that's above the providers."
Dr Warren said she had been impressed with the medical care she had received in Vietnam since she moved a few years ago but the industry had a lot of room for growth.
"That's a story I want to tell to the world about how high level the care is here," she said.
"Vietnam has not been doing a great job of telling that story."
Dr Davis said if the growth plan went ahead, he believed the number of Australians travelling to Vietnam for dental work "would increase".
"My concerns with Vietnam doing this is they are a long way away, the medical legal protections for foreign citizens having care is nowhere near as robust as it is in Australia," he told the ABC.
"So if you do have adverse outcomes, you have very poor opportunities to effectively receive compensation.
"It's possible, but I've been informed it takes years, it's complex, might require multiple visits."
He also warned prospective clients to be wary, saying advertisements "may convey outcomes that are achievable that perhaps may not be achievable".
"Are the testimonials true, is AI being used in the before and after images, are you going to get what you think you're purchasing?" he said.
"That's something you should approach with trepidation."
Calls for dental reform in Australia
For Ms Middleton, the dental work she had done in Vietnam has been life-changing.
She said Australia needed to overhaul its dental industry if it wanted to encourage citizens to stay local.
"This is the best thing I've ever done; the confidence level I now have is through the roof," she told the ABC.
"Australia needs to regulate the price and cut them down.
"I can go back [to Vietnam] 10 times, and I still won't pay $40,000. If they brought their prices down here in Australia, people would stay."
Dr Davis said Australia needed "greater efficiency, simplicity and better support of the industry to allow us to provide health care at a lower price point".
"Regulatory oversight and compliance with the plethora of rules makes health care more expensive generally," he said.
"Governments could do a better job.
"I believe people would rather be treated by someone close to home than a very long distance away and be able to see them if there are complications readily."
Dr Davis warned anyone considering having work done overseas to do their research on the practice, to ensure they were not being advised to have more work done than they actually needed and to check the qualifications and training of the medical professional carrying out the work.
He said just because some clinicians at the practice may have trained in Australia, it did not mean you would be seen by that person.
Australia's Department of Health, Disability and Ageing warned anyone considering dental treatment overseas to understand the risks, seek advice from a registered health practitioner in Australia, and check what aftercare, insurance and consumer protections were available.
A department spokesperson told the ABC it was not responsible for regulation of the dental industry; instead, that fell to the Dental Board of Australia with oversight from the Australian Health Practitioner Agency (AHPA), which both operate independently of government.
Dental Practices are also subject to additional state and territory legislation, including public health and work safety laws.
"Our role is to help protect the public by ensuring dental practitioners are appropriately qualified, trained and safe to practise," an AHPA spokesperson told the ABC.
"Our regulatory responsibilities do not extend to dental practitioners or services provided in overseas jurisdictions."

Frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI all experienced rare outages on Thursday morning, creating downtime for their corresponding AI chatbots. SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, said on Thursday afternoon that the issues with Grok resulted from “an outage at our Memphis compute center this morning.”
The issues initially appeared to be linked because they coincided—perhaps the result of a shared third-party service provider—but neither OpenAI nor Anthropic cited an external source in comments to WIRED on Thursday. SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. But the company said as part of its public comments on Thursday: “We’d also like to apologize to our impacted compute partners.” Anthropic and xAI announced a “compute partnership” with SpaceX in May.
OpenAI spokesperson Kathleen Chaykowski tells WIRED: “A routing error starting around 7:43 am PT on Thursday, September 3, made ChatGPT and Codex unavailable for some users across platforms. As of about 8:17 am PT on Thursday, a solution was successfully implemented and is continuing to be monitored.”
Anthropic declined to comment on the episode. The company began alerting about a “partial outage” at 6:23 am PT on Thursday that involved “elevated errors on requests to Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.” Shortly after, the company said it had “identified the cause” and that “a fix has been deployed.” The company marked the issue as resolved by 9:16 am PT. Claude Sonnet 5 seemed to briefly have similar issues shortly after 9 am PT.
xAI reported Grok outages across all of its platforms and services beginning at 6:30 am PT when the company posted “investigating outage” on its service status page. “Grok is experiencing issues. We are working on restoring service as quickly as possible,” the page said. At 10:05 am PT the episode was marked complete. “We have resolved the situation, and traffic is healthy again,” the company wrote.
There were scattered reports of a possible Google Gemini outage on Thursday morning as well, but the company did not confirm this or record any incidents on its service status dashboard. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment ahead of publication.
Typically, multiple outages in the same sector at the same time would point to a cloud provider, content delivery network, or other third-party vendor having issues affecting multiple customers. But OpenAI and Anthropic did not point to a potential shared cause, and major players in the internet infrastructure space—including Cloudflare, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure—did not report outages on Thursday.

The reasons you procrastinate — and how to finally stop
The reasons you procrastinate -- and how to finally stop
But those things aren't true, says Itamar Shatz, author of a book published in August, Solving Procrastination: The Science of Why We Put Things Off and How to (Finally!) Stop. People have been struggling with getting things done throughout history (Mozart was a serial procrastinator). We also tend to push things off for a variety of reasons, like being a perfectionist.

Swans star Tom Papley says he is "shattered" for his captain Callum Mills after Mills suffered a serious knee injury in the win over Brisbane on Saturday.
Mills limped off the field in the first quarter after a non-contact injury.
What's next?
Scans are expected to confirm an ACL rupture for Mills. Sydney has a week off before playing in a preliminary final against either Fremantle or Geelong at the SCG.
Sydney star Tom Papley says he is "shattered" for Swans skipper Callum Mills as Mills braces to miss the club's push for an unlikely AFL premiership.
Mills's feared ACL rupture added a sour note to Sydney's remarkable 53-point qualifying final demolition of reigning premiers Brisbane at the SCG on Saturday.
Scans are expected to confirm the major knee injury for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss and has dealt with numerous untimely injuries across his 197-game career.
But Sydney have an opportunity to make amends for previous grand final losses, with a preliminary final at the SCG against either Fremantle or Geelong to come.
Loading Twitter content
Papley admitted it "didn't look great" for Mills following the resilient skipper's first-quarter knee injury.
Mills has earned significant praise for leading the club amid the dramatic fallout from the events at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne last month.
"He is an amazing captain," Papley told the Nine Network of his skipper on Sunday.
"[He's] been amazing over the last few weeks.
"He puts this club on his back and wears his heart on his sleeve. It's just shattering for him.
"I'd love nothing more than to win a premiership and have him by my side, albeit he might not be there [playing].
"He deserves it more than anyone."
Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.
Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.
Sydney were given little chance to knock off the Lions, even though they finished the home-and-away season second.
Even club chairman Andrew Pridham conceded the Swans' premiership hopes had been "torpedoed" after suspending the five players.
Loading Twitter content
But all cylinders of the Swans machine fired on Saturday despite those major absences, with Errol Gulden calling the shots in the engine room as Harry Cunningham directed the defence.
Logan McDonald may have led with six goals, but Sydney enjoyed an even contribution from their forward line, with Charlie Curnow and Papley slotting five each.
Tall forward Hayden McLean's three-goal haul is set to further complicate coach Dean Cox's selection conundrum, with Joel Amartey (Achilles) nearing full fitness.
Star winger Justin McInerney is also expected to return from a hamstring strain for the preliminary final.
"They should both be available … and that'll be a decision, like we do every week," Cox said of Amartey and McInerney.
Cox said Saturday's win felt like the most complete four-quarter performance in his tenure.
"With the quality of opposition that we were playing and the ability of the match-winners that they have all over the ground," Cox said.
"I was really proud when we've got some of the young kids that come into our football team to be able to execute the roles they had to play at the right time."

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.
Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.
“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”
Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.
During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.
He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.
The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.
“There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”
Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”
His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.
He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

Padma Shri Dr. Prakash Amte, Dr. Mandakini Amte, Dr. Vitthal Kamat and Achyut Godbole attend the inauguration of Aaji Care’s sixth centre. Pune (Maharashtra) [India], September 4: Aaji Care, an elder-care organisation working across Mumbai, Pune and Goa, inaugurated its sixth Assisted Living Centre and second centre in Pune at Kalyani Nagar on Sunday, 30 August. The new centre marks another milestone in Aaji Care’s journey towards creating compassionate, comprehensive and dignified care environments for India’s growing elderly population.
Spread across a purpose-built seven-storey building with a capacity of 49 beds, the new facility is Aaji Care’s largest centre to date. Designed specifically around the evolving physical, medical, cognitive, emotional and social needs of older adults, the centre brings together different levels of care under one roof, creating a continuum of support as the needs of elders evolve. The centre was inaugurated by Padma Shri Dr. Prakash Amte and Dr. Mandakini Amte, in the presence of renowned hotelier Dr. Vitthal Kamat and author and social thinker Mr. Achyut Godbole. More than 175 guests, including doctors, senior citizens, business leaders, social-sector representatives and members of the media, attended the inauguration.
A centre designed around the changing needs of ageing
Recognising that every elder does not require the same kind or level of support, the seven-storey centre has been thoughtfully designed around different stages and care requirements. Four floors are dedicated to elders living with Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia, with environments designed to support safety, familiarity, routine, comfort and emotional wellbeing. A separate floor is dedicated to high-dependency care, supporting elders who require greater levels of medical and personal assistance.
Two additional floors cater to elders requiring rehabilitation and assisted living, as well as those who remain relatively active and independent but prefer the security, companionship and support of a professionally managed senior living environment. The facility also includes an exclusive physiotherapy unit and dedicated activity spaces designed to support mobility, rehabilitation, cognitive stimulation, socialisation, recreation and meaningful engagement.
The centre has been designed with ageing-in-place architect Rama Sane, with inputs from doctors, geriatric psychologists, physiotherapists and elder-care professionals. The objective has been to bring together professional care and safety with a warm, comfortable and home-like environment. A multidisciplinary team of trained caregivers, nurses, doctors, psychologists and physiotherapists will support elders living with dementia, mobility limitations, chronic medical conditions, post-hospitalisation rehabilitation needs and higher levels of dependency.
Speaking about the vision behind the new centre, Prasad Bhide, Founder of Aaji Care, said that the organisation’s purpose goes beyond simply increasing the number of beds available for senior care. "We don't want to simply add beds; we want to add better days to the lives of our elders and help them age gracefully. "
Elaborating on Aaji Care’s philosophy of ‘Ageing Gracefully’, Bhide said that meaningful elder care cannot be defined only by medical support or infrastructure. "Ageing gracefully is not just about providing good medical care and good infrastructure. It is equally about helping elders maintain their independence and dignity, giving them companionship, keeping them meaningfully engaged and, most importantly, surrounding them with a lot of love. An elder may need assistance, but that should never take away their individuality or their right to make choices about their own life. " According to Bhide, an assisted living centre should therefore be much more than a place to live or receive medical care. It should create an environment where professional care and safety coexist with independence, dignity, companionship, engagement and emotional wellbeing.
A message of active and independent ageing
The inauguration brought together perspectives on ageing, healthcare, compassion and the need to create a society that respects and supports its elders. Speaking at the occasion, Achyut Godbole highlighted the growing need for professionally managed and sensitive assisted living facilities as family structures, lifestyles and social relationships continue to evolve. He noted that an increasingly individualistic society has created a greater need for spaces where senior citizens can receive care and support while continuing to live with companionship, security and dignity. He also appreciated the thought and planning that had gone into the design of Aaji Care’s new Kalyani Nagar facility and its focus on addressing the diverse needs of older adults.
Dr. Prakash Amte and Dr. Mandakini Amte spoke about the importance of action over words and reflected on the legacy of Baba Amte and the work that continues at Hemalkasa through the next generation. They emphasised the importance of remaining physically active, exercising regularly and continuing to do as much of one’s own work as possible even after retirement. They also shared an important message for senior citizens and their families — that younger generations should be given the freedom to make their own decisions, with advice offered when it is sought. Dr. Prakash Amte also recalled the support extended by Aaji Care to their colleague and social worker Nirmala Sathe during the final phase of her life, when she was cared for at Aaji Care’s existing Pune centre. He appreciated the care and support provided to her during that period.
Brain Gym, Neurobics and the celebration of ‘Ageing Gracefully’
The inauguration programme itself reflected Aaji Care’s broader belief that healthy ageing goes well beyond medical care. Naina Oke, Head of Mental Health at Aaji Care, conducted an interactive session on Brain Gym and Neurobics for the guests. Through simple exercises and activities, the session demonstrated ways to stimulate the brain and highlighted the importance of keeping the mind active as we age.
The programme also featured specially presented Kathak performances based on the theme of ‘Ageing Gracefully’. Through classical dance, movement and expression, the performances celebrated ageing not simply as a stage of increasing dependency, but as a meaningful phase of life that can continue to be filled with dignity, expression, joy and engagement. Together, these elements reinforced Aaji Care’s central philosophy — that elder care must address not only medical and physical needs, but also cognitive health, emotional wellbeing, social connection, independence and meaningful participation.
Responding to the changing landscape of elder care
Founded in August 2012, Aaji Care works with senior citizens and their families across Mumbai, Pune and Goa, particularly where medical conditions, dementia, mental-health concerns or mobility limitations make independent living or care at home increasingly difficult. Its services include assisted living, dementia and memory care, post-hospitalisation and rehabilitation care, palliative and high-dependency care, home-based elder care and geriatric mental-health support.
The Kalyani Nagar facility is Aaji Care’s sixth Assisted Living Centre and second centre in Pune. With its combination of specialised care, assisted living, rehabilitation and active senior living, the centre has been envisioned as a continuum of care that can respond to changing needs while helping elders retain as much independence and choice as possible. Following the inauguration ceremony, the chief guests and members of the audience toured the facility and appreciated its thoughtfully designed infrastructure and comprehensive approach to senior care. The new centre will open for admissions from 10 September 2026.
About Aaji Care
Founded in August 2012, Aaji Care is an elder-care organisation providing assisted living, dementia and memory care, home-based elder care, rehabilitation, palliative and high-dependency care, and geriatric mental-health support across Mumbai, Pune and Goa. At the heart of Aaji Care’s approach is the belief that ageing should not merely be viewed as a stage of life requiring care, but as a meaningful chapter that deserves independence, dignity, companionship, comfort, engagement and joy. Through professional and compassionate care, Aaji Care aims to help elders live their better days with greater confidence, purpose and happiness, while giving their families the reassurance and peace of mind that their loved ones are cared for with warmth, respect and dignity.

- The claim that Canada assisted China in avoiding U.S. tariffs by reselling Chinese steel as Canadian is still under investigation.
- U.S. businesses and the U.S. government have accused Canadian companies of acting as a "backdoor" funneling Chinese steel into the United States. President Donald Trump's administration also has accused Canada of being one of China's "biggest enablers" in efforts to avoid tariffs in general.
- In May, the Department of Justice reached a settlement with two Canadian companies accused of falsely labeling Chinese steel as Canadian to avoid customs duties. However, the companies did not admit fault as part of the settlement.
- Some trade experts have expressed skepticism that Canada is enabling Chinese efforts to avoid tariffs on steel. Canada's government also has enacted a number of measures in an attempt to prevent Chinese steel from flooding the Canadian market.
- We have not rated this claim due to a lack of verifiable evidence. We reached out to offices of the U.S. and Canadian trade representatives and will update this story if we hear back.
In the fall and summer of 2026, social media users claimed that Canada resold Chinese steel as Canadian to help China avoid U.S. tariffs.
The rumor spread on Facebook and X (screenshot, screenshot). Snopes readers also contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
It is true that American businesses have accused Canadian companies — not the country's government — of skirting tariffs by selling Chinese goods, including steel, as Canadian. In an August report, Trump's administration also accused Canada of being one of "China's biggest enablers" in helping evade tariffs in general through "transshipment," or the shipment of goods from one country to another via a stop in yet another country.
In May, the Department of Justice reached a $19 million settlement with two Canadian companies over allegations that they "knowingly and improperly" failed to pay duties owed on steel manufactured in European and Asian countries, including China. The defendants denied the allegations and the settlement is not an admission of fault, but it also does not mean the United States' allegations were unfounded, according to the court documents (Page 2).
Snopes relies on independent verification and primary evidence for all of our conclusions. As of this writing, the courts have not determined that any Canadian company or government official has attempted to evade tariffs or help China avoid tariffs through this supposed scheme. Furthermore, there is not enough publicly available evidence that such a scheme has happened or is happening. As such, we have not rated this claim.
We reached out to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Canada's trade minister for the U.S., Dominc LeBlanc, for more information and await a response.
It is also worth noting that the claims connected these allegations to the breakdown in U.S.-Canada trade talks in late summer 2026. That may be because Greer reportedly raised concerns to Canadian officials about the transshipment of Chinese steel through countries Canada is seeking new free-trade deals with.
Here's what we know about the allegations:
US businesses accuse Canadian firms of avoiding tariffs
In December 2025, American industry leaders accused Canadian and Mexican firms of using cheap Chinese materials in ways that undercut U.S. businesses during a public hearing on the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade 
For example, here's what Brandon Farris, vice president of the Steel Manufacturers Association, said, according to Page 135 of the official transcript for the Dec. 4, 2025 hearing:
Some producers of steel-intensive goods in both countries continue to rely on steel sourced from non-market, excess capacity nations such as China. From 2020 to 2024, Mexico's steel imports from China rose by 59 percent, while Canada's increased by nearly 75 percent. Just as Canada and Mexico have experienced rising imports from countries with chronic excess steel capacity, the U.S. has faced its own surge of steel products from both neighbors.
Michael Salmon, CEO of Specialty Steel Works in Indiana, said that "China in particular continues to use Mexico as back door access to key U.S. markets, including steel" (Page 139). And Bob Wahlin, CEO of Stoughton Trailers, an American trailer manufacturer, said the United States must "close loopholes in the agreement" allowing "highly subsidized" Chinese steel to "enter the U.S. market from Canada and Mexico" (Page 244).
DOJ, US government accusations against Canada
The best publicly available evidence that at least some Canadian firms may be skirting tariffs on Chinese steel appears to be the previously mentioned Department of Justice settlement with two Canadian companies, Farjess and Royal Canadian Steel.
According to the Justice Department's complaint, the same people oversee Royal Canadian Steel and Farjess. Royal Canadian Steel imported steel into Canada and supplied that steel to Farjess (PDF pages 4 and 5).
The DOJ alleged that Farjess and/or Royal Canadian Steel personnel removed labels on steel referencing a Chinese company in order to conceal the origin of the steel from customs officials (PDF pages 13 to 15). Allegedly, the companies replaced the Chinese labels with their own. Evidence submitted in court included scans of those labels (see Exhibits 7 and 8).
While this scheme may have helped Chinese companies avoid tariffs, the Justice Department's allegations focused on the benefits to the two Canadian firms — specifically, that they experienced "windfall profits" from the allegedly fraudulent activity (PDF Page 22).
Skepticism of US claims and Canada's response
CBC reported in 2025 that Eric Miller, an expert on Canada-U.S. trade policy with the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, said Canada is "nowhere near as much of a back door for Chinese steel as the American companies make it out to be."
Miller reportedly said Canada is "quite militant" about prevention of Chinese transshipment because it wants to protect its own access to the U.S. market.
"Any objective look at Canada's track record would say that repeatedly over the last decade, Canada has seriously put in place measures to try to control imports of Chinese steel," the CBC quoted Miller as saying.
Indeed, in July 2025, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced measures to restrict and reduce foreign steel from entering the Canadian market amid fears from Canada's steel industry that it would be overwhelmed by an influx of Chinese steel newly subject to U.S. tariffs.

Junior Asia Cup: Men’s team draws 3-3 with Japan
The Indian junior men’s hockey team secured a 3-3 draw against Japan in their second Pool A match of the Junior Asia Cup in Moqi on Sunday.
Fresh from an emphatic 14-0 victory over Indonesia in its opening pool match, India took the lead in the fourth minute through a penalty stroke following a foul. Captain Anmol Ekka stepped up and calmly converted to put India 1-0 ahead.
India continued to build pressure and doubled their advantage in the 10th minute through a penalty corner conversion by Ashu Maurya.
Japan responded almost immediately, winning a penalty corner in the 11th minute. Ryushin Sasaki converted the opportunity to pull one goal back and make it 2-1.
The final quarter saw the intensity rise as Japan pressed for an equaliser. Japan won a penalty corner and, after a re-awarded penalty corner, captain Kazuki Nakanishi converted in the 48th minute to level the score at 2-2.
With time ticking away, Japan won another penalty corner, and Nakanishi stepped up once again, finding the target with a flick in the 59th minute to put Japan ahead 3-2.
India responded by removing its goalkeeper as it desperately searched for an equaliser. Its persistence was rewarded when it won a penalty corner with just 59 seconds remaining.
Anmol once again stepped up and converted the opportunity to make it 3-3.
India will next face Korea on Tuesday in its third Pool A encounter.
Women’s team thrashes Malaysia
Indian women’s team consolidated its position at the top of the points table with an 11-1 hammering of Malaysia. The Indian players scored four goals from field play, five from penalty corners and two from penalty strokes.
The result gives India two wins from two matches and six points, putting them at the top of the Elite Pool standings.
China and Japan are second and third, respectively, with three points each after playing and winning one match.
India will take on Japan in its third pool-stage match on September 8.

Falling debris from a ceiling in the grand foyer of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts may have complicated a battle over renovations of the Washington DC arts center that could result in the building being demolished.
A portion of the ceiling collapsed on Friday evening after heavy rain swept through the area, prompting officials to temporarily close the Edward Durell Stone-designed building. No one was injured by the debris.
Kennedy Center officials posted online on Saturday that the incident showed renovations to the building were urgently needed – an argument that Donald Trump has made in concert with a broader second-term agenda to reshape Washington.
“Another warning we can’t ignore,” the Kennedy Center said in the post. “A section of the Grand Foyer ceiling collapsed after this week’s storms. Thankfully no one was hurt. Decades of deferred maintenance made this inevitable.”
Roma Daravi, the center’s vice-president for public relations, said in a statement that the collapse was “another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed”.
Alongside the White House ballroom, a proposed triumphal arch, fitful renovations to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool and a remodeled golf course on the banks of the Potomac, the Kennedy Center has become a significant project for the president.
The Trump-aligned board has proposed adding Trump’s name to the building’s facade and to close the center for two years as it undergoes $250m in renovations.
Last month, a federal judge expressed doubts about the Kennedy Center’s stated intention to return Trump’s name to the building after a district court blocked the renovations and said Trump’s name had been added to the center illegally and ordered it to be removed.
The board voted earlier this month to inscribe “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J Trump” on the facade by 8 September.
If a fund for the renovations reaches $100m, another inscription would be added, reading: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Congress has approved $257m for the project, and the Trump administration wants to raise an additional $500m through private donations.
Administration attorneys have argued that without Trump’s name on the building it would struggle to raise money for renovations.
Without the Trump-backed funding, they argue, the building “will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years”.
Last week a sculpture titled Blue by American post-minimalist Joel Shapiro was taken down. The Kennedy Center offered no reason for its removal, but said in a statement “we are honored to have been stewards” of the work.
Friday’s debris shower may strengthen the center’s position that the building needs a complete overhaul. Grace Terpstra of Keep the KC, a group fighting the center’s closure, told the Associated Press that the board may seize on the incident “to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down, that it’s going to fall on everybody”.
“I think they’ll try to make it into a bigger thing and show that they’ve found a lot of other things,” said Terpstra.
