What's the difference between volatile and non-volatile memory?
The difference comes down to what happens when the power goes off, but that’s only part of how modern memory works.
Computer specs often use the word "memory" for several different technologies, which can make volatile and non-volatile memory sound more complicated than they are. The basic distinction is whether stored data survives when power disappears.
Volatile memory needs continuous power to retain its contents, while non-volatile memory keeps data after power is removed. That's why conventional system RAM is cleared when you shut down a computer, but files saved to an SSD are still there the next time it starts.
Volatility only describes what happens to the data when power goes away. It does not, by itself, tell you how fast a type of memory is, how much it can hold or what job it performs.
Volatile memory includes DRAM and SRAM
When a laptop or desktop spec lists 16GB or 32GB of RAM, it's referring to dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM. This is the computer's main working memory, which holds data while programs are running. DDR5 is one current form of DRAM in computers, while phones and other mobile devices commonly use low-power DRAM such as LPDDR5X.
Each DRAM cell stores a bit using a capacitor and a transistor. The electrical charge in the capacitor leaks over time, so DRAM has to refresh its contents repeatedly while the system is running. Once power is removed and those refreshes stop, the stored data disappears.
DRAM can come in forms other than the removable sticks commonly found in desktop PCs. AMD's Ryzen AI Max chips, for example, can work with as much as 128GB of unified memory. The underlying job is still temporary working memory, even when the physical layout looks different from a traditional DIMM (the removable stick-shaped circuit board lined with memory chips that plugs into a motherboard slot).
Static random-access memory, or SRAM, is volatile too. "Static" refers to the fact that SRAM can retain its state without the periodic refresh cycles DRAM needs, provided power is still available. SRAM uses latching circuitry with several transistors per bit, which can provide faster access than DRAM's capacitor-and-transistor cell.
That makes SRAM well-suited to processor caches, where relatively small amounts of frequently needed data can sit close to the CPU. The Ryzen 9 9950X3D (our review) is an unusually cache-heavy example, with 144MB of combined L2 and L3 cache. That's still tiny compared with the gigabytes of DRAM used as main memory, which shows how differently the two volatile technologies are used.
Non-volatile memory keeps data after shutdown
Non-volatile memory handles information that needs to remain available when the device loses power. The most familiar example in current consumer hardware is NAND flash, which is used for persistent storage in SSDs, tablets, USB drives and memory cards.
An SSD has two main parts: flash memory, which stores your data even when the power is off, and a controller, which manages how that data is written and read. The controller also helps correct errors and distributes write operations across different memory cells, rather than repeatedly writing to the same cells. This helps prevent some cells from wearing out much faster than others. This basic setup applies to both SATA and NVMe SSDs.
NOR flash is another type of non-volatile memory, but it's usually used for code rather than large files. Devices can use it to store the firmware that starts the hardware and loads the operating system, along with other program code that needs to remain available after shutdown. NOR flash is especially useful in embedded devices because the processor can often run that code directly from the flash chip, without first copying it to RAM.
So, just as DRAM and SRAM are both volatile while serving different purposes, NAND and NOR show that "non-volatile" describes a property rather than a single type of component.
Modern devices move data between both kinds of memory
Opening and using a photo-editing app provides an example of how the memory hierarchy works. The app and saved photo begin on non-volatile storage. As you use them, the system loads the code and data it needs into DRAM. The processor's caches then keep copies of frequently accessed information closer to the CPU, reducing how often it has to reach back into main memory.
None of those temporary copies need to survive a normal shutdown. What matters is that the changes you save eventually reach non-volatile storage.
Hibernation makes the distinction especially easy to see. Windows can write the contents of volatile memory to a hibernation file on non-volatile storage before powering DRAM down. When the computer resumes, Windows reads that file and restores the memory contents. That's distinct from sleep mode, where your session is kept in RAM and lost if the power goes out.
This is why a laptop specification such as "16GB memory | 512GB SSD" describes two separate resources. The first figure tells you how much working space the system has for active tasks. The second tells you how much persistent storage is available for the operating system, apps and files that need to remain after the power is off.

Why Nepal floods should worry India
- Published
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.
India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.
Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.
And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.
Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.
How many Nepal rivers flow into India?
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.
Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.
A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.
Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).
India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.
Which Indian states are most exposed?
Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.
Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.
But the risk extends beyond Bihar.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.
Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.
"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.
Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.
When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate?
Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists.
First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily.
Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.
Second, the river.
Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.
Third, when the water meets India.
How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.
So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.
The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.
So how much depends on Nepal v India?
"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.
How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk
The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration.
Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.
According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.
"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.
The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.
How much warning can India get from Nepal?
For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.
Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.
Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours.
A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.
India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.
But important gaps remain, says Sanyal.
They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.
And then there's, crucially, the last mile.
A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.
For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".
What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India?
A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.
Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.
The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.
But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.
Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.
"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.
Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.
"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.
Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.
The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.
So what should worry India the most?
"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.
In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.
Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".
"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.
A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.
That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.
It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.
And then there's climate change.
Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.
High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.
And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border.
They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

Twin sisters jailed in Iran over anti-regime protests: Ripped-out hair, broken elbows, and a ‘rape threat’
Taraneh Rahimi has been sentenced to death by the Iranian courts, while her twin, Romina Rahimi, has been given a 25-year prison term.
Two teenage twin sisters were taken from their beds in the middle of the night by masked men, later identified as those of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. For what? For reportedly joining millions of protesters in the agitation against the regime led by Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in January 2026.
However, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, the mother of the twins, Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, had no clue where her daughters were for four months. She searched hospitals, state facilities, everywhere she could possibly search for them, only to learn that they had been seized by the IRGC. She had received a call, saying, "We have your girls; come to see them at the prison."
Rape threat in prison
The mother finally got to visit them in prison in May, but she couldn't recognise her own daughters.
A US-based cousin of the twins said they had bruises on their faces, broken elbows, and had extremely patchy scalps from being dragged around by their hair, The Guardian reported.

Taraneh was reportedly told that the prison guards would rape her twin, Romina, in front of her unless they signed a confession.
One sentenced to death, other to 25-year prison term
Around four months have passed since the mother visited her twins at the Dowlatabad prison in Iran's Isfahan city. It has now reportedly been learned that an Iranian court has sentenced Taraneh to death for her participation in the January protests against the regime, while Romina has been given a 25-year prison term.
Since the sentencing, neither of the women has been seen by their family.
The twins' cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in Utah, US, said Iran doesn't follow its own law.

"There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal, but in a lot of (execution) cases recently, that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So, I mean, nothing really makes sense," he was quoted as saying.
The 43-year-old cousin of the twins said he believes Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence, The Guardian reported.
According to him, her kindness is evident in her eyes right away. Speaking about the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Nourmohammadi said, "My sense is like they're looking to put fear within people, to say, 'Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don't come to the streets any more."
Nourmohammadi opened up about his twins despite reportedly receiving death threats via texts and social media from people who say they are aware of his home address. However, he said that the case of his cousins should encourage a determination in people to end the Islamic regime in Iran.
How the twins were taken
The twins, who joined the protests in Isfahan on January 8 and 9 this year, were dragged out of their home with bags over their heads by masked men. Neither the twins nor the family was given any explanation about why they were being taken.
Nourmohammadi said, but when his aunt was finally informed about her daughters and was asked to come to the prison, it turned out to be heartbreaking for her to see her daughters.
"She did not recognise her own children; they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their bodies, broken elbows, knuckles, and feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag it from one cell to another. The twins' mother, Marzieh, was not allowed to attend the trial by herself. However, their lawyers reportedly said that Taraneh told the court that any admissions secured from the twins were obtained through torture. It is claimed that no evidence of their involvement in violence was provided, adding that they had never been involved in protests before.
Executions in Iran
Iran has reportedly executed more than 500 people so far this year, despite the war that broke out following the joint US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic on February 28. Additionally, US President Donald Trump has also been urging Iran to halt executions.
According to a Norway-based NGO, Iran Human Rights, at least 511 people have been executed so far in 2026, including at least 29 in connection with anti-government protests in January.
Among the executions, at least 16 were those of women and at least 13 of "political prisoners" associated with banned opposition groups.

In 2025, Iran executed at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International. However, authorities appear to be intensifying the executions of protesters now.

Opening summary: race to rescue tunnel workers
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

The US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Kyiv for a second day of talks on how to end the war in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, met the pair in Sophia Square, in front of Kyiv’s historic Saint Sophia Cathedral. Zelenskyy greeted Witkoff with a hug, saying: “It’s good to see you, Steve.”
The cathedral is a few hundred metres away from the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency, which was hit by a Russian drone on Friday afternoon, marking an escalation in a conflict that has now dragged on for more than four and a half years.
Witkoff and Kushner are meeting Zelenskyy the day after holding three hours of talks in Moscow with Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
The US envoys have visited Russia several times, but this is their first visit to Ukraine. The trip is intended to mark an intensification of efforts to end the war in Ukraine, although details of any peace proposal remain unclear.
British, French and German national security advisers were reportedly in Kyiv on Sunday before the arrival of Witkoff and Kushner.
Talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending the war have focused on a 20-point peace plan put forward by Washington and Kyiv in December. But the two sides have failed to reach common ground on several sticking points, including control of territory in east Ukraine.
A White House official said on Saturday that the talks with Moscow “discussed substantive plans for next steps” for ending the war and said an announcement would follow in the coming weeks.
The senior Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the talks as “extremely frank” and said there was an acknowledgement of the need to address “the root causes of the conflict”.
Moscow and Kyiv pledged to refrain from strikes on each other’s capital cities for three days to ensure the smooth passage of the negotiators. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that the plans for the US envoys to fly into Moscow had been upended by Russian strikes on Kyiv’s two main airports on Friday evening.
Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Other visiting dignitaries have travelled overland by train from neighbouring countries.
Kyiv and the surrounding areas have been hit by a barrage of daily drone strikes for more than a week, the most sustained attack on Ukraine’s capital in months.
The capital is now enjoying a reprieve from strikes and air raid alerts that had become a daily occurrence, but other parts of the country are still being hit. Ukrainian authorities reported on Sunday that at least eight people were killed and 69 injured across Ukraine in the past day.
Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles that can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones that can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.
Many Ukrainians are worried about the war dragging on into a fifth year and are anxious about the winter ahead. This week, Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, told the Guardian that the government should consider evacuating elderly people from Kyiv as Putin had ordered the Russian military to “prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities.
Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent weeks in an effort to sap morale in each other’s countries.

What’s open and closed on Labor Day? From Costco to banks and UPS pickup
While many workers have the day off, most big consumer-facing businesses are open
The origins of Labor Day, which falls on Monday, date back to the late 19th century, when activists first sought to establish a day that would pay tribute to workers.
The first U.S. Labor Day celebration took place in New York City on September 5, 1882 when some 10,000 workers marched in a parade organized by the Central Labor Union and the Knights of Labor.
A handful of cities and states began to adopt laws recognizing Labor Day in the years that followed, yet it took more than a decade before President Grover Cleveland signed a congressional act in 1894 establishing the first Monday of September as a legal holiday.
While many workers have the day off, most big consumer-facing businesses are open and even offering promotional sales to lure customers.
Here’s what is open and closed this year on Labor Day:
Government buildings
Government offices, post offices, courts and schools are closed.
Banks and the stock market
U.S. stock markets and banks are closed Monday.
Standard FedEx and UPS pickup and delivery services will not be available on Labor Day, although some critical services will be offered at certain locations.
Retailers
Warehouse membership club Costco will be closed on Labor Day, but the vast majority of major national retailers and grocery stores will be open, with many offering promotional sales to lure customers. Hours may vary by location, so check your local store.
Travel
Despite the fact that many schools are back in session and travel costs have risen with higher fuel prices due to the conflict in Iran, millions of Americans will hit the roads and the skies to get away for the last big summer travel weekend.
AAA says that prices for flights to top domestic destinations are nearly 20 percent higher than last year and prices for hotels have also risen. The average U.S. price for a gallon of regular gas, according to the auto club, is just under $4.10, up 90 cents from the same time a year ago.
However, for those traveling by sea, AAA says that cruises departing from U.S. ports are about four percent cheaper than last year.
The auto club doesn’t provide a full travel forecast for Labor Day as it does for Memorial Day and July Fourth. But AAA does offer some useful advice for travelers.
AAA advises travelers to keep an eye on the weather and inspect your vehicle’s tires, battery, and fluid levels before a road trip. It's also a good idea to pack an emergency kit with water, snacks, a flashlight, and jumper cables, AAA says.

Maharashtra Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill (CEB) has no provision to regulate treatment rates charged by private hospitals to patients, highlighted Jan Arogya Abhiyan (JAA), a coalition of NGOs and health professionals, on Friday while launching a statewide campaign appealing public to send objections to Joint Legislative Committee (JLC).
JLC is a committee comprising 21 MLAs, who have been reviewing the objections and suggestions on the Bill. The campaign also includes meetings with all 21 MLAs who are members of the JLC, demanding Health Minister convene a statewide consultation with organisations and networks working in the health sector to discuss the Bill.
JAA pointed out that the Bill must include fixed treatment charges for common procedures, different categories of beds, investigations, ICU services and doctors’ consultations; hospitals violating these rates should face penalties, a refund provision, a mandatory estimated bill by hospital detailing the treatment cost to be given to the patient, and the prescribed limit should not exceed estimated limit more than 5–10%.
The other suggested provision includes, ban withholding of patients or dead bodies over payment issues, establish accessible grievance-redressal system, establish an independent, well staffed regulatory authority, and ensure participation of all stakeholders in the State Council.
CEB was introduced in state Assembly on July 3, advocating compulsory registration of hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic centres transparency in treatment prices, and no deposit mandate for emergency cases. The new bill replaces the 77-years-old Maharashtra Nursing Homes Registration Act, 1949.
According to Arogya Abhiyan representatives, the analysis of hospital data from five major private hospitals in Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur shows that the average treatment charges faced by patients in these hospitals range from ₹24,000 to ₹62,000 per day. “This means just one day’s treatment in a large private hospital can cost as much as the average monthly per-capita income of a person in state,” said Abhay Shukla, the public health expert.
The latest NSS 80th Round data for Maharashtra shows as many as 77% of all hospitalisations in Maharashtra take place in private hospitals, highest among all states in India, average out-of-pocket expenditure on hospitalisation is ₹40,500, and on average rural hospitalisation costs have increased by 87%. 40 lakh people in Maharashtra are estimated to be pushed into poverty because of healthcare expenses.
Jan Arogya Abhiyan appealed to the Joint Legislative Committee to substantially strengthen this Bill in public interest as Section 11-Q of the Maharashtra Nursing Home Registration Act Rules, 2021 states that treatments rates should not exceed rates determined by the government.

Scientists aren’t the only people who participate in Japan’s Antarctica expedition program, which is celebrating its 70th anniversary. Helping to support the research conducted at Syowa Station are teams of engineers, mechanics and doctors.
And then there are chefs.
Their job entails not only keeping 30 fellow expedition members fed all year round but also delighting and uplifting them with occasional parties and events, as the group weathers one of the harshest living environments on Earth with few other forms of entertainment.
All this must be done while keeping limited food supplies in check and making sure that nothing goes to waste.
Despite those challenges, Junko Watanuki, 52, one of two chefs who ran the base’s kitchen in 2016-17, cherishes the experience like no other. She says it taught her invaluable lessons about a simple and sustainable way of living, and it leaves her yearning to go back.
“My values were turned upside down,” Watanuki recalls. “It has made me rethink my lifestyle, to reduce waste and just say ‘no’ to unnecessary giveaways.”
Watanuki, a native of the city of Hachinohe, Aomori Prefecture, has always loved spreading joy through her cooking. She became interested in going to Antarctica in 2003 when she saw an article featuring a female polar region correspondent for the Asahi Shimbun. At that time, Watanuki, who graduated from a culinary school in Tokyo, was a stay-at-home mom after resigning as a cook for the school’s employees.
Years later, she watched “The Chef of South Polar,” a 2009 comedy about a passionate cook stationed at a Japanese station in Antarctica, reigniting her interest in the continent. Now in her late 30s, she was completely overtaken by the desire to join an expedition.
Watanuki began frequenting an eatery run by a former Antarctic chef in Yokohama and listened to tales of culinary pursuits at Syowa Station. While she already had experience handling large volumes of food through her job at the cooking school, Watanuki took up a part-time job at an izakaya to train how to prepare a variety of dishes quickly.
It took her three attempts over three years to pass the exam to join the expedition, which included a high-pressure interview with a National Institute of Polar Research panel.
After months of training and pre-ordering ingredients to ship from Japan, she flew out in the winter of 2016 and boarded the icebreaker Shirase at Fremantle, Australia. On the base, the first couple of months were the hardest, she says, as she had a hard time figuring out how much food she could use each day.
“In Japan, you never experience ordering an entire year’s worth of food and controlling the stock without replenishing it halfway through,” she recalls. “The fear of running out of food was always there, and I would use items conservatively, like 20 eggs at a time instead of 30. After a while, I could grasp the pace of consumption and felt OK.”
She also organized seasonal events, working with other expedition members to prepare food for special occasions such as New Year’s, Halloween and Christmas. She even recreated the famous Jiro ramen shop on the base at the request of a team member.
That project involved months of planning, including visiting the actual Jiro ramen shop while in Japan for research, making chicken broth from scratch and growing 8 kilograms of moyashi bean sprouts in the greenhouse at the Syowa base.
To preserve Antarctica’s natural environment, expedition members must bring all of their waste back home.
Seeing how other members conserved energy and resources — including water — had a profound influence on her.
“In Antarctica, you can instantly understand … how much humans are polluting the environment,” she says. “For example, researchers monitor the atmosphere in real time, displaying data from the observation equipment on their PCs. If a ship approaches Antarctica, you can see carbon dioxide levels go up, even before the ship is visible.
“Also, in Antarctica, the breath you exhale is not white, as there are few aerosols in the air. But the air does look white when exhaust is released from snowmobiles and near power generators. Just by living there, you become aware that you are burdening the environment.”
That sense of guilt haunted her after she came back to Japan. She felt emotionally troubled by the excesses of modern life, and even found herself crying in a supermarket’s deli section, imagining how much of the unsold food there would be discarded after the expiration date.
She also felt disoriented by fast-moving television screens and the bustling streets of Tokyo.
“I learned in Antarctica what it means to know when you have enough,” she says. “I realized that I could get by with just the things I had. I found everyday life back in Japan, where things seem to keep piling up without limit, incredibly suffocating.”
Nearly 10 years on, she remains focused on avoiding waste, from food right down to tissue paper.
Watanuki frequently shares the lessons she learned in Antarctica through lectures on sustainability and food loss. She wrote the 2023 book “Nankyoku no Shokutaku” (“The Antarctic Table”) about her experience cooking in the planet’s most remote region.
“If you are asked to reduce waste from 100 kg to 50 kg, it sounds like such a daunting task,” she says. “But If you just try to reduce the amount of tissue paper you use from two sheets to one at a time, you can also reduce waste by half.
“I also don’t want to waste my experience of going to Antarctica. I want to make full use of it.”

Having appeared in both the penultimate and the final Daniel Craig-era Bond films and in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Two, Léa Seydoux has entered a phase of her career where risk-taking feels paramount. “I like when acting’s a bit dangerous, I think I like to take risks,” she tells me, speaking from her home in Paris.
Seydoux, who shared the best actress prize with Adèle Exarchopoulos at Cannes for Blue is the Warmest Colour, now feels she has “more experience” as an artist. Hence perhaps her decision to take on an extremely weighty, highly-nuanced role in Marie Kreutzer‘s Gentle Monster which is playing at the Telluride Film Festival and was snapped up by Netflix during Cannes.
As Lucy, a musician who shares a nine-year-old son with her director husband Philip (Laurence Rupp), Seydoux plays out the devastating aftermath when he’s suddenly arrested for online activity in child pornography groups. Has he abused their son? How could she have missed the signs? Is it all a mistake? How can this be?
Watch on Deadline
Seydoux hints that she may have sought out a part that’s “so real” because, she concedes, she herself is the mother of two sons, aged nine and 21 months. The children are ”my own personal experience, let’s say,” she tells me. In fact, I can hear her youngest child playing in the background as we talk.
“I think it’s a very interesting age, my age now,” the 41 year-old says. “I don’t like to talk about my age because I don’t want to put myself in a box,” she laughs. “Like, OK, it’s true that this age is very interesting and I feel that I understand things in their complexity more than before.”
She and Kreutzer (Corsage) had many conversations about the film’s highly-charged, sensitive subject matter. “They were about what you can imagine if you were in a similar situation,” noting that, for her, “the movie is very relevant,” with its themes of the betrayal of innocence and the shock of realizing that the man you love, your husband, the father of your young son, has betrayed a sacred trust.
What she had to imagine repelled her, but the discussions that she had with the filmmaker made her realize that she had “to make this film,” she says. “It’s a real problem in society, this problem of pedophilia and families. There was a woman who had a similar story and Marie told me about her and the fact that she spent a lot of time with her.”
Those talks with the woman Kreutzer met helped the director write the film. “It gave her ideas,” Seydoux says, “but for me, when I read the script for the first time, I was immediately touched by the subject and how also what I love is that it’s a statement.” Plus, she was compelled by Marie’s decision “to make this film, and it is important.”
She’s full of admiration, too, for Kreutzer’s “very subtle” script. “And this is what I like, because it’s so difficult to make a movie about that subject, you know, it’s full of complexity.”
Unfortunately, I do have some knowledge of this topic, due to having covered court cases earlier in my career where men, whether they be fathers, brothers, uncles or cousins have appeared in the dock for sexually abusing minors, and I seethed as the accused would attempt to wriggle their way out of the heinous charges against them. And I gained an understanding of the vital work done by the U.K.’s National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children [NSPCC].
None of this makes me a criminal expert, but I did observe women called to give evidence about what their partners did. What I saw in Seydoux’s performance, and what she captures so brilliantly, is the sense of disbelief. Initially, Lucy cannot comprehend what it is her husband might have done. Then it becomes very clear that life for her and her child has been shattered in way that can never be healed.
That’s what I saw in Seydoux’s eyes in the film. I had witnessed such a look in real life, and now here it was in front of me on a big screen as Lucy shed fragile layers with each new revelation.
Seydoux says Kreutzer’s perspective was to hone in on Lucy, making her the “main protagonist” and it’s “through her emotions that we follow the whole thing.” Sighing, she says that sometimes her work allows her to “express something that I feel. I’m not a politician. I cannot really have an opinion and it’s not a subject that I can completely handle in a way, as it’s very, very complex, this subject.”
The situation in the film has “all these contradictions,” she says. “So the fact that she’s in love with this man, but then these horrible things are happening and all these contradictory emotions.”
When we first see Lucy, or rather hear her, she’s at her piano reinterpreting both lyrics and musical arrangements to the Mike Leeson and Peter Vale-written song “Would I Lie To You” (‘Look into my eyes, can’t you see you see they’re open wide? Would I lie to you, baby, would I lie to you?) It was a massive hit in 1992 for Charles & Eddie, but now as sung by Seydoux’s Lucy it’s steeped in unimaginable pain.
Did the director suggest that she study any material related to the topic? “It was very tacit between us,” Seydoux says. “The only thing she asked me was to work on was my German and the piano and the music” But they never really talked about how Lucy felt. “She never gave me intentions.”
Seydoux suggests that the preparations I might have imagined weren’t necessary because “when I read the script, I had an immediate empathy. It was very strong, I really felt that I knew who she was,” a feeling she calls “very rare.” Her voice breaks as she recounts the emotional impact of the experience.
Seydoux is giving a masterclass in acting this awards season, what with both Gentle Monster and in Arthur Harari’s The Unknown. He shared an Oscar as co-writer of Anatomy of a Fall, which was directed and co-written by his wife Justine Triet.
The Unknown is an outrageously sublime movie about a photographer who sleeps with a woman (Seydoux) that he meets at a party, who then awakens to discover that he has transformed into her. I caught both pictures at Cannes and both have stayed with me. The Unknown has two further screenings Sunday at the Sheridan Opera House. Seydoux was attracted to The Unknown because it was both “philosophical and meta physical,” she says. “I like to experience intensity. So making these films, it’s a way to experience intensity.”
Seydoux says of Gentle Monster, “I really love to be able to live inside the film,” and the trick for her is not to over analyze too much. “I was just trying to be her, to be Lucy.”
We discuss how, until laws were changed, men like novelists Gabriel Matzneff were able to go on French television and “boast” of their relationships with underage children. She remembers reading Vanessa Springora’s memoir Consent which detailed her involvement with Matzneff when she was just 14 and he was 49. “I mean, it’s really horrible what he was allowed to do,” Seydoux says. “And to then talk about this pedo pornography on the TV in a brazenly open way. And it’s just crazy when you think of this thing. Everybody was like, ‘Oh, OK,’ and he was making jokes. This horrible man was laughing about it. He seemed to make it acceptable when it’s not,” she says bitterly.
I ask her about Malo Blanchet, who plays Lucy’s son in Gentle Monster. Did he have any idea what the film was about? “Maybe not the whole thing, but I don’t know for sure,” she says. “The parents obviously knew, of course. I don’t think he really knew the story. He’s a kid, too young. I think he was protected,” she says.
However, she was able to discuss the film’s story with Catherine Deneuve who plays Lucy’s mother. “That was a dream of mine to work with her. She’s such an icon,” Seydoux says.
Following Gentle Monster and The Unknown she joined Cate Blanchett in the ridiculously wacky alien comedy Alpha Gang. She lets out a roar of laughter, “I thought it was completely crazy. I needed to do something light after those films.”
And next, she has a project she’s not allowed to talk about. “But it’s a strong story like Gentle Monster and I can’t wait,” she says.
Gentle Monster opens in select U.S. theaters on October 30th and begins streaming on Netflix on November 18th.
The film is produced by Alexander Glehr and Johanna Scherz at Film AG alongside Komplizen Film (Germany), Kazak Productions (France), Kjellson & Wik (Sweden), and Film i Väst.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

It was "horrifying," she says, when Jean, who had a temporary work permit, was laid off from work at the end of July from his position at a nonprofit supporting individuals with developmental and intellectual disabilities. Her son Michael is a 5ft 10in, nonverbal 23-year-old.
"Showering, sleeping, eating, tying his shoes - Michael can't tie his shoes - I mean, there's so much hands-on involvement, and Jean did all of that," she says.
Mancuso was a ball of nerves when she finally agreed to send Michael to residential care, at the age of 19, calling it "the hardest thing I've ever had to do".
When he met Jean in the adult home, however, she felt a sense of peace.
"Certain people just have it," she says of Jean. "He's literally a lifeline."
But Michael lost that lifeline weeks ago, when his employer had to lay Jean off along with 18 other Haitians.
Their temporary protected status (TPS) - which allows eligible foreign nationals from unsafe countries to work in the US - had expired.
The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court.
But America's top judges ruled in favour of the administration, paving the way for 350,000 Haitians to lose their status at the end of July.
The stripping of that status meant that holders can no longer legally work in the US and are at risk of deportation.
The healthcare industry, with a robust Haitian workforce, has been hit particularly hard - with legions of employers forced to fire TPS holders who work directly with patients.
Trump cancelled TPS amid a wave of measures restricting immigration, a central plank of his successful 2024 election campaign.
Immigration was one of the top concerns for voters in that election and, in Long Island, both counties decisively backed Trump.
More than a dozen countries have had their TPS terminated in Trump's second term and Haitians make up nearly a third of all TPS recipients affected.
The care industry is feeling the effects.
Haiti numbers among the top five countries from which immigrants in the direct-care workforce come, says Kezia Scales, vice-president of policy and research at the Paraprofessional Healthcare Institute.
The industry was already under-staffed and waitlists for many care services - from home health aides to assisted living - were already long.
"We simply do not have enough people in our domestic market, when you exclude immigrants, to fill those jobs," she tells BBC News.
National advocacy groups are campaigning for policies that would strengthen the long-term workforce - including ones that "would expand legal pathways for international caregivers".
When asked about the impact of TPS termination, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the BBC that "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that - temporary".
"The assertion that the only way we can support the healthcare industry is by allowing unvetted illegal aliens to remain in the country is grossly false and lazy," the spokesperson said.
At AHRC Nassau, which employed Jean, CEO Stanfort Perry sounds exasperated and exhausted. The organisation let go of 19 Haitian staff this year and 22 last year, amidst other immigration crackdowns, he says.
"It takes us months to recruit one individual to work in this field, train them and prepare them to provide compassionate, caring support to a person with an intellectual and developmental disability," he says.
"I'm competing with fast-food restaurants, grocery stores and retail for staff, because they pay more than what we are able to pay," he adds.
It's an issue across the country. At Jewish Community Services of South Florida, which lost 18 Haitian TPS holders, the remaining aides are also working overtime.
"That is a huge financial strain on a nonprofit like us," says Sarah Katzenstein, the organisation's director of strategic communications and marketing.
The loss of TPS caregivers has been especially damaging to seniors served by the Jewish organisation, as many of them are Holocaust survivors, says Katzenstein.
"They had relationships with these home care aides for years - some of them for decades," she says, adding that Holocaust survivors especially can have difficulty trusting strangers.
"It's a very intimate relationship, so to these clients, the loss of having their Haiti TPS-holding caregivers truly is devastating."
Jewish Community Services has been writing to elected officials to advocate for proposed Senate Bill 4814, which would match a bipartisan bill already passed in the House to extend TPS for Haitians. The effort has currently stalled in the Senate, blocked by Republican opposition.
Hundreds of Haitians have been deported since the Supreme Court ruling, despite widespread gang violence in the country. White House czar Tom Homan defended the deportations in a recent CNN interview.
"The judges made a decision they must go home. And they need to go home... we're just enforcing the law. And we're doing it in a way that the American people voted for."
According to polling released last month by AP-NORC, external, support for Trump's overall immigration policy has fallen 10% since the start of his second term but remains relatively strong compared with other issues like the economy. On deportations, about half of US adults surveyed said Trump had gone too far, which is about the same number as the start of the year.
A Pew Research survey in June 2025, external, before the TPS provision was withdrawn from Haitians, suggested 39% of Americans supported the ending of TPS but 59% disapproved.
Back on Long Island, Mancuso is grieving the loss of a carer who had actually managed to connect with her high-needs son.
"That's one of the things that, as a parent, you worry [about]. Does this kid know that there are other people in the world, other than me, that love him?
"And I think he sensed that from Jean - that it's not just a job."
Her son might not be able to say it, but she knows he misses Jean and doesn't understand why he's no longer there. For Mancuso, her already-high anxiety about her son's well-being is skyrocketing.
"With Jean, I had not a care in the world," she says.
She's worried not just for her son but also for the other families served by the local non-profit - and, of course, for Jean and TPS holders like him who are living with uncertainty, unsure if or when they will be deported.
"I'm hoping against hope that this thing gets resolved," she says. "I care about [Jean] as a human being, he needs a livelihood - and this has been a livelihood for him, and he's good at it, helping my son.
"And it's directly impacting my son by his lack of presence here - and I want him back."

Indian state gives taxi and tuk-tuk drivers a year to learn local language
- Published
An Indian state has given taxi and tuk-tuk drivers one more year to learn the local language after a new rule making it mandatory sparked protests.
Transport officials in the western state of Maharashtra had begun testing drivers' ability to conduct basic conversations in Marathi, the state's official language, on 20 August. Those who failed were given a month to learn the language, after which they risked having their licences suspended or cancelled.
The government said the requirement was meant to improve communication between drivers and passengers and ensure safer journeys.
But the rule alarmed drivers' unions, who argued that workers should not risk losing their livelihoods while they were still learning the language. Many of the drivers are migrants who came to Maharashtra from other parts of India in search of work, including the populous Hindi-speaking states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
Amid protests, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced last week that the drivers would be given another year to learn Marathi, as many had been out of the formal education system for years and needed more time.
State Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik has said that drivers will be expected to learn Marathi during the year and that there will be more extensions.
Maharashtra has almost 979,000 valid tuk-tuk and taxi permits, nearly half of them in the Mumbai metropolitan region.
The extension has brought some relief to drivers who had feared losing their ability to work.
"We were worried that if our licences were suspended, our daily income would be affected," says Lakhan Pandey, a taxi driver in Mumbai. "Now we feel somewhat relieved."
But the row has reopened a much older debate in Maharashtra, where questions of language, migration and jobs have shaped politics for decades.
"The issue is not simply about communication between drivers and passengers, but about Marathi identity, migration and employment," says Prakash Akolkar, a journalist, author and political analyst.
Those tensions stretch back to the creation of Maharashtra itself. The state was formed in 1960 after a long campaign for a Marathi-speaking state.
As Mumbai grew into India's financial centre, it drew generations of migrants from across the country in search of work. Language became increasingly entwined with arguments over jobs and opportunities for Marathi speakers.
In 1966, the Shiv Sena, a regional political party rooted in Marathi nationalism, was founded on a "sons of the soil" platform, arguing that Marathi speakers were losing jobs to migrants. It went on to become one of Maharashtra's most powerful political forces, with Marathi identity at the heart of its appeal.
Today, Maharashtra is governed by a coalition led by Fadnavis's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and one faction of the Shiv Sena, which split in 2022. The rival faction and another regional party, the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS), have also championed the Marathi cause.
Akolkar says it is reasonable to expect people who move to a state to learn some of the local language. But he draws a distinction between that and the politics around it.
"Ordinary people do not always treat language with the same intensity as political parties," he says, adding that parties have often raised the issue when it suits the political circumstances.
Deepak Pawar, a political scientist and president of the Marathi Abhyas Kendra (Marathi Training Centre), which promotes the language, takes a stronger view. He argues that people who have lived in Maharashtra for years should already have acquired at least a basic knowledge of Marathi.
Refusing to learn the local language after living and working in the state for years is "linguistic arrogance", he says.
It's a tension that has played out in other states including Karnataka, where language activists fear their local language - Kannada - is being marginalised as many migrants believe they can get by using Hindi or English.
In Maharashtra, the government says drivers are not expected to read or write Marathi, or to speak it fluently. Under changes to the state's motor vehicle rules, they are required to have a "working knowledge" of the language.
To help them learn, the government has organised classes focused on Marathi words and phrases drivers might need at work - asking passengers where they want to go, discussing fares or giving directions.
Around 166,000 drivers have completed the training and passed an oral test, according to the state's transport department.
Munawar Sheikh, a 58-year-old tuk-tuk driver, was among those who signed up.
Over four days at a training centre in Thane, near Mumbai, he and other drivers learnt 16 commonly used questions and phrases, including "Where do you want to go?", "don't worry" and "the fare will be according to the meter".
At the end, they took an oral test, with those who passed receiving a certificate they could show transport officials during inspections.
Sheikh says the course taught him enough Marathi to manage basic conversations with passengers.
But for some drivers, finding the time to learn is part of the problem.
Ajay Singh, a taxi driver in Mumbai, says he wants to learn Marathi but has struggled to fit classes around his working day.
"From the time we wake up until late at night, we have to drive. Otherwise, there is no food on the table," he says. "Taking a few hours out of the day for a class is financially difficult for me."
Singh says he earns between 1,500 and 2,000 rupees ($17-$23; £13-£17) a day and worries that losing even a few days' income could leave him struggling to pay rent and his children's school fees.
Instead, he is trying to learn while he works - listening to Marathi radio stations while driving and practising with Marathi-speaking passengers.
Lakhan Pandey, also a driver, says the extra year has made a significant difference.
He says he never objected to learning Marathi - he just wanted enough time to do it.
"We live here, we work here. Of course we should learn Marathi," he says. "Just give us the time to learn it without putting our livelihoods at risk."

Since the dawn of Silicon Valley, there’s been a widespread perception that San Francisco is, put gently, not exactly a dating mecca.
The city famously has a skewed male-to-female ratio (per census data, there are about 105 men for every 100 women), and there’s a perception among many women that men who work in tech tend to have poor social and emotional skills and a lack of style—opting for Patagonia vests and Meta glasses rather than putting substantive effort into their appearance.
On August 31, however, Celeste Amadon, the founder of the AI-powered dating app Known, valiantly attempted to reverse that stereotype. In an X thread accompanied by a moody, upward-angled selfie, she announced that she and her team were compiling a list of “SF’s most dateable people,” titled “San Francisco’s Hot List.” She attached a link for people to nominate their single friends according to criteria like “ambition,” “accomplishment,” “reputation,” and “aura.”
The post was skewered online by many in and outside of the tech scene, with some referring to it as “cringe” or mocking the lack of eligible singles in San Francisco: “The solution to dating in SF is to leave SF,” posted one female founder. But it was an extremely effective bit of marketing for Known, garnering more than 15,000 submissions 24 hours after the tweet was posted, according to Amadon. It was also an effective piece of counter-propaganda to the stereotype of San Franciscans, officially heralding that San Francisco Is Hot.
“Not to be cheesy, but I think the SF dating scene deserves some defending,” Amadon tells WIRED. “It gets so much flak for being a place where it’s hard to meet people, but there are many people who are super eligible in not just their physical attractiveness but in their holistic dateability.”
Known’s Hot List is part of a broader conversation focused on the general attractiveness of the San Francisco populace—and why some locals seem to be placing more importance on being perceived as hot.
Last summer, two women who work in tech—Madison Kanna (who is on the Hot List) and Cat Orman—threw an “enforced ratio” party at a Tesla showroom in the city, ensuring that there were as many women as men. The invite stipulated that the vibe would be “unapologetically feminine and fun” and that “Patagonia vests will be turned away at the door.” On August 28, Mantis Biotech startup founder Georgia Witchel posted an X thread titled “Tech Is Having a Hot Girl Renaissance.” In the thread, Witchel describes how social media has been deluged with “young, attractive women taking tastefully slutty duck-faced mirror selfies” to promote their startups, citing Known and the insurance company Corgi as examples.
Witchel says her argument is not so much that she objects to young women using their attractiveness as a marketing strategy—it's more to explain how and why it has emerged as a marketing strategy to begin with, telling WIRED the trend is a result of “a renaissance of sales culture in SF.”
Throughout much of Silicon Valley, software marketing was “nerds selling to other nerds,” she says—but with the emergence of vibe coding, the barrier to entry for the industry has gotten lower, and the standards for marketing a product higher. “The fact that you are able to build a complicated product is not enough to give you the leeway of not being charismatic,” says Witchel. “People are recognizing that.”
When reached for comment, Brooke LeBlanc, head of community at Corgi, who Witchel cites in her thread, referred WIRED to an X post. “My mom just heard about the hot girl in tech renaissance and she’s absolutely thrilled by the news,” she wrote. “No one in my family from Georgia can believe that it’s breaking news for a woman to care about how she looks.”
Amadon says the Hot List has “minimal” connection to Witchel’s thread, but she understands why Known’s marketing “draws interest” (though she notes that X specifically is “not a primary marketing channel” for the app). She concedes that the list was intended to capitalize on the discussion and create “positive discourse” around dating in San Francisco.
And it’s working: On September 1, Known posted the first round of Hot Listers, including LeBlanc and startup founders like Jasper Carmichael-Jack, the CEO of the AI-driven company Artisan. There was nary a Patagonia vest in the bunch.
