You probably don't need two routers — do this instead
Two routers can work in some specific situations, but there are other devices that work better to achieve most network needs.
Adding a second router can seem like an easy fix for weak Wi-Fi. Put another box at the other end of the house, connect it to the first router, and you've got another wireless network. The trouble starts when both devices are left in router mode, because each can create and manage its own private network.
Most homes only need one device doing the actual routing. If you need better coverage or more connections, the cleaner approach is usually to extend the network the existing router already manages, rather than creating another routed network behind it.
Two routers can create a network behind a network
A home router creates your local network, then uses Network Address Translation (NAT) so its connected devices share a connection with the internet. The job of a router isn't just to broadcast Wi-Fi; it sorts the incoming and outgoing traffic on your network so all information arrives at the right place. When you connect a second router in normal router mode behind the first, the second device creates another private network while also performing NAT. This arrangement is known as double NAT.
That doesn't necessarily make normal web browsing or streaming noticeably slower. Double NAT has no major effect on network performance for most cases. Problems are more likely to appear with tasks that depend on connections reaching a particular device, including online gaming, port forwarding and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP).
Running two private networks can also make it harder for devices to find each other. For example, a computer connected to the first router and a printer connected to the second may end up on different networks, even though they're in the same home. This adds unnecessary complication.
Use mesh or access point mode for better Wi-Fi
If coverage is your problem, a mesh Wi-Fi system is built for extending one network throughout a home. Its nodes work together, rather than each creating an independent routed network. This makes mesh a much cleaner solution than placing another router in a weak-signal area.
You may also be able to reuse a router you already own for this task. Many models include access point (AP) mode, which has the device simply act as a Wi-Fi connection point while the primary router continues managing the network. In AP mode, most routers will disable features such as firewall and IP sharing because the main router handles those functions.
If you already have Ethernet in the room with weak Wi-Fi, an router acting as an access point can use that wired connection to extend your network there. This is a viable alternative to dedicated Wi-Fi extenders.
Meanwhile, if Wi-Fi coverage is fine and you're simply out of Ethernet ports, use an Ethernet switch instead. These add wired connections to the existing network without creating another routing layer.
Bridge an ISP gateway if you want your new router in charge
Internet providers often supply a gateway, combining the modem or fiber connection with router functions and Wi-Fi in one box. Connecting your router to that gateway doesn't automatically stop the ISP equipment from routing traffic, so leaving both devices in their default modes can produce double NAT.
If you want your own router or mesh system to control the network, check whether the ISP gateway supports bridge mode. Bridge mode stops the gateway from acting as a router, leaving your own router to manage the network instead. That also avoids double NAT. The exact procedure varies by provider and hardware, so this isn't a setting to change from generic instructions. Check the ISP's documentation first, particularly because bridge mode can affect other functions supplied by its gateway.
The other option is to keep the ISP gateway as your main router and put your own router or mesh system into access point mode. In that setup, the ISP gateway still handles routing, while your secondary device mainly provides Wi-Fi coverage. The downside is that some router-specific features on your device may stop working, which is a particular pain since many routers offer more features than ISP-provided models. TP-Link, for example, says AP mode disables functions such as NAT forwarding, VPN, QoS and some parental controls.
The decision depends on which device you want to manage the network. If you bought a new router specifically for its routing features, bridging the ISP gateway makes more sense. If you're satisfied with the gateway and just want better wireless coverage, AP mode is the simpler arrangement.
Two active routers only make sense in specific setups
There are reasons to run two routers at the same time, but they usually involve deliberately creating two separate networks. A networking hobbyist might use a second router for a home lab, for example, keeping experimental devices and services away from the main home network.
A second router can also be useful when testing new networking hardware or settings. Someone trying a different router, VPN configuration or custom network setup may want to experiment without changing the connection used by everyone else in the house. These are intentional setups where having two networks is part of the goal, rather than an accidental side effect.
That's different from turning an old router into an access point or mesh node. In those setups, the extra device helps extend the network, while your main router remains in charge. For most homes, that's the simpler arrangement when the goal is better Wi-Fi rather than a completely separate network.

Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
- Published
Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.
These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinated vandalism. Yet here, four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.
The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording."
These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California and Georgia.
Proponents say they have made communities safer and have helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have caused concern. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.
They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.
A new age of surveillance
Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.
But little is known about the extent to which Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide and estimates that there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.
Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.
Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.
For example, Houston's Metro Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show Metro has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.
And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year-on-year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.
By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.
Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship - and that's very problematic".
There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.
He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.
Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.
CCTV cameras, licence-plate readers and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice and tune into the capabilities of the technology around them.
With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.
One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that does not mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.
The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI.
The tool includes a database of more than 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a license agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.
Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.
Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. It did not respond to requests for comment.
Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.
"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer."
Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.
Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had gotten lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."
Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.
"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."
'I feel like I'm being stalked'
Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".
The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching for a licence plate.
Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.
"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.
In response, she's changed her commute to work. "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."
But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.
In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.
Hundreds of contracts cancelled
Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle and Austin.
In total, more than 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice, external. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.
Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested that there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.
The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to seven, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.
Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley told the BBC that it was up to individual cities to decide how long to store data and what information to share with whom.
"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.
"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."
Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.
He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find more than 10,000 missing people.
"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".
But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.
The study published Thursday in the journal Science involved tests on rats and certain human tissues as researchers looked at using psilocybin to fight a condition called peripheral neuropathy, which affects millions of people around the world.
It is a nerve ailment that hits about three quarters of all people who undergo chemo and commonly causes numbness and tingling, Patrick Dougherty, a co-author of the study, said in a call with reporters.
But a third of that group will develop non-stop, burning pain, said Dougherty, a pain treatment specialist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
The symptoms can lead to trouble walking and other debilitating complications that can last after a person finishes chemotherapy, and even remain with them for life.
And it is not just a quality-of-life issue. This complication also affects a cancer patient's chances of survival because sometimes the side effects are so bad they force doctors to cut back on chemo or stop it altogether.
Protecting nerves
It was almost by accident that these researchers found that psilocybin can help cancer patients.
The team was initially studying how the disease manages to hijack nerve cells in order to grow.
And the researchers were surprised to see the mushroom ingredient -- it was being used to study a brain pathway regeneration concept called neuroplasticity -- actually prevented the emergence of peripheral neuropathy.
Later experiments highlighted psilocybin's role in protecting nerve cells and stimulating inside them the transport of mitochondria, often referred to as a cell's powerhouse.
This is key because chemo destroys the microscopic railroads that allow mitochondria to send energy all the way to the tips of people's hands and feet, killing off nerve endings there.
Psilocybin also seems to act on the brain, preserving electrical activity that chemotherapy thwarts.
In rodents, taking two doses of psilocybin before chemo was enough to prevent the appearance of painful hypersensitivity during as many as six rounds of treatment. And it did this without affecting the animal's immune system or hindering the cancer-fighting action.
Careful with self-medicating
"This is a highly promising finding," said Kristy Townsend, a professor of neurobiology at The Ohio State University who was not involved in the study.
And psilocybin's nerve-protecting quality does not seem to be linked to its hallucinogenic effects because a non-hallucinogenic analogue had the same effect in a lab test, she added.
Before the treatment can be made standard for people, testing will be needed to see if it is safe and effective, said Townsend.
This will be a long, slow process though it should be eased by a boom in medical research on psychedelic substances and a Trump administration executive order in April to speed up research and regulatory reviews, these scientists say.
The MD Anderson Cancer Center plans to launch clinical tests with psilocybin on cancer patients later this year.
Meanwhile it is important for cancer patients to avoid using magic mushrooms on their own as treatment, the researchers warned.
Psilocybin is legal in a few U.S. states.
The drug has an "amplifier" effect and cancer patients who take it without supervision could feel more stressed and anxious than they already are because of their cancer diagnosis, said Gregory Jones, a psychiatrist who took part in the study released Thursday.
"If you put somebody in adversity under these psychedelic substances, you can get much worse," Jones said.

Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
Universities that hide from the technology will merely secure their irrelevance.
Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college. They are right to be worried. New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work.
Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease. This is how I know it is also curable.
Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test. We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic. Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test.
We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase. AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming. Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat. But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away.
The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes. Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish. In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely.
In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense. But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI. If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively.
In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math. This points to a way forward. When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically. But if higher education opts for prohibition over practice, we will squander the chance to help shape how this technology gets used in the world—ensuring that the private sector will do this for us instead.
Colleges must start by being clear about what a degree is actually worth in the AI age. At Dartmouth, the Ivy League university where I am president, we believe it’s our job to teach students how to do what AI can’t: decide which questions to ask, exercise sound judgment, navigate ethical complexity, reckon with uncertainty, and take responsibility for their decisions. Then, we have to give them the chance to practice these skills in concert with AI.
Harnessing AI ethically and productively requires understanding what the technology is and where it falls short. This is why Dartmouth, along with other schools such as Johns Hopkins University and Rollins College, has employed a critical AI librarian, an educator who helps students and faculty interrogate these models, recognize their biases, and spot unsupported claims. At our DALI Lab, where students design and create technological products, they can now build and stress-test their own AI models, which elevates their understanding of the risks and rewards at play. Our ambition at Dartmouth is for every undergraduate to experience a team-based AI project that relates to their coursework by the time they graduate.
Practice using AI matters even more when students start to specialize. To help prepare business students for AI use in the real world, Dartmouth’s Tuck School of Business now requires that they use the technology to build and test solutions for clients in their First-Year Project. Thanks to this experience, students who lacked AI expertise when they entered the program reported greater confidence using the technology by the end of their first year. At Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine, our faculty developed an AI Patient Actor to help medical-school students sharpen their communication and interpersonal skills with the benefit of real-time feedback. The tool is now being used by more than 100 medical institutions worldwide.
Adapting the college experience for the AI era will be an ongoing process, and there is much work to do. But these examples demonstrate what’s both possible and necessary in higher education. Our job as educators is to teach students how to approach AI critically, help them see what AI can’t answer, and practice using these tools effectively. When these students graduate and are out in the world, employers will certainly expect that they have these skills already.
Globally, jobs that require advanced AI skills are growing eight times faster than the job market overall, according to an analysis from the professional-services network PwC. At the same time, entry-level roles in AI-exposed fields are more than seven times likelier than other entry-level jobs to require the human skills once reserved for senior executives, including discernment, creativity, and leadership. Never before has the ability to harmonize critical thinking and technology mattered more for graduates.
There will not—and should not—be a one-size-fits-all solution to the challenges of supplying this education. One professor may decide that students should write their essays in a blue book in class, while another may ask them to use an AI tool and audit every step of this work. Both choices will serve students when faculty are clear about their ambitions and standards. But outright bans or vague curbs afford no opportunities for students to better understand how to work ethically and effectively with AI.
Seventy years ago, pioneering computer scientists launched the field of artificial intelligence on Dartmouth’s campus. That history gives our institution some responsibility for what comes next—not just to prepare students for a future defined by AI, but to give them the tools to help shape that future themselves. If colleges and universities sit out this revolution, we abdicate a sacred commitment that has guided American higher education for centuries: to prepare the next generation of leaders to navigate an ever-changing, always complicated, and frequently perilous world. In a world that promises to be defined by AI, universities that fail to produce graduates who can use it productively will consign themselves to irrelevance.

New Delhi building collapse kills 1, traps others
At least two people were hospitalised in critical condition, and the cause of the collapse was not immediately known
A building collapsed in New Delhi on Sunday, killing at least one person and trapping several others, officials said.
The five-storey building, which housed a boys’ hostel, collapsed in Satya Niketan, a densely populated neighbourhood known for its private student accommodation near a Delhi University campus.
Fire officer Abhilash Malik said about 30 to 40 people remained trapped in the rubble.
Lawmaker Anil Sharma said some people had been rescued and several others trapped inside were making phone calls for help while rescuers remained in contact with them.
Police, firefighters and crews from India’s disaster response agency searched the rubble as earth movers cleared debris to help rescuers reach those trapped inside.

What China’s Lop Nur desert base expansion means for PLA stealth jets in race with US
Remote site is ideal for quiet testing of sensitive, next-generation aircraft, analysts say, as some forecast faster high-end PLA deployment
Latest satellite photos of the facility near Lop Nur, in China’s western Xinjiang region, show four large new hangars, new taxiway work, a circular pad believed to be an engine-run or turnaround area, and possible fuel-storage infrastructure, according to an August 28 analysis by defence website TWZ.

Not a mistrial, yet. Clancy's lawyer asks for emergency appeal in her murder trial
The judge in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy has granted the request of her defense attorney to appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court to seek an emergency stay in the case. This came moments after the judge said he intended to declare a mistrial Friday morning.
Clancy, 36, was charged with strangling 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in the family's home in Duxbury, Mass. Her defense argued she should not be held criminally liable because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time, an approach often called the insanity defense. The prosecution argued Clancy was well enough to plan and act intentionally.
The jury has been deliberating for six days and told the judge they could not reach a verdict. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan to dismiss a holdout juror on Thursday. Reddington referenced two notes the jury foreperson sent the court about the juror, who, according to Reddington, admitted doubt but refused to join the other 11 jurors in finding Clancy not guilty.
However, Judge William Sullivan denied that request. He did however instruct the jury on the meaning of "reasonable doubt."
When making his request for a stay on Friday, Reddington said of the holdout juror, "I believe that this is a situation where there is a clear and present danger that this individual, for some reason, what it is we don't know, but is taking a position that's intractable, regardless of proof beyond a reasonable doubt."
Reddington also asked the judge to survey the jury to see if they could reach an agreement on a lesser charge, such as second-degree murder or manslaughter, before declaring a mistrial, so that Clancy couldn't be tried again for first-degree murder. The judge denied that request as well.
The judge agreed to give Reddington an hour to make his appeal to the state's top court.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

When Amrit Diyali saw a human hand washed downstream by floodwaters, he was struck by how closely it resembled his younger brother Raj Kumar’s, who has been missing along with his wife and four-year-old son since the devastating floods hit Nepal.
“I found a hand that looks exactly like uncle’s,” Diyali’s nephew Avinash told him after sending him a photograph of the severed hand, according to The Kathmandu Post newspaper.
For Diyali, the discovery brought both hope and dread. A DNA test is now his family’s only chance of knowing whether the remains belong to his brother.
The case reflects a much larger challenge facing Nepal, where authorities are relying on DNA testing to identify hundreds of bodies recovered after the August 26 floods and help families find relatives who remain missing.
Flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.
The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.
It has killed more than 1,300, while around 5,000 people remain missing.
Police have so far collected 2,272 DNA samples -- 1,260 from bodies and 1,012 from relatives -- as they try to establish the identities of those killed in the disaster, The Kathmandu Post reported.
Authorities said 1,030 bodies had been buried after DNA samples were collected and other identification procedures completed. The figure includes 222 women, 355 men and 453 bodies whose sex could not be established, the newspaper reported.
Only 96 bodies have been handed over to families so far after identification, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Identifying the dead has emerged as a major challenge.
Bodies recovered after being swept downstream have often been severely damaged, decomposed or recovered only in parts, making identification by face, clothing or personal belongings difficult, officials said.
Prolonged immersion in water and exposure to mud and debris can destroy identifiable features, while some remains have been fragmented or mixed with other remains. Forensic experts say DNA testing has therefore become crucial, but it is a time-consuming process requiring samples from the remains and biological relatives for comparison.
Fingerprints and dental records can also establish identities, but their usefulness depends on the condition of the remains and the availability of matching records, said officials.
For families such as the Diyali’s, however, identification is not merely a forensic exercise. It is a way of ending days of uncertainty and allowing them to perform the final rites of their loved ones.
Raj Kumar, 33, his 30-year-old wife Shriti and their four-year-old son Siraj were living in Syaphrubesi in Rasuwa district when the Bhotekoshi flood struck. His relatives searched along the river as far as Chitwan and Nawalpur, turning over mud and stones in the hope of finding the family. When they could not find them alive, they began looking for their bodies.
Five days after the flood, Raj Kumar’s nephew, Avinash, found the hand in Nawalpur. The family sent a sample from it to the National Forensic Science Laboratory in Kathmandu on Tuesday for DNA testing. The sample is 182nd in line for testing, according to Diyali.
“We have stopped hoping for anything else,” he told The Kathmandu Post. “Even if that hand turns out to be my brother’s, at least we would know for sure.”
To make the process easier for families, Nepal Police has opened a DNA sample collection centre in Bidur, Nuwakot, allowing relatives of missing people to provide samples without travelling to Kathmandu, the Ratopati news portal reported.
Deputy Inspector General of Nepal Police Hospital Damodar Poudel said samples from close blood relatives such as parents, children and siblings are particularly useful for comparison with DNA obtained from unidentified bodies.
According to Poudel, DNA testing will help in identification, as there are difficulties in identifying the bodies.
Authorities have also uploaded details of 1,270 unidentified bodies on the Nepal Police website so families can check whether their missing relatives are among those recovered, The Kathmandu Post reported.

Naomi Osaka overcomes Achilles issue to advance at US Open, apologises to children after win
In short:
Naomi Osaka has advanced to the fourth round of the US Open after beating Elise Mertens in a three-setter.
Osaka apologised to children for her behaviour during the match after she threw a racquet to the floor at one point.
What's next?
Osaka says the Achilles niggle she suffered is not a "huge injury". She will face No.2 seed Elena Rybakina in the fourth round.
Naomi Osaka continued to impress with her style and staying power at the US Open on Saturday as she shrugged off a late Achilles problem to beat Belgian Elise Mertens 6-3, 3-6, 7-5 and reach the fourth round.
For her latest eye-catching walk-on look, the four-time major champion blended boardroom and locker-room aesthetics in a grey checked blazer-hoodie and wide-leg pants, putting a tailored twist on traditional pre-match attire.
She looked on course for a business-like win after the first set but was dragged into a battle in the third, where she had to fight through the Achilles niggle to advance.
"I wouldn't say it's a huge injury," Osaka told reporters. "I'd say it's this ongoing problem that I've had since the grass season.
"I don't know why it hasn't gone away. I feel I've done a lot of things in order to make it better, but maybe the time off wasn't enough. I'm not really sure what the reason is, but the medical timeout was to address that.
"You know, she massaged my leg and stuff, so that seemed to help, and gave me Tylenol."
The 28-year-old, a two-time champion at Flushing Meadows, reeled off three games in succession to take a 4-1 lead in the first set under the lights of Louis Armstrong Stadium, clinching it with a battling hold thanks to a string of booming serves.
Osaka pushed the 23rd seed hard at the start of the next set with some heavy hitting from the baseline before pouncing with a break in the third game, only to surrender the lead by dropping the next two games.
"Honestly, I can't believe I won this match," Osaka said on court after sealing victory, thanking the crowd for the energy it provided.
"There was a certain point where I put my heart on the court and kept trying in every point. Thank you so much, but honestly, I'm shocked I won. I'm not going to lie."
After levelling the match to force a decider, Mertens capitalised on several unforced errors by a frustrated Osaka to gain the upper hand, but there would be another momentum shift in the match after a medical timeout for the Japanese player.
"I didn't play amazing and it was getting me down, sorry about my behaviour, for the little kids watching," said Osaka, who threw her racket to the floor at one point.
"This is my favourite tournament. I wanted to play well in front of you. I'm just that glad I have the opportunity to play another match.
"I thought I was going to be OK, but clearly I was shaky."
After recovering a break late on, Osaka fired a huge ace to take a 6-5 lead and revved up her forehand in the following game to complete the win and earn a meeting with Elena Rybakina in the next round.

Anthropic’s prospective public-market investors must reckon with an external group of trustees that control the majority of the AI company’s board, as its planned blockbuster initial public offering forces close scrutiny of its experimental governance structure.
The company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) is a small group of advisers created to safeguard the lab’s mission of developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity, even as commercial pressures intensify.
The trust holds no equity in Anthropic, but has significant influence, with the San Francisco-based company planning to preserve its role after a stock market debut that could value the Claude maker at as much as $2 trillion.
The LTBT, which is the controlling governance mechanism of the Anthropic public benefit corporation, has the right to appoint or dismiss the majority of the company’s board. It has selected four of Anthropic’s seven directors, including Netflix’s co-founder Reed Hastings and Vas Narasimhan, chief executive of Novartis.
Currently, the LTBT has three members out of a potential maximum of five, chaired by Neil Buddy Shah, chief executive of the Clinton Health Access Initiative, alongside former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke and Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Mariano-Florentino “Tino” Cuéllar, a former California Supreme Court justice, left the trust after a few months to work as Anthropic’s chief global affairs officer.
Anthropic is attempting to establish a template for future AI governance through the trust, said multiple people close to its plans.
They said the ambition for the LTBT is to provide an industry blueprint, similar to the GAAP accounting principles, which initially emerged as voluntary standards proposed by private companies. Bernanke’s appointment in July signals this intention to build a more institutional body, one person added.
The trustees are required to receive advance notice of major company actions, including the launch of new AI models. They meet weekly among themselves, while also meeting Anthropic’s leadership as frequently as every other week, according to people close to the matter.

Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
- Published
When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".
Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said, so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".
Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?
It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.
Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016., external
It is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.
Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role.
"I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."
De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England.
"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.
London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.
The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sits about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.
According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.
Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic.
But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.
Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.
Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."
There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times.
"Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.
The reason gold storage is such a topic in the minds of central banks is because they have been increasingly buying the stuff. But storing it at home comes at a cost, said Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
"Domestic storage requires investment in physical security, audit infrastructure, and insurance; costs that can be disproportionate for smaller central banks," they said.
Over the past four years, central banks have accumulated an annual average of 1,000 tonnes of gold, up significantly from the 500 tonnes average over the preceding decade, according to the World Gold Council.
The trend stretches back to the global financial crisis. And that is only expected to go up in the next year.
Gold has been having a moment in recent years. Its price has surged to hit a series of record highs, passing $5,000 an ounce in January.
There are several reasons behind its value jumping, but a major factor has been the precious metal's position in the human psyche as a so-called safe haven asset, to invest during periods of financial and geopolitical turmoil caused through trade and military wars.
Inflation and interest rates also influence gold's popularity. Due to the commodity's scarcity and the value placed on it across thousands of years, it is somewhat resistant against rising prices, and so is seen as a good investment.
"Over the past half-century, gold prices have risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) - the most closely watched measure of inflation," according to investment bank Charles Schwab.
While the price of gold has fallen from the record high seen early this year, it still remains at a high level historically.
According to researchers at Goldman, the price is forecast to rise to $4,900 (£3,624) per troy ounce by the end of 2026, $300 more than it was in August.
The demand for gold from central banks is one key reason why prices are surging, according to Thomas and Struyven.

No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive?
- Published
For the fourth time in five majors, there will be no British interest in the second week when the US Open moves into the latter stages.
Underwhelming performances at this year's Australian Open, French Open and Wimbledon led to a series of inquests into what was going wrong.
But there is not quite the same sense of doom and gloom, despite everyone being wiped out after the second round in New York.
"Do I think there could be an inquest? I always think there's things that British tennis could do better. So yes, definitely," said British women's number three Francesca Jones.
"Do I think it's something that's concerning? No, not at all.
"The level is getting better and everyone is dangerous on their day."
With the Grand Slam season now over for the singles players, BBC Sport analyses the positives and negatives in British tennis.
Another Slam semi-final and more top 100 players - the positives
Arthur Fery's extraordinary run to the Wimbledon semi-finals is the clear highlight.
The 24-year-old was ranked 114th in the world and needed a wildcard to play at the All England Club, but took full advantage to produce a performance which nobody could have predicted.
Fery was the only player to reach the second week at a Slam this year and has been heralded by British tennis bosses as proof their talent development pathway is working.
Nine Britons competing in the US Open main-draw singles - the most since 1981- is also highlighted as a sign of recent improvement.
That figure does not include 2021 US Open champion Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper, who both missed out with long-term injuries.
"We obviously want more and more competitors in the second week of Slams - just like the British public," said LTA chief executive Scott Lloyd.
"But the fact we've had four different British players make Grand Slam semi-finals since 2021 - you have to go back 30 years before Andy Murray to have four - shows there is no question that the direction of travel has improved.
"We've just got to keep driving for more - and that's what we're trying to do day in and day out."
Five British men are set to feature in the world top 100 after the US Open, with Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Toby Samuel and Jacob Fearnley representing the highest tally since February 2024.
On the women's side, there will be two players - Katie Boulter and Raducanu - in the top 100, although Jones and Harriet Dart moved back to the cusp after reaching the Flushing Meadows second round.
"We've sent 12 players to the world's top 100 over the past eight years and four of those have played Grand Slam semi-finals," said LTA performance director Michael Bourne.
"I'm not sure what other period in the modern era where we've had that level of productivity. Hopefully the number in the top 100 will rise over the next year."
Injuries, trailing other nations and coaching issues - the negatives
Despite those figures, some will argue that Britain - with its rich tradition and spending power as a Grand Slam nation - is still punching well below its weight.
A glut of injuries for many British players over the past year has not helped the cause.
Former world number four Draper has barely played over the past year because of an arm injury, while Sonay Kartal - who cracked the top 50 last year - has also dropped outside of the top 100 following a long-term back issue.
Britain has fewer players inside the top 100 than the United States, Australia and France, who also benefit from the revenue generated by hosting Grand Slam tournaments.
It also trails nations such as Spain, Italy, the Czech Republic and Argentina, who are all heralded for their talent production.
But Britain cannot simply "pick up a plan" of what others are doing as every country has its own "tennis ecosystem", says Bourne.
Lloyd adds: "We're competing in one of the most internationally elite sports out there and the landscape is vastly different to 40 or 50 years ago in terms of the number of countries which have representation at the top.
"We're ambitious, we want to drive for more, but we honestly believe the indicators are positive. We're moving in the right direction and stronger than where we have been historically."
Encouraging more British children to pick up a racquet from an early age is crucial to developing the next generation of stars.
Draper, Raducanu and Fery - who entered the LTA system at a young age - provide the blueprint.
There are 4.3m juniors playing tennis annually with 1.9m playing every month, which Lloyd says are both all-time records.
But there is a concern that a lack of high-level coaching is stunting the development of many more promising talents.
Bourne admits the UK needs a "higher base" of coaches, adding that one of the LTA's key strategies is "spending time and effort" on developing them.
Chris Marshall, a senior performance coach with over 25 years' experience, fears many youngsters are being priced out of tennis because parents cannot afford quality coaching.

The National Medical Commission’s plan to create a National Medical Register (NMR), is running into rough weather again as doctors are questioning why medical practitioners are being made to pay a fee and register again for entry into the NMR when their database is already available with respective State Medical Councils.
The question assumes significance as the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of the National Medical Commission (NMC) is moving to amend the Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations, 2026.
The NMR is envisaged as a single, reliable national database that would make it easier to verify doctors’ qualifications and registration status and facilitate their practice across State boundaries. The system envisages a unique NMR identification number linked to every doctor’s State registration number.
The dispute now is over how this national database would be created -- is it the task of the State Medical Councils to provide the data for the creation of the NMR or should individual doctors have to put in application afresh, pay a fee and then await EMRB’s verification of credentials?
What the law says
Doctors point out that the NMC Act, 2019, already settles this. In Sections 31(1) , 31 (6) and 31 (7), the NMC Act says that the EMRB “shall maintain a National Register” of all licensed medical practitioners.; the State Medical Councils will maintain and update respective State Registers with the EMRB and that it will be the task of EMRB to maintain the National Register and ensure the electronic synchronisation with the State Registers.
“Nowhere in the NMC Act is it stated that it is the responsibility of registered medical practitioners to apply for NMR registration,” points out the Kannur-based doctor and RTI activist, K.V. Babu. Also, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2025, the Union Health Ministry, quoting the NMC, had said that applying for NMR registration was voluntary.
Doctors therefore argue that the NMR should be populated from the verified data already held by State Medical Councils. “Our data is already with the State Medical Council and it just needs to be handed over to the EMRB. We fail to understand why the NMR database creation should be so complicated and why doctors are being put through the registration and verification formalities all over again,” says the State President of Indian Medical Association, Kerala, M.N. Menon
A registration backlog
The concern raised by doctors is genuine. Applications submitted by several doctors for NMR registration have remained pending before the EMRB for years, raising questions about the practicality of requiring every State-registered doctor to individually apply for national registration. According to the minutes of the NMC’s 17th meeting, fewer than 32,000 registered medical practitioners had applied for NMR registration by December 2025.
The cost angle
The issue also has a financial dimension. Doctors point out that they are already paying a substantial amount as registration and licensing-related charges to State Medical Councils. The registration fee that will be charged in the name of NMR will be another burden on doctors, Dr. Babu says.
Doctors have demanded that the NMC withdraw the proposed draft amendment and ask State Medical Councils to send its database to the EMRB for creating the NMR as well as the unique ID for doctors

- Magnet Fruit is a Natural-type fruit in Blox Fruits that uses Scrap and Magnetic Power to strengthen attacks.
- The fruit has five main moves, with different effects when players tap or hold the ability keys.
- Maximum Overdrive transforms the player into a powerful mech with stronger attacks, faster flight, and increased defense.
The Magnet Fruit is added in Blox Fruits with Update 30, and it brings one of the most unique mechanics to the game. The fruit lets you pull enemies, disarm their swords, fly around with a jetpack, and transform into a massive mech. Wondering how to get the Magnet Fruit in Blox Fruits and what all its moves do? Here is everything you need to know.
How to Get Magnet Fruit in Blox Fruits
You can get the Magnet Fruit through the usual acquisition methods for all fruits in Blox Fruits. The fruit is available through the Blox Fruit Dealer, Fruit Gacha, fruit spawns, and trading with other players.
You can find the Blox Fruit Dealer at several locations across the three seas. If Magnet is not available in the Dealer’s stock, you can try the Fruit Gacha or look for a spawned fruit. Trading is another option if you have another valuable fruit that you are willing to exchange for Magnet.
Blox Fruits Magnet Fruit: All Passive Abilities
Unlike the best fruits in Blox Fruits, Magnet comes with two passive abilities: Magnetic Power and Magnetic Pull. Below we explain how both passive abilities work and are connected to each other.
Magnetic Power
Magnetic Power is the main passive ability of the Magnet Fruit. You build Magnetic Power by collecting Scrap, which appears around you during combat.
As you collect more Scrap, your mechanical arms become larger and move through three different stages. Each stage improves your M1 attacks and gives you more defense. Taking damage drains your Magnetic Power, so you need to keep fighting and collecting Scrap to maintain the higher stages. Here is what each stage does:
- Stage 1: Gives you the basic mechanical arms and your standard M1 attacks.
- Stage 2: Makes the arms larger, increases the M1 combo, and activates Magnetic Pull.
- Stage 3: Gives you the largest arms, the longest M1 combo, stronger Magnetic Pull, and the highest defense.
Magnetic Pull
Magnetic Pull is a passive effect that activates once you reach Stage 2 of Magnetic Power. It automatically pulls nearby enemies toward you.
The effect becomes stronger at Stage 3, with a larger pull radius. This makes it much easier to keep enemies close and connect your other attacks.
Blox Fruits Magnet Fruit Showcase: All Moves and Combos
The Magnet Fruit has five main moves in Blox Fruits, and most of them have different effects depending on whether you tap or hold the key. So, if you have used the Blox Fruits codes to grind the fruit, here is the complete Magnet moveset:
- Z Move or Scrap Arsenal: Tapping Z fires magnetic projectiles that pull enemies toward them. Multiple projectiles can stack together, increasing their area and pulling effect. Holding Z fires a magnetic beam, with a direct hit dealing bonus damage.
- X Move or Magnetic Overcharge: Tapping X traps an enemy inside a magnetic cage before exploding and dealing damage. Holding X creates a larger cage with more range and damage.
- C Move or Polarizing Drop: Tapping C uses the mechanical arms to pull an enemy upward before slamming them into the ground. Holding C pulls nearby Scrap toward you and automatically absorbs it.
- F Move: Tapping F grabs an enemy and forcefully unequips their sword. Holding F activates your jetpack and lets you fly while using your other abilities. Taking repeated damage can cancel the flight. Pressing F again while flying fires the jetpack at an enemy.
- V Move or Maximum Overdrive: Activates the Magnet transformation when you have enough Magnetic Power.
The F move is especially useful against sword users. Catching an opponent with the grab forces them to lose their equipped sword, giving you a chance to follow up with your other attacks.
Blox Fruits Magnet Fruit: Maximum Overdrive Transformation
Maximum Overdrive is the Magnet Fruit’s transformation ability in Blox Fruits. Once you have enough Magnetic Power, you can turn into a large mechanical form with a completely different set of attacks. This makes Magnet slightly stronger than Dragon in Blox Fruits in terms of PvP.
The transformed form gives you much higher defense and makes gun attacks far less effective. However, lightning attacks deal more damage against you, giving the transformation a clear weakness. Here are all the transformed Magnet abilities:
- Z Move or Scrap Arsenal: Tapping Z launches missiles with aim assistance. Holding Z fires a powerful blast from the mech.
- X Move or Magnetic Overcharge: Tapping X fires a large Scrap projectile that explodes over a wide area. Holding X creates Magnetic Room, which pulls enemies toward the center and damages them when they try to escape.
- C Move or Polarizing Drop: Tapping C pulls Scrap toward the mech before slamming it into the ground for massive area damage. Holding C turns the mech into a spinning helicopter attack that can move around while dealing damage.
- F Move: Tapping F releases an area attack that forcefully unequips the swords of enemies caught by it. Holding F activates a faster jetpack flight.
- V Move: Ends Maximum Overdrive and leaves the mech behind. The mech pulls nearby enemies toward it before self-destructing and dealing damage.
Your X and C attacks also cannot be cancelled while you are transformed. This gives the mech super armor while using these attacks.
The Magnetic Power system gives you stronger M1 attacks and better defense as you collect Scrap, while Magnetic Pull helps keep enemies within your attack range. Once you activate Maximum Overdrive, you get an entirely new mech moveset with stronger attacks, faster flight, and plenty of ways to control your enemies.
That is everything you need to know about the Blox Fruits Magnet Fruit. Did you get the fruit yet? Make sure to combine it with strong races in Blox Fruits.
How do you get the Magnet Fruit in Blox Fruits?
You can get the Magnet Fruit through the Blox Fruit Dealer, Fruit Gacha, fruit spawns, or trading with other players.
What does Magnetic Power do in Blox Fruits?
Magnetic Power increases the strength of your mechanical arms as you collect Scrap. It also improves your M1 attacks and defense, with three stages available. Magnetic Pull activates at Stage 2 and becomes stronger at Stage 3.
How many moves does the Magnet Fruit have?
The Magnet Fruit has five main abilities: Scrap Arsenal, Magnetic Overcharge, Polarizing Drop, Disarm, and Maximum Overdrive. Several of these abilities have separate effects when tapped or held.
What is Maximum Overdrive in Blox Fruits?
Maximum Overdrive is the Magnet Fruit’s transformation. It turns you into a large mech with stronger attacks, higher defense, faster flight, and resistance to gun damage. Lightning attacks deal increased damage against the transformed form.
Is Magnet Fruit good for PvP?
Yes, Magnet has several abilities that pull and trap enemies, while its F move can force sword users to unequip their weapons. Magnetic Pull also makes it easier to keep opponents within range of your attacks.

B.C. drought forces volunteers to rescue salmon from drying streams
Rescuers move stranded fish to deeper water, but experts warn the effort has limits
Parts of British Columbia have been hit hard by drought this summer.
In Bessette Creek, severe drought conditions recently prompted orders limiting water use in an effort to protect salmon populations from record-low flows.
Temporary protection orders for the Salmon River watershed were also issued at the end of July, rescinded in early August to address increased wildfire risk in the region and then reissued at the end of August.
And those are just the watersheds struggling to the point of government intervention.
Bob Crandall is treasurer of the Cowichan Lake Salmonid Enhancement Society on Vancouver Island.
The society cares for 16 streams connected to Lake Cowichan, and Crandall says they are getting drier each year.
To help, the society does what they call fry salvage — manually rescuing fish from drying rivers and moving them into other waterways.
"I believe if the hand of man has caused these difficulties in the ecosystems, then the hand of man should be out there, trying to make an improvement to the problems," said Crandall, who has been doing this for over 16 years.
While B.C. communities are embracing this intervention as one of the few options available to them, scientists warn this has limits and may not be a good long-term solution.
Efforts to move fish
Together with the Ts'uubaa-asatx Nation and a variety of volunteers, Crandall works to gather fish — mainly salmon, trout and char — and carry them somewhere with more water.
But the work is becoming more difficult as the climate changes. The society has been doing fry salvage since 1984, and Crandall is used to seeing a kilometre or two of rivers and streams dry up over the course of a summer.
But that is no longer the case.
"We have noticed that streams are drying up farther upstream," he said.
"Now, it seems as though we're going five, six and seven kilometers upstream — it's just a lot more effort."
The process involves aerators and bubblers to ensure the fish have enough oxygen, as well as nets to transport them. Crandall says carrying 23 kilograms (50 pounds) of water, fish and equipment across cobbled, dry streambeds can be challenging in hot weather.
He was born in a rainbow trout hatchery, so he has been around fish his whole life, and it is important to him that they remain part of the ecosystem rather than simply dying.
"You can rescue up to 100,000 or 150,000 fish during the course of a drought summer," he said.
Importance of fish
The Ts'uubaa-asatx Nation is also a major part of the fry salvage efforts. Its members help relocate the fish and use drones to determine where streams are drying up.
Crandall called the Nation the best partner the Society has ever had and says much of the work would not happen without it
"It takes an army of people to do it," said Aaron Hamilton, the Nation's operations manager.
Hamilton said that it's been challenging lately because there is no longer a normal pattern to follow. The weather can be extremely hot one month, followed suddenly by heavy rain.
Michelle Corfield, the lands and resource director and negotiator for Ts'uubaa-asatx, said salmon are a keystone resource for the community. The recovery projects are important to the Nation, she said, and it has also invested its own money in the work.
"Salmon are in our DNA," she said. "And it's up to us to ensure that we have salmon for today and into the future."
Corfield says the Nation takes a full life-cycle approach to salmon conservation, including river restoration and conditions in the oceans, rather than focusing only on individual fish.
Challenges to fry salvage
Similar rescue efforts are facing limits elsewhere as drought and extreme heat intensify.
This year's drought has been especially severe in France, and Jean-Pierre Faure of the Fédération de Pêche du Rhône said relocating fish is no longer working for them.
Faure says that there have been multiple weather events that would normally be expected only once every 50 to 100 years.
"The last one this summer is the worst we have ever had," he said. He added that France's management programs are not prepared for the changing conditions because they rely on the past to plan for the future — an approach he says will no longer work.
"It began very early in the end of May and since that time we have had four or five very big heat waves, reaching temperatures we have never seen before."
River flows were so low that fish were forced to gather in very small volumes of water, intensifying competition for food and shelter and causing more deaths.
Faure said fish experience physiological stress and lose energy when water temperatures rise above 18 or 19 C. He said juvenile fish are first to be affected because they have fewer energy reserves, while temperatures above 25 C can be fatal within hours.
"This summer, due to the combined effects of climate change and warm water discharge from the nuclear power plant industry, the average temperature of the Rhône River reached 25 degrees for more than two months," said Faure.
"It's still the case, it's still going on. This has never been seen before."
He said that instead of focusing on short-term interventions such as rescue fishing, the priority should be ecosystem restoration and water-use management.
Moving fish can add stress and cause injuries or spread disease, he said. The work can also cost at least 1,000 to 2,000 euros a day for each kilometre covered.
"When you have thousands of kilometres of rivers that are drying, it's not realistic to go and do this at a large scale."
He also said that when 90 per cent of the watershed is dry, there may simply be nowhere to move the fish.

Man Utd cannot ignore more dropped points despite positives
- Published
There are positives for Manchester United to take from their 2-2 draw at Everton.
Striker Benjamin Sesko scored his first goal of a season - the start to which has been delayed for longer than anticipated by a shin injury.
Kobbie Mainoo has impressed in the campaign as a whole so far and shows no sign of being affected by his unhappy World Cup experience. The same, in terms of his mental strength, could be said of goakeeper Senne Lammens.
Marcus Rashford has returned to the club with a sense of purpose.
But you cannot ignore the negatives.
After a European based pre-season that should have seen them hit the ground running, Michael Carrick's side have dropped five points from their first three Premier League games.
They have conceded twice in all three. Their opponents are two promoted teams and an Everton outfit whose fans are distraught following a botched deadline day.
Now United must prepare for their Champions League return, against another banana skin-type opponent in Azerbaijan's Sabah FK. After that it is Manchester City.
It is the kind of week they craved 12 months ago. But already, the pressure is on.
Positives and negatives for Carrick
"It's not that bad, you know," was Carrick's assessment of his side's start to the season.
"We were that close to coming away with three points today. That's football. There were little moments we can deal with a bit better, but we'll be fine."
Carrick got support in his assessment from his old friend Wayne Rooney, who analysed the Everton game for BBC Sport.
"I thought it was good away performance," he said.
"Obviously, I'd be disappointed with the result, but I thought there was a lot more control in the performance.
"The midfield three were really good. They were two great strikes from Everton which got two goals, but I think there was encouragement from United's point of view. They'll be very frustrated they haven't won the game, given the performance."
Rooney was right about that.
"It feels like a defeat," said Carrick.
"All the work that went into putting us in that position at different stages to then come away like that. We're disappointed, bitterly disappointed.
"We can't ignore the fact we have taken a point, but it feels that we should have had a lot more."
Man Utd need to stop conceding
If he had wanted, Carrick could have played the 'one of those things' cards about the result at the Hill Dickinson stadium.
After all, the visitors controlled long periods, led twice.
The first equaliser was a brutal strike from Tyrique George. The second a blistering last-gasp effort from Ainsley Maitland-Niles introduced for his debut as a substitute.
It was the first time an Everton player had scored from outside the penalty area on their Premier League debut.
No-one was entirely at fault for either. Lammens might have done better at his near post for the first but George's shot was going at some pace.
But Carrick accepts the optics are not great. He also knows the basic reality if a side concedes twice every time they play, they will not win many Premier League games.
"The mentality is there," he argued.
"It's two really good strikes from distance from their point of view. Sometimes they fly in the top corner, more often than not they probably don't.
"But we obviously can't ignore it. We need to concede fewer goals to give us a better chance of winning games. There's things we need to get better at as a team."
Rooney impressed with Shaw display
Questions have been raised about United's lack of recruitment during the latter days of the transfer window, with no striker signed to support Sesko.
It was interesting to note Joshua Zirkzee remained on the bench for a game he could have played in for Everton had United not ruled out the prospect of the Dutch forward joining on loan because they were unable to secure a replacement.
United also opted not to bring in Rayan Ait-Nouri from Manchester City because they did not want to sign a left-back permanently to put pressure on Luke Shaw.
Shaw was one of the visitors' better performers against Everton. The England defender got forward with regularity and it was encouraging to see him provide the cross for Sesko's late header.
"He was really good," said Rooney.
"Defensively he was leading and he was good going forward as well. He looked more of a threat today in his connection with Marcus [Rashford]."
To that end, Carrick will hope the "something" Rashford felt that led to his second-half exit is not serious.
"Marcus and Luke were particularly dangerous down that side," said Carrick.
"They've played together for quite some time now and have an understanding. We're trying to build partnerships and combinations throughout the team."
Shaw has been ever-present in United's Premier League starting line-up since the start of last season.
Now though, Carrick must navigate through a tricky spell of four games in 11 days.
It is the busiest period he has had as United boss. Last term, neither of his two midweek games were followed by weekend matches.
How involved will Shaw be? If he does not play, who starts? Does Zirkzee really have a meaningful role?
Sesko, presumably, has put himself in line to start against Sabah? Or does Carrick prioritise the derby instead.
These are the unanswered questions that would always come in a campaign that could feature 60 games.
The tricky bit is navigating through, while delivering positive results.
"Not that bad" is a fair assessment after three games. But Carrick knows expectations around Manchester United are huge. We are nowhere near reaching it just yet, but there will come a point where "not that bad" will not be good enough.
