'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

Serbia's ruling populists propose President Vucic switch to prime minister after election
Serbia’s governing party has proposed President Aleksandar Vucic as prime minister if they win an early parliamentary election
BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia ’s governing party on Saturday formally proposed that President Aleksandar Vucic become prime minister if they win an upcoming early parliamentary election that is seen as a major test for the populists after more than a year of street protests.
Vucic is yet to formally dissolve Parliament and call the ballot that is expected to be held on Oct. 25.
Voting will be held nearly two years after a train station canopy collapse in northern Serbia killed 16 people, triggering youth-led demonstrations that blamed government corruption and incompetence for the tragedy. The election will take place in an atmosphere of heightened political tensions as the populists seek to retain power despite widespread popular discontent.
Scores of anti-government protesters on Saturday marched in the city of Nis while Vucic's party held their meeting there. Police surrounded the National Theater building to prevent the protesters from reaching the meeting venue.
Vucic told party officials that he will call the vote in the coming days. He said he will then resign the presidency so he could officially join the campaign. The presidential election will be held later, he said.
More than a year of demonstrations, sometimes drawing hundreds of thousands of people, shook Vucic more than ever during his 14 years in power. The protesters demanded accountability for the Nov. 1, 2024, concrete canopy collapse in Novi Sad and an end to corruption they believed was the cause for bad renovation work.
Vucic has pushed hard against the protesters as the government faced international criticism over police violence and arbitrary detentions of demonstrators. He has repeatedly accused without evidence the Serbian university students and professors behind the protests of an intention to “destroy the state.”
The Serbian president reiterated such claims on Saturday, alleging that the protests have been orchestrated by unspecified foreign powers. “This evil,” Vucic said, "is not coming from the inside, it is coming from the outside.”
The SNS party will face a student-backed election list that is expected to include university professors and experts, though their names have not been made public. Also in the race will be both right-wing and center-left opposition parties, and several smaller groups.
A group of university students said earlier this week they were among at least 14 people targeted with spyware earlier this year in what the Serbian Share Foundation group described as the biggest such incident so far. Vucic's authorities have dismissed the reports.
Serbia is formally seeking European Union entry but the effort has been stalled under Vucic due to democratic backsliding, including election irregularities in previous votes. Vucic has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine and has maintained close relations with China.

White House looks to implement plan that pays parents to stay home and raise their children
The proposal fits into a broader Trump administration effort to promote traditional families and raise the birth rate
The Trump administration is considering a new policy that would provide government childcare subsidies to married couples with a stay-at-home spouse, according to a new report.
Under the draft plan, married couples in certain income brackets could qualify for payments if one spouse works at least 35 hours a week while the other remains home to care for the child, The New York Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Unmarried couples and single parents who do not work would not be eligible.
The funding would come from the $12 billion Child Care and Development Fund, an Department of Health and Human Services program established in the 1990s to help low- and middle-income parents. The fund typically provides about $9,000 per child annually and currently serves roughly 1.3 million children, the vast majority in households headed by single working parents, who are typically mothers.
The proposal fits into a broader White House effort to promote traditional families and raise the birth rate, an effort spearheaded by Vice President JD Vance, who has pushed for more mothers to remain home with their children.
The vice president once wrote on X that “normal” Americans desire a “family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap day care so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force.”
In a 2021 essay, he wrote: “Young children are clearly happier and healthier when they spend the day at home with a parent.”
The plan has drawn criticism from experts who warn that single working parents could be worse off under the changes.
“I am a big proponent of more support for stay-at-home parents. But this is not how I would choose to do it,” Joshua McCabe, the director of social policy at the Niskanen Center, a think tank, told the Times.
“Expanding the eligibility without increasing funding would mean more parents competing for the same dollars, and leaving more parents — particularly single working parents — worse off,” he added.
Some Trump administration attorneys have also discussed whether or not it would be legal to mandate that recipients of the childcare subsidies be married, the outlet reported.
The proposed change does not require congressional approval. If the White House signs off, it would be published online for a public comment period and, if finalized, could potentially be implemented as early as 2027.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

To make it easy for you, we have included each and every icon on every page of Instagram and explained what it does.
Table of Contents
What Do Instagram Symbols and Icons Mean?
Instagram Post Symbols Meaning
Instagram posts are what we see and interact with most on a daily basis while using the app.
They come with several engaging elements. Most of them are easy to understand, but if you are confused, here is what they mean:
- Like: Wherever you see this heart symbol on Instagram, it represents a like for posts, comments, and all
- Comment: This represents a comment on the post. Tapping on it reveals all the comments, and you can also add a comment.
- Repost: Instagram has recently introduced the ability to repost. The reposted post also appears on your feed.
- Save: The save feature lets you save posts; in other words, it works like a bookmark.
Instagram Home Screen and Bottom Navigation Bar Icons Meaning
Now let’s look at what the icons mean on the home screen and on the bottom navigation bar.
You won’t find many icons on the home screen, except for the ability to create a new post and to view all your notifications.
If there is one area that Instagram constantly experiments with, it is the bottom navigation. Meta keeps changing the positions of the icons and also changes their designs frequently.
Here is what they mean:
- Notifications: The heart symbol here represents notifications. Here, you can see all the notifications you receive inside the Instagram app.
- Create: The plus symbol here represents “create,” which you can use to create a post or a story and more.
- Home: Tapping on the home icon takes you to the home screen. It is part of the main bottom navigation. Tapping on it also takes you to the latest posts.
- Reels: Instagram has added a dedicated Reels tab, where you can tap on it to go to the Reels section.
- Messages: Tapping on this icon takes you to the Instagram Messages screen, previously known as DMs.
- Search: Tapping on the search icon takes you to the Explore page.
- Profile: This is a profile icon, which takes you to your profile page.
Instagram Reels Tab Icons Meaning
Instagram offers a dedicated Reels tab where you can see all the latest Instagram Reels. It also comes with several interactive elements, some of which are already used for posts.
Here is what each and every icon means in the Instagram Reels tab:
- Create: You can also add new posts directly from the Reels page. You can tap on the Plus icon.
- Like: It lets you like the Reel you are watching. You can like it, and tapping on it removes your like.
- Comments: Lets you add a comment and see comments for the Reel you are currently watching.
- Repost: It lets you repost the Reel you are currently watching.
- Share: It lets you share the Reel with your friends. You can also copy the Reel link using this option.
- Save: You can save or bookmark the Reel using this icon.
- More options: Gives more options for Reels, including Playback controls, Meta AI, and much more.
- Audio: It represents the audio used for the Reel. Tapping on it reveals more details.
Instagram DM Page Icons Meaning
Instagram DMs are among the most feature-packed, yet Instagram somehow manages to keep them minimal. However, they do come with several icons. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram message space:
- New message: It lets you create a new message. After tapping, you can select the user and send a message.
- Notifications off: It appears if you turned off notifications for Instagram.
We missed highlighting the Instagram Instant feature that the company introduced very recently. It lets you share a random photo with other users without complex editing.
It is turned on by default, and tapping on it shares whatever your phone camera sees, so be careful before pressing it. There is also an option to turn it off completely
Instagram Profile Page Icons Meaning
Instagram profile page also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what they mean:
- Create: Lets you create a new post, Reel, or Story from your profile page too
- Menu: Lets you access main and global Instagram app settings
- Threads: Lets you open the Threads app by Instagram.
- Discover people: The icon lets you discover new friends. It appears when you have a lower following count.
- Posts: Represents the Posts tab
- Reels: It represents the Reels tab
- Tagged posts: It represents the tagged posts where you can see all the posts you were tagged in by your friends.
- Pinned post: It means the user has pinned the post. Instagram lets the user pin up to three posts.
Instagram DM Message Icons Meaning
The chat interface also comes with plenty of icons, which can be confusing for a beginner. Here is what each icon means inside Instagram chats:
- Instagram Blend Feature: This is an Instagram Blend feature where you can invite the user to the Blend, where you can see each other’s suggested Reels, new Reel suggestions based on the chat, and much more.
- Voice call: Lets you make a voice call to the user
- Video call: Lets you make a video call to the user
- Voice message: Lets you send a voice message in the chat
- Photo library: Lets you select the local photos on your phone and send them to the chat
- Stickers: Lets you access the stickers
- More options: Gives you more options, including the ability to send location, draw, and access Meta AI and much more
- Camera: Lets you access the camera, where you can quickly take a photo and share it with the user.
Instagram Share Screen Icons Meaning
The share screen on Instagram is very simple. It is very similar to the other share screens, but it comes with one unique icon that lets you create groups. Here is what that icon means:
- Create group: This is the share screen that appears when you tap on the share button under the post or the Reel. The user icon means you can create a new group.
Instagram Call Screen Icons Meaning
Instagram calling screen also comes with several icons during the call, and here is what each of them means:
- Camera off: During the video call, it lets you control the camera. If you see a cross line, it means your camera is turned off
- Mute microphone: Lets you mute or unmute your camera
- Speaker off: Lets you turn on or off sound from the other user
- End call: End the video or voice call using this button.
Instagram Story Editor Icons Meaning
If you are adding a story for the first time, it can be confusing because Instagram Stories are feature-packed and let you customize everything you upload. Here is what each icon means on the Instagram Stories screen:
- Add text: While adding an Instagram Story, tapping on this icon lets you add text
- Stickers: It lets you add stickers to an Instagram Story
- Music: Lets you add and select music.
- Effects: Lets you add effects
- More tools: More creator tools. Tapping on it lets you access more tools
- Next: Once added, you can move to the next screen while adding a Story
Instagram Profile Bio Options Icons Meaning
Instagram profile bio also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what each icon means and what it does:
- Notifications: Lets you turn on or off notifications for this account.
- More options: Gives you more options about the Instagram profile you are viewing
- Profile link: Instagram lets users add links in their bio. The link icon represents the link the creator added to their Instagram bio. It is also available for regular users.
More Instagram Profile Icons Meaning
Here are more icons that you see when you visit any Instagram profile, including icons in the top right corner of the post and the verified blue checkmark right next to the profile. Here is what they mean:
- Verified badge: Instagram has verified the account, which means it represents the official account. Also, Instagram allows users to pay for the verified badge.
- Video or Reel: If you see this on top of the post, it means the post contains a video or Reel.
- Carousel post: If you see this with a number, it means it is a carousel post.
Instagram Reels Controls Icons Meaning
In the Reels tab, when you pause the Reel, Instagram displays more icons. Here is what they mean, including the recent Friends tab icons:
- Create: The plus icon lets you create a new post or Reel
- Trending audio: If you see an arrow next to the audio file name, it means that audio is trending
- Sound: Lets you turn off sound or turn on sound for the video. It appears when you tap on the video
- Play: It appears when you pause the video. Lets you play the video again
- More options: Again, tapping on this option gives you more Reel options
- Reposted by a friend: If you see a purple arrow icon, it means the Reel is reposted by your friend. If you see the like, it means the Reel is liked by your friends.
More Instagram Messages Icons Meaning
Here is what the different icons mean in the Instagram DM space. If you have multiple accounts and unread messages, Instagram will notify you with different color badges. Here is what they mean:
- Pinned chat: It appears when you pin the chat for any user in your Instagram DMs.
- Muted chat: It means you muted the chat. You won’t receive any notifications for their messages.
- Unread message: It shows the unread messages inside the chat. If it appears, it means you have unread messages.
- Account switcher: Lets you switch between accounts, and if you see the red icon, it means you have unread notifications from the other account
More Instagram Post Icons Meaning
Instagram recently launched collaborations, which allow users to collaborate with each other and publish posts. It joins with older tags, the ability to add music, and much more. Here is what each icon means:
- Collaborative post: Instagram lets you add collaborative posts. If you see multiple profile pictures, it means it is a collaborative post from those accounts.
- More options: It lets you access more options for the posts
- Explicit audio: If you see an E icon right next to the sound or audio, it means the song contains explicit content
- Tagged people: It lets you view all tagged users for the post. Tapping on the user takes you to their profile
- Sound: It lets you mute or unmute the sound for the post.
Paid Instagram Post Icon Meaning
You don’t need a special introduction for the ads on Instagram. If you see a post and you are confused about whether it’s a regular post or not, you can find a little “Ad” label under the profile.
- Ad: If you see Ad, it means it is a sponsored post or ad inside the Instagram feed.
Instagram Story Viewer Icons Meaning
Fortunately, Instagram has kept stories minimal. They also come with several interactive elements. One is the ability to like them and also share the story with others.
- More options: Gives you more options for the Instagram Story you are viewing, which includes options like the ability to report it and more
- Like Story: Like means you can like your friend’s Story
- Share Story: You can also share the Story with others. Tapping on it lets you share the Story with your contacts.
Instagram Close Friends Story Icons Meaning
If you see a green icon in the stories, it means that the user has added you to their close friends list. It comes with an extra “Close Friends” tag, and while the rest of the elements look the same, it doesn’t come with a share option.
Here is what each icon means in the Instagram Close Friends Story screen:
- Close Friends: If you see this green star, it means they have added you to their Close Friends list and shared a Story with you
- More options: Lets you access more Story options
- Like Story: Lets you like your Close Friend’s Story.
Instagram Reels Comments Symbols Meaning
Finally, ending this guide with the post or Reels comments, it also comes with several elements which can be confusing for the beginner. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram post or Reels comments section.
- Sound: You can turn the Reel sound on or off using the icon
- Like comment: You can like any comment made by users. The number below shows how many people liked it.
- Photo: Instagram recently announced the ability to add a photo as a comment.
- GIF: You can also add a GIF in the comments.
- Gift: Send a gift in the comments. You can tap on it and buy points with real money and help the creator to make money.
Instagram Active Status Symbol Meaning
- Green dot: If you see a green dot, it means the user is active on Instagram. If you hide your active status, it won’t appear for you even if others are online.
Story Rings Meaning
- Grey colored ring: If you see a grey-colored ring, it means you have already viewed their story.
- Colorful gradient ring: It means they added a new story or a story you have not watched yet
- Green ring: If you see a green ring, it means a story for a close friend that the user added. In simple words, the user added you to their close friends list and shared a story with close friends.
Still Confused About an Instagram Icon?
Those are the icons and symbols and their meanings on Instagram. Instagram constantly tests new icons and new features, and also changes existing features. As I said before, the platform has undergone several fresh layouts over the years.
To stay updated with the latest, we also update this post regularly when Instagram changes the layout and announces a new feature. We update this post regularly to keep the same layout and make it less confusing compared to what you currently see on your Instagram app.
Fortunately, Instagram also uses the same icons for its desktop version and for the Instagram app on other platforms as well. If you still find any icon confusing on Instagram, you can comment below, and I am happy to guide you.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

The Punjab BJP posted an AI-generated video showing an angry parent slapping Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann inside a government school. In the video, a teacher is seen writing an incorrect spelling on the blackboard while Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann and Aam Aadmi Party convener Arvind Kejriwal watch. Suddenly, the parent spots errors in their child’s notebook and, in a fit of rage, slaps the Chief Minister.
Unlike posts featuring memes from the film KGF or the web series Mirzapur, the Punjab BJP’s post did not use fictional characters to make a point. Instead, it used AI to create a scene depicting a physical attack on a state’s elected Chief Minister, creating a fabricated image of violence directed at a real, identifiable individual. Following widespread criticism, the Punjab BJP deleted the post.
The Origins Of ‘Dimagi Naxal’
The term ‘Dimagi Naxal’ recently entered India’s political vocabulary and is now becoming a weapon wielded by BJP and its affliates to attack dissenters and opposition on social media.
The term originated during Modi’s Independence Day speech at Red Fort, wherein he declared that while the country had eliminated the armed Naxals hiding in the forests, ‘Dimagi Naxals’ remained active within society. He claimed that individuals with a Maoist mindset had entrenched themselves in the corridors of power and influenced policies while serving as advisors on government committees, he emphasised the need to identify and isolate them.
The Prime Minister did not directly mention any specific individual or organisation. However, critics believe that, much like terms such as ‘Urban Naxal,’ ‘Tukde-Tukde Gang,’ and ‘Andolanjeevi’, the term ‘Dimagi Naxal’ is another such label to attack dissenters.
Union Minister Kiren Rijiju tweeted: ‘Dimagi Naxals’ are those who support Maoists and do not accept the Indian Constitution, who stand with separatists and support Article 370, and who want to sever the ‘Chicken’s Neck’ to separate the North-East from India.
In a follow up tweet, Rijiju posted a video of political prisoner Sharjeel Imam, while writing: “…Kapil Sibal and Company who are trying to save this person and his Tukde-Tukde Gang members, P. Chidambaram should clarify if he too supports this statement. Dimagi Naxal can be proven by a person’s actions and expressions. #DimagiNaxal”
Besides Kapil Sibal and Company who are trying to save this person and his Tukde-Tukde Gang members, P. Chidambaram should clarify if he too supports this statement. Dimagi Naxal can be proven by a person’s actions and expressions. #DimagiNaxal pic.twitter.com/jq98cU3Q4s
— Kiren Rijiju (@KirenRijiju) August 17, 2026
The most alarming aspect of the campaign waged against this fabricated concept of ‘Dimagi Naxalism’ is not any single video, but the dangerous pattern underlying it. ‘Dimagi Naxal’ has become a label coined not for actual terrorist groups, but merely for those holding dissenting views, people whom memes have depicted as being brutally beaten or riddled with bullets.

To get started with competitive Pokémon battles, all you need is your phone. But to compete at the highest level, like at the Pokémon World Championships, you’re going to need a Switch. And there doesn’t seem to be a good reason why.
Competitive Pokémon is on phones now, but you still need a Switch to become a champion
The mobile version of Pokémon Champions isn’t allowed at high-level tournaments, but it’s unclear why.
Battle simulator Pokémon Champions originally launched on the Switch and Switch 2 in April, with the mobile version following in June. The experience is nearly identical across the game’s versions; since it’s cross-platform, the choice really comes down to what devices you own and whether you prefer tapping or using a controller. I find myself playing Champions on my phone more often just because it’s always in my pocket and I’m blessed with unlimited data.
But at this year’s World Championships, the mobile version of Champions wasn’t allowed in competition. As of September 1st, certain local tournaments will allow the mobile version, but regional-level tournaments and above will still require Switch hardware to compete.
During a roundtable interview at Worlds last week — before the September 1st rules refresh — Champions producer Masaaki Hoshino addressed its absence from the competition. “The reason why we’re using Switch right now is just because graphics are quite nice on the Switch 2,” he said via an interpreter. “Also, because [with] mobile there’s just so many devices out there, if we allow people to bring their own devices, it can be a bit complicated from that perspective.”
This answer made less sense before the rules were updated. Tournaments at the regional level and higher are streamed on official channels, and VGC — the name for the competitive video game circuit — was the most viewed of the four games featured at Worlds this year, according to Esports Charts. Based on Hoshino’s answer and the new rules, it seems like The Pokémon Company views mobile as fine for smaller tournaments, but maybe not premium enough for the biggest VGC stages. (The Worlds finals took place in the Chase Center in San Francisco this year, only the second time the finals have ever been held in an arena as opposed to a hotel ballroom or convention center hall. Production values and attendance were especially high.)
Champions is certainly sharper on Switch 2 than on my iPhone 14 Pro, and it makes sense to want to present the best version of the flagship VGC game in a series often criticized for its graphics. But while competitors are required to bring their own devices to tournaments, the official VGC rules handbook does call out one case where hardware might be provided: during streamed matches. Players can generate a “team ID” for the battle team they’re using in a tournament, and technically anyone can use that ID to create a “replica” of that team on their own account. The handbook says specifically that “Team IDs may be used for recordkeeping or team checks, and they may be utilized on hardware provided by the Tournament Organizer for streamed matches.” If visual fidelity is a concern, there’s at least a workaround already available.
But is there a technical reason not to allow mobile at every level of competition? “Given that Champions is available on both mobile and Switch, cross-platform play is the trickiest thing,” Hoshino said. “All of the battle calculation is done on the server side, so this is what enables the cross-platform play, but it also was one of the trickiest things in developing Champions.”
So in short, not really. The trickiness of cross-platform play possibly explains the gap between the console and mobile releases of Champions, but that’s solved now that both versions are out (barring things like regular server maintenance, I suppose).
Mobile is also not a problem for other competitive Pokémon games. The mobile version of Pokémon Unite is allowed in high-level competition and it’s worked just fine, though only one player in the finals this year appeared to be playing on a phone as opposed to a Switch. Pokémon Go is only on mobile, and its competitive matches are streamed just like the VGC ones are. These aren’t the best examples in favor of mobile — this was Unite’s last year in the World Championships, and the Pokémon Go spectator experience is by far the worst of the bunch for several reasons — but it’s clearly possible to make mobile work.
Hoshino said that across the Switch 2 and mobile combined, Pokémon Champions has been downloaded around 25 million times. Given that number is higher than the total Switch 2 install base as of June, it’s likely that at least a few million of those downloads were on mobile devices. It’s anyone’s guess how many of those players are exclusively playing on mobile, but with the recent Switch 2 price hike and higher tech prices overall, it’s possible that at least some prospective Champions competitors will own a phone but not have the budget for a Switch.
Building a team and prepping for a tournament is the same whether you’re playing Champions on Switch or your phone. With the single exception of Eternal Flower Floette, which is only obtainable through Pokémon Legends: Z-A, you can get every pokémon you might need for a team within Champions using the gacha-style “recruit” feature. It’s quicker and easier if you already own some Switch Pokémon games, since you can transfer pokémon you caught from those games into Champions via the cloud storage service Pokémon Home, but it’s possible to get the pokémon you need without spending any money on Champions. It’s also easier than ever to train those pokémon and get them battle-ready; what used to take hours in-game now only takes a few minutes.
So it’s not like mobile-only players — or those who’ve only played Champions in general — are majorly disadvantaged in teambuilding. (That said, Eternal Floette was on the winning team this year and many other competitors’ teams besides, and players have criticized it for being a “pay-to-win” pokémon.) If you don’t have a Switch for whatever reason, you could absolutely start your championship run on mobile and potentially qualify for Worlds — and then not have the hardware needed to compete there.
Locking those players out of high-level competition feels like a mistake when the stated ethos of Pokémon Champions is “to be inclusive and accessible to all players.” That’s evident in the game’s design, which makes previously obfuscated information easy to access and understand, and it’s clear from the viewership of this year’s World Championships — in addition to the thousands of spectators in attendance at the arena — that VGC is growing. When I attended the Pokémon World Championships in 2016, the last time they were in San Francisco, it was a niche event held in a hotel; now the official MLB account is posting references to the championship-winning VGC play.
I’ve been playing and following VGC for a long time, and it’s a rich, deep game with a passionate and largely welcoming community — I’m thrilled to see it getting more popular and accessible. It just makes sense to keep tournaments as accessible as possible, too.

Did you buy a beanie from REI recently? The Department of Homeland Security might be looking for you.
New court filings allege that Homeland Security Investigations agents subpoenaed the outdoor retailer in March, requesting the transaction information for “all persons” in the greater Minneapolis–St. Paul area who had purchased a specific type of dark green beanie from the company since 2024. REI did not respond to questions about whether it had complied with the request and, if so, how many people are affected.
The filings are part of a broader lawsuit by the federal government against 39 people who attended an ICE protest at a church whose pastor also worked as an acting ICE field office director. Both protesters and journalists who were attempting to cover the event, including former CNN host Don Lemon, are now defendants.
The subpoena to REI was one of 92 sent as part of HSI’s investigation into the defendants, according to the court filings. Other recipients included social media companies, airlines, telecom providers, a car rental company, and a state employment agency. At least one subpoena sent to an unnamed airline, the filings allege, asked not only for information about a defendant’s past flights, but also requested that the airline give HSI a “lookout notification” about the defendant’s travel in the future. DHS declined to comment. The US Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, which is litigating the case on behalf of the government, did not respond questions about why it was necessary to identify everyone in Minnesota who purchased the beanie from REI, or why it specifically targeted REI customers, since the beanie is sold on other platforms as well.
The subpoenas sent by HSI agents are also known as 1509 customs summons, and are meant to be used to request information related to imports and exports. However, since the start of the Trump administration, WIRED and other news outlets have reported on DHS’s attempts to unmask online critics using the legal tool, which can be sent without the oversight of a judge or a jury.
“It’s flat-out absurd for DHS to demand REI search two years of customer data as part of Trump’s campaign against the people of Minneapolis,” US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon tells WIRED. “Customs summonses only allow DHS to request information directly related to compliance with customs laws, not to conduct unending fishing expeditions into the lives of people critical of Donald Trump.”
The total number of 1509 summonses that have been sent since the start of the Trump administration—and how many people have had their personal information guzzled up by DHS as a result—is unknown. Companies that receive these types of subpoenas are typically asked to keep their existence a secret. When the public has gotten a glimpse of them, it’s usually because the target has contested it in court, either because the recipient company ignored the request for silence and notified the target, or because the target discovered it after the fact.
According to a recent letter written by Wyden and Representative Pramila Jayapal, big tech companies will sometimes ignore the government’s request for silence when not legally required, but other companies in more heavily regulated sectors have told Congress that they’ve complied because of fear of regulatory retaliation.
Court filings, internal DHS documents, and companies’ own public statements show that companies have responded to recent customs summons in different ways.
Attorneys for Georgia Fort, a journalist and one of the defendants in the Minnesota case, wrote in a court filing that they were “stunned” when they realized that the government had obtained logs detailing six months’ of Fort’s calls and text messages from T-Mobile after the government sent a customs summons to the telecom provider. The attorneys allege that Fort was never notified by either T-Mobile nor the government.
“We take our responsibility to protect customers’ privacy and personal information very seriously,” says a T-Mobile spokesperson, who also said the company does not comment on specific legal requests. “Our team carefully reviews government demands for customer information and responds in accordance with the law.”
In the same filing, the attorneys said that Google refused to comply with a customs summons requesting information about Fort’s YouTube viewers and subscribers. A Google spokesperson says that the company reviews each government request for lawfulness and that Google will try to narrow requests or outright reject them when it believes the request is too broad.
Reddit recently announced that during the last half of 2025, it received DHS administrative subpoenas seeking information about 11 different Reddit accounts that made critical posts about ICE actions. After Reddit objected to them on First Amendment grounds, the company said, the agency withdrew them.
“Privacy is central to how Reddit operates, and we take our commitment to protecting it seriously,” says Ben Lee, Reddit’s outgoing chief legal officer. “We routinely push back on law enforcement requests and stand up for users who are exercising their First Amendment rights.”
Meta also pushed back against at least one customs summons, according to internal DHS correspondence obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Meta declined WIRED’s request to comment.
“I think DHS has proved time and time again that they can’t be trusted as the stewards of applying this law correctly,” says Mario Trujillo, a senior staff attorney at the EFF who has been tracking DHS subpoenas sent to tech companies. Congress could pass a law that would restrict how the agency used 1509 customs summons, or add penalties when they are misused, but until then companies and their customers are on their own.

Greeks promised tax relief, wage hikes as protesters take to the streets over cost of living crunch
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has promised more than 2 billion euros or $2.3 billion in tax cuts, salary increases and other support measures before Greece’s general election next year
THESSALONIKI, Greece -- Greece’s conservative government promised sweeping tax breaks and pay hikes before a general election next year, as thousands gathered in protest late Saturday over the high cost of living.
“Our country has overcome stagnation and is now ready to taste the fruits of its efforts,” Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said. “As the country stabilizes, there will be relief from heavy taxes, higher incomes and bold reforms.”
He spoke at an annual speech on the state of the nation’s economy in the northern city of Thessaloniki, where more than 25,000 people took part in union-led protests, according to police estimates.
Labor unions and multiple protest groups staged rallies across the city, with farmers driving tractors into the downtown area. More than 3,000 police officers were on duty, closing streets and subway stations near the venue where the prime minister spoke.
Greece delivered a budget surplus and economic growth of 2.1% last year, while continuing to reduce its high public debt, but its workers had the lowest purchasing power in the European Union.
“Wages are low and prices are soaring, so affordability is the most serious problem,” said Yiannis Panagopoulos, head of Greece’s largest labor union, the GSEE.
The support measures, worth more than 2 billion euros ($2.3 billion) over the next year, include tax breaks for self-employed professionals, farmers and residents of villages, as well as salary and benefit increases for retirees and public sector workers.
Mitsotakis, the 58-year-old son of late conservative Prime Minister Constantine Mitsotakis, has served as prime minister since 2019, as Greece emerged from a major financial crisis.
He's seeking a third term in an election expected next April. But polls suggest that support for his center-right New Democracy party wouldn't give it a governing majority in parliament.
Saturday’s event was overshadowed by a fighter jet crash several hours earlier at an air show near Athens that killed two air force pilots.

BEIJING: The death toll in Tibet from the devastating floods that struck the Himalayas along the China-Nepal border last month has risen from 31 to 43, Chinese state media reported Sunday (Sep 6).
The disaster "left 43 dead and 519 missing, according to the latest count", Xinhua reported, as the death toll on the Chinese side of the border rose.
The glacial and mountain collapse on Aug 26 has killed nearly 1,400 people and left more than 5,500 missing across the two countries.
The huge gap between the death toll and the number of people missing highlights the immense challenge facing rescuers as they push deeper into the devastated border area.
Gyirong Port lies deep in the Himalayas along China's border with Nepal.

Jerusalem, Sep 06: The United States ambassador to Israel condemned Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank again on Saturday, calling the behaviour an “act of terror" as he visited with Palestinian American residents shaken by months of attacks.
Ambassador Mike Huckabee referred to such settlers as “terrorists,” a word that US officials usually reserve for Palestinian militants.
“If there are squatters that come in and put up their own flags and take possession of something that does not belong to them, if they burn a car, if they torch a mosque, if they go into someone’s home and vandalize it, paint graffiti on the walls, that’s a criminal act. But it extends beyond a criminal act. It’s an act of terror,” Huckabee said during his visit to the village of Turmus Ayya, which has reported frequent attacks by settlers over the past year.
Such attacks have surged since the war in Gaza began with the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, according to the United Nations humanitarian office.
Huckabee also used the term “terrorists” last month after weeks of unrest in the West Bank town of Qusra, where settlers surrounded several homes including one owned by a Palestinian American. Days later, residents of the West Bank village of Bazariya said settlers burned a mosque and left a message on a wall in graffiti reading “Huckabee regards from the terrorists" in Hebrew.
“I’m glad they admitted it,” the ambassador said Saturday of the incident, adding: “I don’t think that’s what they intended to do, but I do think that they represent a very tiny minority.”
A week ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the actions of a “handful of rioters,” and the foreign ministry called the settlers’ actions “a disgrace.”
Netanyahu’s government is the most ultranationalist and religious in Israel’s history. It has presided over a surge of settlement construction in the West Bank. Most of the international community views settlements as illegal.
On Saturday's visit to Turmus Ayya, the ambassador began his remarks by making clear he was addressing US citizens, who make up a small percentage of the roughly 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank but a significant part of the village's population.
“I’m very aware that a lot of the American people who live in Turmus Ayya and other communities across this region are not enjoying the life they deserve to live, not enjoying it in a peaceful way,” Huckabee said. “It’s a life that is disturbed by people who have created extraordinary challenges that are unfair and illegal.”
The US Embassy can't investigate criminal activity, he said, but it can tell its host government “there are needs that need to be addressed, there are issues that cannot go unnoticed, and specific crimes and acts of terror that cannot continue without that country doing the investigation and adjudication that every person has a right to expect.”
Huckabee met with about 10 Palestinian American residents who described the impact of the violence on their lives and properties, the municipality told The Associated Press.
Israel captured the West Bank, along with Gaza and east Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state. The UN and much of the international community consider them to be illegally occupied.
Since then, the Israeli government has built nearly 150 settlements that are home to well over 500,000 Jewish settlers. Many settlements resemble developed suburbs.
Israel’s military operates in all parts of the West Bank, but rights groups have said the military frequently turns a blind eye to settler violence. The settlers are Israeli citizens, and Israel’s defense minister recently announced plans to fully transfer law enforcement among settlers to the Israeli police.

How to sideload apps onto Android Auto
You can unlock video streaming on your dashboard, but should you?
Android Auto was built to make your driving sessions simple and easy, but not everyone wants simple. If you've ever wished you could stream YouTube through your dashboard or mirror your phone's screen to your car display, you're not alone. Luckily, there's a way to do it. Sideloading lets you install apps that Google never approved for Android Auto, opening the door to features the platform doesn't officially support right now. The process doesn't require any crazy moves like rooting your phone, but it does come with trade-offs regarding security, reliability and safety.
By design, Google restricts what can run on your dashboard to cut down on driver distraction, which means no YouTube videos, no browser and no screen mirroring. It's a sensible policy, but one that leaves plenty of drivers feeling like their car's display is capable of a lot more than it's being allowed to do.
How do you sideload apps onto Android Auto?
The whole process of sideloading apps on Android Auto is not that complicated, but you do need to go through a few steps to set things up.
- 
First, you'll need to enable Developer Mode on your phone. You can do this by going to Settings > About and rapidly tapping Build number seven times. You'll get a note when Developer Mode is on. This will allow you to install third-party apps on your phone.
- 
Now you have to turn on Developer Mode for Android Auto. Go to Settings > Connected Devices > Android Auto, scroll to the bottom of the page and tap Version and permission info about 10 times in quick succession. Next, you have to tap on the three-dot menu at the top, select Developer settings and check the box for Unknown sources. This will make it possible to load the apps from your phone into Android Auto.
- Next, you need to install Android Auto Apps Downloader (AAAD) from the developer's GitHub. This will make it possible to install popular apps.
  - 
You can also look up the open-source GitHub repositories for popular apps like CarStream, which allows YouTube playback, AAMirror, which lets your phone screen mirror to the dashboard, and Fermata Auto, a media app that handles video, IPTV and a web browser.
- 
What are the risks of sideloading Android Auto apps?
The convenience of being able to install all sorts of apps Google hasn't intended comes with some genuine drawbacks that you should take seriously.
Safety is a major concern. Android Auto YouTube is technically an option even through official channels, but you can only listen to the audio. There's a reason Google hasn't allowed YouTube videos on Android Auto by now and that's because watching videos while driving is not a good idea. In fact, it's illegal in most parts of the world. This is a feature that should only be used when parked.
Malware exposure. Any time you sideload apps and skip Google's security screening, you open your devices to the risk of malware. Google reports that internet-sideloaded sources carry more than 50 times more malware than apps on Google Play. That's one of the reasons why Google will start blocking the sideloading of unverified Android apps, asking developers to verify their identity with the company. These new verification requirements will begin rolling out in late 2026 in a few countries before going global.
For most drivers, the standard Android Auto experience covers everything they actually need. Sideloading is a great capability, but for the vast majority of people, it's best left as a curiosity rather than a daily-use setup. If you do proceed, download only from trusted developers and only use video features when parked.

In Summary
- The Redmi Turbo 5 sees the Redmi brand return to a higher price point. It had earlier released the K series in this segment.
- The Redmi Turbo 5 follows Redmi’s classic formula of offering very good specs at surprisingly affordable prices. Its highlights are a powerful chip and a large Silicon Carbon battery.
- Priced at Rs 41,999, the Redmi Turbo 5 is one of the best options for those looking for something close to a budget flagship in an era of rapidly rising prices.
Redmi is mainly known for its budget-friendly devices, mostly in the mid- and lower-mid segment. It has occasionally released slightly more expensive devices, most notably in its K series, but has then gone back to the comfort of the Redmis and Redmi Notes. Now, as phone prices get on an upward-heading escalator, Redmi is getting back into the higher price zone with the Redmi Turbo 5. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 41,999, and while that may seem a bit on the premium side for a Redmi smartphone, it brings an equally premium spec sheet to the table. But can it help Redmi stretch beyond Note-land? Let’s find out!
Table of Contents
Redmi Turbo 5 design and appearance: Classy, yet not-so-loud appearance
The Redmi Turbo 5 does not come with a radically new design – it looks very similar to its cousin, the Poco X8 Pro. And that is a good thing. The phone has all the design elements that make up a trendy smartphone in today’s day and age – a tall, display dominated front which is surrounded by razor thin bezels, a flat back with two circular camera rings jutting out just a little parked on the top left side, and has those flat sides that have become an essential part of a modern day smartphone’s anatomy.
While not out of the box, the Turbo 5 still has a few distinct design touches that catch attention, the kind that are not obvious or scream for attention, but do not get lost completely either. The right side of the back comes with a thick vertical strip filled with very dainty checkered patterns, and the cameras seem like two independent lenses stacked together, but there is a subtle capsule outline encasing them. The two camera lenses also have LED rings inside them, which is a nice conversation starter.
We received the Turbo White variant of the smartphone, which has a red Redmi logo near the base of the back. The cameras and the power/lock button also come with a very distinct red accent. These subtle touches make the design of the Redmi Turbo 5 give it a personality of sorts, making it stand out in the crowd. The back comes with a matte finish, which keeps smudges and scratches at bay and keeps the phone relatively clean. The metallic frame (a pleasant surprise at this price) is home to a handful of features as well. The top carries an infrared port while the base holds a SIM card tray, a USB Type-C port, and a speaker grille. The left side is bare while the right one bears the volume rocker and the power lock button.
Although relatively light for the size of the battery it carries (more about that later), the phone is not exactly light. It weighs 204 grams, and you can feel the weight in hand and even when the phone is in your pocket. At 157.5 mm, the Redmi Turbo 5 falls somewhere between large (160 mm and above) and compact phones (153 mm and below). It is 75.2 mm wide and, at 8.18 mm, is impressively slim, again considering the size of its battery. It is quite a sturdy phone with Gorilla Glass 7i protection on its front and back, and with IP68 and IP69K ratings for dust and water resistance, which means it can easily survive a fall in the water.
At first glance, the Redmi Turbo 5 might seem routine, but give it more attention, and little details start to pop up, and you start appreciating it for its classy, yet not-so-loud appearance.
Redmi Turbo 5 Specs: Ticks a surprising number of boxes
At a time when brands are cutting spec corners, the Redmi Turbo 5 ticks a surprising number of boxes. The phone is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra processor, which is considered to be in the budget flagship zone, and is paired with 8 GB and 12 GB RAM options and 256 GB of storage. What’s more, the 12 GB RAM variant comes with LPDDR5X RAM, and the storage on both variants is UFS 4.1. On paper, this is a very powerful setup for the price, which can not only run your everyday smartphone tasks but even handle high-end gaming.
The phone comes with a 6.59-inch AMOLED full HD+ (2756 x 1268) display with 120 Hz refresh rate and a peak brightness of 3500 nits, which can actually cover as much as 25 per cent of the display, instead of being isolated to a tiny section. Photography is handled by a dual camera setup on the back comprising a 50 megapixel Sony IMX882 main sensor with OIS, and an 8 megapixel ultrawide sensor, while a 20 megapixel sensor on the front handles selfies.
The Turbo 5 also packs in some very impressive battery numbers – it brings a sizable 7540 mAh Silicon Carbon battery (a rarity at this price, actually at any price) with support for 100W charging and 27W reverse charging. Also on board are stereo speakers, an in-display fingerprint scanner, and an IR blaster. Like all Redmi devices, the Turbo 5 also runs on Android 16 topped with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3. Xiaomi promises four years of software and six years of security updates.
In sheer spec terms, this is one of the best specced devices out there in its segment. Some might find the display a little small, but the power of that processor and the RAM and storage options will attract gamers on a budget.
Redmi Turbo 5 Performance: A smooth, powerful operator
The Redmi Turbo 5’s speedy processor+ RAM+ storage set up, reflects in its performance as well. The phone sails smoothly through everyday duties. It moves from app to app smoothly, handles multi-tasking without a hiccup, keeps going through intense social media scrolls, and binge sessions on OTT. The phone can also handle high-end games like Call of Duty and BGMI at 120 fps for long-ish sessions. Although it does get warm while going through power-hungry tasks, the temperature comes down quickly enough.
The AMOLED display with a 120 Hz refresh rate does not disappoint. It delivers a very rich contrast with vibrant colors and is bright enough not to dull down against a very harsh sun either. The 120 Hz refresh rate kept scrolling through social media breezy. The in-display fingerprint scanner works smoothly as well. This, combined with the loud and clear stereo speakers, makes the phone a multimedia master. We did not face any call drops or connectivity issues with the phone either.
Redmi Turbo 5 Cameras: One sensor show (censor the others)
Cameras are not the forte of the Redmi Turbo 5. There are three sensors on the phone, but all the photography weight rests on the 50-megapixel main sensor’s shoulders. This performs well in daylight conditions, capturing a good amount of detail and producing sharp images, so much so that the photos look decent even after a little zoom-in. The colors seem slightly more vibrant than reality but never to a point of looking unnatural. The details do take a very marginal hit in low light, but the presence of OIS helps, and Night mode on the device also improves results a fair bit. A number of other modes are built right into the native camera app, which offer a lot of scope for creative photography.
The 8-megapixel ultrawide sensor is capable of capturing a wider area, but it does not really do an impressive job. The colors remain nice and vibrant, but the details take a nose dive, resulting in images that look noisier, especially when compared to the main sensor. Matters only get worse as the light dims down. The sensor is usable and will allow you to take some quick snaps for social media in good light conditions, but do not pin your photography hopes on it. The 20-megapixel sensor on the front delivers social media-ready snaps but has the tendency to smooth out skin texture even with no ‘beauty mode’ on. The colors also lean towards being a little oversaturated, but you can get good casual snaps, and video calls are handled well.
The main camera supports 4K video at 60 fps, but the other two cameras are limited to 1080p at 60 fps. The video performance of the main camera sensor is good in daylight and even in low-light conditions, but the others miss the mark a bit. Overall, the 50-megapixel camera is the star of the Redmi Turbo 5’s camera show, while the other two are just supporting staff.
Redmi Turbo 5 software and UI: Very nice HyperOS, but loaded with third-party apps
The Redmi Turbo 5 runs on HyperOS 3. Now, HyperOS has been one of the most intuitive, simple, and functional Android skins since its MIUI days, and while that still largely remains true, the phone comes loaded with a plethora of third-party apps. This really makes the experience feel very cluttered and might even seem overwhelming to those new to the UI. Most of these third-party apps can be uninstalled, thankfully.
That said, features like Xiaomi Interconnectivity that not only allow you to connect your smartphone with other HyperOS products but with other gadgets as well, letting you create a hybrid ecosystem, give HyperOS its productivity edge. Top this with add-ons like Hyper Island (similar to Dynamic Island on the iPhone), and AI features like AI Translate, writing assist, call transcription, and a range of customizations, and HyperOS comes across as a very functionality-forward UI. The LED rings around the camera sensors that light up when you get notifications or calls were actually very handy, even while being a nice party trick as well.
Redmi Turbo 5 Battery: Lasts for days, gets charged in a jiffy
The phone’s massive 7540 mAh battery can see you through even the heaviest work days. Emails, messaging, gaming, photography- we did all of that and more with the smartphone, and it still had some juice left even after a day. If you are someone who does not push their device as much, the phone would easily see off more than two days on a single charge. It comes with 100W fast charging support with a 100W brick in the box, which means you get a fully charged phone in slightly over an hour, while the phone goes from 0-50 percent in about 30 minutes. This makes the Redmi Turbo 5 a device that will not only last for day(s) but will also get charged in a jiffy. The reverse charging feature is quite handy too and charges our TWS at a very decent speed.
Redmi Turbo 5 Price: Typically Redmi!
The Redmi Turbo 5 is available in two RAM variants – 8 GB and 12 GB, while the storage remains 256 GB for both options. Although the phone was initially launched at Rs 37,999, this price has since been revised, given rising costs of inputs. The 8 GB/ 256 GB version of the phone is now priced at Rs. 41,999, while the 12 GB/ 256 GB version is priced at Rs. 46,999.
It might have a much higher starting price than the Redmi Note series, but the Redmi Turbo 5 brings a solid spec sheet to the table at a price tag that is typically Redmi. While there are other devices in its price range, at the time of writing, none quite match its price-to-spec equation.
Perhaps the one that comes closest is its own cousin, the Poco X8 Pro, which comes with a similar processor and a similarly sized display at Rs 39,999, but has a smaller battery. Devices like the OnePlus Nord 6 come with a comparable Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 chip, but are more expensive at Rs 46,999, while the recently launched Vivo S2 brings a sleeker design and bigger display to the table at Rs 39,999 but loses out in terms of processor muscle.
Redmi Turbo 5 Review Verdict: A phone that does everything well
It might come with a higher price tag, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a typical Redmi smartphone in more than one aspect. It delivers a very consistent performance across multiple segments, making it one of the most reliable and powerful options at its price point (typical Redmi!). Its gaming and general performance are both quite smooth; the main camera delivers good snaps, its battery is perhaps its biggest USP, and the display combined with the stereo speakers make it an entertainment master. The price tag is a little higher than some might expect, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a device for those who are looking for a very good everyday phone that does almost everything well.

Old Monk ‘cannot be sold as rum’: What FSSAI told Bombay HC
The FSSAI reportedly informed the Bombay HC that Old Monk cannot be sold as "rum" because the product is made using neutral spirit.
Liquor brand Old Monk cannot sell or market its product as "rum", the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has reportedly told the Bombay high court.
The regulatory body, on Thursday, informed the court that Old Monk cannot be sold as "rum" because the product is made using neutral spirit and artificial rum flavouring, according to a report by LiveMint.
Also Read | FSSAI cracks down on misleading food and alcohol claims; Dabur Honey, Old Monk and more banned
What happened in court?
FSSAI's counsel clarified to the court that the primary issue is the fundamental nature of the product rather than just its labelling, stating that selling it as "rum" is not permitted, according to the report.
The regulator's counsel noted the drink could instead be categorised as a "rum-flavoured spirit".
Old Monk has submitted revised labels, and FSSAI sought more time to review them.
The next hearing is scheduled for September 11.
Ban in Maharashtra, modification of label - What happened?
FSSAI had banned the sale of the product in Maharashtra after detecting artificial flavouring substances mixed into neutral spirits, Bar and Bench reported, further noting that the brand agreed to revise its packaging to prominently display 'added flavor' on the bottles.
Also Read | ‘If there’s a will, there's a way': FSSAI CEO praises Maharashtra FDA's Tukaram Mundhe
FSSAI action against liquor makers over flavour, labelling
According to a statement of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare dated August 2, the FSSAI initiated enforcement action against alcohol beverage manufacturers for the use of non-permitted flavours, age-related claims, and misleading labels.
Enforcement was triggered by manufacturers blending external flavours to imitate the product’s inherent aroma and taste of the standard product, according to the official statement.
"Such products are not only sub-standard but are also misrepresented by using the names of standard categories. At best, they can be identified as Rum-flavoured Spirit or Whisky-flavoured Spirit, etc. Further, the front of the pack completely fails to disclose the true nature of the product," the ministry further stated.
Also Read | ‘Not abrupt’: FSSAI says 5 notices sent to Dabur before order on ‘100%’ claim
The ministry said that laboratory testing of rum and whisky samples from multiple manufacturers found the presence of external artificial or nature-identical flavours.
"The claim of "7 years old blended" in the label of Old monk XXX Rum variant was also found to be misleading. The major ingredient of the rum is neutral (unmatured/unaged) spirit, while the matured rum spirit is only a minor ingredient of the rum (less than 5% as per investigation findings)," the August 2 statement said.
Under the Food Safety and Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Regulations, 2018, the age claim of a blended spirit should be based on the youngest spirit in the blend, it added.
