UN votes to approve new world map which will show true size of Africa
Africa-led campaign asks governments, schools and tech firms to move away from the centuries-old Mercator projection
The UN general assembly has voted to replace the traditional world map with one that more accurately reflects the size of all nations.
The approved resolution calls for the world to move away from the traditional Mercator map, which shrinks the size of Africa and exaggerates northern landmasses.
The "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by Togo, passed with the support of 164 nations, including the UK. The US was the only nation to vote against it, with six other abstentions.
The resolution is non-binding, but asks governments, schools, international organisations, and technology companies to adopt the Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps wherever the true scale of continents matters, with the aim of establishing more proportionally accurate maps as a new global norm. It does not seek to ban the Mercator projection outright.
The Mercator projection, which is currently used worldwide, increases distortion the further a region sits from the equator. Since Africa straddles the equator, it seems comparatively smaller than its actual size, while Europe, North America, Greenland, and Russia all appear substantially larger than they are.
As a result, Africa, along with Latin America, India and other equatorial regions, appear much smaller relative to northern countries than their true area. The map, for example, depicts Africa as similar in size to Greenland, despite the continent being 14 times larger than the Danish territory.
In a briefing to the African Group at the UN this week, Togo's foreign minister Robert Dussey said the importance of the issue went beyond geography.
"A map is never neutral," Mr Dussey reasoned. “It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood, and may, sometimes from the earliest years of schooling, perpetuate representations that do not correspond to geographic reality."
"Africa is not asking for preferential treatment," he said. "Africa is asking that its reality, aspirations and contribution to the international system be duly taken into account."
"I'm an academic before a politician," Mr Dussey said. "As an academic, I say we have to have as large a consensus as possible, because we are here at the UN, we never know.”
A petition on the fundraising platform Change for the campaign, called #CorrectTheMap, had gathered around 11,000 signatures ahead of the vote. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and asked Togo to lead the push for its adoption at the UN.
“As Africa becomes increasingly central to solving global challenges,” the petition says, “it is critical to represent its true scale.”
Historians and geographers have long argued that the Mercator map reflects Western assumptions about the world, and some campaigners have used the term "cartographic colonialism" to denounce what they have described as its negative effects.
German historian Arno Peters was one of the most prominent critics of the projection, launching an alternative map based on the Gall-Peters projection in 1973. Togo's campaign is instead promoting the 2018 Equal Earth map, developed by an international team of cartographers, which supporters say offers a more accurate representation of the size of every continent.
Mr Dussey connected the map campaign to another African Union-backed resolution passed at the UN in March which described the transatlantic slave trade as the "gravest crime against humanity" and was approved by 123 states, with three against and 52 abstentions.
Togo's government is now set to hold an event in the capital, Lomé, with Unesco, the African Union, and technology companies including Google Maps in the first quarter of next year to work out how the change may be implemented.

Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.
According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.
To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.
The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’
Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.
Decline in monsoon related illnesses.
Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.
Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

Prankster built GOP midterm convention lookalike website - that just sends people to the Epstein files
It’s not clear who created the site, but the Republican National Committee pinned the blame on Democrats
A website purporting to host details about the Republican National Committee’s 2026 midterm convention instead redirected visitors’ attention to a subject President Donald Trump has long sought to put behind him, according to a new report.
Google’s preview for the imposter site — gopdallas2026.com — stated that it included “details about the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, Sept. 9-10 including registration, VIP experiences,” The New York Times reported.
But when users clicked the link, they were instead sent to the Department of Justice’s cache of documents related to Jeffrey Epstein, the deceased sex offender.
The fake site appeared far more prominently in Google search results than the RNC’s official convention page, gopconvention.com, drawing immediate attention to the discrepancy.
It remains unclear who created the lookalike website, but the RNC has blamed Democrats.
“Democrats are too broke to have their own midterm convention, so they settled for a sad, fake little website,” RNC spokesperson Zach Parkinson wrote on social media, responding to a Daily Mail report that linked the site to a creative agency run by a former Democratic operative.
As of Saturday afternoon, the site still redirects users to the Justice Department’s website.
The upcoming, first-of-its-kind convention is intended to boost Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November, which historically see the president’s party lose seats in Congress.
However, some GOP lawmakers reportedly have no interest in attending, while Republican operatives have complained about the pricey tickets.
The Independent has contacted the RNC for comment.
Jeffrey Epstein was a financier and convicted sex offender who pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting a minor for prostitution. In 2019, federal prosecutors charged him with trafficking minors. He died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 before trial, leaving many questions unresolved.
The Justice Department’s release of millions of Epstein-related records has renewed scrutiny of his ties to powerful figures, including Trump, who has not been accused of wrongdoing and says he cut ties with Epstein years ago.
Appearance in the files does not indicate wrongdoing.
Trump started the firestorm over Epstein by pledging during the presidential campaign to release more information. However, months into his term, his then-Attorney General Pam Bondi announced no new information would be released. That sparked outrage from his base. Congress passed a law to force the release, and Trump eventually complied and released the documents - despite missing the initial deadline.
A congressional committee continues to investigate the Epstein case.
The president has long sought to move past the Epstein controversy, over which he earned criticism from multiple prominent Republicans.
“Are you still talking about Jeffrey Epstein? This guy's been talked about for years," Trump told a reporter last year. “Are people still talking about this guy? This creep? That is unbelievable.”

OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Astra, its latest frontier model, in a bid to push into AI systems that can use computers and execute tasks more autonomously. OpenAI says that GPT-6 Astra is its most capable model yet. The model supports reasoning efforts ranging from low to maximum and comes with a 1.05 Mn-token context window and a maximum output of 1.28 Lakh tokens. As per the ChatGPT parent, Astra can autonomously navigate websites, interact with software, work with documents and spreadsheets, write and test code, and handle other multi-step workflows. The model is pitched as a significant upgrade for AI interface. "Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helped solve long-standing open problems in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment," the company said. Initially, GPT‑6 Astra will be rolled out to a limited set of organisations and will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, soon. GPT-6 Astra has an April 30, 2026 knowledge cutoff and supports tools including web search, file search, computer use, code execution and image generation. It is priced at $10 per Mn input tokens and $50 per Mn output tokens, with discounted cached-input pricing of $1 per Mn tokens. The company also doubles down on agentic AI with its new model, a segment where it is competing with companies including Anthropic and Google. Instead of requiring users to break down a task into a series of prompts, these systems are designed to perform several steps on their own. OpenAI claimed state-of-the-art results for Astra on benchmarks including Agents’ Last Exam, AutomationBench and ScreenSpot Pro, which measure an AI model’s ability to handle computer-based workflows. “We believe it is the best model in the world for computer use, professional work, science, coding, cybersecurity, and more,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a social media post on X. GPT-6 Astra Steps Up Coding, Science Capabilities ChatGPT parent has also positioned GPT-6 Astra as its strongest model yet for software engineering. There is a rapid growth in modifying AI to perform coding tasks with less to no human intervention, where models like Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3 Pro, Grok Build and Cursor agents have been operating well in recent times. In Codex, OpenAI has introduced a new mechanism that allows Astra to preserve and retrieve information across context windows instead of relying solely on compressed summaries. Beyond coding, Astra has been trained for scientific and mathematical applications. Cybersecurity is another key area of focus for the new model. OpenAI claimed that GPT-6 Astra has reached the "critical" level of cybersecurity capability under its preparedness framework, making it the company's first model to cross this threshold. The launch comes as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and other AI players race to develop increasingly capable AI agents that can move beyond generating text and instead execute tasks on behalf of users. Last year, OpenAI rolled out GPT-5 for users of ChatGPT as well as enterprises leveraging its APIs for artificial intelligence (AI) products, with enhanced features across coding, math, writing, health, visual perception, and others.

Srinagar, Sep 06: In a latest development, the School Education Department (SED) has proposed a comprehensive transfer policy for Rehbar-e-Taleem (RReT), Grade-II and Grade-III teachers wherein a three-year tenure and maximum five-year stay has been prescribed for place of postings.
The department has however introduced the provisions to prevent transfers between these categories and General Line Teachers (GLTs).
The draft Jammu and Kashmir Regularized Teachers (RReTs) Transfer Policy-2026 has been issued inviting objections and suggestions, with the department and the framework is aimed at ensuring need-based, student-centric transfers, staff rationalisation and administrative efficiency.
Under the proposed policy, every RReT teacher covered by it would have to complete three years at a place of posting before he or she becomes eligible for consideration for another transfer.
However, the department has proposed exceptions for compassionate and other exceptional grounds.
"No teacher would ordinarily be allowed to remain at a single place of posting for more than five years. On completion of the maximum tenure, the teacher would become liable for transfer in the interest of administration," reads the draft transfer policy.
The department has also proposed that transfers will be normally conducted once a year through an Annual Transfer Drive (ATD), preferably at the end of the academic session and before commencement of the new session "to minimise disruption to teaching activities."
"Mid-session transfers would be avoided except in cases involving serious medical grounds, security concerns or administrative exigencies," it reads.
The draft categorises transfers into administrative transfers, mutual transfers, security-related deployments and compassionate transfers.
For inter-district mutual transfers, the policy proposes exchanges between teachers of the same cadre, qualification, subject and status, "subject to verification and approval by the competent authority."
"Such transfers would not ordinarily be allowed within two years of a previous transfer," reads the draft transfer policy.
It reads that the teachers transferred under the inter-district mutual transfer provision would retain their lien and promotion prospects in their parent districts.
"Special consideration will be given to teachers facing serious personal or family circumstances. Compassionate consideration will be given to cases involving life-threatening medical conditions, disability, widowhood, single parenthood and spouse unification, particularly where both spouses are government employees serving in different areas," it reads.
As per the draft policy, the deployments on security grounds would be considered by the Administrative Department after following the prescribed procedure.
The draft further proposes that the Cluster Heads will make suitable internal arrangements where a teacher is deployed on compassionate or security grounds to ensure that school functioning is not disrupted.
Another provision seeks to protect reserved-category teachers by ensuring that their mandatory stay period under the Reservation Policy is fulfilled while processing transfers.
The policy has also proposed a 10-day grievance redressal window at the Joint Director level following issuance of transfer orders.
As per the draft policy, the department will restrict frequent transfers, proposing that an employee should ordinarily not be transferred again within two years of the previous transfer, unless necessitated by administrative exigency.
"Employees facing disciplinary proceedings would generally not be considered for transfer, except where their transfer is required in the interest of inquiry or administration," it reads.
As per the draft, key provision specifically deals with RReTs who have not yet attained regularisation status.
"Such teachers would continue within their originally assigned place/zone, keeping in view the nature of their initial engagement," it reads.
"However, once RReTs attain regularisation or are placed as Grade-II or Grade-III teachers, they would be governed fully by the proposed Transfer Policy," the document reads
Department has also proposed a clear separation between RReTs, Grade-II and Grade-III teachers and GLTs.
"Transfers would take place between RReTs to RReTs, Grade-II to Grade-II and Grade-III to Grade-III, with no transfers of any kind between GLTs and ReT teachers, except those who have already been transitioned and adjusted against regular and substantive posts," it reads.
As per the draft policy, the department will decentralise certain transfer powers while retaining administrative control over inter-district movements.
"Transfers within the same zone would be ordered by the concerned Zonal Education Officer after approval from the Chief Education Officer," it reads.
Also, the transfers between zones within a district would be ordered by the concerned Chief Education Officer after approval from the Joint Director.
"Inter-district transfers and deployments would be ordered only by the Administrative Department recommendations of the concerned director," it reads.
The department has proposed that the policy be reviewed every five years, or earlier if required, along with periodic assessment of teacher deployment to ensure rationalisation and effective implementation.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Maggie Bodner, a 28-year-old employee at Spirit Halloween, based in the Fort Lauderdale area. Her identity and employment have been verified by Business Insider. This story has been edited for length and clarity.
I was laid off in June and started to apply for jobs like crazy.
When people say the job market is tough, the job market is tough. It's especially challenging if you do something really specific, like learning and development. It's just rejection email after rejection email, and some of them come in an hour after I applied.
In July, my boyfriend asked me if there was anything I've ever really wanted to do. After thinking about it, I realized I wanted to work at Spirit Halloween. I love shopping at Spirit Halloween and I'm there three or four times a week when it's open.
Sure enough, there was a Spirit Halloween opening right around the corner from me so I applied to the assistant manager position and sales associate position. Three weeks after I applied, I heard from the store manager and went in for an interview. They were still setting up the store and I felt so happy to see it being built.
I heard back a few days after the interview and got the job.
The job provides me with much needed fun
My love for Halloween started with Twilight. I have a Twilight tattoo and Halloween was always a time where I could dress up as a vampire. I love being scared. I'm a big fan of Halloween horror nights, haunted houses, and ghost tours.
I volunteered to work 10 hours in one day, and I came home feeling energized and excited. I enjoy working with the sales associates and my store manager is a great teacher. We have an in-store-experience, which is a haunted house, so people also come in with their kids. The other day, a kid put on a turtle shell costume, got on the ground, and charged at me to scare me. It was really funny and sweet.
Sometimes we have a line of customers waiting outside the door. I was an enthusiast, but I didn't know that people wait outside for the store to open. Some people come in every day because we always put new stuff on the floor.
Spirit hires people who love Halloween. Plus, the Halloween benefits are great. I get 30% off of all my merch, and I can't tell you how much I've gotten already.
I'm still applying to jobs
I've always been an empathetic person, but I think this gave me a little more empathy for people going through layoffs. I used to see posts on LinkedIn of people saying "it's been a year since I've been laid off," and I would think "how could it be a year?" But now that I'm in it, it makes sense.
Two of my colleagues are in high school and working part-time. One of them asked me, "How could you get laid off if you're valuable?" I told him, "You'd be really surprised." The comment itself didn't shock me, but it opened my eyes to the fact that people who haven't experienced a layoff truly don't understand that it can happen to anyone, no matter how valuable you are.
I'm still applying to jobs, but I want to ride this experience out, even if I get another opportunity.
The hours at Spirit get later as it gets closer to Halloween so if I get another opportunity, I would try to change my shift so that I could keep working here for the season.
It's much needed fun during a very stressful time. My biggest takeaway would be that if you find yourself laid off, instead of worrying yourself with the big picture, focus on the moment and find something you truly enjoy doing.

You have, by now, probably come across the notion of maxxing—looks-maxxing, sleep-maxxing, protein-maxxing, potassium-maxxing, sun-maxxing, testosterone-maxxing. Etymologically speaking, maxxing seems to be a descendant of somewhat recent slang—for those of us who remember the late 20th century, “maxin’ and relaxin’ ” and “to the max” both come to mind—but in practice, maxxing is a reductionist worldview cloaked in expansionist language.
The term is often invoked to describe a narrowly focused goal: If you’re maxxing, you’re likely trying to make yourself smaller, sharper, more chiseled. Maxxing requires sacrifice. It requires careful measurement. And in this way, maxxing is a consequence of our broader optimization-obsessed culture, a fixation fueled by every product, device, app, and service that trains people to collect and analyze data generated by their own behavior.
This culture of optimization has been building for some time now, since at least the 19th century, when industrialism made efficiency a core ideal of working life. Later, when offices overtook factories as the emblem of work, efficiency became more abstract. Productivity began to be measured not only in profits maximized, but also in meetings shortened, messages answered, and bottlenecks removed. Over time, workers started managing themselves preemptively in accordance with the mandate of efficiency, optimizing their own calendars and lunch breaks. This optimization mindset leaked out of business and into everything else. People stopped asking what activities were for and started asking how to do them better, faster, or more completely.
Efficiency now infuses every aspect of contemporary life, if you let it. Instacart and DoorDash can replace grocery shopping and dining out. People optimize their vacations, maximizing credit-card points and airport-lounge strategies. Kindle streaks and Goodreads goals have turned books into items on a checklist. Wearables have turned exercise into VO₂ or HRV maximization. The more nutrition-obsessed among us have transformed eating into macronutrient acquisition. Every pleasure can become instrumental—with every instrument focused on the outcomes it might produce.
Optimization is terrific if you want to get somewhere else in the future. But it’s terrible for being where you actually are right now. When goals overtake experience, you lose the freedom to encounter your life as it happens. And when you lose that ability, you are no longer living in full. We used to optimize work so we could do everything else. Now we optimize life as though living were another job. Too many of us seem to be maxxing our way out of the experiences and perspectives that give us maximum meaning.
I’ve come to believe that wonder, the most immense of our sensations, is the antidote. Wonder can rise up anywhere. It might arrive after you hike to Hopi Point, nearly a mile above the Grand Canyon’s river floor. Or as you take in the northern lights from Tromsø, Norway. Or, on a different scale, wonder might be expected while you hold your newborn child for the first time, recognizing human life in its primal form and knowing that your own has now changed entirely. For children themselves, wonder remains abundant—in the bigness of a Tyrannosaurus rex in a museum, or the flicker of fireflies in the summer dusk. But for many adults, wonder is too often compartmentalized: a feeling we associate with extraordinary and rare experiences, banished to a realm outside the mundanities of daily life.
For me, several aspects of modern life have made wonder seem out of reach lately: the rise of “frictionless” automated services for chores; the decline of serendipity in a world where every trip is Google Mapped; the ease with which everything can be done remotely, averting the happenstances and textures of regular routines; the ability to opt out of ambient noise (and impromptu conversations) by popping in AirPods; and, of course, our tendency to fill the gaps in our days by staring at our phones. But most of all, wonder feels scarce because contemporary life has depleted the value of the moment. Time has become instrumentalized, and as a result we have taught ourselves to treat the present primarily as a waiting room in which to plan for—and, yes, optimize—the future.
Efficiency culture has muscled out the present so completely that it feels difficult to occupy a moment at all, let alone fully. Even the seasons, which help us mark the present amid the endless passage of time, seem to be anxious to overcome one another—pumpkin-spice creamers and “Pumking” imperial pumpkin ales now appear in supermarkets in July. Wonder interrupts that impulse to rush to the future before it arrives. It makes the world stop serving our self-centered plans or intentions, and instead offer something worth encountering for its own sake.
For years, I have struggled with the problem myself. The urge to optimize caused me to flee to the future constantly. I realized that I felt best able to overcome efficiency culture when I treated supposedly unimportant sensations, objects, and events as vital ones instead: sliding my feet into the plush softness of slippers in the morning, feeling the warmth of a mug of coffee in my hands, hearing the gravel crunch under my feet as I walked. None of these acts compromised purpose or plans. All they required of me was to construe what I was already doing as valuable.
Eventually I came to recognize that my long-standing obsession with ordinary things—including many that I have written about in The Atlantic, among them toasters, gas-station signs, backpacks, slushies, and gearshifts—offered a reason to take the present seriously. These objects show that beauty and even genius are often expressed through design choices and simple engineering. Tools we might think of as “useful” are in fact wondrous. The A BIT MORE button on modern toasters is a perfect example: so useful that you might overlook it as obvious, yet absolutely transformative in the making of toast. For some readers, this may generate an eye roll. Cynicism is pervasive, and not everyone has time for or interest in the scenic route. But I believe there are more of us wonder-seekers than the cynics and maxxers among us might like to admit. And besides: The route I am suggesting does not require an out-of-the-way trip. It simply asks you to accept gifts that the universe is already handing you.
Wonder may not improve your résumé, make you hotter, or maximize your income. It will simply remind you that you are a body alive in the world, right now, and that is a better place to begin than most self-help advice would have you believe.
Once you allow wonder to arrive, it proves to be astonishingly promiscuous. Over the past year, I’ve made a point of asking people about what inspires daily wonder. I expected themes to emerge, but I also assumed that those themes would be predictable: sunsets and forests; notable structures or works of art.
Many people did describe the familiar icons of awe—the moment when an airplane breaks through the clouds, and all you can see is the great expanse of sky ahead; the experience of strangers gathering silently along a shoreline to watch the sun vanish below the horizon. But just as many have told me that they’ve found wonder in the mundane—watching a procession of ants carrying things they value, for instance. I’ve corresponded with people who described their affection for an old refrigerator; a sewing machine whose hums and clicks became a friend’s familiar voice; pots and pans that carried decades of family meals; and even a toilet whose owner began to admire it after a repair revealed its elegant method of operation.
Whenever you cease treating the world as scenery or equipment, you’ll find that you encounter the world as something inexhaustibly, constantly present. Oceans and ants, sewing machines and sunsets, strangers and screen doors, microwaves and mountains, rocks and racquets, lamps and laughter all prove equally worthy. Our expectations for wonder sometimes wane, but it is with us all along, waiting to be rediscovered.
This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “The Missing Ingredient of Modern Life.”

Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones. The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO.
Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device.
Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air.
Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage, which has made just about everything more expensive. Apple hasn’t been spared. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs.
“Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal, a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.”
Popal says it's a smart strategic move because Apple is aiming to spread out its revenue between a usually very strong fourth quarter and a typically much weaker spring quarter the following year. Apple’s portfolio has also expanded, and the iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup are more enticing for people already prepared to spend the money on a new iPhone.
When components become more expensive, companies have three real options: Eat the costs, raise prices, or, as Apple seems to be doing, lean into it. By moving its cheaper options to a later date, Apple can drum up excitement for its bigger, better, pricier offerings. When it charges more for those, it is likely to be less off-putting than making a cheap phone even more expensive. It’s part of a “premiumization” of devices, as Popal calls it, that Apple hopes to leverage and build hype for its pricier options.
Shawn DuBravac, chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, tells WIRED he is optimistic about what these kinds of rising prices ultimately mean for customers.
“Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer,” DuBravac says. “I'm confident that will be the case again. It just will take some time for the markets to solidify.” In other words, new technologies launch with a high price, but manufacturing efficiencies and competition inevitably drive costs down for consumers.
That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones, which are seeing higher prices than ever. Samsung’s entire 2026 Galaxy Z folding smartphone range saw price increases, as did Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and Motorola’s Razr 2026 models. Apple’s folding iPhone is rumored to cost around $2,000.
To help mitigate those high costs, Apple is turning to financing options and trade-in programs. In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program that lets people pay a monthly fee to rent the newest iPhones, then swap them out when a new device releases. The program will undoubtedly help more people afford the newest devices, but ownership advocates have criticized it, saying it keeps you from truly owning and managing your device. It also fits Apple’s broader effort to turn all of its products into a subscription service.
“The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs,” Popal says. “We can expect a lot more aggressive trade-ins to help cushion that.”
Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases, all smartphones are getting more costly to make. Less expensive phones become less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, and leading smartphone brands have started to see them as far less economical to produce.
On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices has been climbing for a while now, with sales of used devices growing even as new phone sales slow down. More people are looking to save money or purchase more eco-friendly products.
“The days of the cheap smartphone are over,” Popal says.

Abdul El-Sayed is trying to win over undecided Jewish voters in Michigan — without compromising his substantive positions on Israel or disavowing his most radical allies.
The Jewish Democrats trying to get to “yes” on Abdul El-Sayed
A Democratic fundraiser on how the candidate’s charm offensive is going.
During both his primary and general election campaigns, El-Sayed’s opponents have portrayed him as insensitive to Jewish concerns, if not outright antisemitic. These charges have often rested on falsely equating El-Sayed’s opposition to Zionism (he is not committed to Israel’s existence as a majority Jewish state) with a hostility for Jewish people.
But in recent weeks, two other concerns came to the forefront. One was El-Sayed’s response to an antisemitic attack on a Michigan synagogue. In March, a 41-year-old named Ayman Mohamed Ghazali drove a truck into Temple Israel’s Jewish preschool. Days later, El-Sayed condemned the attack, while also noting that Ghazali had recently lost family members to an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon. El-Sayed suggested that these events illustrated how “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle,” one that had led Ghazali to perpetrate “an evil act of displaced rage.”
Separately, El-Sayed had campaigned with the far-left streamer Hasan Piker during his primary campaign. This had always sat poorly with many Jewish and centrist Democrats in Michigan. But Piker made his association with the Democratic Senate candidate more conspicuous in late August. During a broadcast, Piker lambasted Jeremy Moss, a pro-Israel Jewish Democrat running for Congress in Michigan who had not endorsed El-Sayed but was in active conversations with the candidate about how to bridge lingering divides with Jewish voters. More explosively, Piker said, among other things, that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually somebody is going to come around and take action, not against the State of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” He subsequently insisted he was merely spotlighting the hazards of portraying all Jews as ardent Israel supporters, not making some kind of veiled threat, as his detractors alleged.
Nonetheless, this triggered a new round of calls for El-Sayed to both disavow Piker, and to take other measures to reassure Michigan Jews that he cares about their safety.
These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally.
El-Sayed declined to disown the streamer. But he did defend the right of all Americans “to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” saying this was “particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.”
Some Jewish Democrats found this insufficient. In an open letter Wednesday, 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders — including donor Rob Orley — announced that they would be supporting Republican Mike Rogers in their state’s Senate race.
Days earlier, El-Sayed had sought to mend fences with such voters at a summit held by the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus. During his appearance there, he apologized for his remarks following the Temple Israel attack, saying “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.”
Among those in attendance was Charles Gaba, a healthcare analyst and major Democratic fundraiser; Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow has called him “the biggest powerhouse democratic donor wrangler that nobody has ever heard of.”
Gaba was a strong supporter of Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. And he has expressed serious reservations about El-Sayed, even while committing to voting for him and raising money for his candidacy.
These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally: over how far Democrats can and should go in criticizing Israel, whether the left takes antisemitism seriously, and if centrists are using allegations of anti-Jewish bigotry to stigmatize legitimate dissent.
To explore these debates — and clarify the concerns of “Sayed-skeptical” Jews in Michigan — I spoke with Gaba this week.
Our conversation has been edited for clarity and concision.
From your vantage point, what are undecided Jewish Michiganders’ biggest reservations about El-Sayed — and how many are actually addressable by his campaign?
I’d say that there’s probably four main ones. Two are connected to his comments about the Temple Israel attack. And he definitely addressed one of those complaints with his statement: that it was awfully timed. In other words, that days after the attack was not a good moment to raise other issues instead of simply condemning the violence full stop.
But the larger issue to me — and to a lot of other folks I’ve spoken with — is he seemed to be under the impression that timing was the only problem. That it was just too soon and if he’d waited a month and then made the exact same comments about “context,” that would have been fine. He doesn’t seem to get that trying to put it in context at all is the larger problem. Because a bunch of preschoolers at a synagogue in Michigan have absolutely nothing to do with a military conflict overseas, just nothing. If a family member of someone who died in the September 11th attacks had gone and attempted to kill Muslim children, their loss wouldn’t be relevant context. You couldn’t say, “Oh well, but he was upset about that attack.”
I think an El-Sayed supporter might say: There’s a difference between explaining an abominable act and excusing it. In his original statement, El-Sayed did say explicitly that “there is never a justification for attacking innocent people or houses of worship” and described the violence as “heinous” and “evil.” Taken literally, he was arguing that the strike that had killed Ghazali’s family members led to his act of antisemitic terrorism, even as nothing could possibly justify it.
There was just no reason to try to put it in context at all. Pretty much everyone understands that the Israel-Hamas war has brought emotions to a fever pitch for a lot of people.
I don’t think we needed someone to say, “Hey, that whole mess in the Mideast might have inspired this!” Yeah, no shit. Who was the audience for this? Who was he trying to give context to? Certainly the Jewish community understands the situation. I think the Muslim community understands the situation. And so does everyone else. I don’t think it served any purpose other than to upset and offend a bunch of people. So he was lecturing to no one essentially, in my view. Which I get; I have a tendency to do that myself sometimes in other ways. But it isn’t helpful. And shifting the timing wouldn’t have made it helpful.
So, what are the other two big sticking points for Jewish Democrats not sold on El-Sayed?
The third is this Hasan Piker guy. The media certainly seems to be pretty focused on that. If memory serves, El-Sayed seemed to be trailing Mallory McMorrow and Haley Stevens in the primaries up until around March. And then it was announced that he was going to be rallying with Piker at Michigan State and the University of Michigan.
A combination of that and the reaction to it — namely the McMorrow campaign heavily criticizing him for the rally — generated a bunch of attention and certainly raised Abdul’s profile tremendously. I don’t know how much credit to give Piker, but it made some difference. And next thing you know, he’s kind of running in the lead.
So, it’s pretty clear that Piker was brought in specifically to help him win the primary with a very young, progressive crowd. To that effect, it worked. But that doesn’t mean he’s helpful for winning a general election.
So, why do you think El-Sayed refuses to distance himself more explicitly from Piker, if the influencer’s support is not helpful in the general election?
I don’t know. Maybe he thinks that he’s being noble or something by not throwing him under the bus. But the guy just seems to be kind of an asshole, and I would not want to be associated with him in either the primary or the general. And so associating himself with Hasan Piker makes me think less of Abdul.
And I have a lot of respect for Abdul. I’ve met him about a half-dozen times or so, back when he ran for governor and then several times during this campaign. And we’ve also been in contact a few times in between to discuss healthcare policy. And I know he’s a very intelligent guy, very thoughtful guy, and very passionate about universal healthcare. I respect him for all of that. But I think less of him for associating with Piker. And I think a lot of Jewish Michiganders feel that way.
So, what’s the fourth issue?
Well, this is not so much about Abdul specifically as it is about the left. A lot of progressives get that you should condemn antisemitism, or bigotry against the Jewish religion. But many don’t seem to grasp that Judaism is not just a religion; it is also a people. And we do have a several thousand-year connection with the land of Israel — not the leadership, not the current government — but with the land itself. And so that makes the distinction between antisemitism and anti-Zionism complicated. You know, to try to say, “Well, as long as you give up Israel, then Judaism is fine” — many of us can’t do that because it’s an intrinsic part of who we are.
Is there not a distinction between recognizing Jews’ historical and religious connection to Israel — and being committed to the maintenance of a majority Jewish state in the Middle East?
In other words, there are anti-Zionists who deny Jews’ roots in Israel — or the right of Jewish Israelis to live in the region. But I think most progressive anti-Zionists would dispute neither of those things. Rather, they’d argue that Israeli Jews have a right to live in their land — but that maintaining a majority Jewish Israel should not take precedence over allowing Palestinian refugees and their descendants to return to their ancestral territories.
It’s definitely true that there’s more than one type of anti-Zionism. I think there’s several groupings and different shades between them. And that also holds true on the Zionist side. There are right-wing extremists like [Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar] Ben-Gvir who say, “We should annex both the West Bank and Gaza.” And then there’s others that go even more extreme and say that Israel should dominate the entire region, including Lebanon and Egypt.
And then, at the other end, there’s Hamas and other extremists who literally want to either kick out or slaughter every Jew in the region.
And those extremes have led people to think that Zionism means “Jews get to take over the region” and that anti-Zionism means “Jews have to be kicked out.”
I think for most people, it’s somewhere in between. I’ve started calling myself a “small-z Zionist,” which is basically a more mainstream, two-state solution type. I don’t know how feasible that solution is. There’s only a slim chance these days. But the odds of a two-state solution are still better than those of creating a single “kumbaya, let’s all live together in peace” nation, in my view.
How were El-Sayed’s remarks to Michigan’s Jewish Caucus received, from your vantage point?
They were better received than I expected, to be honest. Although, I suspect that those most opposed to him probably didn’t show up at the event at all, since they’ve made up their minds.
Having said that, I did have discussions with several people afterwards, and there was definitely still concern about the whole “context” thing. People were polite and it was a reasonably warm reception. And to his credit, he did stick around afterwards and had one-on-one personal conversations. He was there for quite a while, so I give him credit for that.
From a purely electoral perspective, how much does El-Sayed actually have to lose, if he fails to consolidate the Jewish vote? In demographic terms, the bloc of Jewish voters who are open to voting for El-Sayed — but still need to be persuaded — would seem to be tiny. After all, we’re talking about a small minority of small minority; Jews account for only about 1.4 percent of Michigan’s electorate. So, what’s at stake here politically?
In terms of activism, organizing, and donations, the Jewish community punches far above our weight.
But yeah, we’re a fraction of a fraction. I think the biggest thing is just reassuring moderate Democratic voters in general. Basically, if the headlines start to read, “Jewish leaders seem reassured by Abdul apology,” then some non-Jewish folks — who aren’t sure about El-Sayed — might say, “Oh, well, if the Jews signed off on this guy, I guess he’s okay.”

A common cause given for leg pain is muscle strain, and this may be attributed to standing for a long time, exercising incorrectly, or getting older. But sometimes, there may be something different going on. A pain that begins in the lower back and radiates down the buttock and to the leg, may indicate irritation or pressure on the sciatic nerve, and is referred to as sciatica.
The largest nerve in the body is the sciatic nerve. It extends from the lower back through buttocks and down each leg. If a nerve in the lower back is compressed or inflamed, it may result in pain that radiates down this nerve.
How do you know if you have sciatica pain?
Sciatica isn’t always typical leg pain. It can cause a sudden electric-like, burning or tearing sensation down the back of the thigh and sometimes into the calf or foot from the lower back or buttock.
Some people may also experience tingling, numbness or weakness in the affected leg. The pain can worsen after sitting for prolonged periods, or after coughing, sneezing or certain movements.
In some cases, the discomfort may be primarily experienced in the leg, and there may be very little discomfort in the back. This can be one explanation as to why people may confuse sciatica with leg muscle or joint pain.
What causes sciatica?
A common cause of sciatica is a slipped disc or a bulging disc in the lower portion of the spine. The discs between the bones of our spine work like cushions. If one of them bulges or tears, it can compress an adjacent nerve.
Other reasons include changes in the spine with age, constriction of the spinal canal, bone growth and, less frequently, injury or other spinal diseases.
Not all people suffering from sciatica require a surgery. With the right kind of rest, and the use of the remedies as prescribed by a physician, physiotherapy and a gradual return to normal activity, many people get better. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the symptoms.
When to det a doctor’s advice
Some back or leg pain may get better over time, but certain symptoms shouldn’t be ignored. You should seek medical advice if the pain is severe, keeps returning, lasts for several weeks or is affecting your ability to walk, work or perform everyday activities.
Numbness or worsening weakness in the leg, trouble with urination or defecation or numbness around the inner thighs and genitals are emergencies.
Avoiding making every leg ache a diagnosis of sciatica is also important. Similar symptoms can occur due to problems involving the muscles, joints, blood vessels or other nerves, which is why it is important to consult a doctor. Your doctor can evaluate your symptoms, motion, muscle strength and reflexes and might suggest imaging if needed.
In addition to this, keeping a healthy weight, being physically active, strengthening core muscles and avoiding long periods of sitting can help keep your spine healthy.
The bottom line is: leg pain that radiates from the back or buttock is not necessarily from the leg and can be from the spine. Early identification of warning signs and proper diagnosis can prevent symptoms from becoming severe and can help to expedite a return to normal life.
(Dr. Kalidutta Das is chief and director of spine services, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. Kaliduttadas@gmail.com)

More than a kilometer underground, in what used to be a gold mine, inside a tank filled with tons of liquid xenon, “something” struck the nucleus of an atom. The tiny collision left an unusual energy signature that researchers are still unable to explain, but the scientists behind the experiment believe this could be the most convincing physical evidence of dark matter to date.
Dark matter is one of the most important and elusive substances in astrophysics. Though it makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, we can’t observe it directly because it doesn’t interact with light or much else. Most of the evidence for its existence comes from its gravitational effects, the mass of dark matter having tugged on the atoms of the early universe to form stars, galaxies, and the vast web of intergalactic structures visible today.
But the enigma of dark matter is complex. Scientists don’t even know what it is made of, whether it’s a single type of particle or an entire set of particles that interact with one another in ways we do not yet understand. The most fantastical explanations even suggest that it consists of black holes. One of the most widely studied theories on dark matter has dubbed its components WIMPs, short for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, meaning the particles have a mass and thus a gravitational pull but otherwise interact weakly with conventional matter.
If WIMPs exist and are part of the dark matter of our galaxy, enormous quantities of them could be passing through the Earth continuously without leaving a trace. However, it is possible that, very occasionally, one might interact with an atomic nucleus and transfer some of its energy to it, which is why an inexplicable collision is exciting in the world of particle physics.
In the strange disturbance recorded at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in South Dakota, the detector monitoring the tank recorded that a xenon nucleus received energy and recoiled. Though researchers have not yet been able to satisfactorily explain the cause, some models suggest a WIMP could produce such a reaction.
The scientists stated that this single event is statistically too small to be considered the discovery of a new particle. In 220 days of observations conducted between 2023 and 2024, only one such anomaly occurred. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input,” Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and a member of the team leading the project, said in a press release.
The team behind the experiment has published their study as a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer reviewed. They have, however, presented the results to the scientific community at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics Conference in Japan.
Discoveries made around dark matter tend to elicit this kind of restrained excitement. When in November 2025 a team of Japanese astronomers announced that they had seen signs of dark matter in the Milky Way, they too advised the research community not to count their chickens.
But even if cautious, there are reasons for enthusiasm. If the impact was caused by dark matter, there is enough evidence for researchers to begin characterizing the responsible particle. For example, the team has already calculated that, under the WIMP models they analyzed, the particle is about 200 times more massive than a proton. The impact could help us understand how this type of matter interacts with conventional matter.
The team has also been examining other possible explanations. Paradoxically, in experiments as sensitive as this one, atypical events are not all that uncommon. That’s why SURF has various methods of filtering out background noise and detecting interference caused by known particles or radiation. This event withstood that scrutiny. So far, the researchers have not found an explanation among these known sources that fits what they observed.
“We understand our detector and the backgrounds so well that even a single outstanding event, like the one we found, is important,” said Sam Eriksen, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol and the study’s lead author. “We expect dark matter events to be extremely rare, so only a handful could mark the first detection of WIMP dark matter.”

Scroll down in American Express' TikTok account, and you'll find a video of Ira Galtman popping up from behind a bison at the Bronx Zoo.
"Ira content makes my day," one commenter wrote, evidently already familiar with Galtman, who, as a middle-aged archivist, didn't expect to become a social media hit for the brand when he first started filming "Ira, The Archivist" videos in 2023.
"I don't even have a cat in my video, and people are looking at it! I don't even have to dance in the video to get attention," he said on a video call.
Galtman has served as Amex's brand archivist for three decades, documenting the company's 176-year history and preserving its historic documents and artifacts. He was a bit hesitant when the social media team first approached him about filming videos for LinkedIn, but quickly realized he was relatively comfortable talking about the stories he knows well on camera.
"I can be myself," he said, adding that his authenticity is likely part of the appeal. "I'm not pretending that I'm trying to be an influencer."
Galtman's popularity coincides with Amex's interest in courting younger cardholders, many of whom first encounter brands on their social media feeds. CEO Steve Squeri said on his company's third-quarter earnings call that millennials and Gen Zers accounted 65% of new consumer accounts. As of January, the average age of Platinum cardholders was 33, never mind the $895 annual fee.
'A runaway hit'
Amex's social team started by posting Galtman's videos on LinkedIn and Facebook, mainly for other employees, but expanded to other platforms after they were "a runaway hit," said Aya Kanai, the head of enterprise content and communications.
"Nostalgia does very well online and in social spaces," Kanai said.
The videos originally focused more on the artifacts, but the social media team learned that Galtman is a key part of their appeal. They now all have an endearing, almost jolly vibe, like a mix of the vintage Americana and dad-core posts on the more wholesome corners of the internet.
Galtman always introduces himself in his New York accent, often against "Modern Elevator Music/Cute Electronic Bossanova," and launches into the history of an Amex-related object, periodically raising one eyebrow over his transition lenses. In the zoo video, Galtman explains that, in 1907, Amex helped transport 15 nearly extinct American bison from New York City to a wildlife reserve in Oklahoma.
 @americanexpress In honor of the 60th anniversary of the Gold Card, Ira, the American Express archivist, takes a look back at the Gold Card’s illustrious history in fashion. Link in bio for a deeper dive.

Over time, the social media team has started tying his content to specific business events — in a video honoring the 60th anniversary of the gold card, for example, Galtman talks about a 1995 dress made from the product.
As of September, Amex had posted 20 videos of Galtman, which usually perform about twice as well as the company's social media benchmark, Kanai said. Galtman's videos still perform best on LinkedIn, and also do particularly well with younger audiences on TikTok. Nobody has stopped Galtman on the street yet, but he said colleagues have started coming up to him in the office or cafeteria to ask about their own business line's history or a recent video.
Other corporate leaders have also leaned into social media for the right executives. Blackstone President Jon Gray, for example, regularly goes viral for his running videos, and McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski films taste tests from his office. Kanai said she's keen to expand similar content to other Amex leaders, provided they're comfortable on camera.
Keeping it real
Galtman, however, isn't usually thinking about engagement metrics or customer acquisition when he's filming, and is instead making sure he "feels the content." The same ethos is true for his appearance — he doesn't go through hair and makeup, partly because he wants "to keep it real."
Before each video, Galtman takes time to stretch, swat away any lingering butterflies, and talk through the material in a quiet place, without his notes.
"If anyone sort of overhears me, I guess they may think, 'Ira is really losing it.' But I like to think that that's not a unique thing to do," he said.
Only a handful of people are there for the actual filming, urging him to smile more or coaching him through phrases that trip him up, like "stock certificates."
Galtman's mild social media stardom hasn't changed his own online habits much. He still enjoys keeping up with rock and classical music, and following archive-related content on X. Yet he looks at posts through a different lens, now that he's been on the other side of the camera.
"I can see a video and say that that's really hard to do," he said. "A lot of it is respect for some of the content."

Six Movies to Get You in the Fall Mood
From cozy classics to unlikely favorites, The Atlantic’s writers and editors share their seasonal picks.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
September has arrived, bringing the first hints of fall: cooler days, changing leaves, and the urge to revisit comfort watches. Below, The Atlantic’s writers and editors recommend six films that put them in an autumn spirit.
When Harry Met Sally (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
There’s the cornucopia of cable-knit sweaters, a chocolate-brown velvet bowler hat, the fog of bright-orange leaves streaming through the glass wall at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Autumn in New York is the backdrop of When Harry Met Sally, but that doesn’t fully account for the place that Nora Ephron and Rob Reiner’s classic occupies in my life: For me, it’s the chicken noodle soup of movies. I have my personal reasons for considering it the ultimate comfort watch. Maybe it’s my affinity with Sally (played by Meg Ryan), the curly-haired journalist determined to have life happen to her, though her job is to “write about things that happen to other people.” Or the movie’s love for my hometown, which forms the bedrock of so many of Ephron’s films. Or the weirdly specific fantasy of having your date unwittingly quote to you something you wrote in a magazine.
This time of year, I’m far from the only person who considers a When Harry Met Sally rewatch as inevitable as digging my denim jacket out of the back of my closet. If there’s a universal magic to the movie, maybe some of it comes from magic in real life. The original script saw Sally and Harry’s (Billy Crystal) story ending bittersweetly, with the two apart. But midway through making the film, Reiner fell in love with his wife, Michele Singer. This fall—our first without Reiner and Singer—I’ll be revisiting the movie in large part for the ending he decided on instead: perhaps the most memorable, and certainly my favorite, in the romantic-comedy genre.
— Marie-Rose Sheinerman, assistant editor
Michael Clayton (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Fall is not really about melancholy and the inner life, as the poets would have you believe. It’s that period, after summer’s frivolities, when things get serious again. Michael Clayton, a film I first saw at the urging of my friend and colleague James Parker—and which we both regularly rewatch—is charged with that urban, autumnal, overcoated feeling of things getting serious.
The people in it are grown-ups. If they’re not, as with Timmy—Michael Clayton’s brother, whose feckless behavior leaves Michael exposed to loan sharks—they’re basically ignored. Sydney Pollack? What a performance! What an impeccably serious guy! Tom Wilkinson, Tilda Swinton—they’re brilliant in this. And George Clooney, playing the titular character, is haunted by his own rotting, inky-eyed charm and stymied at every turn, despite his good intentions. He’s at his best in the scene where Michael, working as his law firm’s fixer, advises an affluent, arrogant client who has just committed a hit-and-run. The client, thinking it’s still unfettered summer, throws a childish tantrum. Michael, in his best autumnal mode, sets him straight: “There’s no play here. There’s no angle. There’s no champagne room. And I’m not a miracle worker; I’m a janitor.”
— Sebastian Smee, staff writer
Little Women (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Fall is a happy-sad season: The sunlight is golden (but that’s a sign that the days are getting shorter), the leaves are ochre and maroon (a sign that they’re dying), and the air is crisp (a sign of impending winter). And to me, Greta Gerwig’s 2019 adaptation of Little Women perfectly embodies this feeling. The story follows the four March sisters through the different seasons of their life. Their childhood flashbacks are scenes captured in warm, autumnal tones, and adulthood flash-forwards are shot in cooler, harsher light, to reflect the girls’ feelings about the passage of time.
Jo March wants to grow up, and yet she clings to girlhood, panicking as those around her—such as her sister Meg, who gets married—seem content to let the past go. In one pivotal scene, Jo tells her mother that she wishes she could still want what she wanted as a child, when simply being with her family was enough. Now her aspirations for a career and romantic love seem at odds, and her sense of independence has become inextricable from an acute sense of loneliness. For those of us who also cling to the past (even if that past is just “summer”), this film will comfort you and remind you that change is inevitable.
— Nancy Walecki, staff writer
You’ve Got Mail (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
The first 30 minutes of You’ve Got Mail are an unabashed ode to autumn. “Don’t you love New York in the fall?” the film’s romantic hero, Joe (Tom Hanks), writes in an email to the heroine, Kathleen (Meg Ryan). When Kathleen arrives at work a few minutes later with a perfect orange pumpkin under her arm, she breathlessly repeats the question: “Don’t you just love New York in the fall?” And how could you not? The film shows children bobbing for apples at a street fair, a tree with copper leaves set against a row of brownstones, and characters walking around the Upper West Side in good knits, blazers, and fleeces.
Even when the movie shifts to winter and then spring, You’ve Got Mail still feels autumnal. That feeling goes beyond the scenery: It’s a wistful movie, and at times a sad one. Characters major and minor express regret over lost loves, broken family relationships, and unrealized dreams. Kathleen and Joe spend most of the film in relationships with people they clearly do not love. These notes of melancholy make it a perfect romantic comedy to turn to as the days get shorter.
— Eleanor Barkhorn, senior editor
Point Break (streaming on Peacock)
I grew up in Los Angeles, and as a result, I do not really understand seasons, weather, or people’s fear of being seen perspiring. Since I moved to the East Coast eight years ago, I have found autumn to be a cute but unwelcome reminder that winter is real and, even worse, that I will soon be forced to experience it.
The 1991 action thriller Point Break is also about Angeleno men who do not condone the end of summer. In the movie, they take this aversion one step further, robbing banks to fund the travel necessary to never stop surfing under the hot sun. The dialogue is clunky, albeit quotable, and almost nothing about the plot is believable. And yet, it’s so fun to watch these guys, and the FBI agent who tails them, try to make one summer weekend last forever. That is how I will be spending the fall: in denial, doing as much hiking, paddleboarding, and swimming as possible, until I am forced to stop.
— Marc Novicoff, staff writer
Silent Friend (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Silent Friend is a meandering film that has nudged me toward accepting slowness and inevitable change. The historical drama follows three environmentalists at a German university across three epochs as each tries to uncover the secret life of plants: In 1908, Grete navigates sexism and her own position as one of the first female students in the university’s botany department; in 1972, a young man named Hannes, immersed in his college campus’s Cold War–era counterculture, develops sensors to understand how a potted geranium perceives him; and in 2020, a neuroscientist runs an experiment connecting a tree’s electrical activity with his own after the COVID lockdown cuts off his access to human subjects.
At the center of it all is a nearly 200-year-old ginkgo tree that provides quiet solace to the three characters. The tree becomes a central figure in the story, observing, listening, and breathing alongside its subjects. Its presence embodies the spirit of the film, which is more sensory-driven than narrative-driven and makes it easy to lose yourself in the foliage. Now every time I see a leaf change color, I’m reminded to pay closer attention to the natural world around me and all of the life that brims within it.
— Kim Jao, assistant editor

The Measles-Stricken Mother Who Lost Her Newborn Son
By Tom Bartlett
When the Amish man emerged from his barn to greet me, he had no idea that his newborn son’s death had become national news. The man wore a straw hat, black trousers, and suspenders over a long-sleeved blue shirt; one of his similarly dressed sons was guiding a horse-drawn plow in a nearby field.
The man told me that, like most Amish people, he and his family don’t watch TV or use the internet. They don’t read the newspaper either. So they didn’t know until I told them that last Tuesday, Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, held a press conference to announce the first two “measles-associated” deaths in the state in 35 years.

For generations of rum drinkers, Old Monk has simply been rum. But the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has now told the Bombay High Court that the popular alcoholic beverage cannot be sold as "rum" because it is made using neutral spirit and rum flavouring. The regulator's counsel told the court on Thursday that its objection was not merely about the product's labelling but about the nature of the beverage itself. "What is not permitted is to sell this product as rum," FSSAI's counsel said. The regulator said the product could instead be described as a "rum-flavoured spirit". And suddenly, for those who first discovered rum through Old Monk, a rather strange question emerges: Was everything we knew about our first rum wrong? The Merriam-Webster dictionary defines rum as "an alcoholic beverage distilled from a fermented cane product (such as molasses)". For the famous Romantic poet Lord Byron, the definition was less technical and far more comforting. In his epic poem Don Juan, Byron wrote: "There's naught, no doubt, so much the spirit calms as rum and true religion." So, rum has had its definitions, from the technical to the poetic. But the current Old Monk dispute is about whether a product containing neutral spirit and added rum flavouring can legally be sold as rum in India. This author, too, had his first rum in the form of Old Monk during college, in the company of friends who, like countless others, praised the spirit. Old Monk wasn't merely a drink that appeared at college gatherings. It became part of conversations whenever this author met those friends later. It was one of those shared experiences that stayed with the group long after college ended. So when FSSAI's position became known, this author spoke to one of those friends. His first reaction was disbelief: "Sab jhooth tha?" This friend has a habit of recording every event of his life that happened for the first time. "Now I no longer know, when I drank actual rum," he said. Social media users were equally in disbelief amid FSSAI's assertions. For a group that had spent years calling Old Monk rum, the regulator's description of it as a "rum-flavoured spirit" was difficult to process. The dispute goes beyond what is printed on the bottle. FSSAI told the HC that its laboratory tests found external artificial or nature-identical flavouring substances in the products. According to the regulator, these additives masked the beverages' natural characteristics. The regulator cited the Food Safety and Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Regulations, 2018, which require standardised alcoholic beverages such as rum and whisky to retain their characteristic taste and aroma. FSSAI argued that adding "rum flavour" to rum or "whisky flavour" to whisky misrepresents these standardised products. Based on its findings, the regulator prohibited the sale of specific variants of McDowell's No. 1 Rum, Antiquity Blue Whisky and Royal Challenge Whisky manufactured by United Spirits; select Old Monk rum variants produced by Mohan Rocky Springwater; and Bagpiper Deluxe Whisky and Old Cask Deluxe XXX Rum made by Inbrew Beverages. The dispute over Old Monk's classification is also tied to its product labels. During a previous hearing on Monday, the company told the court it was prepared to modify its labels and remove the phrase "7 years old blended". The division bench of acting Chief Justice Ravindra V Ghuge and Justice Gautam A. Ankhad directed the company to present a revised label. The court also asked FSSAI to specify the details and requirements that needed to appear on the packaging so consumers could clearly distinguish the product. The state excise department was directed to review the modified label and expedite the approval process. The bench observed that consumers could be misled into believing that the rum was aged for seven years. It also questioned the company over text on the label, noting that it was "so small that nobody can read [it]". Old Monk submitted revised labels to the court on Thursday. FSSAI sought additional time to examine them and consider whether they could be approved. The matter will next be heard on September 11. Senior counsel Navroz H Seervai, representing the company, told the court that it had suffered a loss of ₹1 crore per day for the 120 days that the ban had been in force, according to an earlier Mint report. The Old Monk case is part of a broader dispute involving alcoholic beverages and FSSAI's objections to added flavouring. United Spirits, which faced a similar ban, withdrew its case on August 24. Its parent company, Diageo, along with other liquor manufacturers, agreed to comply with FSSAI directives by either removing disputed flavouring agents or modifying product labels. For the regulator, the issue is that a standardised alcoholic beverage such as rum must retain its characteristic taste and aroma, and adding rum flavouring to a product does not meet that requirement. For generations of drinkers, however, Old Monk has been their introduction to, and perhaps their most familiar idea of, rum. Which brings us back to that college friend. For him, however, the regulatory distinction remains difficult to digest.
