'Not Football Manager' - De Zerbi says misfiring Spurs need time
- Published
It has been more than half a century since Tottenham have gone this long without a league goal to start the season.
A City Ground stalemate at Nottingham Forest at least gets Roberto de Zerbi's side their first point of the season but not to the extent they would want.
It followed defeats to Brentford and Newcastle which means Spurs have failed to score in their opening three league games for the first time since 1974-75.
Spurs did not play badly - they were the better side - but after their huge summer transfer outlay more is needed and expected.
De Zerbi preached patience and he is right - 10 senior arrivals means his team is still to find an identity.
And they did leave Forest with a point, something they have failed to do for almost three years.
Indeed, the video assistant referee's call to rule out Neco Williams' bundled second-half effort ensured it was not a third-straight Premier League defeat for Spurs.
Yet they have now failed to score in three successive Premier League games for the first time since November 2021, and improvement is needed at misfiring Spurs.
Last March's 3-0 win for Forest at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium provided the platform for the visitors' survival bid while leaving Spurs floundering until the final day.
Since then Spurs have spent over £300m on new players - contributing to the record £3.49bn Premier League outlay this summer.
Sandro Tonali, Jon Paul Van Hecke, Savio and Omar Marmoush were the new signings who started on Saturday, with De Zerbi remaining calm after another blank.
"We bought very, very good players but you can't just build the team with the names like in Football Manager," he told Sky Sports.
"We are disappointed for the result but for the performance very happy. Considering we started to work together last Thursday for the first time, for the first day.
"We have to improve in every part of football, organisation with and without the ball. Even today I thought we defended very well.
"We have to work because I think we played very well with the ball, we found the solution. I think we can be much better in the final third."
De Zerbi bemoaned Tottenham's decision-making with Marmoush a culprit, blazing over in the second half with Andy Robertson on an overlap and Mohammed Kudus waiting for a far-post tap in.
The former Brighton boss could see the positives but needs his men to discover their composure.
"I think we played well, in the last third we have to improve, we have to take better decisions, maybe keep calmer when we are close to doing something important.
"The chance when Marmoush shot, we had Robertson overlapping. If we take the right decision and if we play with Robertson on the second post there is Kudus to score.
"I am very happy with the spirit, with the organisation, their style of play is very clear, long ball and second ball, even the second ball we won many duels. They are good players.
"Taking a point in this stadium is not so easy. We are not happy because we didn't win but this is the right spirit and the right way to move on in this moment."
A draw was Tottenham's eighth in the league this year, their most across a calendar year since 2020, and they failed to have a shot on target in a top-flight match for the first time since April 2022 against Brentford under Antonio Conte.
Spurs have had 38 shots in the league this season with an expected goals of 3.3 and former midfielder Danny Murphy agreed with De Zerbi over what the visitors lacked.
"When Spurs did get in really good areas, they just rushed it and shot when they maybe should've passed," he told BBC Sport.
"They made the wrong choice on pullbacks or crosses when they're getting in wide areas, taking men on one too many times when they've already got the space.
"They were just missing that little bit of calmness and composure that you expect from top quality players.
"It takes time for some players [to find chemistry]. You could argue that Marmoush and Savio know each other anyway and bright footballers quickly learn each other's runs and movements.
"From a midfielder to a forward perspective, you're not always sure what they're going to do. Whereas if you played with someone for a while, it comes more naturally. So those relationships will build."
Mudryk makes his Premier League return
Mykhailo Mudryk arrived on deadline day, on an initial loan from Chelsea, looking to revive his career following his four-year ban for testing positive for banned substance meldonium in 2024, something he denied knowingly ingesting.
The Ukraine international came off the bench, his first Premier League appearance since being a second-half substitute in a 1-1 draw against Arsenal in November 2024.
"He needs time and he needs work, we have in that position Mathys Tel - big potential - but also Tel takes too many wrong decisions," added De Zerbi.
"Two big players with potential."
It was part of a second-half shake-up with Savio and Destiny Udogie being withdrawn after an hour in a planned double substitution on medical advice.
De Zerbi added: "Before the game the plan for Savio and Udogie was around 60 minutes. I'm not happy but football is like this, Savio not in the best physical condition to play 90 mins, he's a crucial player for us.
"Destiny is another crucial player. Kudus and Robertson played well but to start one game like today is not so easy to come inside from the bench and adapt immediately.
"I'm not happy when we have the plan but it's not my business, the management of players after injuries."

Rain swept across large parts of Andhra Pradesh on Sunday, offering relief to a State reeling under a substantial seasonal deficit, with automatic rain gauge stations of the Directorate of Economics and Statistics recording cumulative rainfall of more than 50 mm at several locations between 8.30 a.m. and 9 p.m.
Musunuru in Eluru district recorded the highest rainfall in the State at 52.69 mm, followed by Pallamalli in Prakasam district’s Chimakurthy mandal with 46 mm. Ipuru and Machavaram in Palnadu district recorded 42.64 mm and 42.49 mm, respectively. Darlapudi in Anakapalli district’s S. Rayavaram mandal received 42 mm, while Rajamahendravaram Urban in East Godavari recorded 38.25 mm.
Anakapalli district accounted for a large share of the readings above 20 mm, with several gauges in Paravada, Nakkapalli and Anakapalli mandals recording between 20 mm and 34 mm. Palnadu, Kakinada, East Godavari and Guntur districts also featured prominently among the Directorate’s top 50 stations, drawn from its network of 2,218 automatic rain gauges.
Among the India Meteorological Department (IMD) observatories, Amaravati recorded 27 mm, one of the highest figures in the State. Machilipatnam and Bapatla received 11 mm and 16 mm, respectively.
The spell occurred against the backdrop of a trough extending from south Telangana across Rayalaseema and Tamil Nadu to the Gulf of Mannar, persisting at 0.9 km above mean sea level, the Meteorological Centre, Amaravati, said. An upper-air cyclonic circulation over north coastal Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and the west-central Bay of Bengal had weakened.
The Cyclone Warning Centre, Visakhapatnam, had forecast moderate to severe thunderstorms accompanied by gusty and squally winds during the afternoon. It briefly issued a red alert for Anakapalli, Kakinada, East Godavari, West Godavari, Eluru, NTR and Krishna districts.
Maximum temperatures varied widely across the State on Sunday. Nellore recorded 39.2°C, which was 3.8°C above normal, followed by Tirupati (AP) at 39.4°C and Kavali at 39°C. Jangamaheswarapuram and Arogyavaram recorded the lowest maximum temperature at 34.5°C each, followed by Kalingapatnam at 34.9°C. Amaravati recorded 37.3°C and Visakhapatnam 35°C.
The rain came against the backdrop of a pronounced monsoon deficit. The State’s cumulative rainfall since June 1 remained 47% below normal, with every district classified as either ‘deficient’ or ‘large deficient’. Guntur and Krishna, despite recording steep single-day surpluses of 388% and 188%, respectively, remained in seasonal deficit at 30% and 37%.
In Vijayawada, the Municipal Corporation said its monsoon response team cleared waterlogging at Labbipeta, the bridge area and Bandar Road soon after the rain began, following directions from Commissioner Dhyanachandra.
The IMD’s seven-day outlook indicates isolated to scattered rainfall over coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema through September 12.

Eleven people sentenced to death in Vietnam drug trafficking case
- Published
Eleven people have been sentenced to death by a court in Vietnam in one of the country's largest drug trafficking cases, state media report.
They are among 227 people accused in total, with prison sentences ranging from 18 months to life behind bars.
Among those sentenced to death was the person purported to be the mastermind behind the drug trafficking network, Ha Danh Nam, who investigators said arranged for the drugs to be brought from France to Vietnam.
The case began in March 2023 when four Vietnam Airlines flight attendants - arriving in Ho Chi Minh City from Paris - were caught carrying more than 10kg of drugs in 157 toothpaste tubes.
Legal affairs newspaper Bao Cong Ly reported that authorities found the flight attendants - who were not prosecuted - had unknowingly transported the drugs, which included MDMA and ketamine.
Nam was found to have hidden the drugs inside consumer goods - including dietary supplements, laundry detergent, mouthwash and coffee - and then arranged for people in France to carry them in their luggage or transported via delivery service to Vietnam.
Nam targeted Vietnamese nationals living or studying in France to act as drug mules, local media report.
Prosecutors said those involved in this transnational drug trafficking network used encrypted messaging platforms and bank accounts registered under other people's names to facilitate their smuggling efforts.
Transactions linked to the network were worth nearly 29 trillion Vietnamese dong ($1.1bn; £815m), they said.
The court found the defendants played varying roles in the network - from leaders to accomplices - and penalties were imposed according to the seriousness of their involvement.
Around 20 others on trial were sentenced to life imprisonment for the illegal buying, selling, transporting and organising of drugs.
Vietnam is one of 54 countries that still have the death penalty, rights groups say.
The government does not publish how many people are on death row as that is considered a state secret, though human rights groups say there are more than 1,000 awaiting execution.
Last month, the Vietnamese government proposed abolishing the death penalty for six offences including drug trafficking. These proposed changes are yet to take effect.
The proposal follows changes to the criminal code in 2025 that removed the death penalty for eight offences - including embezzlement, espionage and overthrowing the government.
One of the most high-profile figures to be handed the death penalty was tycoon Truong My Lan, who was found guilty of embezzlement and sentenced to death in 2024.
The 2025 change in the law led to her death penalty being commuted to life imprisonment.

Is the Steam Deck still worth it in 2026?
The Steam Deck was the king of gaming handhelds when it arrived. But with more competition (and a higher price), is it still worth the cost?
We're still deep in the trenches of RAMageddon, the memory shortage driven by AI companies utilizing massive amounts of it in data centers, and virtually no sector of the tech world has been spared. This is particularly true for the gaming industry, where console prices have risen in recent months (compared to historically, when they would fall over time). The Steam Deck has seen a $300 price increase, and with a new generation of handheld competitors on the market, it's easy to wonder if the hefty price tag is still worth it in 2026.
The gaming landscape has changed a lot since the Steam Deck was first released in February 2022. Unreal Engine 5 released just a few months after, drastically expanding the tools at developers' fingertips to make increasingly complex game graphics, and in turn how taxing they are on a machine. Even the Steam Deck OLED — now the only model available — didn't see any real performance improvements when it was released in 2023, with changes instead focusing more on the screen and battery life.
However, the Steam Deck still has features that help it stand out amongst its competitors in 2026.
The Steam Deck's main competitors
Arguably the biggest competitors for the Steam Deck in 2026 are the Asus ROG Xbox Ally (and Ally X) and the Lenovo Legion Go line of products. Both boast generally higher performance: in testing, all models in both lines tend to deliver better frame rates than the Steam Deck. All achieved a higher raw 3DMark Time Spy score — a common benchmark test for GPUs and CPUs — except for the Legion Go S and Legion Go model that features the less powerful Z2 AMD chip. However, it's worth noting that sometimes these differences with the Steam Deck can be very minimal depending on the game (even down to a few frames).
The two competitors do have some distinctions between them. The Xbox Ally or Ally X are clear picks for gamers who skew towards Xbox titles (though not every title supports Xbox Play Anywhere). However, the Xbox Ally is somewhat held back by its frequently criticized Windows OS, something the Legion Go has circumvented by introducing models that run SteamOS. The Legion Go line (sans the S models) is also set apart with its detachable, Joy-Con-esque controllers, making it an especially good option for those interested in docked gaming.
Though it may not be for everyone due to its limited title pool, the Nintendo Switch 2 is another viable alternative. "Prices are ludicrous," says Jessica Conditt, who wrote our review for the Steam Deck OLED. "I feel like Switch 2 is the only handheld that makes sense for its price at the moment, honestly."
Even with its own price increase — rising from $450 to $500 in September 2026 — it still beats the prices of the Xbox Ally and Legion Go product lineups. There are a few other standout differences: The Switch 2 is the sole handheld in this discussion that can support Nvidia's DLSS rendering technology, and the only one besides the Steam Deck to support HDR.
Is the Steam Deck still worth it?
One of the biggest considerations when purchasing a Steam Deck is the sort of games you want to play. "If you only want to play Steam games and you're not too worried about bleeding-edge graphics," Conditt says, "Steam Deck is still a great little machine, even with the price increase." For those who tend to play less-intensive titles, and are content with what the library has to offer, it's a fine option. Bear in mind that SteamOS can't run games like Fortnite or CoD: Warzone that utilize certain forms of anti-cheating software, though.
Another point of deliberation is battery life. Though the Xbox Ally and Legion Go (S and 2) lines offer larger batteries than the Steam Deck OLED, in real-world applications, Valve's handheld often comes out on top. As soon as the Xbox Ally or Legion Go stop operating in low-power settings and utilize their full potential, they tend to die faster. If you're someone who wants to use their handheld for hours on end, the Steam Deck offers you the best shot at a handheld console that lasts. You may also find the Steam Deck most comfortable for long gaming sessions — besides the Switch 2, it's the lightest of the bunch.
Price-wise, the Switch 2 is by far the cheapest option. The regular Xbox Ally is the most affordable choice that has access to a PC library, but with the tradeoff of the Windows-based operating system. From there, the Steam Deck OLED is less expensive than the Xbox Ally X and every product in the Lenovo Legion Go line's current generation (at least when buying straight from the source — occasionally a Legion Go S can be found on sites like Amazon for less than MSRP). If price is your biggest deciding factor, Lenovo's line is effectively ruled out. From there, it really comes down to whether you prefer Nintendo, Windows, or Steam OS, and how much you're willing to pay for it.

In short:
Russia's foreign minister has called accusations that Moscow was implicated in last month's drone incident at Leipzig Airport in Germany "the start of a real war".
The German government concluded last week that Russia was responsible for the alleged drone attack.
What's next?
Germany has ordered a raft of security measures after the incident, including installing an anti-sabotage "cyberdome".
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov says the accusations levelled at Moscow that Russia was involved in the drone incident at Germany's Leipzig airport were "by and large, the start of a real war."
"All these statements by [German Chancellor Friedrich] Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again — they are being put into practice," Mr Lavrov said on Sunday, state news agency TASS reported.
"He is, in effect, declaring war on us."
The German government said on September 1 it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an alleged drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a consulate and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
Russia has long rejected allegations it is carrying out operations in Western Europe and has denied involvement in the German airport attack, accusing Berlin of planting evidence to frame Russia for the attack.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Saturday, local time, that the incident shows Germany is facing a "profound rupture", with far-reaching consequences that will only become clear in retrospect.
Speaking at a party event near Hanover, Mr Merz said the German government's attribution of the attack to Russia was "clear and legally sound" and sent a clear warning to Russia not to continue this type of hybrid warfare.
Germany to install anti-sabotage 'cyberdome'
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper that one of the measures the country would take in response to incident involved an anti-sabotage shield called a "cyberdome".
Mr Dobrindt added that Russia's hybrid attacks had become a part of daily reality.
"These attacks will increase, but we can defend and protect ourselves,"
Police mobile drone defence capabilities would be expanded under the plan, a military spokesperson said, with rapidly deployable counter-drone units stationed in cities to protect the airspace above critical transport hubs and government districts.
Companies operating critical infrastructure, such as power utilities and defence manufacturers, would be granted the legal authority to not merely detect drones but also actively fend them off.
A national protective shield — or "cyberdome" — would be established, involving a network of digital sensors designed to detect and intercept attempted hacking attacks.
The government also intends to expand the use of AI-supported technologies, biometric facial recognition and video surveillance to identify suspected attackers preparing acts of sabotage.
NATO should not tolerate 'hybrid' war
Also on Saturday, US ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said members should not tolerate deliberate actions of hybrid war.
Mr Whitaker said the incident last month was more worrying than other recent incidents NATO members have faced due to Russian drones targeting Ukraine that strayed off course.
"Then you have what I would call the more concerning hybrid actions like we saw in Leipzig, like we have seen in Poland," Mr Whitaker said speaking on the sidelines of a business conference in Italy.
"If we can identify who's doing it — which Germany did — we make sure we express strongly that is unacceptable and we will not tolerate it."
Critical infrastructure, including energy assets, could be targeted and should be monitored by national authorities, he added.
The response to these challenges is primarily national, but the United States supports countries when they are dealing with these acts, he said.

Steve Irwin's family celebrates 'superhero' dad, 20 years after shock death
- Published
Australian conservationist Bindi Irwin has marked the 20th anniversary of her famous father's death with a touching tribute to the man best known as the "Crocodile Hunter".
Steve Irwin died on 4 September 2006, aged 44, after a stingray fatally pierced his chest while he was underwater filming a documentary at the Great Barrier Reef.
Bindi, who was eight when her father died, called Steve a "superhero" in an online post on Friday, saying she has "watched the world mourn my dad with our family" for the past two decades.
"I always thought that my dad's legacy is wildlife conservation; it turns out, his legacy is love. For our planet and for each other," Bindi, 28, wrote on Instagram.
She described the impact of her father's death on her mother Terri and her younger brother Robert, 22.
"My mum lost the love of her life; my brother and I lost the greatest dad," she wrote. "Grief never truly leaves us; we walk alongside it every day."
Bindi also shared details on how her daughter connects with the grandfather she never got to meet.
"I have a 5-year-old daughter who watches his documentaries every morning. She feels utterly loved by her 'grandpa crocodile' without ever having met him."
Since Steve's death, the Irwins have continued to run Australia Zoo in Queensland.
"My dad left a lasting impact so poignant that it will ripple out for generations to come," Bindi wrote, saying his life and legacy were "worth celebrating".
She thanked Steve for being the family's "guardian angel" and signed off her message saying she loved him "with my whole heart".
Steve's wife Terri also took to social media to mark the day, posting an interview where the khaki-clad wildlife advocate recounted Bindi's birth and its impact on him.
"The most incredible wildlife encounter of my life was the birth of my daughter, Bindi," Steve says in the interview, with his signature enthusiasm.
The first time he held his newborn child, the inspiration for her name hit him.
"I was flabbergasted and it was then that her name evolved. I've gone, 'Bindi!' after my favourite crocodile, Bindi," he said, with a wide grin.
Robert Irwin also posted a tribute to his father, with a photo of Steve holding him when he was a baby, alongside the caption, "Your legacy is forever".
Last November, Robert was crowned the winner of US dance competition Dancing with the Stars, a decade after his sister won the same title.

Several videos have gone viral on social media following the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, 2026. Some users shared a video claiming that after the disaster, the world’s largest Shaligram, said to be more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath.
In this context, Zee News put out a report with a screenshot from the viral video and, along with the hashtags #Nepal, #Flood and #Shaligram, wrote: “Viral Video: Floods have revealed a secret, a 170-million-year-old Shaligram has been found.”
Shaligrams are naturally formed stones traditionally found in Nepal’s Kali Gandaki River, and revered by Hindus as representations of the deity, Vishnu.
Right-wing X user Amitabh Choudhary (@MithilaWaaala), who has been found spreading misinformation and comminal propaganda several times in the past, shared a video and wrote: “Stone older than dinosaurs. Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal.”
Kisi ne sahi hi kaha hai, “शुरुआत भी वही, सफ़र भी वही, और अंत भी वही।”
Stone older than dinosaurs !!
Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal 🇳🇵 pic.twitter.com/GIv851LJbV
— Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala) August 29, 2026
X user Shashank Shekhar Jha, who claims to be a Supreme Court lawyer, and others such as @Nalanda_index, @CodexZeroTR, @Krishnavallabhi, @bhaktSenapati, along with several Facebook and Instagram users, too, shared videos and photos with similar claims.
Fact Check
To find out the truth behind the viral claim, we performed a relevant keyword search. This led us to reports published on June 30, 2026, by Himalaya Times and Online Khabar featuring images of the giant sculpture seen in the viral video.
The reports stated that a 22-foot-tall Shaligram sculpture in Nepal’s Mustang district was gradually becoming a centre of religious faith. According to the reports, sculptors from the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts carved a huge rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom in Gharpajhong rural municipality area and created the 22-foot-tall Shaligram replica between April 20 and May 4, 2026.
During our investigation, we found a report by a website called Desh Sanchar. According to the report, the 22-foot-tall sculpture had been unveiled on the evening of May 28, 2026, after religious rituals on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River.
We also located a video uploaded on April 23, 2026 on the Facebook page, Nepal Raibar, in which artists could be seen carving a rock to create a Shaligram statue.
We also geolocated the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video. It’s located on the Kali Gandaki River, opposite ‘Thakkhola Lodge & Jimihendrix Restaurant in Jomsom. When we compared Google Street View images from 2025 with the viral video, we found that the 2025 image only showed a large rock.
This makes it clear that the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video is not a natural or ancient stone. Rather, it is a statue created by carving a rock.
We also tried to look for the sources of all the variants of the now-viral visuals. We found the original version of the video and the screenshots shared by Zee News on the Instagram account of a user named Durga Prasad Poudel. It was posted on June 2, 2026.
View this post on Instagram
Similarly, we found the second viral video uploaded on June 30, 2026, on the Instagram account of a user named Rijan Dongol.
View this post on Instagram
The third viral video was shared on June 8, 2026, on the Facebook account of a user named Arjun Singh. Its caption reads: “A huge 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue is located on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom, Mustang. This monumental work, inaugurated by Jagadguru Shankaracharya Mahaswami Vidushekara Bharati, attracts a large number of pilgrims and stands as a major spiritual and cultural site in Nepal.”
Thus, all three viral videos featuring the Shaligram statue have been available on social media since June 2026. They have absolutely no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal in August.
Overall, the claim by Zee News and other users that after the recent disaster in Nepal, the world’s largest Shaligram, more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath is completely misleading. In reality, the 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue seen in the viral video was created by carving a rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Mustang district, during April–May 2026. The videos of the Shaligram statue circulating on social media are also from June 2026 and have no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal.

For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation. Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. About 64% of the listed new-age tech companies, 41 to be precise, are currently profitable. In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42's purview are about a decade old. From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra's IPO materialised within four years of its operations. Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal. Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem. The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups. While fintech leads the race with 13 listings, enterprise tech and ecommerce sectors dominates new-age tech IPOs with 12 listings and 11 listings, respectively, so far The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of PhonePe, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts. Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 256listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru's fifteen and Mumbai's eleven. While sixteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. Delhi NCR contributes $112.3 Bn in the cumulative $190 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. A devastating flash flood on Wednesday, August 26, near the Nepal-Tibet border, resulted in massive destruction in several districts of Nepal, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, with over 700 dead and over 2,500 people still missing. Reportedly, a glacial landslide of ice and rock caused the flash floods, which destroyed homes roads, bridges and power plants.
In the days following the catastrophe, social media was rife with video clips showing the extent of devastation — from gigantic waves of floodwater gushing through entire villages, to buildings collapsing, and people being swept away under the debris.
However, Alt News found that a large number of these videos circulating on social media were not authentic. Several of these videos were not from Nepal at all, but drawn from various other calamities which occurred across the world in the last few years.
Clip From 2025 Uttarakhand Floods
An X user, Said Ercan (@saidercan), posted a compilation clip on August 27 showing the havoc wreaked by large flood waves. The first clip shows a torrential river flowing through a mountainous area, and eventually sweeping through the houses on the banks, destroying them in an instant. The post has garnered over 5.8 million views and been reshared over 5,000 times at the time of publishing. (Archive)
To verify whether the video is of the Nepal floods, we broke it down into keyframes and ran a reverse image search. This led us to an Instagram post uploaded by The Times of India, on August 5, 2025, featuring the same footage.
View this post on Instagram
The caption states that the footage is of the Uttarakhand cloudburst havoc. “At least four people have died and many are feared missing after a devastating flash flood triggered by a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga river caused large-scale destruction in Dharali village in Uttarkashi district…,” read the caption.
A Dainik Bhaskar report also features the same video to show the scale of damage caused by the cloudburst in Uttarkashi. We ran relevant keyword searches, and found news reports from sources like Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, The Hindu, and others, that corroborated this finding. Thus, the video footage shared by the X user is actually of the 2025 Uttarakhand flash floods, and not of the recent Nepal havoc.
AI-generated Clip
In another instance, X user Ayesha Khan (@Ayesha0Khaan) posted a video clip, of huge waves sweeping away cars, building structures, and people. The clip received over 1 million views. (Archive)
X user Ravi Shankar Singh (@Ravishanka34381) also posted the clip with the same claim. However, we noticed some discrepancies in the video — for instance, around the 0:05 timestamp, a tree log appears out of nowhere in the debris flowing through the floodwater, indicating that the clip could be AI-generated.
We ran the video through Hive’s AI detection tool, which confirmed our suspicion, showing a 99.9% possibility of the video containing AI-generated content.
Clip From 2024 China Incident
News outlet Medya Post (@medya_post) uploaded a clip on X, which showed around 15 people getting swept away by powerful flood waves. The caption stated: “Tourists who wanted to take videos and photos during the flood disaster that occurred in Nepal were swept away by the current and disappeared.” The post had seen massive traction on social media, with over 1.5 million views. (Archive)
Two other X users with the handles (@JMNewsNetwork_) and (@redpillmd) had uploaded the same video, with the former having deleted it after it had been viewed over 45,000 times.
To verify the clip’s authencity, we ran a reverse image search, which led us to an X post, originally uploaded by an user with the handle (@Arab_Storms) on September 8, 2024.
التصوير اصبح اهم من الحياة #شاهد ❗️#الصين جرف المد القوي لنهر تشيانتانج العديد من الزوار الذين كانوا يحاولون التقاط صورة ،،،#Yagi pic.twitter.com/bdiEj7fk9b
— طقس_العالم ⚡️ (@Arab_Storms) September 8, 2024
According to the caption, the video had been taken in China, showing the powerful waves of the Qiantang River overpowering tourists on the shore who were clicking photos. The incident, which occured in the days following Asia’s most powerful storm in 2024, the Super Typhoon Yagi, had also been reported on by The Indian Express, and Newsflare.
Video From West Bengal Landslide
A news outlet TNT Media (@TNT_Media1) posted a clip which showed a mudslide from a vantage point. It also features the narrow escape of some vehicles and people gathered at the spot. The caption, written in Arabic, claims that horrifying scenes correspond to the recent Nepal flash floods. (Archive)
مشاهد مروعة من نيبال.. 😯😯 pic.twitter.com/N7f5jBl4i6
— 𝐓𝐍𝐓 (@TNT_Media1) August 26, 2026
We noticed that the car, visible in parts of the video, bears a number plate whose state code (WB) corresponds with that of West Bengal. Moreover, the recorder of the video, while shooting the clip, speaks in Bengali to warn people to get away from the waves.
A reverse image search on several keyframes of the video led us to this X post, uploaded by The Daily Jagran on August 17.
A biker had a narrow escape after a massive landslide struck the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district. Huge rocks, soil and debris suddenly came crashing onto the road as vehicles passed through.#Kalimpong #Landslide #WestBengal #Biker #ViralVideo #Monsoon pic.twitter.com/HgFLY7Dhjy
— The Daily Jagran (@TheDailyJagran) August 17, 2026
The caption states that the video shows a landslide in the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district, thereby proving that this video clip is not related to the Nepal flash floods.
Compilation Clip From Various Calamities
An X user named “Leonard Sardua $TOR” (@lsardua) posted a compilation of clips showing structures collapsing under the deluge, claiming they showed the devastation caused by the flash flood in Nepal. The clip garnered over 3.3 million views and 3,700 reshares. (Archive)
Two more users, “HadY Azmy” (@HadYAzmy1) and Ahmad Ansari (@Ahmadansari2233), amplified the same clip on August 27. The former video, which has now been deleted, had garnered over than 2.5 million views and over 3,000 reshares.
On running a reverse image search on one keyframe from the viral clip, we were led to an article published by The Times of India on July 21. The report shows the same building structure collapse under the force of floodwater, and states that the video was from the Budgam district of Jammu and Kashmir.
Another segment of the compilation shows a red building being engulfed by the gushing floodwater, sweeping away cars and other structures amid the debris.
Running a reverse image search on this keyframe, we found that the clip could be traced back to a mudslide in Japan’s Atami city from July 2021. An X user with the handle @d_t_dcg_sdh had uploaded several clips showing the mudslide sweeping away houses and vehicles. We also found news reports from Al Jazeera and Spanish news outlet La Nacion, corroborating that the clip was recorded during a mudslide in Japan in 2021.
The same compilation video also included a segment which showed a bridge being torn down by the raging floodwater.
This, we found, was in fact from an incident in Indonesia, showing the collapse of the wooden Molintogupo Bridge, owing to the overflowing of the Bone River. A video uploaded by Newsflare on Dailymotion, notes that the incident occurred on June 11, 2020. It was also reported on by VGTV.
Another segment of the same clip shows two men watching a bridge being dismantled and swept away by floodwater.
We found that this video was from Argentina. A reverse image search on a keyframe led us to this X post by AccuWeather on December 25, 2023, which shows a bridge in Argentina’s Catamarca being blown away by the turbulent floodwater.
A bridge was swept away in Catamarca, Argentina, on Christmas Day, leaving a city completely isolated.  pic.twitter.com/hVdwxmQ7QU
— AccuWeather (@accuweather) December 27, 2023
Another video, showing a white car being dragged along by the torrential flow of mud water, was also part of this compilation.
This, Alt News found, was originally from Islamabad, in Pakistan, dating back to a devastating flood that took place in July 2025.
Similarly, a segment showing a woman overlooking a building structure being swept away by flood water, was also part of this compilation, alleging that it was from Nepal.
A reverse image search proved that the image has existed on X since at least September 2024. On further investigation, we found that it showed the damage caused by Hurricane Helene in North Carolina, United States.
Don’t worry guys, weather modification isn’t real! It’s just a coincidence that Hurricane Helene is one of the most devastating “inland damage storms” in history and that hundreds of pro-Trump counties are being massively impacted during the most important election of our… pic.twitter.com/lyi8YZXB8A
— Matt Wallace (@MattWallace888) September 28, 2024
Another clip showing a submerged bus making its way through the floodwater was also featured in the compilation.
We found that this video was shot during a downpour in Pakistan’s Karachi, which left the city flooded and resulted in at least 16 deaths. Pakistani news media outlet 24 News HD, in their report on the flood dated March 19, used the same clip of the submerged bus.
Thus, the compilation clip uploaded by users “Leonard Sardua $TOR”, “HadY Azmy”, and Ahmad Ansari, with the claim that the footage depicts the havoc in Nepal is fake and misleading. The entire compilation stitches together footage from real calamities, occuring in various other parts of the world in the past few years, to wrongly claim that they are visuals from the Nepal flash floods on August 26.

Komal Nahta had a conversation with Adnan Sami, in which he gave a detailed answer about plagiarism in music. He began by saying, “I am against plagiarism in any form. But I feel bad for the composers who emerged in this millennium; they have been unfairly targeted. If you are only criticizing them for copying and forgiving the rest, that is unfair. In the last 20 years, there has been a lot of access to information thanks to the internet. So, if a composer gets ‘inspired’ and composes a tune, he gets immediately caught.”
“HUGE fan of Shankar-Jaikishan, R D Burman, Bappi Lahiri etc but they also lifted songs; Sholay’s ‘Mehbooba’ was inspired…agar aap original composer ka naam daal dete, toh aapke shaan mein koi kami nahin aati” – Adnan Sami
Adnan continued, “Some people tend to hail our yesteryear musicians. They’d say ‘Woh toh kaafi genius log the’. And there’s no doubt that they were indeed geniuses. I am their biggest fan. But what happens is that a child may think that his father is a superhero. When the child grows up, he realizes that mera baap jo hai, aakhir woh insaan hai. You still respect him because he’s your father. Hence, you can’t single out new composers and assume that the rest were doodh ke dhoole hue.”
Adnan confessed, “Whether it's Shankar-Jaikishan, Naushad, S D Burman, R D Burman or Bappi Lahiri, I am their biggest fan and have learned a lot from them. But each one of them lifted songs. Yet, I still love and respect them as they made a beautiful version of that song.”
Adnan Sami remarked that the composers should have given due credit, “Dean Martin’s famous song ‘Sway’ was inspired by an Italian song. But he gave credit to the original composer. Our problem is that our composers did not. They just gave their own name to the track, without acknowledging the original creator. Aap kahin se chhote nahin ho jaate by acknowledging.”
Adann continued, “Even today, I enjoy the song ‘Mehbooba’ from Sholay (1975). But it's not R D Burman’s original composition. It was inspired by Demis Roussos’ song ‘Say You Love Me’. Agar aap Demis Roussos ka naam daal dete, toh aapke shaan mein koi kami nahin aati (smiles). People would have respected you more if you gave due credit. Later, the same happened with them as well and they felt about it.”
He added, “This happened even with films. Kaala Patthar (1979) is a great film, but it was originally Gold (1974), featuring Roger Moore (smiles).”

US rejects claim it sought to influence Malaysian politics
PAS chief Abdul Hadi Awang claimed on Saturday that the US had offered to help the party topple Malaysia's government in 2014.
SINGAPORE: The United States Embassy in Malaysia on Sunday (Sep 6) pushed back against a claim that it sought to influence Malaysian politics.
In a statement posted on the embassy's Facebook page, its charge d'affaires David H Gamble Jr said: "The United States has never sought to decide Malaysia's political leadership.
"Any account to the contrary is false."
This comes after Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) chief Abdul Hadi Awang said that the US had offered to help the party topple Malaysia's government in 2014.
Malaysian media reported Hadi as saying at the party's annual congress on Saturday that this occurred around the time of former US President Barack Obama's visit to Malaysia that year.
Hadi said that several PAS leaders had been invited to a meeting at the US Embassy in Kuala Lumpur while the party was still part of the Pakatan Rakyat coalition.
PAS assistant secretary-general Takiyuddin Hassan and Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, then his political secretary, attended the meeting, he was reported to have said.
According to The Malay Mail, Hadi said US Embassy representatives raised the possibility of helping PAS topple and take over the government at the meeting.
However, the party leaders rejected any foreign interference of this kind, he said.
Hadi said that the US ambassador to Malaysia at the time also asked him separately who PAS would propose as prime minister if it took over the government.
According to The Star, he said he responded by asking the ambassador: "Who does America agree with?"
His response was met with approval by Mahathir Mohamad, Hadi was reported as saying.
Takiyuddin confirmed that the meeting with the US Embassy representatives took place but said their discussion did not go beyond whether PAS had plans to topple the Barisan Nasional government, The New Straits Times reported.
The party representatives did not state whether or not it had the intention of doing so, he added.

Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov on Sunday accused Germany of seeking another war and dismissed Berlin’s allegation that Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
On September 1, Germany had accused Russia of orchestrating a drone attack. They stated that their investigation had found Russia responsible for the August 4 incident, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at the airport. Berlin said the attack was part of a wider Russian “hybrid” campaign and announced measures including the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt confirmed that the drone configuration, components, explosives, and detonation systems matched patterns from previous Russian hybrid operations. German foreign minister Johann Wadephul also announced on September 2 that Berlin will push for further EU travel restrictions against Russian nationals and increase pressure on Russia's "shadow fleet" of oil tankers.
Calling the latest escalation “by and large, the start of a real war”, Lavrov said Germany “wants war again”, drawing a comparison with the period before World War II. He also accused Germany of Nazism and said the Russian leadership would draw “appropriate conclusions”.
"All these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again – they are being put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov said, referring to German chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Moscow has rejected Germany’s accusations as baseless and accused Berlin of fabricating evidence.
The dispute has further strained ties between the two countries, with Moscow and Berlin closing each other’s cultural institutions and European countries summoning Russian envoys.

After 12 years of dominating American politics — either as president, as a candidate, or from the sidelines — Donald Trump will finally exit the stage in 2028, and it’s anybody’s guess what will come next. But one thing we do know is that Gen Z, many of whom were children during Trump’s first campaign, will play a large role in shaping that future.
Gen Z’s politics aren’t what people think
Is it time to update our understanding of Gen Z?
What’s less clear is what direction they might choose or what their politics are in the first place.
We do know a few things, thanks to a Vox collaboration with the polling firm Murmuration. For one, they’re highly independent: Almost 30 percent answered “none of the above” when they were asked to choose their political label in Murmuration’s survey. They’re an economically insecure cohort, at least for now; Murmuration found that only 28 percent of respondents between the ages of 18 and 30 said they could cover an unexpected expense of $500. And they had the largest gender gap of any age group when it came to supporting the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 — women preferred Kamala Harris by 17 percentage points over men.
To find out more, Vox’s Astead Herndon spoke with Gen Z researcher Rachel Janfaza for a recent episode of America, Actually. They discussed the group’s political identities, preferences, and top issues, and what that all could mean for politics going forward. They discussed an important distinction between two versions of Gen Z, and whether its infamous gender gap is shifting. They also touched on how, contrary to seemingly everyone else, Gen Z is hope-maxxing.
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Janfaza, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
You’ve done a lot of work around the different Gen Zs. I’ve heard you talk about Gen Z 1 versus Gen Z 2. How would we describe those differences?
I call this the theory of the two Gen Zs. I really started to cultivate it doing focus groups with young people in 2022, hearing the way that high school students at the time and college students at the time just had a different outlook, and I realized that those who had graduated high school before the start of the pandemic, those Gen Z-ers, just had a different worldview than the younger half of Gen Z, who were still in high school at the time that the pandemic hit.
And that is because of the taste of independence that people on the older cusp of Gen Z had prior to the lockdown situation. Anyone who is between roughly 29 and 22, I would say, is Gen Z 1.0, and anyone younger than that would be Gen Z 2.0.
And there’s no official end date to Gen Z right now. Like, it’s sort of 1997 to 2012, so it’s not very clear yet.
Can you just name for me what the difference was between the generations? How did that shape a different form of politics?
Gen Z 1.0 really came of age during Trump’s first term in office. This was a new phenomenon. He was breaking down past barriers, and we saw a lot of youth-led activism in response to actions or inaction from the first Trump administration.
You saw things like the March for Our Lives and climate strikes and the Black Lives Matter movement. And there was this very real sense that, you know, if we protest and demand change, perhaps there could be a difference.
Whereas Gen Z 2.0 came of age during the Biden era. This was a post-Covid sort of upbringing. And they really grew resistant to authority because they saw Democrats in charge during the time when kids went back to school and when there were things like mask mandates and vaccine mandates, especially in blue areas across the country where Democrats were handling the way that schools were reopening.
Young people whose lives and childhoods were on the line felt like they were guinea pigs in an experiment that they didn’t sign up for, and I think this is when we saw a movement away from Democrats. I don’t necessarily think that was toward Republicans.
Trump capitalized on this in 2024. Broadly speaking, Gen Z 2.0 is far less trusting of authority and institutions, far more independent. They hate labels, and this isn’t just political. They hate labels when it comes to gender, their relationships. No one wants to be boxed in. I hear this all the time in my focus groups, and so they just moved away from both parties writ large.
I also want to ask a couple of questions specifically about the gender divide, because that was such a big topic in the 2024 election.
We heard at that time, and I reported on, the change among young men that we saw manifested in that race. There was a 17-point gap between the votes of Gen Z men and Gen Z women. Before we get to where we are now, what do you think drove that gap?
No. The easy thing to say is it’s the algorithm, but that’s not the whole picture. I think a lot of young women felt like their bodily autonomy, freedom, rights were on the line. And a lot of young men care about that, but when I asked them, “What’s the top issue in the 2024 election?” few said abortion. They were like, “I care about that, but that’s not an issue that personally affects me.” And so I think that’s sort of what it came down to.
Women literally felt like it was their futures that were in question. And when you talk about the gender gap, you noted that young men shifted to the right, and that’s of course true.
Young women, since 2017, have remarkably moved to the left. And there have been a number of different causes to that, but every time there’s been a social wedge issue, whether it was early with immigration during Trump’s first term, the MeToo movement, the conversation about reproductive healthcare access and the fall of Roe v. Wade and the Dobbs decision … there have been so many examples of things that have pushed women further to the left, and then also a frustration with the way that Trump talks about women or accusations that have been made against him.
This is part of what I think makes this political period for Gen Z so fascinating. The Trump era will shape history across every generation, but Gen Z are the ones whose ideology was forming. And so there was this real sisterhood that emerged between young women during this time, where both on social media and in person, they were finding camaraderie around this shared fear for their future, but also appreciation of their individual rights and freedoms.
And young men didn’t see that same sort of bonding happening. And we talked a lot in 2024 about how Democrats had a problem with young men because they weren’t actively reaching out to young men. I’m the first person to say that Democrats really screwed that up, and that was a problem. But I think that there were not shared spaces for young men to come together in that way as there were for young women. I think that was part of what has driven this gap as well.
Should we update our thinking, though, of that gender divide from then to now? Like, are we still seeing the same big gaps between voting and political behavior from Gen Z men and women?
No. So largely, when I ask young people about the gender gap, they acknowledge that it exists, but they don’t like it. They don’t want to be stuck in this divide. Gen Z wants out of the gender war. They do.
We’re also now seeing a generation unite around a new set of issues that are pretty communal, that everyone can kind of agree upon. There’s a new shared set of issues that are less gendered and more affecting everybody.
AI? What are you talking about?
AI and the economy. Gen Z now agrees that the two main issues are AI and the economy. And obviously those are related.
I see this. You’re saying the gender gap among young people was at its peak because the parties were positioning themselves on gendered lines as well. And now, because of the consensus about issues that touch everyone, mainly the economy and AI, it’s a little bit of a permission structure to put the knives down in the gender fight because everyone’s lives are affected by this.
I think a lot of the gender war in the first place was kind of manufactured by people who were talking about Gen Z and not to them. You had the main candidates for president playing into that, too, and it was a man versus a woman, and it was kind of like, “These are your two options.” And we’re far past that.
I’ve talked about how Gen Z is hope-maxxing. You can say, “Oh, like it’s giving Obama,” but they really are looking for something to feel excited about. It’s enough of the doom and gloom. Growing up in this era has been exhausting.
The division and the vitriol isn’t fun for anyone. And maybe it’s the hopeless optimist in me, but I think that there is a real appetite for a post-Trumpian era of politics that is just less toxic. And that feels more hopeful and gives you something to rally around and unite around, rather than to be divided.

Kenya's chai lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
- Published
Kenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage.
A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. It is often served at meetings and during social visits, with many people taking the hot brew several times a day.
But now some may have to do without as supermarket chilled sections are nearly empty. Retailers have upped the price and are limiting how much shoppers can take home.
The government has put the dearth of milk in recent months down to drought, which has significantly reduced pasture and hampered production.
But the recent shortages are unusual, with the country's industry regulator itself admitting to "supply constraints" and "low stock levels" across the country.
Muthoni Macharia, who runs a restaurant in the capital, Nairobi, usually buys more than 70 packets of fresh milk - and is desperate and puzzled by the scarcity.
"Where has the milk gone?" she asked when the BBC spoke to her as she was out searching for at least a few packets to quench her customers thirst for chai.
Macharia says there have been shortages for about a week - and it was especially affecting her morning rush hour. Her regulars are not happy: some opting to take their tea black - but many will not.
"If they come in groups, and there's no milk tea, you see that's a loss for me," she said.
Kenya is one of the leading milk producers on the continent.
A long-established commercial dairy industry has led to pasteurised milk being very popular, particularly in urban areas, with Kenyans ranked among Africa's highest consumers, according to industry data.
Raw and fermented milk is more widely drunk in rural areas.
The milk shortage has sparked widespread public concern with some people promoting unfounded conspiracy theories about supermarkets deliberately trying to profit.
According to the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB), the government body that oversees the dairy sector, formal milk deliveries to processors fell by 3.7% from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July, while preliminary investigations suggest deliveries declined further in August.
The Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek) says there has been a downward trend of supply since the beginning of the year.
It attributes this to a delay in the seasonal rains, which has reduced the grazing ground available, coupled with a 45% rise in the cost of animal feed.
Cofek has expressed concern over the rationing as well as the increasing cost, saying fresh milk prices have risen from 70 to 80 Kenyan shillings ($0.54 to $0.62; £0.40 to £0.46) a litre.
"This shortage was foreseeable, and in material part, avoidable," it says.
The consumer body says dairy processor New KCC, a state-owned company, and the KDB did not adequately absorb the milk surplus last year, adding that powder processed from the excess milk would have helped resolve the current crisis.
Some of the milk processors in Kenya often reconvert the powder into the more-preferred liquid milk during dry seasons when the supply of fresh milk goes down.
"Had these buffers been in place, today's supply shock would have been substantially cushioned," Cofek says.
It has demanded a recovery plan to include fodder and subsidy support for farmers.
This would include waiving of taxes on animal feed inputs, as well as "active retail price monitoring to deter opportunity price gouging and rationing".
In response to media enquiries, the dairy board's managing director William Maritim assured that despite the "temporary supply constraint", milk continued to be available.
Fresh pasteurised milk, which has a shorter shelf life, had been more affected than the more long-life UHT milk, he said.
Customers at Nairobi supermarkets on the hunt for milk told the BBC they were worried about rising costs.
"Sometimes when I go to the supermarket I find there is none. When I do find some, the price has gone up. Today it is this price, tomorrow it has gone up again," said Bernard Abok, who does his shopping after finishing work.
Patricia Gathoni said if the prices kept going up she would have to rethink what she gave her children, saying she had resorted to adding water to the milk that she managed to buy.
On Thursday, agriculture ministry officials held a meeting with the association of dairy processors about the problem, with the ministry committing to support farmers, stabilise milk supply and protect consumers.
The ministry's top official in charge of livestock development, Jonathan Mueke, said the immediate focus was to get more feed for farmers, including through duty-free importation of yellow maize.
He said they were also looking at longer-term solutions that would manage stability across periods when there was surplus milk and when there were shortages.
Reports of milk going to waste are not uncommon during periods of a dairy glut. Farmers have often complained about how little they are paid for their perishable produce at such times - but they have few options because of limited processing or storage capacity.
According to Mueke, the government is considering setting up a fund to help support the preservation of milk during such periods.
In the meantime, the government is also considering temporarily importing milk from the neighbouring countries to ease the shortage.
For the devoted Kenyan chai lover, that may offer some respite.

Early spring fire bans have been put in place as Australia’s eastern states reckon with unseasonably hot conditions for the start of the season.
The Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) warned of unseasonal heat in the low to mid-30s in north-eastern New South Wales and south-east Queensland.
Brisbane had a forecast top of 34C, while Sydney had some respite from the recent record temperatures, with a forecast top of 23C, as that heat moved north.
If Brisbane reaches its predicted temperature peak, it would be the hottest September day in the city since 2019. Brisbane recorded a temperature of 31.6C in the late morning, the weather bureau said, while the Ipswich suburb of Amberley recorded a peak of 35.7C in the early afternoon.
“It’s a bit of an ‘all eyes on the temperatures this afternoon’ type [of] thing until that south-easterly change gets in, which is probably about 6 or 7pm tonight,” the BoM’s Steve Hadley said.
The Queensland fire department has issued local fire bans for Ipswich and the Lockyer Valley as the state comes close to shattering records for the highest temperatures seen in early September.
Areas from Gladstone to the Gold Coast were likely to come a few degrees shy of breaking the record for the state’s highest recorded temperatures for the start of spring.
The state had experienced its third-warmest winter on record with temperatures 1.8C above the long-term average.
BoM meteorologist Jonathan How said over the past 24 hours, a cold front swept across south-eastern Australia bringing damaging winds, rain and storms.
“At the same time, parts of eastern NSW saw their warmest early spring day on record,” he said.
But a dry cool change was moving up the east coast, bringing milder temperatures from Monday. Western Australia is set to get more rain this week, while Tasmania and Victoria can expect some showers.
South-east Queensland’s fire bans came a day after a similar ban was issued for the greater Sydney region, with early spring temperatures climbing to 33C on Saturday in the NSW capital.
Maximum temperatures across the city during the first days of September matched the midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since observations began.
Severe weather warnings were in place for south-eastern Australia over the weekend as damaging winds fuelled the hot conditions.
Jumping castles were picked up by strong winds in two separate incidents in NSW and Victoria on Saturday.
Two children were treated for head injuries at a scene in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, before being transported to hospital.
An infant with minor injuries was also hospitalised, while a woman was treated at the scene.
Two children in Mount Duneed, near Geelong in Victoria’s south-west, were hospitalised after the jumping castle they were using was lifted into the air.
Temperatures are expected to drop in the coming days across both NSW and Queensland.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, eleven new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty four startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub.
