Capital, SBI Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. ESDS Software Solution Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida. The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh. Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025. As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. SEDEMAC Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X, with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price. SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. Shadowfax Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses. Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital. Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator's nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹907 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X, receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹113, down 8.87% below the issue price. In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹21 Cr from ₹9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹1,805.6 Cr during the period. Shiprocket Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Vishesh Khurana, Akshay Gulati, and Gautam Kapoor, Shiprocket aggregates third-party logistics providers. It claims to partner 17 courier firms like Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, and Shadowfax and serves over 24,000 pin codes across India. The logistics unicorn has raised over $323 Mn to date from investors like Temasek, Bertelsmann, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, and Zomato. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the Zomato-backed unicorn in May 2025 confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI and received the regulator’s approval in October 2025. Shiprocket then filed its RHP with the markets regulator in August 2026. The logistics major’s ₹1,617 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹732 Cr. Subsequently, in mid-August 2026, Shiprocket’s public issue opened to healthy market response and closed with an oversubscription of 99.38X, receiving bidding for 938.53 Cr shares against 9.44 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a strong debut on the D-Street on August 19. The stock listed at ₹131 on the NSE, marking a premium of 35.05% to the issue price of ₹97. Turtlemint Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. Startups That Have Filed DRHP AceVector Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands. The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025. A month later at the fag end of the year, AceVector filed its updated DRHP, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹300 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 6.39 Cr shares. On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue leapt nearly 35% to ₹244.4 Cr in the first half (H1) of the financial year 2025-26 (FY26) from ₹181.1 Cr the year ago period. Meanwhile, losses also shrank almost 80% to ₹22.4 Cr versus ₹110.3 Cr in H1 FY25. Atomberg Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg began as a B2B supplier of energy-efficient BLDC fans before entering the D2C segment in 2016. It has since expanded to manufacture mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances. The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date. Taking the first step towards its public listing, the D2C appliance brand, in July 2026, converted into a public entity and changed the name of its parent entity from Atomberg Technologies Pvt Ltd to Atomberg Technologies Ltd. In August 2026, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. The startup is also considering raising up to ₹90 Cr through a pre-IPO placement. On the financial front, Atomberg’s losses widened 26.5% to ₹149 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹117.8 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. AVPL International (AITMC Ventures) Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AITMC sits at the intersection of agriculture and drones. It manufactures drones, offers drone-as-a-service, and runs more than 70 drone training centres across 16 states. In July 2025, AITMC once again kicked off its IPO plans as the company’s board approved a proposal to increase the fresh issue size of its IPO to ₹200 Cr from ₹125 Cr previously. AITMC then filed its draft papers with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in October 2025. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. Notably, this marks its second attempt at going public. Previously in December 2023, the company was eyeing an NSE Emerge listing, which comprised solely of a fresh issue of up to 2.1 Cr shares. That earlier plan was shelved after AITMC signed a term sheet in January 2025 for a strategic merger with BSE SME-listed DroneAcharya, a deal that ultimately fell through. On the financial front, AITMC Ventures’ net profit climbed 59% to ₹14 Cr in FY25 from ₹8.8 Cr a fiscal earlier, while operating revenue zoomed 87% to ₹87.5 Cr as against ₹46.8 Cr in FY24. boAt Founded in 2016 by Aman Gupta and Sameer Mehta, boAt is a D2C consumer electronics brand that sells headphones, smartwatches, speakers, and other audio wearables. The company has raised over $171 Mn across multiple rounds from investors such as Warburg Pincus, Qualcomm Ventures, Malabar Investments, Innoven Capital, and Fireside Ventures. boAt has pursued an IPO for several years now. It first filed its DRHP with SEBI in 2022 for a ₹2,000 Cr public issue, but later shelved the plan amid challenging market conditions. Taking a second shot, the boAt’s parent, Imagine Marketing, pre-filed its DRHP confidentially with the SEBI in April 2025, and secured SEBI approval in August. In October 2025, boAt filed its updated DRHP for an ₹1,500 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to ₹500 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹1,000 Cr. On the financial front, boAt saw its revenue from operations grow 10.7% YoY to ₹628.1 Cr in Q1 FY26, while profit stood at ₹21.3 Cr compared to a ₹31 Cr loss in Q1 FY25. C5i Founded in 2000 by Ashwin Mittal, C5i (formerly known as Course5 Intelligence) is an enterprise AI company that helps large businesses automate tasks and turn data into actionable insights. Backed by names such as Nuvama Asset Management and 360 ONE, the startup has raised more than $55 Mn in funding to date. The platform first attempted to go public in 2022, targeting a ₹600 Cr IPO, but later shelved the plans due to weak market conditions. Reigniting its IPO ambitions, the startup once again filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in July 2026. C5i is now looking to raise about ₹1,000-1,200 Cr via the public issue. On the financial front, C5i’s consolidated net profit declined 15% to ₹48.3 Cr in FY25 as against ₹56.7 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile its operating revenue surged 26% to ₹545.3 Cr from ₹431.4 Cr in FY24. Curefoods Founded in 2020 by Ankit Nagori, Curefoods is a cloud kitchen unicorn that manages brands like EatFit, CakeZone, Nomad Pizza, Sharief Bhai Biryani, and Frozen Bottle. It claims to operate over 200 cloud kitchens and offline outlets across 70 Indian cities. The startup has raised over $175 Mn from backers including Iron Pillar, Accel, Three State Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, and ASK Finance. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Curefoods filed its DRHP with SEBI in late June 2025 and received markets regulator’s approval in late October. As per the DRHP, the proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to ₹800 Cr and an offer-for-sale of up to 4.85 Cr equity shares. However, in June 2026, the startup took a U-turn and put its IPO plans on hold amid the turmoil in the Indian equities market and concerns over its potential valuation. As per reports, mutual funds were not aligned with the ₹4,000 Cr (about $419 Mn) valuation sought by Curefoods during its roadshows. On the financial front, Curefoods' net loss remained steady at ₹169.9 Cr in FY25 as against ₹172.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 27.4% to ₹745.8 Cr compared to ₹585.1 Cr in FY24. Fibe Founded in 2015 by Akshay Mehrotra and Ashish Goyal as EarlySalary, Fibe initially offered salary advances and small-ticket personal loans to young working professionals. Since then, it has evolved into a diversified consumer finance platform. Today, it offers personal loans and purpose-driven financing solutions across sectors such as education, insurance, healthcare, rooftop solar and travel. It claims to operate a merchant network spanning 10,387 touchpoints across India, and claims to have ₹8,603 Cr in assets under management as of March 2026. It has raised more than $266 Mn from a host of marquee names such as TPG, Norwest Venture Partners, Eight Roads Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, TR Capital, and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). In June 2026, the lending tech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of over 4 Cr shares. On the financial front, Fibe saw its net profit more than double to ₹257.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹113.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 31% to ₹1,584.6 Cr from ₹1,208.9 Cr in FY25. Garuda Aerospace Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash and Rithika Mohann, Garuda Aerospace manufactures over 30 types of drones, while also offering drone-as-a-service (DaaS) solutions. It claims to have trained over 1 Lakh drone pilots, serving more than 100 government agencies along with over 500 enterprises. The startup currently operates a fleet of over 400 drones and has a manufacturing capacity of up to 15,000 units annually. Backed by cricketer MS Dhoni, Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle and Ocgrow Ventures, Garuda Aerospace has raised more than $37.1 Mn in funding to date. It was last pegged at a post-money valuation of $250 Mn during its last fundraise last year. The company first signalled its intent to go public in 2023. At the time, Jayaprakash told Inc42 that the company would list on the bourses within two years. Eventually in April 2026, the Chennai-based dronetech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. While the exact size of the IPO is yet to be determined, the company’s board, in March, approved a proposal to raise up to ₹750 Cr via fresh issue of shares and an undisclosed OFS component. The startup bagged SEBI’s approval for its IPO in August 2026. On the financial front, Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹11 Cr in H1 FY26 against an operating revenue of ₹41.2 Cr. InCred Holdings Founded in 2016 by Bhupinder Singh, InCred Group runs three distinct business verticals. InCred Finance handles lending, InCred Capital is focussed on wealth and asset management, while InCred Money specialises in retail bonds and alternative investments. The company boasts backing from heavyweights like Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), OAKS, Investcorp, Moore Capital, and Elevar Equity, among others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in September 2025, InCred Holdings, the parent of InCred Financial Services, sought shareholder approval to raise up to ₹ 1,500 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. By November 2025, InCred Holdings filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup received the markets regulator's nod for its IPO in February 2026. In May 2026, the company filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a public issue, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,250 Cr and an OFS of up to 9.9 Cr equity shares. InCred Holdings reported a 5.3% jump in net profit to ₹290 Cr in 9M FY26 from ₹275.5 Cr during the same period last fiscal. Operating revenue also surged 38.6% to ₹1,848.9 Cr from ₹1,333.9 Cr in 9M FY25. Infra.Market Founded in 2016 by Souvik Sengupta and Aaditya Sharda, Infra.Market runs a B2B marketplace that helps customers procure construction materials like concrete, steel, pipes, fittings, and chemicals. The startup has raised over $415 Mn till date from investors such as Tiger Global, Accel, and Nexus Ventures. In October 2025, Infra.Market confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI for a nearly ₹5,000 Cr ($563.3 Mn) listing. It received SEBI’s go-ahead in January 2026. However, the platform now appears to have ditched plans for a standalone IPO and is exploring a reverse-listing route via its listed subsidiary Shalimar Paints. In August 2026, the paint manufacturing giant proposed that it would acquire shares and CCPS of Infra.Market through a swap, involving securities worth around ₹10,545 Cr. The two companies are also exploring a potential “unification” at a later stage, subject to applicable laws and requisite approvals. Infra.Market’s net profit dwindled 42% to ₹219.7 Cr in FY25 from ₹378 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, revenue from operations rose 27% to ₹18,472 Cr versus ₹14,530.2 Cr in FY24. Kuku Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu,Vikas Goyal and Vinod Kumar Meena, Kuku is an audio-centric OTT platform that hosts audiobooks, podcasts, and original shows under Kuku FM in multiple Indian languages. It also operates a vernacular short-video app under Kuku TV brand and a microlearning platform Guru. The startup claims to have raised more than $156 Mn in funding to date and is backed by marquee names such as Vertex Ventures, Krafton, IFC and Paramark Ventures. In December 2025, reports first emerged that the OTT soonicorn was looking to list on the bourses. The company is said to have appointed Kotak Mahindra Capital, Axis Bank and Morgan Stanley as bankers to helm its potential IPO. In June 2026, Inc42 reported that Kuku filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr to ₹3,500 Cr (about $261 Mn to $366 Mn) through its IPO. The startup is targeting a valuation of up to ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn) for the public listing. The IPO will comprise both a fresh issue of shares and an offer-for-sale component. Kuku FM’s net losses soared 59% to ₹153 Cr in FY25 from ₹96 Cr the prior fiscal, while operating revenue soared 175% to ₹242 Cr from ₹88 Cr in FY24. MakeMyTrip Launched in 2000 by Keyur Joshi, Rajesh Magow, and Deep Kalra, MakeMyTrip is an online travel aggregator (OTA) that operates an end-to-end platform for booking flights, hotels and holiday packages. It also offers ancillary services such as forex cards and travel insurance. Over the years, it acquired rivals such as Goibibo and redBus to complement its primary business of air ticketing and hotels. More recently, it also acquired a minority stake in Visa processing platform Atlys and holiday packages business Flamingo Transworld. Since its inception, the company claims to have processed over 8.7 Cr transactions for retail consumers and onboarded 77,000 SME and large corporate customers. It was also one of the first Indian startups to list on Nasdaq in 2010. After Nasdaq, the travel tech major is now eyeing an Indian IPO. In April 2026, reports surfaced that the company appointed Axis Capital, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan as advisers for the IPO. Subsequently in July 2026, the travel tech major filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route for a $1 Bn OFS-only listing. On the financial front, MakeMyTrip reported a nearly 46% YoY decline in its net profit to $51.7 Mn in FY26, while operating revenue rose a mere 6.7% YoY to $1.04 Bn during the fiscal under review. NoPaperForms A brainchild of Naveen Goyal and Suraj Sapra, Meritto parent NoPaperForms helps educational institutions and edtech businesses automate student enrollment and fee collection processes. Founded in 2017, the startup catered to 1,183 educational institutions, including Manipal University, Shiv Nadar University and PhysicsWallah, in FY26. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Meritto turned into a public entity in May 2025 after its board and shareholders passed a resolution to approve the conversion. Subsequently, in November 2025, the company filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential route for an IPO, and received approval from the markets regulator to go ahead with its IPO in March 2026. In September 2026, NoPaperForms filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹375 Cr and an OFS component of up to 3.8 Cr equity shares. On the financial front, NoPaperForms reported an operating revenue of ₹115.6 Cr in FY26, up 25.2% from ₹92.3 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, the startup’s profits surged 534% to ₹11.9 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹1.9 Cr in FY25. Moneyview Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance. The company claims to manage over ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. Moneyview entered the unicorn club in 2024 after a ₹38.6 Cr infusion from Accel India and Nexus Ventures. In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹1,500 Cr and an OFS of up to 13.61 Cr equity shares. It received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026. Moneyview clocked a revenue of ₹2,409 Cr in the nine month period ended December 2025 against a net profit of ₹245 Cr. OYO (PRISM) Founded in 2012 by Ritesh Agarwal, OYO, rebranded as PRISM in 2025, is a travel tech major that operates budget hotels, vacation homes, casino hotels, coworking spaces, and corporate stays. After postponing its IPO plans multiple times, the hospitality giant’s parent entity PRISM secured shareholder nod in December 2025 to raise up to ₹6,650 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. Days later, the company confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI. It eventually received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in June 2026. Right after, the hospitality major filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO, which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares. The company is targeting a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn and has appointed ICICI Securities, Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, and Citibank to helm the issue. OYO's IPO journey has been a turbulent one so far. It first filed its DRHP in September 2021 for a $1.2 Bn public issue, but later shelved the plans amid market volatility. It once again filed its DRHP via the confidential route for a $600 Mn IPO in 2023, but later withdrew the papers again in May 2024. On the financial front, PRISM reported a profit of ₹748 Cr in 9M FY26, almost 3X of the ₹245 Cr profit it reported in the full year FY25. Its operating revenue stood at ₹6,941 Cr in 9M FY26, up from ₹6,253 Cr in FY25. PhonePe Founded in 2015 by Sameer Nigam, Rahul Chari, and Burzin Engineer, PhonePe is India's leading digital payments platform. It regularly accounts for nearly half of all Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions processed in the country. Originally focussed on digital payments, the fintech giant has since evolved into a comprehensive financial services provider, offering insurance products, broking services, and more. PhonePe was acquired by Flipkart in 2016. Six years later, US retail giant and parent Walmart spun it off as a separate entity from Flipkart. The fintech major redomiciled back to India in late 2022, setting the stage for its eventual listing on the Indian exchanges. In January this year, the fintech major filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for its IPO, which will comprise solely of an OFS component. Walmart, Tiger Global, Microsoft and General Atlantic will offload their stakes as part of the offer for sale. However, raking a U-Turn, the fintech major, in March 2026, temporarily paused its IPO plans amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in the global equity markets. While the company plans to restart the IPO process once global capital markets regain stability, sources told Inc42 that PhonePe has pushed the IPO till at least June 2026. Financially, PhonePe’s net loss widened by 62% to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 as against ₹1,727.4 Cr reported in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25. PlaySimple Games Founded in 2014 by Siddharth Jain, Siddhanth Jain, Preeti Reddy, and Suraj Nalin, PlaySimple Games is a casual mobile gaming studio. It operates a portfolio of 30 live mobile games across five categories – search, crossword, anagram, other word games, and non-word puzzles. It claims to have a presence in more than 110 countries. The startup was acquired by Swedish gaming company MTG for more than $360 Mn in 2021. Prior to the acquisition, PlaySimple raised $4.5 Mn in funding from the likes of Elevation Capital and Chiratae Ventures. None of the original cofounders remain with the company today, and it is currently led by MTG's Yoav Ecker as MD and CEO. In April 2026, PlaySimple filed its DRHP with SEBI for a public issue which will comprise solely an OFS component of ₹3,150 Cr. MTGx Gaming Holding AB will be the lone seller during the listing. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in August 2026. If listed, PlaySimple will become the second gaming company to go public in India, after Nazara Technologies. On the financial front, PlaySimple reported an operating revenue of ₹2,259.8 Cr in CY2025, up 20% YoY. However, net profit declined 31% YoY to ₹359 Cr, largely due to a 54% surge in advertising and sales commission costs. Purple Style Labs Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia's Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia's Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India. Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date. In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consists entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. It has also set a price band of ₹546 to ₹575 per equity share for its IPO, valuing the company at ₹4,604 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Subsequently, Purple Style Labs wrapped up its public issue with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. It will now tentatively list on the bourses on September 7. On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25. Razorpay Founded in 2014 by IIT-Roorkee alumni Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar, Razorpay has evolved from a simple payment gateway to an omnichannel fintech giant for payments, banking, SME payroll, lending, insurance, and more. It claims to process an annualised total payment volume (TPV) exceeding $180 Bn and caters to a majority of India’s unicorns. Kicking off its IPO plans, the company reverse flipped back to India in May 2025 by merging its US-based entity with its Indian arm Razorpay Software Pvt Ltd. In February 2026, the fintech major roped in Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi as investment bankers to helm its upcoming IPO. In June 2026, the unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup is said to be looking to raise anywhere between $500 Mn to $700 Mn at a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, lower than its last private valuation of $7.5 Bn. Razorpay has so far raised nearly $740 Mn from heavyweights such as Y Combinator, Tiger Global, Peak XV Partners, Lone Pine Capital, Alkeon Capital, and GIC. The startup’s net profit skyrocketed 365% to ₹33.5 Cr in FY24 from ₹7.2 Cr in the year-ago period, even as operating revenue shot up a mere 9% to ₹2,475 Cr from ₹2,283 Cr in FY23. Razorpay claimed that it slipped into the red in FY25 due to an ESOP expense of ₹1,209 Cr and tax payments linked to its reverse flip to India. Meanwhile, operating revenue is said to have surged 65% YoY to ₹3,783 Cr in FY25. RentoMojo Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date. Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in September 2025, RentoMojo enlisted IIFL and Motilal Oswal enlisted as bankers for its IPO. A few months later in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It has also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its upcoming public issue, which will value RentoMojo at around ₹4,206 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. The IPO will open for bidding on September 9 and close on September 11. Meanwhile, right before RentoMojo filed its draft papers, its cofounder and former COO Nain filed a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio. On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. Table Space Founded in 2017 by the late Amit Banerji and Karan Chopra, Table Space offers enterprise managed workspace to companies across multiple Indian cities. It counts the likes of EY, Dell, Fujitsu, AMD, Shell, and JCI among its clients. The startup has so far raised $407 Mn from the likes of Hillhouse Capital, Rava Partners, and Alta Capital. The Bengaluru-based startup first attempted to go public in 2025, but the plans were delayed after cofounder Banerji passed away in January 2025. In the aftermath, it appointed cofounders Chopra and Mehra as co-CEOs. Reigniting its listing plans, the managed workspace provider, in August 2026, filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹800 Cr and an OFS of up to 6.55 Cr shares. On the financial front, Table Space managed to narrow its loss by 74% to ₹402.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,555.4 in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 66.3% to ₹2,262.3 Cr from ₹1,360.5 Cr in FY25. Tonbo Imaging Founded in 2012 by Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D'Souza, Tonbo Imaging is a defence tech startup that designs and builds advanced imaging and sensor systems. Its product portfolio includes smart thermal weapon sights, see-through armors, AI-based seekers, and gun shock simulators. The company has raised over $59 Mn to date from investors such as Artiman Ventures, Celesta Capital, and Qualcomm Ventures. It was last valued at $175 Mn during its $20.4 Mn pre-IPO fundraise in April 2025. With presence across Europe, APAC region, the US, Australia, and Israel, the startup counts NATO, US Navy SEALs, Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), the defence ministries of India and Armenia, among others, as its customers. Tonbo Imaging’s IPO plans came to light in May 2025 after CEO Lakshmikumar, in May 2025, said that the startup was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI for up to ₹1,000 Cr IPO. The company filed its draft papers a few months later in December. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In August 2026, the company refiled its DRHP with the markets regulator, with the offer size largely unchanged from the previous DRHP. Tonbo’s net profit declined 30% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in the previous year. Operating revenue slumped 22.7% to ₹299.9 Cr from ₹374.3 Cr in FY25. Travelstack Tech Founded in 2014 by Vaibhav Aggarwal and Adarssh Mnpuria, FabHotels runs a chain of 1,379 budget hotels across 50 Indian cities. In 2020, the startup entered the travel-focussed SaaS segment with TravelPlus, an enterprise platform for booking travel, managing approvals, and processing expenses. TravelPlus counts names such as Eternal, Infra.Market, Zepto, Titan Company, and UnifyApps as customers. Both verticals operate under the consolidated entity Travelstack Tech. Kicking off its IPO process, Travelstack filed its DRHP with SEBI in mid-December 2025. The company received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in March 2026. The proposed IPO will comprise a fresh issue of up to ₹250 Cr alongside an OFS of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Fresh proceeds will fund working capital, repay borrowings, and support general corporate purposes. Financially, Travelstack posted a net profit of ₹32.2 Cr in H1 FY26, driven by a ₹37.4 Cr deferred tax gain, on an operating revenue of ₹400.4 Cr. For the full FY25, the company slashed its net loss by 95% to ₹6.3 Cr from ₹114.1 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue surged 31% to ₹716.4 Cr from ₹547.8 Cr in FY24. Zepto Founded in 2021 by Aadit Palicha and Kaivalya Vohra, Zepto is a quick commerce startup that delivers groceries and other essentials. Backed by Y Combinator, Nexus Venture Partners, Glade Brook Capital, and Motilal Oswal AMC, the quick commerce unicorn has raised nearly $2.5 Bn to date. The quick commerce major has been planning its IPO for some time now, with no clear timeline in sight. It was first planning to list on the bourses in 2025 but paused the plans in June 2025 for a year to trim cash burn and improve profitability. The startup revived its IPO ambitions in November 2025 and confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. The quick commerce major then received SEBI’s approval to float its proposed IPO in May 2026, and subsequently, it filed its updated DRHP in July 2026. As per its UDRHP, Zepto’s public offering was supposed to comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹8,010 Cr and an OFS component of 11.35 Cr shares. However, taking another U-turn, Zepto once again put its IPO plans on hold in August 2026. Cofounder and CEO Palich internally told employees that the startup was now aiming to list on the bourses between February 2027 and May 2027. In the meantime, the quick commerce major plans to raise $105 Mn via a pre-IPO funding round and fix its cash burn problem. On the financial front, Zepto’s net loss widened 26% to ₹5,905.2 Cr in FY26 as against ₹4,699.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Iran fuel tanker explosion leaves 11 dead and seven injured
The fuel tanker explosion occurred late on Saturday night
At least 11 people have been killed and seven injured after a fuel tanker exploded in western Iran, state media said.
State news agency IRNA reported late on Saturday that the vehicle suffered a brake fault and struck several cars before catching fire near a traffic police station outside Sanandaj, a Kurdish city roughly 400 kilometres (248 miles) west of Tehran.
The injured were taken to hospital.
A similar collision involving a fuel tanker and a passenger bus near Sanandaj in 2018 killed 15 people and injured four.
Road accidents claim over 17,000 lives annually in Iran, with experts blaming unsafe vehicles, disregard for driving laws and inadequate emergency services for the high mortality rate.
The explosion comes at a time when tensions have escalated between Iran and the US in recent days.
The two nations have traded strikes on ships in the latest round of attacks since the conflict flared a week ago after a period of relative calm.
US Central Command, which oversees the nation’s military in the Middle East, said it struck three Iranian oil tankers, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near the nation’s oil export hub, after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, said: “Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.”
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against US military vessels in the region, and later said it targeted three tankers that Tehran claimed were on unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as as three US-linked vessels in other areas.
The exchange of attacks followed an escalation in the past week that threatens to deepen a conflict that has continued since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February.
They also come after US president Donald Trump insisted the Iran conflict is a relatively minor operation, rather than a full-on war.
"I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us,” the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday. “It’s not a big thing.”

Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
- Published
Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity to India and Bangladesh.
But the very glaciers and mountains giving Nepal this massive natural advantage are succumbing to global warming - and last Wednesday's deadly floods have laid bare the risks to the nation's hydropower ambitions.
More than 1,300 people were killed, while thousands more are still missing.
The floods, which destroyed entire villages near the border of Nepal and Tibet, severely damaged 12 hydropower plants in the Trishuli River basin and knocked out more than 10% of Nepal's total power generation capacity. Operators tell the BBC they don't yet know if any of these facilities can be brought back to operation.
The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority, which owns six of the 12 damaged facilities, has assured Nepalese households that supply remains adequate. But its spokesman Rajan Dhakal acknowledges that with climate-related disasters becoming more frequent, "the time has come for a rethink of our hydropower policy".
Only two-thirds of people in Nepal had access to electricity in 2010, and even connected households would face power cuts for up to 16 hours a day.
An expansion of hydropower infrastructure alongside efforts to tackle corruption and boost energy imports from India to fill seasonal gaps meant that by 2018, most of Nepal was enjoying 24 hours of power supply per day.
At present, there are 225 hydropower plants across Nepal with more than 3,900MW of installed capacity, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority - capable of powering some three million households simultaneously.
Hundreds more such facilities are either being constructed or in the pipeline. Most of them are built high up in the mountains, where they can seize fast-flowing currents to generate power. These projects require little to no storage system.
However, with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50% faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks. Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier and its bedrock as the cause of last week's flash flood.
While scientists say it is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority previously said more than nine in 10 disaster events recorded between 2018 and 2024 were "related to climate".
Nepal's former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising, who called the catastrophic deluge a "once-in-a-century" event, says it holds lessons for designing plants and picking sites where they are built.
"We need to design the plants [to be more] resilient to the floods and, most importantly, adopt early-warning systems as well as robust emergency evacuation measures," he told environmental news outlet Mongabay.
Potentially hundreds of hydropower labourers, engineers and residents are thought to be trapped inside the mud-filled tunnels of these plants since the floods hit.
A "rethink" of Nepal's hydropower strategy could involve reservoir-based plants that need not be situated up in the mountains, says Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority. These could allow water to be stored and released as needed, but would also involve significant economic and environmental costs.
'All our eggs in one basket'
Some question if Nepal has been too reliant on hydropower.
"We should not be putting all our eggs in one basket in these dangerous times," says renewable energy expert Kushal Gurung, who founded the clean tech firm WindPower Nepal.
"We need to seriously embrace other alternatives as well, like solar and wind. And for that we will need to revise our energy policy that is at the moment very pro-hydropower," he says.
The claim is echoed by Vivek Shastry, researcher at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who argues that "meaningful additions of wind and solar generation is a resilience strategy that can limit single-point or interconnected electricity system failures in the future".
A report from the German aid agency suggests the technical potential for energy production from solar power in Nepal is around 10 times larger, external than that of hydropower.
Puspa Sharma, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore's Institute of South Asian Studies, agrees Nepal has to diversify its energy sources, but warns this can be done "only to a limited extent".
"While there is untapped capacity in wind and solar, hydropower really is the one that gives Nepal massive competitive advantage vis-a-vis its South Asian neighbours," he says, citing various studies comparing renewable energy potential in the region.
Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.
The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.
The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.
Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape".
"Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.
History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.
Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.
Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly".
"Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.
Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.
He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".
This disaster shows climate risks are international and cannot be managed by Nepal alone, suggests Manjeet Dhakal, a member of the country's climate delegation at the UN Climate Change Conference.
Governments and international organisations must share data, assess impacts and develop early-warning systems together, he urges.
"Nepal is among the least responsible for the greenhouse emissions that led to these exacerbated risks.
"Ironically, our hydropower industry is an attempt to reduce our already minimal emissions... We cannot, and should not, be made to respond to these risks alone."

Why are iPhones more expensive than iPads?
You can get an iPad for less than any iPhone, but that doesn’t mean the iPad is a low-cost device.
At first thought, you would expect an iPad to cost more than an iPhone due to the size difference. This is the case with other devices like TVs, laptops and smartwatches: a larger model comes with a higher price tag. However, at the time of writing, the lowest-cost iPhone (iPhone 17e) is $599, quite a bit higher than the most affordable iPad (11th generation) at $449.
The reason for this is a combination of design, hardware, demand and market segments. An iPad isn't simply a larger iPhone in the same way as a 65-inch TV compares to its 55-inch counterpart. And depending on which ones you consider, an iPad can actually come at a higher cost than any iPhone.
Smaller components are more complex to design
An iPhone's relatively small size presents design challenges; all the essential components must fit into a tiny space. It takes a lot of engineering work to design a motherboard, battery, SoC, radios, sensors, speakers and everything else to fit inside an iPhone without being bulky. It all has to be carefully arranged to avoid components interfering with each other and heat building up — not to mention the battery being able to power it all.
In comparison, an iPad gives engineers a lot more space to work with, reducing the costs. Designers don't have to be as strict with how they lay out components, and heat dissipation is simpler with more internal space. This doesn't mean the iPad is a free-for-all internally, but it also doesn't require as intensive research as the iPhone (especially with ultra-thin models, which have their own compromises, as our iPhone Air review noted).
iPhones include premium hardware
Aside from size, the biggest difference between the iPhone and iPad is the technology inside. Every iPhone contains lots of elements that most iPad models lack, such as all the radios and antennas required for phone calls. While you can make calls on your iPad using Wi-Fi calling or routing through your iPhone, even cellular iPad models are data-only; they can't make traditional phone calls.
Cameras on the iPhone are far superior to the iPad's offerings; the iPhone 17's camera is much better than even an iPad Pro's. The iPhone 17's rear cameras are both 48MP, compared to the 12MP camera on the M5 iPad Pro. iPad cameras lack optical zoom, have worse performance in the dark, and lack features like Cinematic video mode. An iPad camera is serviceable in a pinch or for scanning documents, but it's not meant for everyday picture-taking.
Every model in the iPhone 17 series has an OLED screen, which is more expensive than the LCD screens of all iPad models outside the Pro line. Each iPhone 17 model also offers a ProMotion screen that goes up to 120Hz, while all iPads except for the Pro line have 60Hz screens. Lower-end iPads usually get older chips, too. The 11th-gen iPad, released in 2025, uses the A16 chip first seen in 2022's iPhone 14 Pro. That's not to mention iPads lacking MagSafe charging, NFC and an IP water-resistance rating.
Different competition spaces and markets
Even though the iPhone and iPad run a similar OS and many of the same apps, they don't compete in the same field. Smartphones are essentially a necessity for most people today given how many roles they play: calling and messaging, music player, GPS, entertainment, camera and much more.
An iPad isn't nearly as vital. For many people, a tablet is a secondary device for streaming, reading and maybe taking notes. They can be great for students and those in creative fields, but they don't feel necessary in the way phones do. You could opt for a "phablet"-sized phone, a Chromebook or even a laptop like the surprisingly solid MacBook Neo for the same purposes.
Because of all this, Apple has good reasons to offer a low-cost iPad. Fewer people would buy a tablet if the starting price were prohibitively high, which means the company would miss out on newcomers to the Apple ecosystem spending on services like iCloud and Apple Music. The iPad also competes against Chromebooks in the education market, where Apple wants schools to buy its devices and get them into families' hands.
The iPhone represents Apple's highest source of income by far, meaning it's sensible for the company to spend the most time and money improving it. Apple has always positioned the iPhone as a premium phone and knows what people are willing to pay for it. Selling an ultra-cheap iPhone would devalue the framing Apple has built up over decades; even the "affordable" iPhone 17e is hundreds more than budget Android phones.
There's also the matter of how people buy these devices. The majority of US buyers purchase an iPhone through mobile carriers, which offer "free" phones through monthly bill credits in exchange for staying on an expensive plan for several years. This obfuscates the true price. People also tend to upgrade their tablets less often than their phones.
iPads can still get quite expensive
We've contrasted the iPhone to the base model iPad for most of this discussion, but looking at other iPad models shows that the iPhone isn't always more expensive. The base iPad starts at $449 for the 128GB model and goes up to $749 for 512GB of storage; you'll pay another $150 for a model with cellular connectivity. This means a 256GB iPad with cellular costs $700 — already $100 more than the iPhone 17e for a device with a worse screen and inferior camera that can't make calls without Wi-Fi.
Other iPad models are even more expensive, as they pack better specs that start to exceed the iPhone's power. The M4 iPad Air starts at $749 for 128GB, while the iPad mini (more affected by the size considerations mentioned earlier) begins at $600 for 128GB. Meanwhile, the iPad Pro can far exceed the cost of any iPhone given its Apple silicon chip and premium OLED screen. A maxed-out 2TB iPhone 17 Pro Max is $2,000, while the 13-inch M5 iPad Pro with 2TB of storage is $2,600 — and that's before the optional nano-texture glass for another $100 and cellular connectivity for another $200. These models compete against laptops and desktops for professional work, rather than the more casual usage of phones.
Prior to the Apple price hikes of June 2026, this wasn't as bad. The base iPad and iPad mini's prices each jumped by $100, while the iPad Air and Pro went up by $150 to $200 each. These increases haven't hit the iPhone yet, though that might change soon.

The "last vacant lot" northside of the Brisbane River is slated for nearly 2,200 homes, as well as a 50-bed hotel and supermarket.
Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, who dumped the former government's housing affordability mandate last year, says his government "doesn't discriminate" about types of housing.
What's next?
The first residents are expected to move in in 2031, but Mr Bleijie says the development is not "required" to be finished for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
Queensland's deputy premier says he's "pulling every lever possible" to relieve the housing crisis after confirming a 13-tower development on the "last vacant lot" northside of the Brisbane river won't have affordable homes.
Today, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie announced the Northshore Hamilton former industrial site would be parcelled off to five developers, who between them would build almost 2,200 homes.
Mr Bleijie, who is also minister for state development, infrastructure and planning, dumped the former Labor government's affordable housing mandate from the state facilitated development program last year.
He said mandates "stopped development", suggesting homeowners in the outer suburbs would downsize to riverfront units, freeing up more houses.
"You need all forms of housing, that's why we are not discriminating on the types of housing we build across the state,"
he said.
"We are in a housing crisis still, we inherited a housing crisis from the Labor government, and we are doing everything we can — we are pulling every lever possible."
Mr Bleijie was unable to say what the land had sold for, only that it had gone for "market value".
Under Labor, the long-vacant 6.1 hectare site was tipped to become the athletes village for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
The first residents are expected to move in in 2031.
Mr Bleijie said the towers weren't "required" to be built ahead of 2032, "but having them done before 2032 would be great".
Member for Clayfield Tim Nicholls said it was "the last major development site available" near the CBD, "close to all the things people need and want".
The development will include a 50-bed hotel as well as a supermarket and shops.
"[It's] on the last outstanding northside of the river property location," Mr Nicholls said.
"It is the last vacant space and it's the great opportunity Brisbane has been crying out for."

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

Iran claims a strike on a U.S. ship in the Strait of Hormuz, which the U.S. denies
Purported attack the latest salvo in new flare-up of fighting between the two countries.
Iran said Sunday it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim that the U.S. military dismissed as a "total lie."
It was the latest salvo in a new flare-up of fighting between the two countries.
The purported attack came a day after the U.S. military said forces struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to a missile attack on Navy warships.
The war began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. But since a ceasefire agreement was announced in June, on-and-off fighting has persisted, with both sides trying to inflict military and economic pain as negotiations have collapsed.
Strikes come about a week after fighting resumed
The U.S. and Iran resumed attacks last week, following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian communities along it again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a U.S. bombardment of southern Iran.
The Trump administration appears to have adopted a dual-prong approach to the conflict, responding militarily to attacks on the strait while going after foreign financial institutions that handle Iran's money.
- U.S. military hits 3 Iranian oil tankers after saying its navy warships were targeted
- Iran attacks U.S. bases across Gulf after reports of deadly strike on wedding
But Tehran's hardline new senior leaders have signalled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions.
Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions — and now the U.S. blockade — and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.
Meanwhile, Iran's nuclear program, the issue that contributed to the outbreak of the war, was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.
Diplomats say the U.S., Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations.
Instead, Tehran's new leverage focuses on the Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

Researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras (IIT Madras), and Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, have developed a set of AI-based tools designed to assist in the early detection and assessment of kidney diseases, a press release said.
The team has developed three technologies that complement each other. The first is a machine learning model that uses clinical and laboratory information to predict the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). This CKD prediction model is implemented in a user-friendly prototype interface to facilitate future clinical translation.
The second is a deep learning system that automatically analyses CT scans and classifies them into four categories: normal kidney, kidney cyst, kidney stone, and kidney tumour. The image classifier has been trained with over 12,000 images and can distinguish healthy kidneys from cysts, stones, and tumours.
And the third is a 3D imaging platform that recreates kidneys from CT scans to precisely assess tumour volume and the percentage of kidney involvement. The 3D imaging framework was developed using open-source software and is a step toward the development of a kidney ‘digital twin’, integrating AI-assisted image analysis with patient-specific 3D anatomical models for personalised clinical decision-making.
Kidney diseases are often asymptomatic in their early stages and are not diagnosed until substantial damage has occurred. The AI tools aim to assist physicians for earlier diagnosis, which could help slow the disease process and reduce the need for expensive interventions like dialysis.
The research was led by G.L. Samuel, department of mechanical engineering, IIT Madras, and Jennifer Delighta, research scholar, IIT Madras, in collaboration with Santosh Varughese from the department of nephrology, CMC Vellore. The research received institutional support from IIT Madras and the SPARC (Scheme for Promotion of Academic and Research Collaboration) project, the press release said.

The Greens have criticised inflammatory statements from the former Israel Defense Forces officer who ordered the attack which killed Zomi Frankcom, accusing the Albanese government of weakness over its failure to halt military exports and impose new sanctions.
Australian aid worker Frankcom and six of her colleagues were killed in 2024 while bringing food to the people of Gaza. Former IDF reserve colonel Nochi Mendel has said he would do “exactly the same thing” again and that those killed in the World Central Kitchen (WCK) humanitarian convoy in Gaza were “not innocent”.
The statements have been condemned as “utterly disgraceful” by Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, and as an “outrageous smear” by WCK’s humanitarian chief.
But the Greens’ defence spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said the government’s response was insufficient in the face of Mendel’s “reprehensible” statements. He said the comments “reflect the rhetoric and policy of the Israeli government, where collective punishment of aid workers, doctors and innocent civilians is occurring daily”.
“I do not care what minister Wong’s personal feelings are, I don’t care about her outrage, I care about the actions taken as foreign minister,” Shoebridge told Guardian Australia.
“Anyone can condemn the actions of the Israeli military, but only the government can impose the sanctions and material responses needed. Until they do their words are distractions.”
He called for material reprimand for members of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and for the sale of parts for the F-35 fighter jet to be immediately halted.
José Andrés, the WCK founder, said Mendel had smeared Frankcom and her colleagues.
“Now, one of the officers involved says he isn’t sorry for what happened. He said we are not a neutral organisation,” he said in a statement published online this week.
“Really? Let me be very clear, to him and to the whole world. We are humanitarians. We are friends of humanity. We believe that food is a universal human right.”
Mendel, then the chief of staff of the Nahal brigade, said he gave the order to attack a humanitarian convoy delivering hundreds of tonnes of food to Gaza on the night of 1 April 2024.
Three vehicles in the convoy were attacked along Gaza’s coast road, in successive drone strikes, each about two minutes apart.
One after another, the three vehicles were bombed, as survivors from the initial strikes ran to the untouched cars, seeking sanctuary.
An IDF investigation found the attack was a grave mistake, identifying specific errors made by a handful of officers, in particular Mendel, who was removed from his position. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect the food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.
Last month, Israel’s advocate general declined to press charges against anyone for the deaths, saying there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”.
Mendel has given interviews to the ABC and the Guardian saying he did not regret the attacks. He told the Guardian he was following IDF protocol, and the humanitarians were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association.
Mendel was referring to a general policy of haflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion in designating a person a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association.
Mendel told the Guardian while he didn’t plan to kill aid workers, those killed “were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas”.
He did not support this assertion with any evidence. Investigations by the IDF itself and the former head of the Australian military have found no suggestion of any connection between Hamas and World Central Kitchen.
Mendel said he fought in the war in Gaza “to defeat Hamas”, and dismissed the seriousness of the killing of seven humanitarians.
“If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing,” he told the Guardian.
“I think it’s an idiotic side event. It really isn’t a serious event.”
Wong, asked about earlier comments from Mendel that he was unapologetic over the strikes, said his statements were extremely distressing for Frankcom’s family.
“I thought those comments were disgraceful, utterly disgraceful,” she told the ABC. “I don’t even want to go into some of the detail of them because I don’t want to give them any credence.”
Wong said the Australian government was dissatisfied with Israel’s decision not to lay criminal charges against those responsible, and would continue to “press for justice”.
“We do want to see full accountability for the deaths of Zomi Frankcom and her colleagues. They were humanitarian workers working to deliver aid and they are protected under the Geneva conventions.”
Restaurateur Andrés, whose charity has provided more than 600m meals to people affected by natural disasters, climate emergencies and conflict around the world, said the deaths of humanitarian workers who were just trying to feed hungry people was inexcusable.
“Enough with the outrageous smears. Enough with excuses. Enough with the shifting of blame.
“From the start, we have demanded truth, truth and justice for our friends and their families. We want an independent investigation with all the video and audio released in public so the world can know the truth, because we continue to grieve for our friends. We will never forget them or stop fighting for them.”
Frankcom’s family issued a statement following Israel’s decision not to lay criminal charges, saying they were “deeply disappointed” by the decision.
