As Rachael Leigh Cook celebrated the 25th anniversary of Josie and the Pussycats, it was the voice behind the character that got her flowers.
During Cinespia‘s screening of the 2001 cult musical comedy on Saturday at Hollywood Forever Cemetary, the actress praised Letters to Cleo frontwoman Kay Hanley for providing the vocals for Josie and the film’s iconic soundtrack, as they were joined by the film’s writing/director duo Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont.
“I have never felt more pride for being in a film that’s sort of also in excess with unearned ownership of that product, because I am only half of this role,” said Cook. “So, I want to take this moment to just shout out Kay Hanley for the rest of my days. The only reason I can watch myself in this movie is because [Josie’s] spirit is you. I love your work in this movie so much.”
Hanley explained that the movie “literally changed my life,” noting that she was in attendance with her 27-year-old daughter, who was a baby going to work with her when she recorded the soundtrack.
Watch on Deadline
In June, Hanley detailed her struggles trying to obtain residuals and health insurance through SAG after the film’s producers allegedly failed to submit her paperwork to the union.
Although the 2001 big-screen adaptation of the Archie Comic only grossed $14.8 million when it was first released, the camp, stylized comedy has earned a massive cult following over the years, thanks to its fierce takedown of capitalism through subliminal messaging, in-your-face product placement and an iconic original soundtrack, performed by Hanley.
The movie, which recently marked its milestone 25th anniversary, also featured a perfect ensemble, including Cook as Josie, Rosario Dawson as Val and Tara Reid as Mel, as well as Alan Cumming and Parker Posey as evil Mega Records execs Wyatt and Fiona.
Hanley has been the lead singer and songwriter for Letters to Cleo since 1990, also appearing on the soundtracks for The Craft (1996) and 10 Things I Hate About You (1999), in which she also made a musical cameo as herself.

Body of world's youngest traditional king returns home to Uganda amid succession row
- Published
The body of a popular traditional ruler who was the world's youngest reigning monarch has been flown home to Uganda where President Yoweri Musveni was amongst the mourners gathered at Entebbe airport to pay their respects.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV died in the US last week aged 34 after receiving treatment for an aggressive form of cancer.
The Tooro king will be buried next Saturday - the day he had hoped to celebrate the anniversary of his coronation. He had ascended the throne aged just three and was crowned when he turned 18.
The return of his body marks the start of the Tooro kingdom's official nine-day mourning period amid a growing dispute over who should succeed him.
Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, but it has several traditional kingdoms that continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.
Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.
After a brief ceremony at the airport, his body was flown by military helicopter to Kyegegwa in western Uganda, where the Tooro Kingdom is located, before being taken by road to the royal palace in Fort Portal.
It will lie in state at Karuziika Palace for the mourning period and members of the public will be allowed to pay their respects and prayers will be held there each evening.
On Thursday, Uganda's parliament held a special tribute to King Oyo, with MPs remembering him as a modernising monarch who championed education, health and opportunities for young people.
Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja described him as a "symbol of unity" and praised his work raising awareness about HIV and Aids among young people.
Opposition MPs also paid tribute, with acting opposition leader Patrick Nsamba Oshabe saying: "Heritage and development were never rivals in his hands."
President Museveni has ordered an official burial for the monarch and national flags will fly at half-mast for three days around the funeral.
On Wednesday, the Tooro kingdom's Prime Minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said the king had asked officials not to disclose the seriousness of his illness because he believed he would recover and return to his people.
He said the monarch had hoped to return home for this year's Empango - the annual celebration of his coronation - on 12 September.
"He was confident in his recovery," Akiiki said.
His death has triggered uncertainty over the future of the monarchy as Oyo was not officially married.
But Akiiki has said the king had a young son, whose identity would be revealed later in accordance with Tooro customs.
President Museveni also said the king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, had told him that her son had left an heir.
But Charles Kamurasi, who is head of the Babiito royal clan from which Tooro's kings are chosen, said he knew nothing about the reported child, prompting an unusual public disagreement among senior figures in the kingdom.
Others within the royal clan have questioned why they were apparently unaware of the child.
"The prime minister is not supposed to talk about the king's heir. It is a cultural process," one royal clan member was quoted as saying by Uganda's state-owned New Vision newspaper.
"How can we, blood relatives, not know of the child, and the prime minister says he knows? That is totally out of order," the clan member added.
Akiiki has since appealed for the dispute to be dealt with privately, saying he wanted to meet other elders to resolve their differences.
"Words spoken in moments of grief can deepen divisions that may take years to repair," he warned.
The Ugandan government has also intervened, urging people not to spread speculation about the succession on social media.
Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde said Ugandans should rely on official information from the government and the Tooro Kingdom, adding that any dispute would be dealt with under law governing traditional and cultural leaders.
"The whole world is watching how Uganda mourns its king," he said, urging people to show "restraint and respect".
The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.
King Oyo ascended the throne in 1995 and became an international curiosity because of his young age.
Before his burial, a church funeral service will be held at a local church.
His body will then be carried in a traditional procession to the Karambi Royal Tombs, with burial is expected to be completed by 14:00 local time.
According to Tooro tradition, kings are not buried in the evening.

India is ageing, and the most recent official figures show how quickly this is happening. The National Family Health Survey - 6 factsheets, released in August 2026, indicate that the proportion of Indians aged 60 years or older has reached 12.9%, up from 11.8% in NFHS-5, some four years earlier. This represents a small national increase, and while significant, is not the most interesting aspect of what the data reveal.
The more important conclusion is that India is not ageing as one country. Keralam, which was already the oldest state, now has 20.7% of its population aged 60 and over; Goa is at 17.2%, Himachal Pradesh at 16.4%, and Tamil Nadu at 16.3%. On the other hand, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh had their proportions of elderly people increase by only 0.4 and 0.3 percentage points, respectively and remain young by any measure. There is also the case of Ladakh, where the percentage of people over 60 rose from 8.9% to 14.6% in four years, a 5.7 percentage-point increase, which is greater than the increase Kerala achieved over the same period.
It is impossible to apply a single national template to such different populations. In States that are already ageing, there will be increases in the demand for care of chronic diseases, geriatric services and long-term care. Although younger States have more time ahead of them, that time is exactly when preparation should take place. Putting off action until the elderly population is large enough to be seen when looked at as a group, means responding to demographic change rather than predicting it.
What the fact sheets cannot tell us
The NFHS-6 State and national fact sheets include 101 key indicators. The only one of these relating to older Indians is the proportion of the population aged 60 and over; all the other information that could tell us about their health is either included in age groups that are too broad to be of any use or is given in a form that does not allow linkage to individuals.
When it comes to hypertension and high blood sugar, the two main indicators of India’s burden of non-communicable diseases, both conditions are recorded for adults aged 15 and over. Thus, a 25-year-old and an 85-year-old are placed in the same statistical category. Based on the available fact sheets, there is no way to know how common hypertension is among the elderly in India, how this prevalence differs from State to State, or whether the States ageing most rapidly are also experiencing the steepest increase in chronic disease among older adults.
When it comes to nutrition, the gap is even more apparent. Body mass index is reported only for adults between the ages of 15 and 49, and not because older adults were measured and then left out of the tables. They were never weighed. Height and weight are recorded only for women up to 49 and men up to 54. The population whose nutritional and functional status matters most as a society ages does not appear in the data at all.
With regard to health insurance and financing indicators, they are provided at the household level. These indicators tell us whether a household has coverage, but they tell us very little about whether the older person in that household is financially protected when their healthcare needs become intensive and long-term.
There is a deeper design issue underneath this. NFHS interviews women up to 49 and men up to 54. Above that age, Indians appear in the survey only as a line in the household roster and, if selected, a blood pressure cuff and a glucose reading. So even where we have a measurement for a 70-year-old, we have very little to explain it with: nothing on their tobacco or alcohol use, whether they are on treatment, whether they sought care, whether they still work. The elderly are enumerated. They are not interviewed.
This does not mean that NFHS-6 is a flawed survey; it is, in fact, one of the most valuable sources of information on population health available anywhere in the world, and it was intended to track overall population health rather than to answer all the questions raised by an ageing society. But as India’s age structure changes, so must the information system used to formulate health policy.
The evidence is older than the policy
This is no longer just a theoretical issue: since the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) has been extended to all citizens aged 70 and over, the government has now assumed responsibility for financing the health of a very large number of elderly people.
To serve that population adequately we need to know more than simply how many people are eligible. How many live with chronic diseases? How many need help with everyday activities? How much are they paying out of pocket? Only on the basis of this information can we tell whether the money and the services are being directed towards the right needs in the right States.
India possesses the necessary equipment to deal with these questions. The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India, conducted by the International Institute for Population Sciences, was designed precisely for this purpose. In its first phase, it included more than 73,000 adults aged 45 and over, gathering information on their health conditions, their use of and expenditure on healthcare, economic circumstances, social networks, functional health, and biomarkers. It is a major piece of infrastructure.
The problem is that the first wave covers the period 2017 to 2018. For a policy programme being expanded this year, a baseline that is eight years old cannot be considered up-to-date evidence. Once data has been collected, it loses relevance over time, and this decline in value is most rapid in cases where the underlying population is changing quickly.
Staying current
When a gap in data is identified, the reflex is to call for a new survey. That is the wrong instinct here. India already runs two surveys. The NFHS gives a regular, broad picture of population health across the country. The LASI does a deep dive into ageing and its social and economic consequences. They were built to do different jobs, and turning the NFHS into a second LASI would be expensive and would damage what it already does well.
What is needed is more modest. Keep the ageing data current, rather than letting a decade pass between one wave and the next. Report the numbers by age where the NFHS already collects them, particularly for hypertension and blood sugar. And design the two surveys so they can be read against each other, instead of sitting in separate silos.
An ageing India will have to do more than simply count its older population; it will also need to find out what their requirements are, where these needs are appearing first, and whether the health system is able to meet them. With regard to the first of these questions the data are now fairly good, but with respect to the others we are still making guesses.

SUNDAY AM: Forget about any of the new films at the Labor Day weekend box office. They didn’t really dazzle. All that matters is whether or not we ring in a record summer, beating 2013’s $4.756 billion.
According to Rentrak, the 3-day domestic marketplace of $88M gets us to $4.732 billion by end of today, still the second best summer ever. From the chart below, Rentrak is forecasting a photo-finish. If the 4-day marketplace in North America rings up between $114.1M-$115.9M, then 2026 has claimed a new all-time record for summer between $4.758B and $4.759B.
Note this past August hit an all-time record stateside with $1.276 billion per Rentrak, unseating August 2016 which previously grossed $1.02B, that month led by Warner Bros/DC’s David Ayer directed Suicide Squad (which finaled at $325M domestic). It was the third time that August cracked $1 billion at the domestic B.O., the previous time being 2014 ($1.016B).

SATURDAY AM: Rentrak reports that we’re $112.2 million away from having a record summer at the domestic box office, the previous high being 2013 with $4.756 billion. Per sources this morning, it looks like we’re going to get there with the Friday-Monday Labor Day frame ringing up over $118M.
For the period of May 1-Sept 3, Rentrak had the domestic marketplace at $4.643 billion and if we hit the forecast that studios are seeing for the weekend, we’ll be at $4.76B. Rentrak had a footnote on its summer note yesterday saying that there’s a chance that summer 2026 could finish $8 million–$23 million below the 2013 record of $4.756B. Remember, this summer was longer than 2013’s record: 130 days versus 123 days.
It’s not often that Labor Day becomes this nail-biting at the box office. Studios often use the frame as a dumping ground, rarely attempting to lure moviegoers out. The only time really they appealed to the masses was 2021 when Disney booked Destin Daniel Cretton’s Marvel title Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings in an effort to get moviegoers back into cinemas post Covid, that title still owning the best opening for the holiday at $94.6M.
With an eye at $22M (and maybe $23M) over 4-days, Sony/Marvel Studio’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day is one of the best holdovers for the holiday frame after The Sixth Sense ($29.2M), Crazy Rich Asians ($28.5M), and Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy ($22.9M). As we’ve already written, the movie is chasing history, and ultimately in the next few weeks, or even days, will step on 2015’s Star Wars: Force Awakens ($936.6M) to become the highest grossing movie of all-time at the domestic B.O.
Also, let’s not ignore the holdover power of Universal’s The Odyssey which by the end of this weekend after its eighth sesh of $16.4M over 4-days, will stand at $588.1M, Universal’s second-highest grossing movie at the domestic box office after Jurassic World ($653.4M) and ahead of Super Mario Bros Movie ($574.1M).
The rest of the newcomers are quite light, though Paramount’s Mark Wahlberg-Yahya Abdul-Mateen II Civil rights action thriller By Any Means is coming in higher than the $6M spotted with $8.5M over 4-days and a B+ CinemaScore. Lionsgate Grindstone’s Fall 2: Deadpoint is looking at $2.7M over 4-days in 12th place with a B- while A24’s Onslaught isn’t igniting hipsters with $2.3M over 4-days and a C CinemaScore.
Busting into the top 10 is Sony Pictures/Crunchyroll’s re-release of the 1988 Akira which made $1.215 million on Friday from 787 locations for what’s looking $3.5M over 4-days, $2.8M over 3-days.
For all the pom-poms about the comeback of theatrical, smaller films have a very hard time, bad reviews or good reviews. To have something akin to A24’s specialty win, The Invite, ($25.6M, 96% critical Rotten Tomatoes score, 89% audience), a distributor needs to invest and push. However, the reality of the situation for many who aren’t opting for an awards season or even a genre audience pull is that they’re often using theatrical as a means of marketing to get a film into the next home window. It’s the primary financial model for many distributors, even the big studios.
That said, one of the exceptions is Roadside Attractions and Saban’s Buddy which is having an exceptional hold and speaking to its under 25 audience (at a huge 44% per PostTrak). Buddy could wind up as the distributor’s second or third highest grossing movie ever behind I Can Only Imagine ($83.4M domestic) and ahead of either Judy ($24.3M) or Peanut Butter Falcon ($20.4M). This is all with a P&A spend under $5M for the Sundance acquisition. The 3-day on Buddy is $5.9M (+9%) while the 4-day is looking like $7.4M in 7th for a running total by EOD Monday of $15.98M at 1,771 theaters. The 18-34 crowd here alone is driving 73% of business. Pic is drawing mostly men at 52% and it has a 55% definite recommend. Best definite recommends of 66% and 67% are respectively coming from the 25-34 and 45-54 age brackets.

Electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric has opened its first dealer-operated stores across India, less than a month after announcing a shift from its company-owned retail model. The first dealer-led outlets have gone live across Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Bihar, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh. The company said the stores will cater to local demand for its electric scooters and motorcycles while expanding its presence across regional markets. Ola Electric is now looking to build a network of more than 500 dealerships over the next two quarters. Meanwhile, its existing company-owned stores will transition into product experience centres. The development marks the beginning of a major overhaul of the Bhavish Aggarwal-led company’s distribution strategy. Ola Electric opened its sales and service network to dealers on August 6, five years after launching its first escooter through a fully company-owned retail network. Under the new model, dealers will handle local sales and service, while the company’s outlets will largely focus on showcasing its products and building the brand. The partner-led model is expected to allow Ola Electric to expand across cities and towns without incurring the costs associated with setting up and operating company-owned stores. The company had earlier said that it received more than 1,200 expressions of interest from prospective dealer partners. It added that the dealer network would help the EV maker take its products deeper into regional markets. The dealership push is also expected to support Ola Electric’s attempt to address its long-standing after-sales service issues. The company has faced sustained customer complaints related to delayed repairs, inadequate spare parts, and service centre capacity. Under the dealer-led model, partners will handle both sales and service and maintain Ola Electric’s spare-parts inventory locally. While announcing its Q4 FY26 financials, the company said service was the largest constraint on demand and brand trust through the fiscal year, but claimed that average service turnaround time fell 88% from around nine days in October 2025 to nearly one day in March 2026. Service backlog declined from 14 days to six days, while same-day closures reached about 87%. The rollout comes as Ola Electric looks to regain lost ground in India’s increasingly competitive electric two-wheeler market. The OEM has seen a turnaround in recent months, and commanded a 7.6% market share in E2W registrations in August. To penetrate further into the mass market segment, Ola Electric launched the new S1Z range, priced from ₹79,999. Offered with 3.1 kWh and 5.1 kWh battery options, the scooters have claimed ranges of up to 179 km and 301 km, respectively. Beyond new models, the EV major is also using the S1Z to showcase its battery technology, with the scooter becoming its first model to use its indigenously developed Bharat Cell LFP technology.

Foodborne illnesses have been a trending headline for most of 2026, leading many readers to write in to Snopes asking for clarification on exactly what they should and shouldn't eat. As of this writing, the CDC listed 36 active investigations into contaminated foods resulting in 11 recall notifications thus far in the year.
For instance, amid an outbreak of thousands of cases of an intestinal disease called cyclosporiasis across the United States, readers asked whether U.S. President Donald Trump's administration cut programs tracking the surveillance of cyclospora, the parasite that causes the illness. Trump's alleged monetary connections to Taylor Farms, the supplier linked to the outbreak, also were a hot topic.
Food contamination claims can run the gamut from alleged heavy metals in Girl Scout cookies to microscopic bugs on Oreos — but as you'll find in Snopes' food investigations, things aren't always as cut and dried as they appear.

Masked men block traffic to UK's port of Dover, site of past anti-immigrant protests
Masked men have blocked the entrance to Britain’s busiest ferry port, Dover
LONDON -- A group of masked men blocked the entrance to Britain’s busiest ferry port on Saturday. Police said they were “engaging with the protesters."
The Port of Dover said all traffic in and out “is stopped due to an ongoing public order incident.”
Footage on social media showed several dozen men in black, their faces covered, standing across a major road near the port.
It was not immediately clear what they were demanding.
The National Highways agency said the protests caused a 4-mile (6.4-kilometer) traffic jam, causing delays of up to 45 minutes.
P&O Ferries, which runs services between Dover and Calais in France, said its boats were running on schedule, and passengers who missed their ferry would be offered the next available crossing.
Dover, about 70 miles (110 kilometers) southeast of London, has been the site of previous anti-immigrant protests focused on migrants who cross the Channel from France in small boats. Some politicians, including Nigel Farage of hard-right party Reform UK, have seized on the issue. He branded the asylum seekers “an invasion” in a Friday speech.
The Labour Party government says stepped-up law enforcement cooperation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing this year by more than 40% compared to 2025.
Mike Tapp, a Labour lawmaker who represents Dover in Parliament, criticized “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.”
“I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossing are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess,” he wrote on Facebook on Saturday. “Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”

US military hits 3 Iranian oil tankers after saying Navy warships were targeted with missiles
The U.S. military says it has struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy warships were targeted with missiles
CAIRO -- The U.S. military on Saturday said it struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy warships were targeted with missiles, warning that it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
The military’s statement said a U.S. aircraft carrier and a destroyer evaded “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling in the region and no U.S. personnel were hurt. It said two Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled” and the third, unladen one, was destroyed.
The U.S. statement said the tankers were part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region.
Earlier, Iran accused the U.S. of attacking an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf.
The U.S. said one tanker was struck off Kharg Island and another was struck near Jask. The unladen tanker was hit in the Gulf of Oman. The statement shared what it called video footage of the strikes.
The strikes came nearly a week after the U.S. and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm in the on-again, off-again war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. Both sides have sought to inflict both military and economic pain, and negotiations have collapsed.
“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” the head of U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper said.

'It cannot happen': Why Quebec fans and actors fought to save their own version of The Simpsons
Quebec’s identity, language and creative livelihoods are preserved through the dubbed show
Growing up in Quebec, Joshua Biasotto fell in love with watching The Simpsons after discovering the version of the show that's dubbed in the French dialect, Québécois.
He says he not only lived for the long-running American animated sitcom’s quirky characters, irreverent humour and satirical take on life, but he also "developed a big love for Quebec dubbing."
"I've done my research," said Biasotto. "I know which actor is doing the voice of which character."
But last August, after 35 years, Corus Entertainment’s Télétoon, which held the Canadian broadcast rights to the show and oversaw its dubbing, decided not to renew those rights for the 36th season.
This put Les Simpson in jeopardy.
Distraught, Biasotto sprang into action, creating an online petition on Change.org called Sauvons le doublage québécois des Simpsons — “Let's save the Quebec dub of The Simpsons.”
“I was like, it cannot happen,” said Biasotto. “It’s a part of our identity that we lose.”
The Quebec version, he says, was adapted to incorporate local expressions and cultural references that made it feel uniquely theirs.
For example, the characters spoke in regional Quebec accents, including joual, the colloquial dialect associated with working-class Montreal, while U.S. people and places were swapped out for local references.
In one episode, a sketch involving upstate New York — including the cities of Utica and Albany — is replaced in the Québécois version with the Lac-Saint-Jean region and the towns of Jonquière and Alma.
Ian Lafrenière, Quebec’s deputy premier and a longtime Simpsons fan, even wrote in a Facebook post that the Quebec version must be saved, describing the cultural and geographical references in the show as "sublime."
And the public outcry to save Les Simpson tapped into something bigger than just nostalgia.
Dubbing is part of a long tradition in Quebec to adapt entertainment from around the world to reflect the province’s language, humour and culture.
Dubbing as Quebec identity
In Quebec, watching American and other English-language shows and films in French has long been part of the culture, says Daniel Béland, director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada at McGill University in Montreal.
A dubbing industry emerged in the province after the Second World War, he says, allowing audiences to experience international entertainment in their own language, along with voices, expressions and cultural references that felt familiar.
Although French-language content from France was readily available, Quebec’s distinct culture and language meant that those productions could often feel foreign to local audiences.
“For people to shift from the Quebec version to the French version from France would be really a culture shock,” said Béland.
Dubbing, he says, is also about more than translating dialogue word for word, particularly when it comes to humour. Some jokes simply don’t land when translated directly, so they have to be tweaked or replaced with references that local audiences can relate to.
"It will not be the same experience," he said. "“Humour, like poetry, is really hard to translate."
Quebec, is home to the vast majority of Canada's French speakers, with 84.1 per cent of the province's population speaking French, according to Statistics Canada’s census in 2021.
Keeping the dubbing industry, says Béland, is also a way of preserving the province’s mother tongue.
“There's a sense that Quebec is a French island surrounded by an anglophone sea, so there's this sense of a vulnerability of the French language.”
For the voice actors, it was personal
The possibility that Les Simpson might not return spurred a reaction in Quebec that seemed like “an earthquake,” says Thiéry Dubé, who has voiced Québécois Homer Simpson, the famously bumbling patriarch of the family, since 2017.
“Because for [Quebecers], it's something like poutine, you know? It's so part of our culture and cultural identity here.”
The news had also come during a particularly difficult year for the Quebec dubbing team, says Dubé.
Béatrice Picard, who voiced Homer’s wife, Marge, died in December at 96.
A few months later, in April, Benoît Rousseau, who voiced several prominent characters, including Grampa Simpson, Mr. Burns and Duffman, and served as the show’s main adapter, also died.
Dubé says the uncertainty over the show’s future made an already difficult period even harder.
“We were living day-to-day and waiting, and it was crazy for me, because one day couldn't pass without having somebody just stopping me in the street and saying, ‘Are you guys going to come back?’”
It was the fans’ fierce loyalty that offered some solace.
“[They said] I don't want it to be in French from France, and it was very touching, having all the people cheering for it.”
Bringing Les Simpson back
The campaign worked.
Biasotto’s petition drew more than 35,000 signatures, and Les Simpson was revived in May after Bell Media struck a deal with Disney Entertainment to broadcast the show. The new season is set to premiere Sept. 9 on Noovo.
“It had a bigger impact than I could imagine,” said Biasotto.
The return was also welcome news for difuze, the largest French dubbing facility in Canada, which has studios in Montreal and Toronto, and dubs Les Simpson.
Elizabeth Pélissier, vice-president of dubbing at difuze, says the studio is happy to be a part of bringing back the show in the language Quebec audiences know and love.
“We're just proud to make sure that we can call back all the actors and be part of the art process,” she said.
Les Simpson is returning at a time when Quebec’s dubbing industry is busier than ever.
difuze, founded in 2018, has seen the volume of content it dubs increase, says Pélissier. As streaming platforms such as Disney, Netflix, Amazon and Crave release more television series, the French studio has taken on more work than it once did with films alone.
The studio’s credits include Stranger Things, Moana and Toy Story 5. But the growth, she says, has also brought new challenges. There is more work to dub, but production timelines have become tighter, causing teams to “work really hard on overtime.”
Joey Galimi, president of the National Association of Professional Dubbers, which has represented dubbing professionals across Canada for 50 years, says the industry is “very healthy.”
But he says he’s concerned about the effect AI-generated dubbing could have on human voice actors.
In an emailed statement to CBC, Walt Disney Studios Canada says that under its new agreement, the broadcasting and dubbing of Les Simpson "will continue to be dubbed in Quebec by the local talent."
For Galimi, the revival of Les Simpson is more than a testament to the show’s popularity: it showcases the power of its fans.

Woman kills sister-in-law over jailed brother's insult, dumps body in tank
Vandana had allegedly mocked Parvati over her brother, who is currently in Damoh Jail in connection with a rape case.
A woman allegedly stabbed her newlywed sister-in-law to death in Indore’s Nehru Nagar on Thursday after a dispute over an insulting remark about her brother, who is lodged in Damoh Jail in a rape case, police said.
The accused, identified as Parvati Bai Kushwaha, allegedly attacked her sister-in-law Vandana with a kitchen knife, striking her twice on the neck.

Dragged, dumped into water tank
She then allegedly dragged Vandana’s body outside the house and dumped it into a water tank before leaving the premises to visit her husband, who was undergoing treatment at Aurobindo Hospital.
According to police, the incident was the culmination of tensions between the two women that had been building since Raksha Bandhan.
Vandana had allegedly mocked Parvati over her brother, who is currently in Damoh Jail in connection with a rape case. The remark reportedly angered Parvati and led to a dispute between the two.
The tension resurfaced on Thursday and escalated into a confrontation, police said. During the argument, Vandana allegedly told Parvati that her husband was under her control and that she would be thrown out of the house. Five dead after consuming spurious liquor in MP’s Sagar, over 12 hospitalised
Five people died and over 12 were hospitalised after alleged spurious liquor consumption in Sagar, Madhya Pradesh, with six in serious condition.

The incident comes days after a licensed liquor contractor had lodged a complaint with the Excise Office alleging the sale of counterfeit liquor branded as ‘Bombay Whisky’ in the area. Four days ago, during an excise department meeting, licensed contractors had raised strong objections over the alleged supply of illicit and spurious liquor in the district.
The collector has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident.

Volcano eruption triggers flight suspensions at Indonesia's main airport
- Published
A volcanic eruption has halted hundreds of flights at Indonesia's main international airport, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.
Authorities said 209 flights were suspended after ash from Mount Anak Krakatoa was detected in airspace near Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Sunday morning.
The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said.
More than 22,000 people have been impacted by the suspension of flights, which has been extended until 13:30 (0630 GMT).
The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.
Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where there is high volcanic and seismic activity.

OpenAI announced Thursday the launch of its next generation AI model, GPT-6 Astra, which the company claims is state of the art at navigating computers and web browsers, writing software, and solving difficult math problems.
It plans to make GPT-6 Astra available to paid customers in the coming days, starting with enterprise clients in its Daybreak early access program, followed by ChatGPT Plus, Pro, and Business plan subscribers. OpenAI did not say whether GPT-6 Astra will be available to free users of ChatGPT.
In a press briefing with reporters, OpenAI executives made it clear that they feel very confident about the company’s latest AI model. President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he personally believes the world is now in the era of artificial general intelligence, or AI systems that are generally smarter than humans.
“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” Brockman told reporters. “I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."
OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Astra at a critical moment for the company. The ChatGPT maker is trying to rapidly advance its technology and boost sales ahead of a planned initial offering while simultaneously avoiding compromising on safety and security. OpenAI is also facing stiff competition from Anthropic, its most important rival, which is also working on an upcoming IPO.
In a blog post, OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming it can navigate computers and web browsers on behalf of humans far better than its predecessors. AI companies have historically struggled to make models that can reliably browse websites, fill out forms, and manipulate software tools quickly and accurately enough to replace humans. In tests, OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra was able to book DMV appointments, search for job listings, and apartment hunt faster than the average person could.
The company also claims GPT-6 Astra is also the most safe and aligned AI model OpenAI has ever released. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company is monitoring GPT-6 Astra’s chain-of-thought—the model’s internal scratchpad it uses to work through problems—to ensure it is deployed safely. However, Pachocki said that making sure advanced AI models don’t cause unintended harm is increasingly a challenge, and may present a bottleneck to further AI progress.
“We kind of take this visibility for granted, and we are seeing that as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging,” said Pachocki. “We think confidence in monitoring may constrain further development, because we would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We would withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.”

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet after an ice-and-rock avalanche triggered a surge of water and debris through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster destroyed homes, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other infrastructure. As of 04 September, at least 1,252 people have died in Nepal, and more than 4,200 remain missing. Search and rescue operations are continuing, with two hydropower workers rescued alive from a tunnel on 4 September, nine days after the disaster (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this, a photo is being widely shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a young girl being protected by her brother, who were victims of the Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind the photo in this article.
Claim: The photo shows a young girl being protected by her brother, who are victims of the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: The photo is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. Vietnamese photojournalist Na Son Nguyen took it in October 2007 in Can Ty, a remote village in Hà Giang province, Vietnam. The photo shows two Hmong siblings, with the boy comforting his younger sister while their parents were away working in the fields. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A Google Lens search of the viral photo led us to a BBC report (archived) dated 4 May 2015 featuring the same photo, confirming that it predates the 2026 Nepal floods. According to the report, Vietnamese photographer Na Son Nguyen took the photo in October 2007 in Can Ty, a remote village in Ha Giang province, Vietnam. Talking to the BBC, he said the photo shows two Hmong siblings, with the boy comforting his crying sister while their parents were away working in the fields. He also said this was his most-shared photo, but unfortunately, it was repeatedly circulated online in the wrong context.
We also found (archived) an Instagram post by Vietnam-based photojournalist Na Son Nguyen featuring the same photo, published on 2 April 2015. The post states that Nguyen captured the photo in October 2007 in a mountainous village in Hà Giang province, Vietnam. He said the photo shows a young boy comforting his younger sister while their parents were away working in the fields. This confirms that the viral photo is unrelated to the recent floods in Nepal.
To sum up, this viral photo does not show children affected by the August 2026 Nepal floods; it was taken in Vietnam in 2007.

Two killed as Greek air force jet crashes at annual air show near Athens
The crash of the twin-seat Phantom F4 jet occurred during a low-altitude manoeuvre
Two pilots were killed when a Greek air force jet crashed at an annual air show north of Athens on Saturday, officials said.
Thousands of people were in attendance at Athens Flying Week, which attracts military and civilian aviation teams from dozens of countries, where the twin-seat Phantom F-4 jet crashed during a low-altitude manoeuvre.
A fire after the crash sent up large plumes of black smoke. There were no injuries among the spectators or residents in the wider area.
“The sense of grief is widespread, and our thoughts are with the families of the two pilots we lost,” Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said. “It is a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greece’s aviators, who remain on constant standby to protect Greece's skies.”
Air force officials in Greece said the bodies of the two pilots were located during a rescue operation, hampered in the early stages by the fire on the grounds of Tanagra air force base, 60 kilometres (about 40 miles) north of Athens.
Eleven water-dropping planes and helicopters assisted 85 firefighters to contain the blaze, which remained at some distance from the viewing area at the event.
Organisers cancelled remaining events planned over the weekend, while the fire prompted an evacuation order in an area near the base.
"We were all stunned. It hadn't been airborne for more than three minutes," an eyewitness told ERT.
Video footage of the crash showed a plume of smoke rising from the point of impact, followed by a larger, second explosion that occurred nearby as the plane broke apart.
Cyprus' Defence Minister Vasilis Palmas said that he had called his Greek counterpart, Nikos Dendias, to express the condolences of his government.
“It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base,” Palmas wrote in an online post.
The air force declared three days of mourning following the crash.

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”

Last month, I injected myself with a GLP-1 drug and became my own lab rat for three weeks.
As a fitness coach with my weight well under control, I didn’t need this. And yet, I took it. Why?
I work with people to treat their metabolic disease — obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, PMOS, metabolic syndrome. GLP-1 medicines, including semaglutide (the drug in Ozempic) and tirzepatide (the drug in Mounjaro), are among the tools we use. My job is to guide users to a healthy lifestyle (the right kind of activity, better food, improved sleep), while my medical team monitors their health markers. Our goal is to get them off the drug, with their health intact.
For the last 15 years, I’ve coached thousands of people on their strength and health. The single biggest pattern, which shows in their urgency and commitment to the cause, is the trigger moment. A doctor check-up, a wedding, or even a small event like finding themselves unable to bend down and tie their shoelaces helps them prioritise their health and wellness. As they get stronger and start building good lifestyle habits, good things happen.
But for a large percentage, the struggle with weight is real. And it never really ends. While people who lose weight see improvement in their quality of life across the board, maintaining that weight is an uphill struggle, especially when the reality and demands of life hit. As work mounts and stress amplifies, many of these habits crack, especially given the tremendous strain on our time and mental health and the way the environment is structured around us. You may have the best intentions, but you may still end up skimping on sleep or reaching for junk food.
Which is where GLP-1 drugs come in: this new tool in a weight loss toolbox, which I recently tried firsthand – something I always do, even when it comes to designing training plans. I always test-drive anything I recommend for my clients to coach well; I don’t know any other way.
How it went
I’ll start with a caveat: do not do this yourself. While I had no prescription and did not medically need the drug, I did this systematically. I tracked my vitals daily and weekly and reported my subjective and objective experience nearly every day to my doctor and my dietitian.
The drug I opted for was Mounjaro, the most advanced GLP-1 drug on the market today, opting for a starter dose of around 2.5 mg/ week, after consulting with my doctor. Honestly, I did not expect much, since my baseline lifestyle is good. I eat well 85% of the time; I’m active five or six days a week; my sleep hygiene is decent (even if my sleep, lately, hasn't been). But the experience surprised me more than I expected.
Food noise — the constant background hum of thinking about food — simply disappeared. I wanted simple, sattvic food, finding anything greasy immediately unappetising. Over-eating was not possible, whether it was my favourite dessert or the potato chips with my rice. The ease with which I could move through a world of hyper-palatable food, whether I was eating out, ordering in, or eating home-cooked meals, was mind-blowing.
That is the beauty of these drugs: they allow for mindful eating, making that admittedly woo-woo term accessible to all. I wasn't constantly thinking about food or tempted by the package of cupcakes being passed around at work, and I made sensible, adult decisions about food quite naturally, indulging in my favourite snacks without overeating.
In fact, I naturally wanted to eat more nutritious meals because they make me feel good. And I paid attention to my body and how it responded. Also, because I simply could not overeat, my energy levels started to improve, making it a truly liberating time.
Add a doctor, diet and activity
Dr Arun Raghavan, diabetologist and co-founder of Chennai’s Revivo Clinic, which focusses on metabolic care for obesity and diabetes, explains that GLP-1s in India are for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher who have at least one weight-related condition, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or Type 2 diabetes. “They work alongside diet and activity. They are not a stand-alone fix,” he cautions.
And yes, some people should not touch them at all, he adds: anyone with a personal or family history of certain thyroid cancers or a rare inherited hormone disorder, and those with a history of pancreatitis or gallbladder disease. “Most bad reactions come down to the wrong patient, no baseline work-up, or no monitoring.”
The side effects are mostly gastrointestinal and are worse when starting or increasing the dose. His real warning is about stopping. “Come off the drug without having built the lifestyle, and the hunger returns. People lose muscle and regain the weight, often as fat.”
Battling the side effects
It was not all rosy. For the entire three weeks I was on the medication, I had a mild headache and low-grade nausea. It eased after the first week, but it never fully left. My resting heart rate climbed 15%. My heart rate variability — a marker of recovery, where higher is better — dropped 15%. I had frequent palpitations and a mild brain fog, all symptoms that I discussed with Dr Arun Raghavan.
While there is nothing particularly abnormal about these patterns, these were indeed high costs for someone who did not need the drug. For someone who does, going unmonitored is a gamble.
So, did it work?
The results of all this weren’t insignificant: my muscle mass increased by 1.2 kg (a lot!), and fat decreased by 3.2 kg. I was active six days a week, following a hybrid (strength plus conditioning) protocol I developed, which translated to about four 4-hour sessions a week. (Disclaimer: These measurements were taken with a high-end body composition machine, and while the data is reasonably accurate, what we can look at are trends only)
The downside, however, was that my sleep was affected a fair bit, especially at first. Practising some pranayama helped, and it did get better once my body got used to the drug, but the first few days were a struggle.
So, will I recommend this to my clients? It depends.
For people who struggle with weight loss, the first step is to understand the underlying reason for their struggle, whether it be environment, lifestyle, psychological, or an underlying health condition. Only then can an action plan be structured, and GLP-1 could be a valid tool for some people. While you are on the drug, you need to do physical activity, get enough sleep and manage nutrition.
Sure, the last may become easier than before, but it still requires discipline – adding adequate protein, avoiding junk food, increasing your vegetable intake and drinking enough water. And during this window (we see this as a six- to 24-month window, depending on the person), shift your lifestyle to one that is sustainable and significantly better.
Shedding that old lifestyle and identity is a relevant part of this metamorphosis. It is not possible to undergo a simplistic change, i.e. take the drug, lose weight, be happy forever and ever. That isn’t going to happen, because there is a very high chance you will put it back on.
Is using Mounjaro a short cut?
I see a lot of moral dilemmas around taking this drug. Do I want to use a crutch? Do I want others to know that I use a crutch? How will this affect my social life? And of course, the wariness in taking a drug in a world where trust in Big Pharma is rightfully eroding.
I understand and empathise with most of these dilemmas. After all, would I trust a drug to only do positive things for me? I don’t think so. But if it serves the purpose and there’s no long-term cause for concern, then I would use the tool for the job. Because every day with subpar health is affecting you: that’s my simplistic thinking.
I also see people taking the drug and not seeing results because they refuse to take responsibility for their actions and lifestyle. These are people that no drug or coaching can help, until they choose to help themselves.
Most of us eat too much. We think about food too much. We have too many options. Year on year, our weight-loss resolutions don’t change. And neither does our weight. We don’t struggle with knowing what to do. The people I’ve coached over 15 years struggle with food noise. With an environment that makes it hard to be healthy. And life getting in the way — work, stress, kids, the usual.
The drug silences that noise, and that’s why it feels like magic. It’s also why selling only the drug is dangerous: the day you stop, the struggle comes back. The injection is the simple part, but life isn’t always that way. Even Johann Hari, a journalist who took these drugs, lost 20 kilos, and wrote a book about them, refuses to call it a miracle. He calls himself one of the “guinea pigs” in a “mass experiment.”
It is a tool.
I profit from saying this, but I’m saying it anyway: the people selling you only the needle are selling a return ticket and calling it a journey. It buys you a window. What you build in that window is everything.
Disclaimer: This is a first-person account of a three-week self-experiment. It is not medical advice or a recommendation to use GLP-1 medicines without a prescription or medical supervision.
Arvind Ashok has coached strength and fitness for over 15 years. He is co-founder of The Quad and of Revivo Clinic, a metabolic-health practice that pairs medical care with lifestyle change.

Beloved Alice Springs car festival the Red CentreNATS has drawn about 700 registered entrants for this year's event.
The event's program featured street cruising, drag races, burnout competitions and a street parade.
According to estimates, the festival — now in its 12th year — boosts the Alice Springs local economy by about $5 million each year.
Sitting in the passenger seat as her dad lined up in his classic Ford Falcon XC 393 Stroker to drag race at the 12th annual Red CentreNATS, Montana Taylor looked jubilant, and proud.
The teen and her dad, Ben, had travelled from South Australia to be a part of the festival that celebrates all things horsepower.
"I love it so much, I'm so glad I get to come and experience this," she said, with a massive grin.
She said she could not wait to drive her dad's car.
"Maybe one day," Mr Taylor said.
The Taylors are among the 700 registered entrants into this year's Red CentreNATS — more than half of whom come from interstate, boosting the local economy by about $5 million each year.
The weekend's program was huge, featuring street cruising, show and shines of the incredible array of vintage and new muscle cars, drag races, burnout competitions and a street parade that stopped the town.
Labours of love
A pale blue 1984 Holden Kingswood ute shone bright against the red-brown of the dirt dragway.
It was right at home — it had been in Alice Springs its whole life, according to owner Paul Totani.
Mr Totani, whose family has been in town since the 1960s, is a licensed aircraft engineer and pilot. But on Saturday he swapped the sky for the dirt, tearing down the drag strip, dust flying.
"It's a family heirloom. It will go to the kids later on, but we get it out once a year for Red CentreNATS," he said.
At the show and shine car display, dozens of automobiles sparkled in the sun and inside the Alice Springs Convention Centre.
Proud owners stood beside their lovingly cared-for cars, excited to share their stories.
Parading the past
Sitting on the back of utes, in deckchairs and on car roof-racks, Alice Springs turned out in force and lined the streets for the annual Red CentreNATS street parade.
Hundreds of cars rolled around the town's largest roundabout at the base of the MacDonnell Ranges, which glistened in the afternoon sun.
One of the spectators was Alice Springs local Lisa Morgan, who said events like the Red CentreNATS helped Alice Springs to shine.
She has volunteered for the event for years.
"Everyone bands together for the excitement, and the rumbles," she said.

A closely watched cardiovascular drug from Novartis failed in a pivotal study, the company said Friday, a major blow to the firm and to efforts to target a common heart disease risk factor.
The drug, called pelacarsen, had shown in earlier trials that it could drastically lower levels of what’s called Lp(a), a little blob of lipids and proteins that at elevated concentrations increases the likelihood of severe heart problems.
But Novartis said that in the Phase 3 HORIZON trial, pelacarsen failed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death or emergencies like heart attacks or stroke compared to placebo.
